TITLE: African Peacebuilding and Developmental Dynamics Individual Research Fellowship 2026: Up to $12,000 for African Researchers, Policy Analysts and Practitioners

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Social Science Research Council (SSRC), through its African Peacebuilding and Developmental Dynamics (APDD) program, is inviting applications for the Individual Research Fellowship (IRF). The fellowship is designed to support African researchers, policy analysts, and practitioners whose work focuses on conflict, peacebuilding, governance, and developmental dynamics across the African continent.

In 2026, the program plans to award up to nine individual research fellowships, with each fellowship providing a maximum award of $12,000.

The Individual Research Fellowship is intended to strengthen the quality, visibility, and impact of independent African peacebuilding research. It provides fellows with an opportunity to undertake field-based research, analyze and communicate their findings, participate in professional workshops, receive mentorship, build networks with other African scholars and practitioners, and contribute to important conversations around peacebuilding policy and practice.

The fellowship is particularly valuable for professionals seeking to ensure that African perspectives and evidence-based research play a stronger role in regional and global discussions concerning peace, governance, development, and conflict transformation.

About the African Peacebuilding and Developmental Dynamics Program

The African Peacebuilding and Developmental Dynamics (APDD) program is part of the Social Science Research Council’s work to strengthen social science research and make research-based knowledge more accessible to policymakers, practitioners, researchers, and other stakeholders.

Since its establishment in 2012, the Individual Research Fellowship has served as a mechanism for improving the quality and visibility of independent African peacebuilding research both within Africa and internationally.

The program also seeks to bridge the gap between research, policy, and practice. Rather than limiting research to academic audiences, the fellowship encourages fellows to produce knowledge that can be used by policymakers, practitioners, research institutions, civil society organizations, and other peacebuilding constituencies.

Through the program, fellows are expected to contribute evidence and African perspectives to regional and global debates concerning peacebuilding.

Individual Research Fellowship 2026 at a Glance

The major details of the fellowship include:

Program: African Peacebuilding and Developmental Dynamics (APDD)

Fellowship: Individual Research Fellowship (IRF)

Host organization: Social Science Research Council (SSRC)

Number of awards: Up to nine fellowships

Maximum fellowship award: $12,000 per fellow

Research duration: Six months of field-based research

Analysis and writing period: Three months

Total fellowship period: Nine months

Program period stated: July 2026 to March 2027

Target applicants: African researchers, academics, policy analysts, and practitioners

Geographic eligibility: African citizens currently residing in an African country

Research focus: Conflict, peacebuilding, governance, and developmental dynamics

Workshops: Two mandatory APDD workshops

Funding: Andrew Carnegie Foundation

Application: Online application

Application deadline: Not stated in the information provided

What Does the Individual Research Fellowship Offer?

The APDD Individual Research Fellowship goes beyond financial support for research. Fellows become part of a broader professional and intellectual community focused on strengthening African knowledge production and peacebuilding practice.

The program has several major components.

1. Field-Based Research and Thought Leadership

One of the central elements of the fellowship is the opportunity to conduct substantial field-based research.

Fellows commit to:

Six months of field-based research; and

Three months dedicated to analysis and writing.

This represents a total fellowship period of nine months, running from July 2026 to March 2027, according to the information provided.

The research undertaken through the fellowship is expected to generate knowledge that is relevant to peacebuilding scholarship, policy, and practice in Africa.

The program seeks research that can have a meaningful impact rather than research that remains confined to academic discussions. Fellows are therefore expected to produce evidence-based knowledge capable of contributing to regional and global conversations about peacebuilding.

This provides researchers with an opportunity to examine important peace and conflict-related issues from African perspectives while generating evidence that can potentially inform policy and practice.

2. Mandatory APDD Workshops

Fellows will participate in two mandatory APDD workshops, scheduled to take place in July and January in different regions of Africa.

These workshops are an important part of the fellowship experience because they provide fellows with opportunities to develop both their research and professional capabilities.

During the workshops, fellows can:

Refine their research designs.

Improve their research focus.

Strengthen their research methodologies.

Present and discuss research findings.

Receive feedback from experienced academics and practitioners.

Explore strategies for making their research accessible to broader audiences.

Discuss opportunities for publication.

Network with other fellows.

Develop professional relationships with senior scholars.

Engage with practitioners working in peacebuilding.

Learn from facilitators with relevant expertise.

The workshops therefore provide an environment where fellows can test their ideas, receive constructive feedback, and strengthen their research before communicating their findings to wider audiences.

3. Contribution to African Scholarship and Knowledge Production

Another major component of the fellowship is knowledge dissemination.

Fellows are expected to contribute to the broader APDD knowledge-production ecosystem. This includes opportunities to contribute to:

The APDD Working Paper series.

The African Peacebuilding Policy Review and Analysis.

APDD digital forums.

Kujenga Amani.

APDD social media platforms, including Facebook and X.

Fellows may also have opportunities to contribute to external academic and public-facing platforms.

These may include:

International peer-reviewed journals.

Books.

Academic articles.

Essays.

Blogs.

Feature articles.

Opinion and editorial articles.

Podcasts.

This aspect of the fellowship can be particularly valuable for researchers and practitioners seeking to increase the visibility and accessibility of their work.

Rather than producing research solely for specialist academic audiences, fellows are encouraged to explore different formats and platforms through which their findings can reach policymakers, practitioners, researchers, communities, and the broader public.

4. Professional Development and Career Advancement

The fellowship also provides opportunities for professional development.

Fellows will gain new knowledge and skills that can help advance their careers as academics or practitioners.

For academics, this can provide an opportunity to strengthen their research portfolios, develop publications, expand professional networks, and increase their visibility within African and international peacebuilding scholarship.

For policy analysts and practitioners, the fellowship can provide an opportunity to deepen research capabilities and develop evidence-based approaches to peacebuilding-related work.

The combination of research, workshops, mentorship, publication opportunities, and networking makes the fellowship relevant to professionals interested in building long-term careers around peacebuilding, governance, development, conflict analysis, research, and policy.

5. Networking and Building an African Peacebuilding Community

Fellows become part of a network of active African scholars and practitioners working on peacebuilding.

The program seeks to develop a community capable of bringing African perspectives into global discussions about peacebuilding, conflict, governance, and development.

Through this network, fellows can potentially establish relationships with:

Other African researchers.

Senior academics.

Policy professionals.

Peacebuilding practitioners.

Research institutions.

Regional organizations.

Civil society professionals.

Other experts working on peace and development issues.

These relationships can provide opportunities for peer learning, collaboration, knowledge exchange, and future research partnerships.

6. Mentorship from Senior Scholars

Fellows will receive mentorship from experienced senior scholars working in the field.

Mentorship is an important component because fellows can benefit from the experience of established researchers while developing their own research and professional careers.

The program also emphasizes peer-to-peer learning, meaning fellows can learn not only from senior experts but also from one another.

This creates an environment where researchers and practitioners working on different peacebuilding issues can exchange perspectives and develop collaborative relationships.

Who Can Apply for the APDD Individual Research Fellowship?

The fellowship is specifically designed for African citizens currently residing in an African country.

The competition is open to African academics as well as policy analysts and practitioners working on relevant peacebuilding issues.

However, eligibility requirements differ depending on whether an applicant is applying as an academic or as a policy analyst/practitioner.

Eligibility Requirements for Academic Applicants

Applicants applying as academics must meet specific educational and professional requirements.

They must:

Be an African citizen.

Currently reside in an African country.

Hold a full-time faculty or research position.

Work at an African university or research organization.

Hold a PhD obtained no earlier than January 2016.

The fellowship therefore targets established researchers who are already professionally connected to an African university or research institution.

PhD Requirement

The fellowship specifies that academic applicants must have obtained their PhD no earlier than January 2016.

The information also states that applicants who had not been awarded their PhDs by June 2026 would not have their cases prioritized for eligibility as academics.

Applicants should therefore carefully review the official application guidance concerning their PhD completion status and eligibility before applying.

Eligibility Requirements for Policy Analysts and Practitioners

The fellowship is also open to African policy analysts and practitioners working in peacebuilding-related fields.

Applicants in this category must:

Be African citizens.

Currently reside in an African country.

Be based in Africa.

Work at an eligible regional or sub-regional institution, government agency, nongovernmental organization, media organization, or civil society organization.

Hold at least a master’s degree.

Have obtained the master’s degree before January 2021.

Have at least five years of proven research and work experience in peacebuilding-related activities on the African continent.

This pathway makes the fellowship accessible to experienced professionals whose careers may be based outside traditional academic institutions.

Where Must Applicants Be Based?

Applicants must currently be residing in an African country.

For policy analysts and practitioners, the relevant organization or institution must also be based in Africa, including eligible:

Regional institutions.

Sub-regional institutions.

Government agencies.

Nongovernmental organizations.

Media organizations.

Civil society organizations.

The fellowship is therefore geographically focused on African professionals and African-based institutions.

What Areas of Research Does the Fellowship Support?

The APDD Individual Research Fellowship is intended for applicants working on issues related to conflict and peacebuilding.

The broader fellowship description also identifies peacebuilding, governance, and developmental dynamics as key areas.

Applicants should therefore ensure that their proposed research demonstrates a clear connection to the fellowship’s thematic priorities.

Potential research questions may examine issues such as:

Conflict prevention.

Peacebuilding processes.

Post-conflict recovery.

Governance and peace.

Development and conflict.

Community-level peacebuilding.

Institutional responses to conflict.

Policy approaches to peace and stability.

Regional peace and security.

Civil society and peacebuilding.

Evidence-based approaches to conflict transformation.

The fellowship information provided does not prescribe a single research topic. Instead, applicants are expected to demonstrate how their proposed research contributes to the broader understanding of peacebuilding, governance, and developmental dynamics in Africa.

Fellowship Research Timeline

The fellowship follows a nine-month structure.

July 2026

The fellowship period begins, with fellows undertaking field-based research and participating in an APDD workshop.

July to December 2026

Fellows conduct approximately six months of field-based research.

During this period, fellows are expected to gather the evidence and information necessary to develop their research findings.

January 2027

Fellows participate in the second mandatory APDD workshop, which provides an opportunity to present findings, receive feedback, and consider how the research can be effectively disseminated.

January to March 2027

The final three months are dedicated to analysis and writing.

March 2027

The stated nine-month fellowship period concludes.

Applicants should note that the timeline described above comes directly from the program information provided and that the official application guide should be consulted for detailed expectations and scheduling.

How Much Funding Is Available?

In 2026, the APDD program plans to award up to nine individual fellowships.

Each fellowship carries a maximum award of $12,000.

If all nine fellowships are awarded at the maximum amount, the program could provide up to $108,000 in total fellowship awards.

Applicants should carefully review the official fellowship application guidebook for detailed information about eligible expenses, budget requirements, and how the proposed research budget should be prepared.

What Documents Are Required to Apply?

According to the fellowship information provided, applications consist of several important components.

Applicants should prepare:

Online application form

Research proposal

Research bibliography

Current CV

Proposed research timeline

Proposed research budget

Two reference letters

Language evaluation(s), if required

Each component plays an important role in demonstrating the applicant’s qualifications and the feasibility and significance of the proposed research.

Research Proposal

The research proposal is likely to be one of the most important parts of the application.

Applicants should use the proposal to clearly explain the research question or problem they intend to investigate, why the topic matters, how the research will be conducted, and how the expected findings can contribute to peacebuilding scholarship, policy, or practice.

A strong proposal should demonstrate a clear connection between the proposed research and the APDD program’s focus.

Bibliography

Applicants must also provide a bibliography supporting their proposed research.

The bibliography should demonstrate that the applicant understands the existing scholarship and relevant evidence surrounding the proposed research topic.

Current CV

Applicants must submit a current curriculum vitae.

The CV should clearly demonstrate the applicant’s relevant academic, professional, research, and peacebuilding experience.

For policy analysts and practitioners, the CV should be particularly useful in demonstrating the required five years of proven research and work experience in peacebuilding-related activities.

Research Timeline

Applicants must submit a proposed research timeline.

The timeline should demonstrate how the applicant intends to organize the research activities during the fellowship period.

A realistic timeline can help demonstrate that the proposed project is achievable within the fellowship’s nine-month structure.

Research Budget

Applicants must also submit a proposed research budget.

The budget should clearly explain how the requested fellowship support will be used to undertake the proposed research.

Applicants should ensure that their budget is realistic, clearly justified, and aligned with their proposed research activities.

Two Reference Letters

The application requires two reference letters.

Applicants should identify referees who can provide meaningful assessments of their academic, professional, research, or peacebuilding experience and their ability to successfully undertake the proposed fellowship research.

Language Evaluation

Language evaluation(s) may also be required where applicable.

Applicants should consult the official APDD Fellowship Application Guidebook to determine whether a language evaluation is necessary for their particular application.

How to Apply for the APDD Individual Research Fellowship

Interested applicants should consult the APDD Fellowship Application Guidebook for the complete application instructions and requirements.

The application involves an online application process and requires applicants to submit their research proposal, bibliography, CV, research timeline, budget, reference letters, and any required language evaluation.

Because the fellowship has specific eligibility requirements for academics, policy analysts, and practitioners, prospective applicants should carefully review the official guidance before beginning their application.

Applicants with technical questions about the online application portal can contact the APDD team by email at: apdd@ssrc.org

or visit their website HERE

More fellowship opportunities can be found HERE

Fellowship Funding and Institutional Support

The APDD program is funded by the Andrew Carnegie Foundation.

The funding support allows the program to provide individual research fellowships while also facilitating workshops, mentorship, professional development, knowledge production, and networking opportunities for selected fellows.

The fellowship is administered through the Social Science Research Council, an organization focused on mobilizing social science research for the public good.

Why Should African Researchers and Peacebuilding Professionals Consider This Fellowship?

The APDD Individual Research Fellowship offers several potential advantages for professionals working in peacebuilding and related fields.

Financial Support for Research

The maximum fellowship award of $12,000 can provide significant support for an independent research project.

Dedicated Research Period

The nine-month structure provides fellows with dedicated time for field-based research, analysis, and writing.

Professional Visibility

Contributing to APDD publications, forums, and digital platforms can help fellows increase the visibility of their research and professional work.

Academic Publication Opportunities

Fellows may have opportunities to develop their work for peer-reviewed journals, books, articles, essays, blogs, features, and other forms of publication.

Mentorship

Access to experienced senior scholars can help fellows strengthen their research and professional development.

Networking

The fellowship connects participants with African scholars, practitioners, researchers, and other professionals working on peacebuilding issues.

Policy Impact

The program emphasizes research that can inform peacebuilding policy and practice, giving fellows an opportunity to connect their research with real-world challenges.

African Perspectives in Global Debates

The fellowship seeks to strengthen African voices and perspectives in regional and international discussions concerning peacebuilding.

Important Considerations Before Applying

Prospective applicants should pay close attention to the eligibility requirements before preparing their applications.

In particular, academic applicants should verify their:

African citizenship.

Current residence in an African country.

Full-time faculty or research position.

Institutional affiliation.

PhD award date.

Policy analysts and practitioners should verify their:

African citizenship.

Current residence in Africa.

Institutional or organizational affiliation.

Master’s degree award date.

Five or more years of relevant research and work experience.

Experience specifically related to peacebuilding activities on the continent.

Applicants should also ensure that their proposed research has a strong connection to the fellowship’s focus on peacebuilding, governance, conflict, and developmental dynamics.

Application Deadline

No application deadline is provided in the information supplied for this article.

Applicants should therefore check the official APDD Fellowship Application Guidebook and application portal for the current deadline before submitting an application.

Prospective applicants should not assume a deadline based on previous editions of the fellowship, as application dates can change between competition cycles.

Contact Information

For questions or technical issues concerning the online application portal, applicants can contact the APDD team.

Email: apdd@ssrc.org

Applicants can also consult the following resources:

Individual Research Fellowship FAQs

APDD Fellowship Award Application Guidebook

About the Social Science Research Council

The Social Science Research Council (SSRC) is the organization behind the APDD Individual Research Fellowship.

The organization describes its mission as mobilizing social science for the public good.

The SSRC works to support research and knowledge that can contribute to understanding important social, political, economic, and developmental challenges.

The APDD fellowship reflects this broader mission by supporting African researchers and practitioners whose work addresses peacebuilding and related challenges across the continent.

Conclusion

The African Peacebuilding and Developmental Dynamics (APDD) Individual Research Fellowship 2026 represents a significant opportunity for African researchers, policy analysts, and practitioners working on conflict, peacebuilding, governance, and developmental dynamics.

With up to nine fellowships available and awards of up to $12,000 each, the program provides financial support alongside a broader professional development experience. Selected fellows will undertake six months of field-based research followed by three months of analysis and writing, participate in two mandatory APDD workshops, receive mentorship, build professional networks, and contribute to African and international knowledge production.

The fellowship is particularly suited to African academics with eligible PhD qualifications and full-time positions at African universities or research organizations, as well as experienced policy analysts and practitioners with the required master’s degree, organizational affiliation, and peacebuilding experience.

Beyond the financial award, the program offers an opportunity to strengthen research capacity, increase professional visibility, develop meaningful relationships with scholars and practitioners, and ensure that African evidence and perspectives contribute more strongly to peacebuilding policy and practice.

Interested applicants should carefully review the APDD Fellowship Application Guidebook, prepare all required application materials, verify their eligibility, and confirm the current application deadline before submitting their applications.

For technical questions regarding the application portal, prospective applicants can contact the APDD team at apdd@ssrc.org.

TITLE: Olympic Studies Centre PhD Students & Early Career Academics Research Grant Programme 2027

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 22, 2026

Applications are invited for the Olympic Studies Centre PhD Students & Early Career Academics Research Grant Programme 2027. The Olympic Studies Centre (OSC) organises an annual research grant programme intended for PhD Students and Early Career Academics engaged in scholarly research on the Olympic Movement, its history and ideals, and the impact of the Olympic Games on the various aspects of contemporary society and culture.

The objectives of the programme are as follows:

Support PhD Students and Early Career Academics and foster excellence in Olympic related research with a humanities and/or social sciences perspective.

Facilitate a research and study visit at the Olympic Studies Centre in Lausanne, Switzerland (the Olympic Capital), and the consultation of the OSC’s collections (including primary sources and the IOC historical archives).

Support the next generation of scholars in the field of Olympic studies.

Grant

Successful applicants will receive a research grant of a maximum of USD $6,000. The total amount to be awarded will be decided by the Grant Programme Selection Committee after full consideration of all elements of the application.

Eligibility

Students enrolled in a PhD degree programme, with a humanities and/or social sciences perspective, with Olympism, the Olympic Movement or the Olympic Games as, at least, one of the research foci. Students must remain enrolled in the PhD degree programme for the entire duration of the grant, from submission of the application to delivery of the final report.

The project presented should demonstrate a clear contribution to the candidate’s doctoral thesis.

Academic staff and postdoctoral fellows who completed their doctorate or equivalent highest degree with a humanities and/or social sciences perspective (including masters, depending on the field) in or after 2024 (named or referred to in this programme as “Early Career Academics” (ECA)).

ECA applicants must hold a university appointment covering the period of the grant (from submission of the application to delivery of the final report).

Application

Applications and all supporting documentation must be submitted in either French or English, the two official languages of the Olympic Movement. Completed application files must include the following documents:

Official application form duly completed

Proof of registration covering the period of the grant (from submission of the application to delivery of the final report), issued by the university administration on institutional letterhead:

for PhD students: current proof of doctoral enrolment;

for ECA: current proof of a university appointment, including academic/research status.

Letter of recommendation written on institutional letterhead, signed and sent by the applicant’s supervisor (for PhD students) or mentor (for ECA).

The Selection Committee is particularly interested in the supervisor’s/mentor’s assessment of the following points: the scholarly significance of the research project; the methodology and original nature of the study; the impact of the project on the Olympic Movement; the candidate’s training, abilities, achievements to date and motivation for the research proposed; and the likelihood that the applicant will complete the project on time.

If the research proposal includes interviews, surveys or any other methodologies that involve human subjects, human data and/or fieldwork, or as required by the applicant’s home institution, a certificate stating that the project has been approved by the university’s ethics committee must be included.

Applicants are requested to take note of the Guidelines concerning the use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools and disclose if they have used an AI tool to develop their application.

For more information, see official rules or visit Olympic Studies Centre Research Grant.

TITLE: Sign up today for the Climate Action Policy course

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Course Name: Climate Action Policy

Duration: 6 weeks

Target group:

OVERVIEW OF THE COURSE

Climate change is arguably one of the most important global issues we face in the 21st century. It is widely recognized by scientists and many policymakers as posing significant risks, not only to the environment but also to society and the global economy. Governments have been attempting to address this difficult challenge since at least 1992—cooperatively through the United Nations and through national and subnational policy. Most governments are also making plans to adapt to the climate change that is likely to occur. The outcome of any significant climate change will be varied rather than simply an overall increase in average or nocturnal temperatures. Climate researchers have designed models to predict the longer-term consequences both in air and ocean circulation patterns. This course will (in six modules) explore the facts about climate change and its impacts; potential policies to address climate change; why some governments might choose to address climate change more or less vigorously; and how sub-national governments and non-governmental actors might complement action by national governments.

TITLE: Join us for the 2025 International Women’s Day Celebration

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Theme: ‘Accelerate Action: Advancing Gender Equality in African Higher Education’

The Women in Higher Education Network (WoHEN), hosted by the Association of African Universities (AAU), invites all stakeholders to join us in commemorating the 2025 International Women’s Day. This year’s theme, “Accelerate Action: Advancing Gender Equality in African Higher Education,” underscores the urgent need to address systemic barriers and biases while taking decisive steps to foster gender equity across the African higher education landscape.

Event Details:

• Date: March 7, 2025

• Time: 10:00 a.m. – 12:00 p.m. GMT

• Venue: Virtual Event – Register here – https://bit.ly/3F9mPyl

This interactive event will offer a dynamic platform to spotlight gender inequalities in African higher education institutions, assess progress, and chart actionable strategies to accelerate gender equality. Participants will engage with thought leaders and practitioners to explore ways of fostering inclusive academic environments, dismantling systemic barriers, and advancing the leadership of women in African higher education.

Why This Matters:

Gender equality in higher education is central to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals, particularly those related to equity, access, and the democratization of education (Inter-Agency and Expert Group on SDG Indicators, 2017). While significant progress has been made in closing gender gaps in tertiary enrolment, disparities persist in specific fields and leadership positions, with STEM disciplines being particularly affected (Directorate-General for Research and Innovation Horizon, 2020; Tomassini, 2021; UNESCO Institute for Statistics, 2018).

Women remain significantly underrepresented in STEM-related programs. Data from the UNESCO Institute for Statistics indicate that between 2015 and 2018, female students comprised only 6% to 7% of those enrolled in engineering, manufacturing, and construction programs, compared to 20% to 21% of male students. Across sub-Saharan Africa, 2.5% of vice-chancellors are women and 5% of CEOs are women. Women make up 43% of those who receive tertiary education but hold 28% of formal sector jobs (McKinsey Global Institute, 2019). Only 24% of academic staff in tertiary education across sub-Saharan Africa are female (UNESCO, 2019). This lack of representation leads to the exclusion of diverse perspectives, limiting innovation and economic potential (García-Holgado, González-González, & Peixoto, 2020). Addressing this imbalance is not only a matter of fairness but also an economic imperative, as increasing the participation of women in digital and STEM careers has been linked to economic growth (Seo, Huang, & Han, 2017).

The gender gap in higher education is not just about access—it is also about career progression. Women face multiple barriers at different stages of their academic and professional journeys, with their representation diminishing from university enrolment to labour market participation and leadership roles (Seo, Huang, & Han, 2017; Amon, 2017). These challenges are influenced by structural and cultural factors, including self-efficacy, institutional biases, and socio-economic constraints (Leaper & Starr, 2019; Cadaret, Hartung, Subich, & Weigold, 2017; Salas-Morera et al., 2019).

Globally, no country has yet achieved full gender parity. The Global Gender Gap Report (2021) indicates that only 67.7% of gender disparities have been closed, leaving a 32.3% gap still to be addressed (World Economic Forum, 2021). While 95% of educational attainment gaps have been closed, gender disparities in academic leadership and STEM fields remain entrenched (García-Holgado & García-Peñalvo, 2022).

This year’s International Women’s Day underscores the need for accelerated action to eliminate these systemic barriers. Addressing gender inequality in African higher education will not only foster more inclusive institutions but also drive broader social and economic transformation. By tackling biases, supporting women’s career progression, and promoting institutional policies that advance gender equality, we can ensure that women are not only present but thrive as leaders, educators, and innovators in higher education.

Objectives of the 2025 International Women’s Day Celebration:

1. Raise Awareness: Illuminate the systemic barriers that hinder gender equality in African higher education.

2. Promote Actionable Strategies: Foster dialogue on pragmatic approaches to accelerate gender equity and inclusion.

3. Showcase Best Practices: Share successful models and initiatives that advance women’s participation and leadership in African higher education institutions.

4. Engage Stakeholders: Encourage collaboration among policymakers, educators, researchers, and advocates to drive sustainable change.

Expected Outcomes:

• A comprehensive documentation of the challenges and opportunities in advancing gender equality in African higher education as discussed during the session.

• Identification of actionable solutions and policy recommendations to accelerate progress.

• Generation of a communique for dissemination to key stakeholders and decision-makers.

Target Audience:

The event is open to all stakeholders in African higher education, including:

• Female and male Vice Chancellors, Presidents, Rectors, and other senior leaders

• Academic and administrative staff

• Policymakers and government representatives

• Civil society organizations

• Students and researchers

• Development partners

All stakeholders interested in the theme

Organizers:

• Women in Higher Education Network (WoHEN): WoHEN supports the effective participation of women across all thematic areas in higher education, including leadership, STEM, and the humanities.

• Association of African Universities (AAU): As the apex higher education organization in Africa with close to 450 member universities, AAU provides a platform for African universities to collaborate. The advancement of gender-responsive policies and practices in Africa’s higher education institutions is of prime importance to the AAU.

Join Us:

We invite you to be a part of this transformative conversation and to contribute your voice and expertise as we work together to accelerate action for gender equality in African higher education.

Register Now – https://bit.ly/3F9mPyl

For inquiries, please contact fnkrumah@aau.org or +233 246425147. Together, let’s accelerate action and drive meaningful change for women in African higher education.

TITLE: Chatham House Research in Practice – PhD placement 2026/2027

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 7, 2026

Applications are open for the Chatham House Research in Practice – PhD placement 2026/2027. Chatham House, the Royal Institute of International Affairs, is an independent policy institute and world-leading think tank based in London. It conducts in-depth research and analysis on global affairs, aiming to help governments, businesses and the public make informed decisions.

The Queen Elizabeth II Academy for Leadership and the Next Generation at Chatham House empowers aspiring young leaders to address global challenges and influence a better world. We are now looking to welcome PhD students to the Chatham House research community to offer aspiring researchers an enriching working experience in a leading policy institute.

Placement Details

As part of the placement, the student will be expected to:

Work on and contribute to a research project – either a paper, series of convenings or other similar work – for the duration of the placement. This could include but is not limited to desk research and literature reviews, helping with drafting publications, designing and undertaking research interviews and collating feedback; designing, developing and delivering a research roundtable(s); synthesising high-level workshop and conference discussions, etc.;

Support the programme in responding to important international developments related to the programme’s focus by undertaking research, writing briefs or monitoring issue(s) in a timely fashion;

Where appropriate, collaborate with colleagues from across other regional and thematic research areas to draw together complementary research and explore avenues for potential collaboration;

Work with the team to identify and pursue opportunities for developing research and grant proposals. With support from the programme, contribute to research proposals for submission to a breadth of potential funders, including governments, businesses and foundations;

As appropriate, gain experience in drafting, monitoring and reconciling project reports and budgets; and

As appropriate, support with Chatham House events including identifying topics, suggesting speakers and planning.

In addition to their work in a research team, the student will take part in The Queen Elizabeth II Academy’s Leadership Masterclass Programme for the duration of the placement. The programme takes place every Thursday and includes skills workshops, thematic sessions and leadership training. The student will also gain access to Chatham House’s wider networks, library and busy events schedule featuring world-leading experts.

Eligibility

Open only to PhD students affiliated with the following DTPs:

UCL, Bloomsbury and East London Doctoral Training Programme

London School of Economics Doctoral Training Programme

London Interdisciplinary Social Science Doctoral Training Programme

Applicants may apply to one of the five Chatham House research programmes:

Europe Programme

Global Health Programme

International Law Programme

International Security Programme

US and North America Programme

Application

Application closing date is Monday 7 September 2026, 23:59 GMT. Placement duration is 1 October 2026 – 8 January 2027 (3 months, full-time).

Click here to apply

For more information, visit Research in Practice – PhD placement.

TITLE: IOM Ethical Migration Journalism Fellowship Programme 2026: Apply for a USD 1,000 Reporting Grant in Chiang Rai, Thailand

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are open for the IOM Ethical Migration Journalism Fellowship Programme 2026, a three-month reporting initiative designed to support original, accurate, evidence-based and ethically produced journalism about migration in Chiang Rai and surrounding areas of northern Thailand.

Organized by the International Organization for Migration in Thailand, the programme will select five fellows, each of whom will receive a USD 1,000 reporting grant alongside professional mentorship, editorial guidance, programme check-ins, a field visit and potential publication through IOM platforms.

The fellowship will run from 1 October to 31 December 2026, while completed stories must be submitted by 8 January 2027. Applications must be submitted no later than 22 September 2026. The official announcement does not specify a closing time, so candidates should avoid waiting until the final day. Review the official IOM Thailand announcement.

About the Ethical Migration Journalism Fellowship Programme

Migration is an important part of Thailand’s social, economic and demographic landscape. Its significance is particularly visible in Chiang Rai, a northern border province where communities, economies and personal experiences are closely connected to cross-border mobility.

Despite the importance of migration, public discussion can sometimes be shaped by incomplete information, stereotypes, sensational reporting or narratives that fail to reflect the realities and contributions of migrants. Journalism plays a significant role in determining how migration is understood by communities, institutions and policymakers.

The Ethical Migration Journalism Fellowship Programme seeks to strengthen the ability of local journalists and emerging media practitioners to produce reporting that is:

Accurate and based on credible evidence.

Balanced in its treatment of complex migration issues.

Sensitive to the dignity, safety and rights of migrants.

Connected to the realities of Chiang Rai and surrounding areas.

Constructive in how it contributes to public understanding.

Professionally and ethically produced.

Capable of challenging stereotypes and misleading migration narratives.

The programme’s central theme is the reframing of migration narratives and public perceptions to encourage greater inclusion of migrants. Through well-researched stories grounded in evidence, local realities and migrants’ experiences, fellows are expected to help build a more informed and constructive understanding of migration at the local level. Read the official call for proposals.

The initiative is made possible through financial support from the Government of Japan. See the programme announcement from IOM Thailand.

Main Objectives of the Programme

The fellowship is intended to move beyond short-term awareness raising by providing selected participants with practical support to research, produce and complete substantial migration stories.

Its main objectives include:

Supporting local migration journalism

The programme provides financial and professional assistance for reporting on migration issues connected to Chiang Rai and nearby areas.

Improving the accuracy of migration reporting

Fellows will be encouraged to use reliable evidence, appropriate sources and properly verified information when developing their stories.

Promoting balanced and ethical storytelling

The programme emphasizes journalism that avoids harmful stereotypes, respects the dignity of migrants and accurately represents complex migration experiences.

Connecting national migration issues with local realities

Proposed stories should be relevant to Chiang Rai or its surrounding areas rather than addressing migration only as a broad or abstract international issue.

Strengthening the practical capacity of journalists and emerging storytellers

Through mentorship, editorial guidance, orientation sessions and programme check-ins, fellows will receive structured support throughout the reporting process.

Expanding public access to evidence-based migration stories

Completed work may be published through IOM platforms, giving selected fellows an opportunity to reach wider audiences.

What Selected Fellows Will Receive

1. USD 1,000 Reporting Grant

Each of the five selected fellows will receive a reporting grant of USD 1,000 to support the production of an original migration story.

The grant is intended to assist with the reporting and production process. Applicants should therefore present a story idea that is realistic, properly planned and achievable within the available funding and programme period.

This is a reporting grant rather than a salary, academic scholarship or general cash award. It is connected to the successful production of the proposed journalism project. See IOM Thailand’s official fellowship information.

2. Professional Mentorship

Selected fellows will receive mentorship while developing their stories. This support can help participants strengthen their research plans, refine their angles, address gaps in evidence and improve the overall quality of their reporting.

Mentorship is especially valuable for participants working on sensitive migration topics that require careful consideration of informed consent, confidentiality, source protection, representation and the potential consequences of publication.

3. Editorial Guidance

IOM and designated mentors will provide editorial feedback during the reporting process.

Fellows will be expected to respond constructively to this guidance and incorporate relevant recommendations into their work. Editorial support may help participants improve the structure, clarity, factual accuracy, balance and ethical quality of their final stories.

4. Online Orientation and Monthly Check-Ins

Selected participants will take part in an online orientation session at the beginning of the programme.

IOM will also organize monthly check-ins throughout the fellowship period. These sessions are intended to monitor progress, provide guidance, identify emerging challenges and help fellows remain on schedule.

5. Field Visit in Chiang Rai

The programme includes a field visit within Chiang Rai organized by IOM.

The field visit is designed to deepen participants’ understanding of migration dynamics in the province. It will also provide opportunities to exchange experiences with foreign correspondents and other relevant stakeholders. Consult the official call for the participation requirements.

6. Opportunity for Publication

Fellows may have their completed stories published through IOM platforms.

Publication can increase the visibility of the participant’s work while contributing to broader public understanding of migration. It may also strengthen the fellow’s professional portfolio and demonstrate an ability to produce responsible, evidence-based reporting on a complex social issue.

Publication is not automatic or unconditional. Materials developed through the programme will be reviewed by IOM before they are published or otherwise disseminated.

Expected Journalism Project

Applicants must propose an original and feasible story related to migration in Chiang Rai and/or surrounding areas.

A strong project should establish a clear connection between the proposed subject and the local migration context. The idea should be narrow enough to investigate properly within the programme period but significant enough to contribute meaningfully to public understanding.

The proposed story should ultimately demonstrate:

A clearly defined migration issue or reporting question.

Relevance to Chiang Rai or surrounding communities.

A practical reporting and production plan.

Credible sources and evidence.

Appropriate inclusion of migrant experiences and perspectives.

Balanced treatment of the people and institutions involved.

Ethical interviewing and reporting practices.

Realistic completion within the three-month fellowship.

Responsiveness to editorial feedback.

Compliance with the final format and supporting-material requirements established by IOM.

Applicants should avoid submitting broad proposals that attempt to cover every dimension of migration. A focused story with identifiable sources, a clear audience and a realistic reporting plan is more likely to be completed effectively.

Responsibilities of Selected Fellows

Receiving the grant carries clear professional and programme obligations. Successful applicants will be expected to:

Produce a high-quality migration story by the agreed deadline.

Participate in the programme’s online orientation.

Attend monthly check-ins organized by IOM.

Participate in the IOM-organized field visit in Chiang Rai.

Remain engaged throughout the fellowship period.

Incorporate appropriate editorial guidance from IOM or designated mentors.

Complete the proposed story within the approved timeline.

Follow applicable professional and ethical journalism standards.

Submit all required supporting materials with the final story.

Ensure that the completed work meets the minimum format requirements stated in the programme documents.

Submit the final story by 8 January 2027.

All materials produced through the programme will be subject to IOM review and approval before publication or dissemination. This review is intended to confirm that funded stories remain within the approved scope, meet ethical and professional standards and comply with relevant IOM requirements. Read the official terms in the call for proposals.

Documents Required for the Application

Applicants should prepare the complete application package before opening the online submission form.

The required materials include:

1. Updated Resume or CV

The resume or CV should clearly present the applicant’s education, journalism or media experience, relevant training, publications, reporting interests and other experience connected to migration, social issues or public-interest communication.

2. Cover Letter

Applicants must provide a cover letter explaining:

Their motivation for applying.

Their interest in ethical migration journalism.

Their proposed story idea.

Why the subject is relevant to Chiang Rai or surrounding areas.

How they intend to complete the project.

The cover letter and proposed story description should be concise and should not exceed one page.

3. Completed Story Proposal Form

Candidates must download and complete the official Story Proposal Form available through the programme webpage.

The proposal should be internally consistent with the information provided in the cover letter and online application form.

4. Certificate of Relevant IOM Training

Applicants must provide evidence that they completed the qualifying IOM training or e-learning route.

For the e-learning route, both the Migration Explained and Reporting Migration in Thailand modules must be completed.

5. Previous Work Samples

Journalist applicants must provide two relevant samples of previous work.

This requirement is specifically identified for journalist applicants. The samples should demonstrate the applicant’s ability to research, structure and communicate a story professionally. Whenever possible, applicants should select work relevant to migration, human rights, border communities, social inclusion or another complex public-interest issue. Confirm the complete application requirements on the official IOM page.

How to Apply

Interested candidates should follow these steps:

Review the official programme announcement and call for proposals.

Confirm that all location and training requirements are met.

Develop an original and feasible migration story connected to Chiang Rai or surrounding areas.

Update the resume or CV.

Prepare a focused cover letter of no more than one page.

Download and complete the official Story Proposal Form.

Obtain the certificate showing completion of the required training or e-learning modules.

Prepare two relevant work samples if applying as a journalist.

Complete the online application form available through the official IOM Thailand programme page.

Submit the entire application no later than 22 September 2026.

Apply through the official IOM Thailand opportunity page

Candidates should carefully check uploaded documents before submitting. The story title, subject, proposed activities and timeline should remain consistent across the cover letter, proposal form and online application.

Important Programme Dates

Programme stage
Date

Applications opened
1 September 2026

Application deadline
22 September 2026

Shortlisting and interviews
23–25 September 2026

Selection announcement
29 September 2026

Fellowship period
1 October–31 December 2026

Final story submission
8 January 2027

The short period between the application deadline and interviews means applicants should remain available and regularly monitor the email address and telephone number provided in their application.

How to Prepare a Strong Story Proposal

Although applicants should follow the official Story Proposal Form, the following practical steps can help produce a clearer and more competitive submission.

Define a Focused Local Issue

Identify a specific migration-related issue that can be examined within Chiang Rai or nearby areas. Avoid a subject that is too broad to research properly within three months.

Explain Why the Story Matters

Clearly describe why the proposed story is relevant to local communities and how it could improve public understanding of migration.

Present a Credible Reporting Plan

Explain which people, communities, experts, institutions, documents and other sources may be consulted. Applicants should demonstrate that the proposed reporting process is realistic.

Center Accuracy and Ethics

The proposal should explain how information will be verified and how the dignity, privacy and safety of migrants or other potentially vulnerable sources will be protected.

Include Migrant Perspectives Responsibly

Migration stories should not treat migrants only as statistics or passive subjects. Where appropriate and safe, the proposal should create space for migrants to explain their experiences in their own words.

Demonstrate Feasibility

The reporting scope, production method and expected output should be achievable between October and December 2026 and within the USD 1,000 grant.

Prepare for Editorial Collaboration

Applicants should demonstrate openness to mentorship, review and constructive editorial feedback. The fellowship is structured as a supported reporting process rather than an unrestricted financial award.

Review Every Document for Consistency

The CV, cover letter, proposal form, work samples and online application should support the same professional narrative. Conflicting titles, timelines or project descriptions could weaken the application.

Contact for Questions

Questions about the programme or application process may be directed to:

Email: mediathailand@iom.int

Applicants should first review the official announcement and call for proposals before contacting IOM. Questions should be clear, specific and directly related to information not already addressed in the published materials.

Application Deadline

The application deadline is:

22 September 2026

No specific closing time or time zone is stated in the accessible programme announcement. Applicants should submit early to avoid technical problems or uncertainty on the final day.

Conclusion

The IOM Ethical Migration Journalism Fellowship Programme 2026 offers an important opportunity to transform a strong local story idea into professionally supported, evidence-based journalism.

Five selected fellows will receive USD 1,000 each, along with mentorship, editorial guidance, structured check-ins, a field visit in Chiang Rai and potential publication through IOM platforms. More importantly, participants will contribute to a wider effort to improve how migration is reported and understood in northern Thailand.

This is a project-based programme with meaningful responsibilities. A successful fellow must be prepared to conduct careful research, engage ethically with sources, respond to editorial feedback and submit a completed story by 8 January 2027.

Interested candidates should prepare their application documents carefully and submit the online form by 22 September 2026.

The goal of the program is to identify current students from Big Ten Academic Alliance universities who have been admitted into doctoral candidacy and satisfied all requirements except completion of dissertation. Folklife

History of science and technology

Materials research

Molecular biology

Social and cultural history of the United States

TITLE: Latin American Scholars Grants 2026: Up to £1,750 for Researchers to Attend and Present at the SLAS Conference

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Society for Latin American Studies (SLAS) is offering the Latin American Scholars Grants 2026, a funding opportunity designed to support scholars based in Latin America who wish to attend the SLAS conference in person, present their research, and develop meaningful academic collaborations with SLAS members.

The scheme normally provides 10 awards of up to £1,750 each. The funding is intended to contribute towards eligible costs associated with attending the conference, including registration, travel and accommodation. Although the grant is not expected to cover the full cost of conference participation, recipients can combine the funding with other sources of financial support.

The opportunity is particularly relevant to researchers whose work focuses on Latin America and who would benefit from presenting their research internationally, expanding their academic networks and establishing collaborative relationships with scholars connected to SLAS.

About the Latin American Scholars Grants

The Latin American Scholars Grants are administered by the Society for Latin American Studies (SLAS) as part of its efforts to facilitate greater participation by scholars based in Latin America in its annual conference.

The grants are intended to reduce some of the financial barriers associated with international academic conference participation. Successful applicants receive financial assistance towards attending the SLAS conference and are expected to use the opportunity not only to present their research but also to develop closer collaboration with members of the Society.

The scheme normally makes ten awards, with each recipient eligible to receive up to £1,750.

Funding can contribute towards:

Conference registration costs

Travel expenses

Accommodation costs

Other appropriate costs connected to attending the conference

Certain additional care-related expenses where applicable

Applicants should understand that the grant is a contribution rather than a full conference sponsorship. SLAS explicitly recognises that £1,750 may not cover the entire cost of attending the conference, meaning applicants may combine the grant with other funding sources where necessary.

Who Can Apply for the SLAS Latin American Scholars Grants?

The funding scheme is specifically intended for scholars based in Latin America.

Applicants must demonstrate that they are based in Latin America through their address and institutional affiliation. The scheme accommodates researchers working in different academic circumstances and does not restrict applications only to scholars holding conventional university positions.

Eligible applicants can include:

Independent researchers based in Latin America

PhD students

University-affiliated scholars

Researchers affiliated with other academic or research institutions

Early-career scholars who meet the relevant requirements

Other scholars based in Latin America who are able to participate in the SLAS conference in person

Applicants are not required to be members of SLAS in order to apply.

However, non-members and other applicants are encouraged to consider joining the Society.

Requirement to Attend the Conference in Person

One of the central conditions of the funding scheme is that grant recipients must attend the SLAS conference in person.

The funding is intended to facilitate physical participation in the conference, including the presentation of the recipient’s research and opportunities for networking and collaboration.

Award holders must therefore register to attend both days of the conference.

This requirement is important for applicants to consider when preparing their budgets and planning their travel.

What Does the Grant Fund?

Each successful scholar can receive up to £1,750 to contribute towards the costs associated with participating in the conference.

The funding may be used to help meet costs such as:

Conference Registration

A portion of the grant can contribute towards the cost of registering for the SLAS conference.

Travel

Funding may help scholars meet the costs of travelling to the conference location. Applicants should provide a realistic estimate of anticipated travel expenses in their application.

Accommodation

The grant can also contribute towards accommodation costs associated with attending the conference.

Caring Responsibilities

SLAS recognises that caring responsibilities can create additional financial barriers to conference participation.

Applicants can therefore include eligible costs associated with caring responsibilities in their proposed budgets.

Examples mentioned by SLAS include:

Additional care required while the applicant is away

Travel expenses for accompanying children

Other appropriate costs arising from caring responsibilities

Applicants who have such requirements are encouraged to include them in the outline budget rather than excluding them from consideration.

SLAS Membership Is Not Mandatory

An important feature of the opportunity is that applicants do not have to be SLAS members to apply.

Nevertheless, the Society encourages applicants to become members.

The grant is particularly focused on building stronger links between scholars based in Latin America and the wider SLAS academic community. Consequently, applicants are expected to explain how the proposed conference participation could create opportunities for collaboration and academic networking.

SLAS Member Support Requirement

Applications must be supported by a member of SLAS who is not the applicant.

This means prospective applicants should identify an SLAS member who can support their application and contribute to the strategic case for the proposed collaboration.

The support requirement is connected to one of the main purposes of the scheme: encouraging closer academic relationships between Latin American scholars and members of SLAS.

Applicants should therefore approach this part of the application strategically and identify a potential collaborator whose academic interests or expertise have a meaningful connection with their proposed research.

What If You Do Not Know an SLAS Member?

Applicants who do not already have contacts within SLAS are encouraged to contact Prof Marieke Riethof, former SLAS President, for support.

This provides a potential route for researchers who are interested in applying but do not already have an established relationship with an SLAS member.

Strategic Case for Collaboration

The application should go beyond simply explaining why the applicant needs financial assistance.

Applicants are expected to make a strategic case for the proposed collaboration.

This is an important component of the selection process because the grant aims to maximise both:

Networking opportunities for the applicant.

The potential impact of activities associated with the funded trip.

A strong application should therefore clearly explain the academic value of attending the conference and the potential benefits of connecting with SLAS members.

Applicants may wish to demonstrate:

Why their research is relevant to the SLAS community

How attending the conference will advance their academic work

Which academic connections they hope to develop

How the proposed collaboration could develop beyond the conference

Why in-person participation is valuable to their research or career development

How the funding will enable participation that might otherwise be financially difficult

Early-Career Scholar Consideration

SLAS aims, wherever possible and where the relevant criteria are met, to reserve two of the awards for early-career scholars.

This provision is intended for researchers who are within five years of completing their thesis or dissertation.

Applicants who fall within this category should clearly indicate this in their short professional biography.

For PhD holders, applicants who are within five years of completing their PhD should therefore make the date of completion clear in their application materials.

This information can help the assessment committee determine the applicant’s career stage when considering the application.

Application Languages

The application process provides flexibility regarding language.

Completed application forms may be submitted in:

English

Portuguese

Spanish

This multilingual application provision is particularly relevant given the geographical focus of the scheme and its aim of supporting scholars based in Latin America.

Applicants should nevertheless ensure that all required information is provided clearly and that the application addresses the assessment criteria regardless of the language selected.

Assessment Criteria

Applications for the Latin American Scholars Grants are assessed using four principal criteria.

1. Strategic Case for Support — 10 Points

The strategic case for support carries the highest weighting, with a maximum of 10 points.

Applicants should clearly explain the purpose of the proposed conference participation and the potential value of collaboration and networking with SLAS members.

The application should demonstrate that the proposed trip has a clear academic and collaborative purpose.

2. Quality of Abstract — 10 Points

The quality of the research abstract is also worth 10 points.

Applicants should therefore pay close attention to the clarity, relevance and academic quality of the abstract submitted with the application.

The abstract should communicate the research topic and its significance effectively while giving the assessment committee a clear understanding of the proposed conference contribution.

3. Profile Relative to Career Stage — 5 Points

Applicants can receive up to 5 points for their profile in relation to their career stage.

This criterion allows the committee to consider applicants within the context of their academic development.

Early-career applicants should ensure that relevant information about their career stage, including whether they completed their PhD within the previous five years, is clearly presented.

4. Justification of Budget — 5 Points

The proposed budget is worth 5 points.

Applicants should therefore provide a clear and realistic explanation of how the requested funding will be used.

A well-prepared budget should distinguish the anticipated expenses and provide sufficient justification for the requested support.

Application Timeline

Applicants should be aware of the broader timeline surrounding the SLAS conference and the grant application process.

October — Conference Call for Papers

The deadline for the SLAS conference Call for Papers normally falls in October.

SLAS generally aims to notify applicants about whether their conference paper has been accepted before the funding application deadline.

However, if the outcome of the Call for Papers has not yet been communicated, applicants are advised to submit the funding application while awaiting the outcome rather than missing the grant deadline.

November — Grant Application Deadline

The deadline for the Latin American Scholars Grant is in November.

For the 2026 application cycle, the stated deadline is:

27 November 2026

Applicants should leave enough time for both the Latin American scholar and the supporting SLAS member to complete the required parts of the application.

Applications submitted after the deadline will not be considered.

December/January — Notification of Results

Applicants will normally be informed of the outcome in December.

However, applicants should expect to receive the final notification by the end of January at the latest.

February — Conference Registration and Travel Arrangements

Successful applicants should then proceed with conference preparations.

This stage includes:

Registering for the full conference

Booking travel

Making accommodation arrangements

Completing and submitting the grant acceptance form

Providing the information required for the SLAS Treasurer to arrange the bank transfer

April/May/June — Post-Conference Blog Contribution

Grant recipients are expected to prepare and submit a short blog post following their participation.

The blog should discuss their conference paper and the research collaboration developed through the funded trip.

Post-Grant Blog Requirement

Receiving the grant comes with a post-conference communication requirement.

Grant recipients are expected to write a blog post of approximately 500–750 words covering:

Their conference paper

The research collaboration

Relevant experiences or outcomes from the funded trip

The blog may be published on the SLAS website.

The post can be submitted in:

English

Spanish

Portuguese

Recipients are encouraged to include photographs or other images where they have the appropriate permissions to use them.

The blog should be submitted to the SLAS Secretary within three months of receiving the funding.

Encouragement to Publish in the Bulletin of Latin American Research

In addition to the blog requirement, SLAS strongly encourages grant recipients to consider submitting an article to the Bulletin of Latin American Research.

This provides recipients with an opportunity to develop their conference research into a more substantial academic publication.

Applicants and eventual grant recipients should therefore consider how their conference presentation could form part of a broader research and publication strategy.

Application Submission and Confirmation

Completed application forms should be submitted to the SLAS Secretary before the stated deadline.

Applicants will normally receive confirmation that their application has been received within three working days.

Applicants should retain evidence of their submission and ensure that they have provided all required information before the deadline.

Because applications arriving after the deadline will not be considered under any circumstances, applicants should avoid waiting until the final hours to submit their materials.

Application Retention and Assessment

SLAS states that applications will be retained for up to one year.

The applications will be shared with members of the SLAS committee for assessment.

Applicants should therefore ensure that their submissions are prepared specifically for the selection criteria and contain information that clearly demonstrates the academic and collaborative value of the proposed conference participation.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Applicants can improve the clarity of their submissions by addressing each assessment criterion directly.

1. Develop a Clear Collaboration Strategy

The strategic case is worth the largest number of points, so applicants should clearly explain the proposed collaboration.

Rather than focusing exclusively on the need for financial support, explain what academic relationships could result from attending the conference.

2. Prepare a Strong Research Abstract

Since the quality of the abstract is worth 10 points, applicants should ensure that the abstract is coherent, focused and representative of the research they intend to present.

3. Explain Your Career Stage

Applicants should provide an accurate professional biography and clearly indicate relevant career-stage information.

Early-career scholars within five years of completing their thesis or dissertation should make this particularly clear.

4. Prepare a Realistic Budget

The budget should be detailed enough for the assessment committee to understand how the £1,750 contribution would be used.

Applicants should consider the anticipated costs of:

Registration

Transportation

Accommodation

Other legitimate conference-related expenses

Eligible caring responsibilities, where applicable

5. Plan the SLAS Member Support Early

Because applications require support from an SLAS member, applicants should not leave this requirement until the last minute.

Applicants without existing SLAS contacts should consider using the support route suggested by the Society.

6. Consider Other Sources of Funding

The grant is not intended to cover the entire cost of attending the conference.

Applicants should therefore consider whether university departments, research institutions, professional organisations or other funding bodies can provide additional financial support.

APPLY HERE

Deadline for the Latin American Scholars Grants

The application deadline is: 27 November 2026

Applications received after the deadline will not be considered.

Applicants should also allow sufficient time for the supporting SLAS member to complete their part of the application before submission.

Why This Opportunity Matters for Latin American Researchers

International academic conferences can provide researchers with opportunities to present their work to specialist audiences, receive feedback, develop research collaborations and build professional networks.

For scholars based in Latin America, travel and conference costs can present significant barriers to participating in international academic events.

The Latin American Scholars Grants seek to address part of this challenge by providing financial assistance while placing particular emphasis on collaboration between scholars based in Latin America and members of SLAS.

The combination of financial support, conference participation, networking and potential publication opportunities can make the programme relevant to researchers seeking to expand the international reach of their academic work.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Latin American Scholars Grants 2026.

Conclusion

The SLAS Latin American Scholars Grants 2026 provide up to £1,750 for scholars based in Latin America to contribute towards registration, travel and accommodation costs associated with attending and presenting at the SLAS conference in person.

The programme is open to a broad range of scholars, including independent researchers, PhD students and researchers affiliated with universities and other institutions. Applicants do not need to be SLAS members, although membership is encouraged. Each application must be supported by an SLAS member and must present a strategic case for collaboration and networking.

The application is assessed on the strategic case for support, quality of the research abstract, the applicant’s profile relative to career stage and the justification of the proposed budget. Where criteria are met, two awards are normally reserved for early-career scholars within five years of completing their thesis or dissertation.

Applicants should also take note of the post-award requirements, including attending both days of the conference and submitting a 500–750-word blog post about their conference paper and research collaboration within three months of receiving the funding.

With the 27 November 2026 deadline approaching, eligible scholars should begin preparing their abstract, collaboration strategy, budget and SLAS member support well in advance of the closing date.
