TITLE: NIH Graduate Partnerships Program 2026: Funded Doctoral Research Opportunities for PhD Students in the U.S. and Abroad

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
NIH Graduate Partnerships Program (GPP) offers doctoral students interested in conducting advanced biomedical, behavioral, social science, and health-related research an extensive research training opportunity to undertake all or part of their dissertation research within the NIH Intramural Research Program.

The Graduate Partnerships Program connects doctoral education at universities in the United States and abroad with the research environment, facilities, scientists, and resources available across NIH Institutes and Centers. Through the program, participating students remain enrolled as full-time doctoral students at their universities while completing dissertation research under the guidance of NIH researchers.

The opportunity is particularly relevant to doctoral researchers working across fields such as biology, engineering, epidemiology, psychology, mathematics, chemistry, pharmaceutical sciences, nursing, physics, computer science, bioinformatics, and other disciplines related to health and biomedical research.

Importantly, the NIH Graduate Partnerships Program provides financial support to participating students. Graduate student stipends are adjusted annually and based on relevant experience after completion of an undergraduate degree. Additional support includes health insurance coverage and, for eligible new fellows relocating near an NIH campus, a one-time relocation benefit of $1,500.

There are two primary routes into the Graduate Partnerships Program: Individual Partnerships and Institutional Partnerships. The appropriate pathway depends on a student’s university, current doctoral status, and the structure through which they plan to undertake their NIH dissertation research.

About the NIH Graduate Partnerships Program

The NIH Graduate Partnerships Program is designed to give doctoral students an opportunity to perform dissertation research within the NIH Intramural Research Program while continuing their academic studies through their home universities.

Students participating through institutional partnerships benefit from both the academic resources of their universities and the research environment of NIH. Under these arrangements, students complete their academic requirements through their universities while performing all or part of their dissertation research within an NIH research group.

Rather than replacing a student’s university doctoral programme, the NIH experience becomes an important component of it. Participants remain responsible for satisfying the academic requirements established by their home institution while simultaneously undertaking research at NIH.

This model can provide doctoral researchers with access to a broad scientific community while allowing them to maintain their existing academic affiliation.

Two Ways to Participate in the NIH Graduate Partnerships Program

Prospective participants should understand that the Graduate Partnerships Program offers two main pathways.

1. Individual Partnerships

Individual Partnerships are intended for students who are already enrolled in doctoral programmes at universities around the world.

Through this pathway, currently enrolled doctoral students may undertake all or part of their dissertation research at NIH.

Individual Partnerships can include:

U.S. citizens;

U.S. permanent residents; and

foreign nationals.

This makes the Individual Partnership pathway particularly significant for doctoral students studying outside the United States who are interested in conducting dissertation research within the NIH Intramural Research Program.

Individual Partnership applications are open year-round.

Students should review the specific Individual Partnership eligibility requirements and application process before submitting an application.

2. Institutional Partnerships

Institutional Partnerships are established collaborative arrangements between NIH and specific university programmes.

Students participating in these partnerships are jointly selected through NIH and university processes, complete their academic requirements at the relevant university, and undertake all or part of their dissertation research in an NIH Intramural Research Program research group.

The listed partner programmes include partnerships involving:

Brown University;

Georgetown University;

Johns Hopkins University;

University of Pennsylvania;

University College London;

University of Oxford and University of Cambridge; and

the Consortia of Universities – NIH Comparative Biomedical Scientist Training Program.

Applicants should note that eligibility requirements, university application requirements, programme structures, and deadlines can differ significantly between individual institutional partnerships.

What Degrees Are Eligible for the NIH Graduate Partnerships Program?

The broader NIH Graduate Partnerships Program is designed for doctoral-level students.

According to the NIH programme information provided, students pursuing the following degrees may participate:

PhD;

DPhil;

PharmD;

DrPH;

PsyD;

MD/PhD; and

DVM/PhD.

Students pursuing a master’s degree are not the intended participants for the Graduate Partnerships Program and are instead directed by NIH towards its Academic Internship Program.

The Graduate Partnerships Program is also not intended for students pursuing stand-alone professional degrees such as:

MD;

DO;

DDS; or

other professional degrees that do not fit the programme’s doctoral research structure.

Applicants should carefully review the requirements of the specific Individual or Institutional Partnership they intend to pursue, as individual pathways may have additional eligibility conditions.

Research Opportunities Available Through the NIH GPP

Graduate students participating in the programme undertake research within one of the NIH Institutes or Centers that form part of the NIH Intramural Research Program.

Research groups operate across NIH campuses, including the main NIH campus in Bethesda, Maryland.

Graduate students work within research groups directed by NIH Principal Investigators (PIs).

The programme encompasses research opportunities across the:

biomedical sciences;

behavioral sciences;

social sciences;

basic sciences;

translational research; and

clinical research.

The institutional programme specifically invites graduate students interested in fields including biology, engineering, epidemiology, psychology, mathematics, chemistry, pharmaceutical sciences, nursing, physics, computer science, bioinformatics, and other health-related disciplines.

This multidisciplinary structure means the NIH Graduate Partnerships Program is not restricted solely to traditional laboratory-based biomedical research.

Fields of Study Relevant to the Programme

Students with academic or research experience across a wide variety of scientific and health-related disciplines may find relevant opportunities through the programme.

These include, but are not necessarily limited to:

Biology

Biomedical sciences

Engineering

Epidemiology

Psychology

Mathematics

Chemistry

Pharmaceutical sciences

Nursing

Physics

Computer science

Bioinformatics

Behavioral sciences

Social sciences

Other health-related disciplines

Applicants should research the NIH Institutes and Centers carefully to identify research groups whose scientific focus aligns with their doctoral research interests and long-term academic or professional goals.

Where Will Graduate Students Conduct Their Research?

Graduate students can work within research groups across NIH campuses.

The programme is therefore not limited exclusively to one research building or scientific department. Students should research the different NIH campuses and understand the specific areas of work conducted at each location before pursuing a placement.

For Institutional Partnerships, these are full-time research positions within NIH Institutes and Centers, and participating students may work across NIH campuses, including the main campus in Bethesda, Maryland.

Students should also remember that their university remains an important part of their doctoral education.

Depending on the partnership, students may be required to divide their time between their university and NIH.

Professional Development Beyond Dissertation Research

The NIH Graduate Partnerships Program extends beyond laboratory or research training.

Participating graduate students also gain access to professional and personal development resources intended to support their progress as researchers and future professionals.

NIH graduate students have access to:

professional development programmes focused on competencies needed for research and healthcare careers;

educational and career advising; and

a comprehensive well-being and resilience programme.

These resources can complement the student’s scientific training by helping them consider career pathways, strengthen professional competencies, and navigate the demands associated with doctoral research.

NIH Graduate Partnerships Program Stipend

One of the major features of the Graduate Partnerships Program is the financial support available to participating graduate researchers.

NIH graduate student stipends are adjusted annually and determined based on the amount of relevant experience accumulated after completion of an undergraduate degree.

Students participating in the broader GPP while conducting dissertation research at NIH are required to be paid according to the NIH graduate stipend structure, including where funding originates from a university or doctoral fellowship.

Because stipend levels depend on experience and are adjusted annually, prospective applicants should consult the current NIH stipend information rather than assuming that all GPP students receive an identical amount.

Health Insurance Support

In addition to the graduate stipend, NIH provides a stipend supplement designed to cover the full cost of health insurance offered through the Foundation for Advanced Education in the Sciences (FAES).

The insurance provision includes coverage for:

medical needs;

dental needs; and

vision needs.

Coverage is available for individuals and families.

Applicants should review the applicable NIH and FAES information to understand the specific terms of health insurance coverage.

$1,500 Relocation Benefit

New fellows who need to relocate to the vicinity of an NIH campus may qualify for a one-time relocation benefit of $1,500.

This support is particularly relevant to students who must move in order to begin their research training at an NIH location.

Applicants should review the applicable relocation conditions to determine whether they qualify.

Transportation and Travel Support

Free parking is available on each NIH campus.

Graduate students at some campuses may also qualify to participate in the Transhare Program, which provides another transportation-related option for eligible participants.

Students participating through institutional agreements additionally receive funding for travel between NIH and their university. However, the specific arrangements vary according to the partnership.

Prospective applicants should therefore review the details of their particular institutional partnership rather than assuming identical travel benefits across every programme.

Eligibility Requirements

There is no single set of detailed eligibility requirements that applies identically to every GPP pathway.

Eligibility requirements for Individual Partnerships and Institutional Partnerships differ.

For Institutional Partnerships specifically, NIH states that eligibility requirements vary according to the partnership. Applicants must therefore consult the individual programme information for the university partnership that interests them.

At the broader programme level, applicants should pay particular attention to their:

doctoral enrolment status;

degree type;

academic discipline;

research interests;

university;

citizenship or immigration circumstances where applicable;

requirements of the particular partnership; and

ability to fulfil NIH onboarding requirements.

Federal Background Check Requirement

Regardless of the pathway through which a graduate student enters NIH, participants must be able to pass the required federal background check.

Applicants should take this requirement seriously and review NIH’s full terms and conditions before committing to the programme.

Meeting academic or research requirements alone does not remove the requirement to satisfy applicable NIH onboarding and federal requirements.

Important Considerations Before Applying

Participating in the Graduate Partnerships Program involves significant responsibilities.

A GPP participant remains a full-time student at their university while undertaking dissertation research through NIH.

For Institutional Partnerships, the student is simultaneously a full-time university student and a trainee working onsite at an NIH campus. Institutional partnerships require students to spend time at their university, and some arrangements require the establishment of collaboration between an NIH Principal Investigator and a university Principal Investigator.

Students must continue meeting the academic requirements of their graduate programme while conducting their dissertation research at NIH.

Prospective applicants should therefore carefully investigate:

How much time they will spend at NIH.

How much time they will need to spend at their university.

Their university’s doctoral requirements.

NIH research expectations.

The requirements of their specific partnership.

Whether collaboration between university and NIH investigators is required.

The research group and Principal Investigator they may work with.

Funding, relocation, travel, and other practical considerations.

Understanding these requirements before applying can help students determine whether the structure is compatible with their doctoral programme.

NIH Graduate Partnerships Program 2026 Application Deadline

Deadlines depend on whether an applicant is pursuing an Individual Partnership or an Institutional Partnership.

Individual Partnerships

Applications are open year-round.

This means there is no single annual closing date for the Individual Partnership pathway based on the programme information provided.

Institutional Partnerships

The 2026 Institutional Partnership application is currently open.

The main applicant deadline is:

Tuesday, December 1, 2026 at 12:00 noon Eastern Time.

The general deadline for references to submit recommendation letters is:

Thursday, December 3, 2026 at 12:00 noon Eastern Time.

However, NIH lists exceptions for certain institutional partnerships:

University of Pennsylvania: Tuesday, December 1, 2026 at 12:00 noon ET.

Johns Hopkins University: Friday, December 4, 2026 at 12:00 noon ET.

NIH also notes that the Consortia of Universities – NIH Comparative Biomedical Scientist Training Program (CBSTP) operates two submission rounds, and prospective applicants should consult the CBSTP programme directly for its applicable deadline.

Because deadlines and requirements vary, applicants should verify the schedule for their selected partnership well before beginning the application.

How to Apply for the NIH Graduate Partnerships Program

Applicants should first determine whether they are applying through an Individual Partnership or Institutional Partnership.

They should then carefully review the eligibility and admission requirements associated with that pathway.

Applying for an Institutional Partnership

Applicants pursuing an Institutional Partnership must complete the NIH GPP application.

University application requirements can differ depending on the selected partnership.

The NIH online application includes several important components.

1. Undergraduate Experience

Applicants must provide information about their undergraduate educational experience.

2. Coursework and Grades

Applicants must provide a list of their coursework and grades.

Candidates should ensure that the academic information entered into the application is complete and accurate.

3. Curriculum Vitae

A current CV must be included.

Applicants should ensure that their CV clearly communicates relevant academic, research, technical, professional, and other experiences appropriate to the programme.

4. Personal Statement

Applicants must submit a personal statement.

According to the NIH application requirements, the statement should address:

previous research experiences;

why the applicant is interested in the particular institutional agreement;

long-term career goals; and

barriers experienced during the applicant’s educational journey.

The personal statement therefore provides applicants with an opportunity to explain both their scientific preparation and their motivation for pursuing the specific NIH-university partnership.

5. Three References

Applicants must provide the names and contact information of three references.

Applicants should pay close attention to recommendation deadlines, particularly because references generally have a separate deadline from the applicant.

6. Complete the Partner University’s Application Where Required

Submitting the NIH application may not be the only requirement.

Applicants may also need to submit a separate application to the relevant partner university.

The exact requirements differ between institutional partnerships, making it essential to review the programme-specific instructions before applying.

Institutional Partner Programmes

The NIH information provided identifies several established Institutional Partnership programmes.

They include:

Brown University Graduate Partnership Program

Georgetown University Graduate Partnership Program

Johns Hopkins University Graduate Partnership Program

University of Pennsylvania Graduate Partnership Program

University College London PhD – England

University of Oxford-Cambridge PhD – England

University of Oxford/Cambridge MD/PhD – Track 1 and Track 2, England

Consortia of Universities – NIH Comparative Biomedical Scientist Training Program (CBSTP)

Each partnership should be treated as a distinct opportunity within the broader GPP structure because eligibility, academic arrangements, university requirements, and deadlines may vary.

Why Applicants Should Research NIH Institutes and Centers Before Applying

A strong application should be informed by an understanding of the NIH research environment.

Prospective applicants are encouraged to investigate the NIH Intramural Research Program, individual NIH Institutes and Centers, NIH campuses, and the specific research conducted at those locations.

This is especially important because doctoral students work within research groups led by Principal Investigators.

Applicants should consider how their dissertation interests connect with:

a particular NIH Institute or Center;

an NIH research group;

the work of relevant Principal Investigators;

their university research programme; and

their long-term scientific and professional goals.

This preparation can also help applicants explain why a particular partnership or research environment is appropriate for their doctoral development.

Key Benefits of the NIH Graduate Partnerships Program

Depending on the applicable partnership and individual circumstances, major features of the programme include:

The opportunity to undertake all or part of doctoral dissertation research within the NIH Intramural Research Program.

Access to research groups across NIH Institutes and Centers.

Research training under NIH Principal Investigators.

Opportunities spanning biomedical, behavioral, social, basic, translational, and clinical research.

NIH graduate student stipend support.

Annual stipend adjustments based on post-undergraduate experience.

A stipend supplement covering eligible FAES health insurance costs.

Medical, dental, and vision coverage through the applicable insurance arrangement.

A one-time $1,500 relocation benefit for eligible new fellows moving near an NIH campus.

Free parking at NIH campuses.

Potential access to Transhare at eligible campuses.

Travel support between NIH and the university for students participating in institutional agreements, subject to partnership-specific arrangements.

Professional development programmes.

Educational and career advising.

Well-being and resilience resources.

The opportunity to combine university-based doctoral education with research experience in the NIH Intramural Research Program.

Application Checklist

Before submitting an application, prospective candidates should consider completing the following steps:

Determine whether the Individual or Institutional Partnership route applies to you.

Confirm that your doctoral degree is compatible with the GPP.

Review the specific eligibility requirements for your chosen pathway.

Research the NIH Intramural Research Program.

Explore relevant NIH Institutes and Centers.

Investigate NIH campuses and research areas.

Review the requirements of the relevant university partnership, where applicable.

Prepare information about your undergraduate experience.

Compile your coursework and grades.

Update your CV.

Prepare your personal statement if applying through the relevant institutional route.

Identify three appropriate references.

Confirm recommendation letter deadlines.

Determine whether a separate university application is required.

Review federal background check requirements.

Verify the deadline applicable to your particular partnership.

Submit all required materials through the appropriate NIH application system.

APPLY NOW

Important Deadline Summary

Applicants should not assume that every Graduate Partnerships Program pathway follows the same application calendar.

For the current cycle described by NIH:

Individual Partnerships: Applications are open year-round.

Institutional Partnerships: Applications are open, with the main applicant deadline of December 1, 2026 at 12:00 noon ET.

General recommendation letter deadline: December 3, 2026 at 12:00 noon ET, with partnership-specific exceptions.

Prospective applicants should confirm the requirements of their chosen programme before submission because certain institutional partnerships operate under different deadlines and procedures.

Contact for Questions

Applicants with questions about the Graduate Partnerships Program can consult the NIH Office of Intramural Training & Education’s frequently asked questions or contact the programme directly at:

Email: gpp@nih.gov

Applicants are strongly encouraged to use official NIH information when checking eligibility requirements, deadlines, programme structures, and application procedures.

Conclusion

The NIH Graduate Partnerships Program 2026 offers doctoral researchers an opportunity to integrate university-based graduate education with dissertation research in the National Institutes of Health Intramural Research Program.

Through Individual and Institutional Partnerships, students can undertake research across biomedical, behavioral, social, computational, engineering, pharmaceutical, and other health-related fields while working within NIH research groups led by Principal Investigators.

The programme also provides substantial support for participating graduate researchers. Depending on eligibility and partnership arrangements, this can include an NIH graduate stipend, health insurance support covering medical, dental and vision needs, a $1,500 relocation benefit for eligible new fellows, transportation provisions, professional development, career advising, and additional support resources.

For prospective applicants, choosing the correct pathway is essential. Individual Partnership applications remain open throughout the year, while the current Institutional Partnership cycle has a principal applicant deadline of December 1, 2026 at noon ET, with recommendation letters and certain partner programmes following separate deadlines.

Doctoral students interested in the programme should carefully examine the relevant partnership, research NIH Institutes and Centers that align with their interests, prepare the required academic and application materials, and verify all programme-specific requirements before submitting an application.

TITLE: MFWA Training Workshop 2026 on Critical Coverage of Africa-China Trade, Investment & Political Relations for Journalists in Anglophone West Africa

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: July 30, 2026

Applications are open for the MFWA Training Workshop 2026 on Critical Coverage of Africa-China Trade, Investment & Political Relations for Journalists in Anglophone West Africa. The Media Foundation for West Africa (MFWA), in partnership with South Africa-based Wits Centre for Journalism (WCJ), invites applications from journalists across Anglophone West Africa for a three-day capacity-building workshop on reporting critically on the multiple dimensions of Africa-China relations. Dubbed “Building Capacity to Cover a Complex Story – Africa and China relations”, the workshop is scheduled to take place in Accra, Ghana in the last quarter of 2026.

Africa has long been a site of geopolitical competition among global powers. China’s growing global influence and engagement across Africa has intensified debates around trade, infrastructure, development financing, natural resources, technology, labour, governance, and international cooperation. As global power relations continue to shift, journalists across Africa must be equipped to critically examine these developments and report on them with depth, nuance, and strong public interest perspectives grounded in African realities.

The workshop, funded by the University of Witwatersrand, therefore aims at strengthening the capacity of journalists to better understand Africa-China relations in an increasingly multipolar global setting, and the implications of these developments for African communities and development. It will offer both subject matter knowledge and journalism techniques in covering stories pertaining to Africa-China relations.

Costs

All costs related to participation in the workshop will be covered by the organisers. These include:

A return flight ticket (economy class)

Accommodation and Meals

Local transportation

Story Grants

Beyond the training, participating journalists will have the opportunity to apply for reporting grants to support the production and publication of in-depth stories on Africa-China relations and related issues. Three (3) excelling journalists may also have a fully-funded opportunity to participate in the Africa Investigative Journalism Conference (AIJC) scheduled for 10-12 November, 2026 in Kenya to speak to their stories.

Eligibility

Applications are invited from journalists who:

Are based in an Anglophone West African country (ie: Ghana, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Liberia and the Gambia).

Work in print, radio, television, or digital media.

Report on areas such as politics, economy, business, trade, development, environment, extractives, infrastructure, or international affairs.

Are available in the last quarter of 2026 (September – October) and can secure a formal permission letter from their editor to participate fully in the training workshop in Accra.

Can produce in-depth stories upon completion of the training.

Application

Interested applicants should fill the application form. Only shortlisted candidates will be contacted. The deadline for applications is July 30, 2026.

As a Youth Ambassador, you have the chance to shape your ideas for a self-determined Europe into impactful policy recommendations that are heard by politicians and other decision-makers in Brussels and beyond!

The Rise to Lead summit is designed around this changing understanding of leadership.

Rather than focusing only on traditional ideas of leadership, the event invites participants to consider an important question:

What kind of leadership does the movement for gender justice need right now, and what role can young people play in shaping what comes next?

The summit will create a space for young people to listen, learn, exchange ideas, and connect with others who are interested in gender justice and youth leadership.

Through conversations involving youth voices and different generations, participants will have the opportunity to explore how leadership can be practiced in different ways and how young people can contribute to movements for meaningful change.

The Rise to Lead Global Leadership Summit is part of Girl Up’s broader leadership and community-building activities and will launch the organization’s 2026 Summit Series.

The virtual event will therefore serve not only as a standalone global gathering but also as the beginning of a wider series of leadership events taking place in different regions around the world.

TITLE: Africa Higher Education Centers of Excellence for Development Impact (ACE Impact) Stakeholders Convene in Morocco to Foster Partnerships with Moroccan Universities and the Private Sector

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The World Bank Group, the Association of African Universities (AAU), and the French Development Agency (AFD), in close collaboration with the Ministry of Higher Education, Scientific Research and Innovation, the Mohammed VI Polytechnic University (UM6P), and OCP Africa are currently hosting the 9th bi-annual ACE Impact Regional Workshop and Morocco ACE Impact Higher Education Partnership Forum at the Palm Plaza Resort in Marrakech, Morocco. The event, which started from May 29 and runs through till June 2, 2023 marks the first time the ACE Impact project’s regional workshop is being hosted outside the eleven participating countries. Morocco, like other thriving African countries, harbors all ingredients for fostering inter-institutional and private-sector partnerships, crucial for advancing collaborative research development and innovation. “Given the successes of the ACE Impact project in contributing to research, innovations, and improving the quality of education in the sub-region, it has become imminent to forge sustainable partnerships with institutions and the private sector in other regions of the continent, particularly in North Africa, for concerted knowledge transfer and peer learning.”- Prof. Olusola B. Oyewole, AAU Secretary-General.

Several universities in Morocco have been instrumental in aligning technological innovations with transformative research to drive national development. The UM6P is a paradigm of Moroccan institutions that have taken impressive strides in the priority areas of Agriculture, Renewable Energy, Mining, and Digital Technology and Innovation. The university offers an interdisciplinary ecosystem of scientific research, entrepreneurship, and innovation aimed at advancing knowledge and promoting the emergence of resilient businesses across the globe. Hosting the workshop in Morocco provides a unique opportunity for cross-learning and partnership development with UM6P, as well as other Moroccan universities and Morocco’s private sector markets. “The strategy of decompartmentalizing knowledge and expertise must be taken beyond the UM6P ecosystem to give impetus to a common African ambition. As an institution driven by the determination to improve the impact of research and training on the development of our continent, we adhere to the program’s vision and express our willingness to make our knowledge and academic competencies available to the ACE Impact centers.“- Mr. Hicham El Habti, President of UM6P.

The event has brought together the project government representatives from the eleven participating African countries, the leaders of the fifty-three Centers of Excellence, subject matter experts, experts in research commercialization among other priority fields, key higher education stakeholders, policy think tanks and industry players. OCP Africa is a principal industry partner for the Higher Education Partnership Forum. “At OCP Africa, we’re dedicated to supporting R&D in agriculture across Africa through a systematic approach integrating research and education. We’re excited to explore collaboration opportunities with ACEs at the Forum, driving sustainable solutions ‘In Africa, by Africa.’ With 20 ongoing R&D projects and partnerships with a dozen universities continent-wide, we aim to make a transformative impact.” – Dr Mohamed Anouar Jamali, CEO of OCP Africa.

The first two days (May 29 & 30) are focusing on ACE Impact implementation sessions, whereas the remaining days (May 31 – June 2) will be dedicated to fostering cross-country partnerships and networks.

The workshop acts as one of many preparatory events, “On the Road to Marrakech,” building the path to the World Bank Group and the International Monetary Fund Annual Meetings to be held in Marrakech from October 9-15, 2023. “High-quality human capital and scientific research can act as catalysts for diversifying economic output and accelerating economic growth. Higher Education Institutions and their participation in international research partnerships and networks can play a key role in addressing national development challenges and promoting research quality, commercialization, and technology transfer. The Morocco ACE Impact Higher Education Partnership Forum will contribute towards fostering such cross-country partnerships and networks between the African Centers of Excellence and Moroccan universities and private sector stakeholders for joint research, co-creation of programs, and innovation opportunities.” Jesko Hentschel, Country Director for the Maghreb and Malta at the World Bank.

Virtual participation is available for stakeholders who wish to participate online. The opening and closing sessions of the workshop will be held on May 31 and June 2, respectively, at 9:00 GMT +1, and members of the press are cordially invited to take part in the event. Opening the sessions will be given by key partners such as the Ministry of Higher Education, Scientific Research, and Innovation in Morocco, represented by the Director of Cooperation and Partnerships, Mrs. Sanaa Zebakh (representing the Secretary General of the Ministry, M. Mohamed Khalfaoui) and Mr. Jesko Hentschel, Country Director for the Maghreb and Malta at the World Bank.

Please register here to participate.

For further information, contact

Ministry of Higher Education, Scientific Research and Innovation: i.hannouche@enssup.ma

UM6P: rachid.serraj@um6p.ma

The World Bank: eallano@worldbankgroup.org

OCP Africa: g.benazzouz@ocpafrica.com

The AAU: makyei@aau.org

Background Information

The Africa Higher Education Centers of Excellence (ACE) is a World Bank initiative in collaboration with governments of participating countries to support higher education institutions specializing in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM), Agriculture, Health, Environment and Social Science/Applied Science and Education. It is the first World Bank project aimed at building the capacities of higher education institutions in Africa through the promotion of regional specialization among participating universities in areas that address specific common regional development challenges. It further aims to strengthen the capacities of these universities to deliver high-quality training and applied research, as well as meet the demand for skills required for Africa’s development. The first phase (ACE I) was launched in 2014 with 22 Centers of Excellence in Nine (9) West and Central African countries while the second phase (ACE II) was launched in East and Southern Africa with 24 centers. Based on the initial successes, the World Bank, and the French Development Agency (AFD) in collaboration with the African governments, launched the ACE Impact Project in 2019 to further strengthen post-graduate training and applied research in existing fields and support new fields that are essential for Africa’s economic growth. Under the ACE Impact, there are 53 Centers specializing in the broad thematic areas of STEM, agriculture, health, environment and social/applied science and education. For more information on the ACE Impact Project, visit https://ace.aau.org

About the Organizers

Ministry of Higher Education, Morocco: The Ministry of Higher Education, Scientific Research and Professional Training is a government ministry in Morocco that is responsible for overseeing and regulating higher education in the country. The ministry plays a crucial role in shaping the future of education in Morocco by developing policies and strategies that promote academic excellence, scientific research, and innovation. One of the primary functions of the ministry is to ensure that higher education institutions in Morocco are providing quality education to students. The ministry sets standards for academic programs, faculty qualifications, and research activities and monitors compliance with these standards through regular evaluations and inspections. It also works closely with universities and other institutions to develop curricula that are relevant to the needs of the job market and the country’s economic development.

Mohammed VI Polytechnic University (UM6P): The Mohammed VI Polytechnic University is an institution oriented towards applied research and innovation. Focused on Africa, it aims to place itself among the world-renowned universities in these fields. More than a classic academic institution, the Mohammed VI Polytechnic University is a platform for experimentation and a breeding ground for opportunities that students like to call quite rightly “The school of life”.

The OCP Africa: Created in 2016, OCP Africa, a subsidiary of the OCP Group, aims to contribute to the development of integrated agricultural ecosystems in Africa.

OCP Africa works hand in hand with farmers to help grow the agricultural potential of the African continent through solutions adapted to local conditions and to the needs of soils and crops. In partnership with a network of partners, including governments, non-profit organizations, and companies, OCP Africa works continuously to put all the necessary conditions for the benefit of farmers.

OCP Africa has local offices in many African countries (Côte d’Ivoire, Senegal, Cameroon, Kenya, Ghana, Nigeria, Zambia, Benin, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Burkina Faso, and Rwanda) and is present on the ground in many others. It is also helping to secure the production of competitive fertilizers near major agricultural regions, to strengthen its logistical capacities and to develop new local distribution networks. Learn more: www.ocpafrica.com

Association of African Universities (AAU): The Association of African Universities is an international non-profit, non-governmental organization created by African Universities to promote cooperation among them on the one hand, and between them and the international academic community on the other. Created in 1967, the AAU is the Voice of Higher Education in Africa. AAU aims to improve the quality of African Higher Education and to strengthen its contribution to Africa’s development by supporting the core functions of Higher Education Institutions and facilitating critical reflection and consensus building on issues affecting Higher Education in Africa. The AAU is the Regional Facilitating Unit of the Africa Higher Education Centers of Excellence for Development Impact project.

World Bank Group: The World Bank Group is a multilateral development institution that works to reduce poverty and boost shared prosperity. Its subsidiary IDA (International Development Association) finances the Africa Centers of Excellence series of projects. The World Bank’s International Development Association (IDA), established in 1960, helps the world’s poorest countries by providing grants and low to zero-interest loans for projects and programs that boost economic growth, reduce poverty, and improve poor people’s lives. IDA is one of the largest sources of assistance for the world’s 74 poorest countries, 39 of which are in Africa. Resources from IDA bring positive change to the 1.3 billion people who live in IDA countries. Since 1960, IDA has provided $458 billion to 114 countries. Annual commitments have averaged about $29 billion over the last three years (FY19-FY21), with about 70 percent going to Africa. Learn more: www.worldbank.org

French Development Agency (AFD): For more than 75 years, the French Development Agency (AFD) has been fighting global poverty by supporting policies and investments that benefit the poorest populations. Strengthening the social link between individuals, groups, and territories are now at the heart of its actions in education, health, employment, urban planning, climate, and biodiversity. The French Development Agency (AFD) is the ACE Impact project co-financier. Learn more: https://www.afd.fr/en

TITLE: Oceanic seabirds chase tropical cyclones

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Ventura, F., Sander, N., Catry, P., Wakefield, E., De Pascalis, F., Richardson, P. L., Granadeiro, J. P., Silva, M. C., & Ummenhofer, C. C. (2024). Oceanic seabirds chase tropical cyclones. Current Biology, 34. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2024.06.022

Panel A: Map showing the path of hurricane Gaston (in red) and the concurrent foraging movements (in black) of a petrel from the breeding colony of Bugio (yellow dot). The underlying colors depict the sea surface temperature anomaly (blue = cold anomalies). The sea surface temperatures are anomalously low in the cyclone’s wake. Panel B: Tracks of 9 petrels that followed cyclone wakes over the greatest distance. The yellow dot is the breeding colony of Bugio; the cyclones are shown as a solid red line, with the shaded red area depicting the associated area of maximum wind speeds. The black tracks depict the petrel movements, and the blue segments are those within a maximum of 200 km from the storm’s wake. Image provided by Francesco Ventura.

In late summer and autumn, the passage of intense tropical cyclones can profoundly perturb oceanic and coastal ecosystems. Direct negative effects on individuals and marine communities can be dramatic, but cyclones can also enhance pelagic primary and secondary production. However, cyclone impacts on open ocean marine life remain poorly understood. In our latest article, we investigate their effects on the foraging movements of a wide-ranging higher predator, the Desertas petrel (Pterodroma deserta), in the mid-latitude North Atlantic during hurricane season. Contrary to previously studied pelagic seabirds in tropical and mid-latitude regions, Desertas petrels did not avoid cyclones by altering course, nor did they seek calmer conditions within the cyclone eye. Approximately one-third of petrels tracked from their breeding colony interacted with approaching cyclones. Upon encountering strong winds, the birds reduced ground speed, likely by spending less time in flight. A quarter of birds followed cyclone wakes for days and over thousands of kilometers, a behavior documented here for the first time. Within these wakes, tailwind support was higher than along alternative routes. Furthermore, at the mesoscale (hours–weeks and hundreds of kilometers), sea surface temperature dropped and surface chlorophyll sharply increased, suggesting direct effects on ocean stratification, primary production, and therefore presumably prey abundance and accessibility for surface-feeding petrels. We therefore hypothesize that cyclone wakes provide both predictably favorable wind conditions and foraging opportunities. As such, cyclones may have positive net effects on the demography of many mid-latitude pelagic seabirds and, likely, other marine top-predators. TITLE: University of Konstanz Zukunftskolleg Postdoctoral Fellowships 2027: Four Fully Funded 2-Year Research Positions in Germany

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the 2027 Zukunftskolleg Postdoctoral Fellowships at the University of Konstanz in Germany, offering four outstanding early-career researchers the opportunity to pursue independent research for two years within one of the University’s most interdisciplinary academic environments.

The Zukunftskolleg is the Institute for Advanced Study for early-career postdoctoral researchers at the University of Konstanz. It brings together researchers from the natural sciences, humanities and social sciences and is designed to give early-career scholars the independence, institutional resources, interdisciplinary networks and professional development opportunities needed to establish their own research profiles.

For the 2026 call, the Zukunftskolleg is recruiting four Postdoctoral Fellows for two-year appointments. The positions are full-time and remunerated at E13 TV-L, the German public-sector academic salary scale. The preferred starting date is 1 April 2027. Under certain conditions, the fellowship may be extended for an additional year when the Fellow has submitted an external grant application intended to fund their own position.

The opportunity is open across academic disciplines represented at the University of Konstanz. Applicants must propose an independent research project that can be appropriately affiliated with a University department. The call is particularly intended for excellent early-career researchers who demonstrate scientific excellence, research independence, teamwork and strong potential for a successful academic career.

The application deadline is 12 October 2026 at 11:00 AM Central European Time (CET). Applications and supporting materials must be submitted in English through the University of Konstanz online application portal.

About the Zukunftskolleg at the University of Konstanz

The Zukunftskolleg is an Institute for Advanced Study embedded within the University of Konstanz.

Its model is based on giving promising early-career researchers sufficient independence to pursue ambitious projects while remaining integrated into a larger university research environment.

Unlike a narrowly disciplinary postdoctoral programme, the Zukunftskolleg brings together researchers from:

Natural sciences

Humanities

Social sciences

The programme places particular emphasis on independent research, interdisciplinary and intergenerational exchange, integration across the University, and international academic connections. English is the working language of the Zukunftskolleg.

This structure can be especially valuable for researchers who have completed their doctorates and are now seeking to transition from doctoral work toward a more independent scholarly profile.

Four 2-Year Postdoctoral Fellowships Available

The current call offers:

Four two-year Postdoctoral Fellowships

The positions are full-time.

The official vacancy classifies the positions as:

E13 TV-L

This is the German collective public-service salary framework commonly used for academic research positions at public universities.

The official call does not provide a single fixed euro amount because remuneration under TV-L depends on the applicable salary stage and employment circumstances.

Applicants should therefore describe the opportunity as a salaried E13 TV-L postdoctoral position, rather than assigning an unofficial fixed annual salary.

Preferred Starting Date

The preferred start date is:

1 April 2027

The normal initial fellowship period is two years.

The call also creates a possible pathway toward:

2+1 years

because Fellows who apply for external funding to finance their own position may, under the Zukunftskolleg’s rules, receive financial support for an additional fellowship year while awaiting the outcome of that external grant application.

Possibility of a Third Year

The initial fellowship is for two years, but the Zukunftskolleg actively encourages Fellows to pursue external funding during their appointment.

According to the programme information, Postdoctoral Fellows who submit an external funding or grant application covering their own position can potentially receive support for one additional fellowship year while waiting for the funding decision.

This makes the fellowship not only a two-year research opportunity but also a platform for developing the external funding record required for longer-term academic independence.

Full-Time Appointment

The advertised positions are:

Full-time

However, the formal call notes that, in principle, a position may be divided into two half-time positions.

Candidates interested in such an arrangement should consult the official call or contact the Zukunftskolleg directly regarding individual circumstances.

Who Is the Fellowship Designed For?

The target group consists of excellent early-career postdoctoral researchers.

The Zukunftskolleg is particularly interested in candidates who demonstrate:

Scientific excellence

Research independence

Strong teamwork

Academic ambition

Capacity to develop an independent research profile

Potential for a successful academic career

Interest in interdisciplinary exchange

Applications are assessed through a two-stage international review process. Candidates are expected to be informed of the selection decision around mid-February 2027.

PhD Eligibility Window

One of the most important eligibility requirements concerns the date on which the applicant received their doctorate.

Normally, applicants must hold a doctoral degree granted between:

30 September 2024 and 1 October 2026

This means the fellowship is specifically targeted at researchers at a very early postdoctoral career stage.

Exceptions to the Doctoral-Date Rule

Earlier PhD completion dates may potentially be accepted in cases involving:

Maternity leave

Paternity leave

Employment contracts outside academia

Candidates whose doctorate falls outside the normal eligibility period but who believe one of these exceptions applies should consult the formal call and FAQs carefully.

Maximum Postdoctoral Experience

In practical terms, the eligibility period means the call is directed toward researchers with approximately no more than two years of postdoctoral experience under the normal timeline.

The focus is therefore firmly on scholars transitioning from doctoral study into the early stages of independent academic research.

Permanent Professors Are Not Eligible

Applicants must not:

Hold a permanent professorship

Have completed a habilitation

Hold an equivalent qualification such as Venia legendi

The programme is intended to support researchers who have not yet reached a permanently established senior academic career stage.

Candidates With External Funding May Also Apply

Researchers who already have their own position funded through another programme may still be eligible if that funding can be transferred to the University of Konstanz.

This allows the Zukunftskolleg to accommodate certain candidates who bring portable external funding while still seeking the Institute’s interdisciplinary research environment.

Open Across Disciplines

One of the strongest features of the Zukunftskolleg Postdoctoral Fellowship is its disciplinary breadth.

Applicants must propose a research project that connects with:

A discipline represented at the University of Konstanz.

The programme is therefore not limited to one field.

Potential applicants may come from the:

Humanities

Social sciences

Natural sciences

Other academic disciplines represented at the University of Konstanz

Applicants should verify that an appropriate disciplinary home and potential host exist at the University before applying.

Finding a Local Host at the University of Konstanz

Applicants are expected to contact a potential local host among researchers at the University of Konstanz.

The purpose is to ensure that the proposed project has an appropriate institutional and disciplinary affiliation.

This is an important strategic step in the application process.

Candidates should not simply write a research proposal and identify the University generically.

Instead, they should investigate:

Which department best fits the project

Which faculty members work in related research areas

Whether a potential host sees intellectual compatibility

How the project could become integrated into departmental research

The official call notes that support from a department strengthens the application.

How to Approach a Potential Host

Applicants should consider contacting potential hosts well before the October deadline.

A concise initial message could include:

Brief academic introduction

Current institution

PhD field and completion date

Short description of the proposed postdoctoral project

Explanation of the intellectual connection with the potential host

Mention of the Zukunftskolleg fellowship

Request to discuss possible institutional affiliation

The goal should not simply be to obtain a nominal endorsement. A strong host relationship should demonstrate genuine research alignment.

Relationship to the UN Sustainable Development Goals

Applicants are invited to include in their motivation letter a brief reflection on how their research relates to the 17 United Nations Sustainable Development Goals.

This does not mean every project needs to be directly framed as development research.

Rather, candidates can consider whether their research connects meaningfully with themes such as:

Health

Education

Inequality

Peace and institutions

Climate

Sustainability

Gender equality

Innovation

Sustainable communities

Responsible production

International partnerships

Applicants should avoid manufacturing an artificial SDG connection. The reflection will likely be stronger if it identifies a genuine relationship between the project and one or more goals.

International Experience Is an Asset

International teaching or research experience is considered advantageous.

A strong interest in interdisciplinary research is also an asset.

International experience might include:

Research conducted abroad

International academic collaboration

Visiting research stays

International conferences

Teaching in another country

Cross-national research projects

However, the official wording describes these elements as assets rather than absolute requirements.

Research Independence

The fellowship is designed specifically to help researchers develop and implement their own independent research projects.

Successful Fellows are expected to:

Develop their project

Implement the research

Establish an independent research profile

Engage actively with the Zukunftskolleg community

Applicants should therefore demonstrate intellectual independence from their doctoral supervisors and dissertation projects.

A proposal may build on previous expertise, but it should demonstrate a credible next stage in the candidate’s development as an independent researcher.

Responsibilities of Zukunftskolleg Postdoctoral Fellows

Successful Fellows will have several important responsibilities.

Develop and Implement the Research Project

The primary responsibility is to carry out the independent project proposed in the application.

The fellowship provides the institutional infrastructure needed to make that project central to the Fellow’s academic work.

Build an Independent Research Profile

The Zukunftskolleg explicitly expects Fellows to strengthen their own scholarly identity.

This may involve:

Publishing research

Developing collaborations

Presenting at conferences

Building new methodologies

Preparing grant applications

Expanding research networks

Developing future projects

Participate in Weekly Zukunftskolleg Meetings

Fellows are expected to participate actively in the Zukunftskolleg’s regular weekly meetings, known as the Jour Fixe.

These meetings are a key element of the Institute’s interdisciplinary model.

Participants should therefore be genuinely interested in engaging with research outside their own discipline.

Contribute to the Postdoctoral Community

Fellows are expected to help create an active interdisciplinary community rather than focusing exclusively on their individual projects.

This may involve:

Discussing colleagues’ research

Participating in events

Building collaborations

Sharing methods and ideas

Contributing to joint initiatives

Residence Requirement

Successful Fellows must have their:

Place of residence in Konstanz or the surrounding area.

The fellowship is therefore not a remote postdoctoral programme.

International candidates should be prepared to relocate to the Konstanz region in Germany if selected.

Research Allowance

Every Postdoctoral Fellow receives an:

Annual research allowance

The allowance may be used, for example, to support:

Research assistants

Equipment

The official page does not state a single universal monetary amount for the allowance in the public summary.

Additional Research Funding

Fellows may also gain access to funding pools supporting:

Cooperative projects

Research assistants

Travel

Equipment purchases

This funding structure can help researchers build projects beyond what could be achieved through salary support alone.

Co-Funding Opportunities

Zukunftskolleg Fellows are eligible to apply for additional co-funding opportunities available through the Institute.

This may help support activities extending beyond the core fellowship budget.

International Research Visits

The Zukunftskolleg maintains support mechanisms for research mobility.

Fellows can:

Undertake temporary research visits abroad

Nominate international early-career researchers for research visits to the Zukunftskolleg

These opportunities help strengthen international research connections during the fellowship.

Senior Fellows and Mentorship

The Institute’s support structure also allows Fellows to connect with distinguished senior scholars.

Through mechanisms including:

Senior Fellowships

Mentorship Programme

Fellows can help bring experienced researchers to Konstanz and develop relationships useful to their own research and career development.

Career Development Support

The Zukunftskolleg provides professional development beyond direct research funding.

Available support can include:

Coaching

Professional career counselling

Grant proposal writing support

Academic staff development

Research support

This is particularly important for early-career researchers navigating the transition from postdoctoral work toward independent academic positions.

Scientific Retreat Funding

Fellows may also receive financial support to organize and run a scientific retreat.

This can provide an opportunity to bring collaborators together around a focused research question, network or emerging project.

No Teaching Obligation

An attractive feature of the fellowship is that there is:

No mandatory teaching obligation.

However, Fellows have the opportunity to teach in collaboration with a University of Konstanz department if doing so supports their professional development.

This allows researchers to protect substantial time for research while still gaining teaching experience when strategically useful.

Cluster of Excellence Affiliations

Each Fellow becomes a member of both:

The Zukunftskolleg

A relevant University of Konstanz department

Fellows may additionally become affiliated with one of the University’s Clusters of Excellence:

Politics of Inequality

or:

Centre for the Advanced Study of Collective Behaviour

This provides another pathway into high-level interdisciplinary research networks.

The programme information also notes that up to two Cluster-Zukunftskolleg Fellowships connected with collective behaviour may be funded directly by the Centre for the Advanced Study of Collective Behaviour.

Application Requirements

Every application must contain five main components.

1. Motivation Letter

Maximum length:

1 page

This is an eligibility criterion.

The motivation letter should explain:

Why the applicant wants to join the Zukunftskolleg

How the programme supports their research trajectory

Why the University of Konstanz is a strong institutional fit

How interdisciplinary collaboration may benefit their research

Relevant connection with the UN Sustainable Development Goals, where appropriate

Applicants must respect the page limit.

2. Research Proposal

Maximum length:

5 pages, including references

This is also an eligibility criterion.

The proposal should clearly explain:

Central research problem

Research questions

Existing scholarship

Original contribution

Theoretical or conceptual framework

Methodology

Work plan

Feasibility

Connection to a discipline at Konstanz

Potential wider significance

Because references count within the five-page maximum, applicants need to write efficiently.

3. Curriculum Vitae

A complete academic CV is required.

Candidates should highlight:

Academic qualifications

PhD completion date

Publications

Research projects

Grants

Awards

Teaching

International experience

Conference activity

Relevant methods

Academic service

4. Writing Sample

The writing sample may not exceed:

30 single pages

This is another eligibility criterion.

The writing sample should showcase the candidate’s strongest academic work.

Applicants may wish to choose material that demonstrates:

Research independence

Analytical sophistication

Methodological ability

Clear academic writing

Potential for future research

5. Two Reference Letters

Applicants must provide:

Two letters of reference

The official vacancy states that only recommendation letters may be sent directly by referees to the Zukunftskolleg application email by the deadline.

All other materials should be submitted through the online application portal.

Page Limits Are Strict

Applicants should pay extremely close attention to the page requirements.

If any of the following exceed the published limits:

Motivation letter

Research proposal

Writing sample

the application will be considered ineligible and will not receive further consideration.

This is not merely a stylistic recommendation.

It is an eligibility condition.

Application Language

All applications and supporting materials must be submitted in:

English

English is also the working language of the Zukunftskolleg.

Application Process

Applications should be submitted through the official University of Konstanz online application platform.

The vacancy reference number is:

2026/138

Applicants should ensure that all materials are complete and uploaded before the deadline.

Apply through the University of Konstanz portal

Application Deadline

The final deadline is:

12 October 2026 at 11:00 AM CET

Candidates should note that this is an 11:00 AM deadline, not midnight.

International applicants should carefully convert the deadline into their own local time and avoid submitting at the last moment.

Selection Process

Applications are evaluated in a:

Two-stage process

by:

International reviewers

The programme expects candidates to be informed of the decision around:

Mid-February 2027

Selected Fellows are then expected to begin around April 1, 2027.

Tips for Preparing a Competitive Application

1. Secure a Potential Host Early

Do not wait until October to search for a host.

Identify University of Konstanz researchers whose work genuinely overlaps with your project and approach them with a concise, well-developed research concept.

2. Demonstrate Independence From Your PhD

Reviewers are seeking evidence that you can develop an independent academic identity.

Your postdoctoral proposal should represent a meaningful intellectual progression beyond your doctoral thesis.

3. Explain Why Konstanz Specifically

Avoid writing an application that could be sent unchanged to any university.

Explain why:

The specific department

Potential host

Zukunftskolleg

Relevant research networks

Possible Cluster of Excellence

make Konstanz uniquely appropriate for the project.

4. Use the Five Proposal Pages Strategically

Because references count toward the page limit, every paragraph needs to serve a purpose.

A strong structure could include:

Problem and research question

State of the field

Proposed contribution

Methods

Work programme

Fit with Konstanz

Expected outcomes

5. Demonstrate Interdisciplinary Potential

Zukunftskolleg is fundamentally interdisciplinary.

Explain what other disciplines could learn from your research and what your project could gain from discussions beyond your own field.

6. Address the SDGs Thoughtfully

If your research has a meaningful connection with one or more SDGs, explain it succinctly.

Avoid listing several goals without explaining the substantive relationship.

7. Respect Every Formal Requirement

Remember that exceeding the page limit can result in automatic ineligibility.

Check:

Motivation letter: maximum one page

Proposal: maximum five pages including references

Writing sample: maximum 30 pages

Two references

English-language submission

October 12 deadline at 11:00 AM CET

Why the Zukunftskolleg Fellowship Stands Out

The Fellowship offers considerably more than a temporary research salary.

Selected Fellows receive a combination of:

Independent research time

Salaried full-time employment

Individual research allowance

Access to additional project funding

Research mobility

International networks

Mentorship

Career counselling

Grant-writing assistance

Potential Cluster of Excellence affiliations

Opportunity rather than obligation to teach

A possible additional third year linked to an external funding application

The structure is designed to help postdoctoral researchers make the difficult transition from completing a PhD to establishing an internationally visible and externally funded independent research career.

Important Details at a Glance

Host: University of Konstanz

Institute: Zukunftskolleg – Institute for Advanced Study

Location: Konstanz, Germany

Positions: Four

Duration: Two years

Preferred start: April 1, 2027

Employment: Full-time

Salary classification: E13 TV-L

Working language: English

Teaching: No teaching obligation

Residence requirement: Konstanz or surrounding area

Normal PhD eligibility window: September 30, 2024–October 1, 2026

Selection: Two-stage international review

Expected decision: Mid-February 2027

Deadline: October 12, 2026 at 11:00 AM CET

Reference: 2026/138

Application contact: zukunftskolleg-application@uni-konstanz.de

Conclusion

The University of Konstanz Zukunftskolleg Postdoctoral Fellowships 2027 provide an outstanding opportunity for researchers at the very beginning of their postdoctoral careers to establish independent research profiles within an internationally oriented and interdisciplinary academic environment.

Four researchers will be selected for two-year full-time positions at E13 TV-L, with a preferred start date of April 1, 2027.

The programme is open across the natural sciences, social sciences and humanities, provided the proposed project connects with a discipline represented at the University of Konstanz. Fellows join both the Zukunftskolleg and a University department and may additionally connect with major research networks such as the Politics of Inequality or Collective Behaviour Clusters of Excellence.

Beyond salary and research infrastructure, Fellows receive an annual research allowance, access to funding for research assistance, travel and equipment, international research-visit opportunities, mentorship, career development, grant-writing support and additional collaborative funding possibilities. There is no compulsory teaching load, although Fellows may teach if they wish to develop their experience.

The normal eligibility window requires candidates to have received their doctorate between September 30, 2024 and October 1, 2026, subject to specified exceptions for parental leave or employment outside academia. Applicants must not hold a permanent professorship or habilitation.

A strong application will combine an ambitious but feasible independent research project with clear evidence of scientific excellence, an appropriate host and disciplinary connection at Konstanz, interdisciplinary potential, and a credible trajectory toward academic independence.

Candidates should begin contacting potential local hosts well before preparing the final application.

TITLE: When Unexpected Costs Hit: Your Financial Options Explained

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Unexpected expenses can disrupt even the most carefully planned budget. A vehicle may need repairs before the next workday, a laptop may fail during an important semester, or a medical bill may arrive without much warning. These situations rarely happen when money is readily available.

When unexpected costs arise, it is easy to focus on finding the quickest solution. Taking a little time to understand the available financial options, however, can make a meaningful difference. The best approach depends on the nature of the expense, the amount involved, and the resources already available. Understanding the available choices before making a financial decision can help reduce stress while limiting financial pressure in the months ahead.

Building a Clear Picture of the Expense

The first step is understanding exactly what the expense involves before deciding how to pay for it. Knowing whether the cost is urgent, essential, or flexible helps narrow the available financial options.

Some expenses require immediate attention because delaying them can create larger problems. Emergency medical treatment, essential vehicle repairs, or a broken heating system during winter are common examples. Waiting may increase both the inconvenience and the eventual cost.

Other expenses allow more flexibility. A home décor upgrade, elective purchase, or nonessential subscription may feel important in the moment, though postponing it often has little lasting impact. Recognizing that difference helps prevent unnecessary borrowing.

It also helps to estimate the full cost before making a decision. Looking beyond the initial invoice to include taxes, repair fees, or related expenses provides a clearer picture of how much financial assistance, if any, is actually needed.

Using Savings and Emergency Funds First

Savings are often the simplest financial resource to use when unexpected costs arise. If money has already been set aside for emergencies, using those funds may eliminate the need to borrow altogether.

Emergency savings exist because unexpected situations are part of life. Drawing from those funds for a necessary repair or medical expense allows the problem to be addressed without creating a repayment obligation that continues for months afterward.

Not every household has a fully funded emergency savings account, making it important to consider all available financial options. Even a modest savings balance, however, may reduce the amount that ultimately needs to be borrowed, making future repayment easier.

Using savings does not mean abandoning long-term financial goals. After the emergency has passed, gradually rebuilding an emergency fund can help prepare for future unexpected expenses without placing extra strain on the monthly budget.

Exploring Payment Plans and Financial Assistance

Borrowing is not always the first solution worth considering. Many organizations offer payment arrangements or financial assistance programs that allow essential expenses to be managed over time.

Medical providers frequently offer payment plans that divide larger bills into smaller monthly amounts. Colleges and universities may offer tuition payment plans, while utility companies sometimes provide hardship programs for customers facing temporary financial difficulties.

Students may also have access to emergency grants or institutional assistance, depending on their school. Asking about available resources before committing to a loan can sometimes uncover solutions that were not immediately obvious.

Exploring these alternatives may take a little extra time, though it can reduce the amount that needs to be financed. Even if they do not fully cover the expense, they may work alongside other financial options to make the situation easier to manage.

Personal Loans as a Financing Option

Personal loans can become a practical option when savings are limited and an essential expense cannot reasonably wait. Unlike revolving credit, they typically provide a fixed amount that is repaid through scheduled monthly installments.

This repayment structure allows borrowers to understand from the beginning how much they will owe each month and how long repayment is expected to continue. That predictability can make budgeting easier after the emergency has passed.

If borrowing becomes the most practical solution, it also helps to understand what to say when applying for a personal loan, since lenders may ask about the purpose of the funds during the application process. Being prepared to explain the need clearly and honestly can help the application process move more smoothly.

A personal loan should still fit comfortably within the household budget. Borrowing only what is necessary and reviewing the full loan agreement carefully helps ensure that today’s solution does not create unnecessary financial challenges later.

Comparing Your Financial Options Before Deciding

Choosing the right financial option means looking beyond immediate access to money. Comparing the long-term impact of each solution often leads to better financial decisions.

Before deciding, consider:

The urgency of the expense,

Available savings,

Monthly repayment obligations,

Total borrowing costs,

Payment flexibility,

The long-term effect on your budget.

No single solution works for every situation. Someone facing a short-term cash shortage may benefit from a payment plan, while another person dealing with an emergency repair may find that a personal loan better fits the circumstances.

Taking time to compare options does not necessarily delay solving the problem. Instead, it increases the likelihood of choosing a solution that addresses both the immediate expense and future financial stability.

Preparing for Future Financial Surprises

Unexpected expenses cannot always be prevented, though it is possible to become better prepared for them over time. Small financial habits often make the next emergency easier to manage. Building an emergency fund gradually is one example. Setting aside even modest amounts on a regular basis can reduce dependence on borrowing when future costs appear unexpectedly.

Reviewing household budgets periodically also creates opportunities to identify unnecessary spending and redirect those funds toward savings. Over time, those small adjustments can strengthen overall financial resilience. Planning ahead will not eliminate every financial surprise. It can, however, provide greater flexibility when unexpected costs arise and make future decisions feel less overwhelming.

Moving Forward After an Unexpected Expense

Unexpected costs are part of life, whether they involve education, transportation, health, or everyday living. Understanding the available financial options can make it easier to choose an approach that fits the situation.

Savings, payment arrangements, financial assistance programs, and personal loans each have situations where they may be appropriate. Looking at the full picture before making a decision often leads to better outcomes. A thoughtful financial decision is rarely about finding the fastest solution. It is about choosing the option that addresses today’s needs while supporting financial stability in the months that follow.
