TITLE: Verizon Small Business Digital Ready $10,000 National Grant 2026: Applications Open for U.S. Small Business Owners

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Small business owners across the United States and eligible U.S. territories can now apply for the Verizon Small Business Digital Ready $10,000 National Grant 2026, a major funding opportunity designed to help entrepreneurs strengthen, stabilize, and grow their businesses.

Through Verizon Small Business Digital Ready, Verizon is partnering with the Local Initiatives Support Corporation (LISC) to award $10,000 grants to selected small businesses throughout 2026. Unlike a traditional loan, the grant does not have to be repaid.

The 2026 funding model is particularly attractive because applicants do not have to repeatedly submit applications for every monthly funding round. An eligible entrepreneur can complete the required Digital Ready activities, unlock the grant application, apply once, and remain under consideration for subsequent selections during the year if they are not initially selected.

Verizon states that 10 small businesses will be selected each month from June through December 2026 to receive $10,000 grants. The initiative forms part of Verizon’s broader effort to equip small businesses with resources, education, expertise, and access to capital needed to compete in an increasingly digital economy.

About the Verizon Small Business Digital Ready Grant 2026

The Verizon Small Business Digital Ready $10,000 National Grant is a funding initiative offered through Verizon’s Small Business Digital Ready platform.

The Digital Ready initiative combines business education, events, expert resources, networking opportunities, and funding opportunities for entrepreneurs. Verizon reports that since 2021 it has awarded $15 million in grants to small businesses through its Digital Ready efforts, while more than 1,500 unique small businesses have received Digital Ready grants.

For 2026, Verizon and LISC have introduced a rolling application model intended to make applying simpler for small business owners.

Rather than having to prepare a separate grant application for multiple funding rounds, qualified entrepreneurs can submit one application and continue to be considered throughout the remaining 2026 selection periods.

How Much Funding Is Available?

Each selected business receives a $10,000 grant.

Verizon and LISC plan to select 10 small businesses per month between June and December 2026 under the national grant program.

Because this is grant funding rather than debt financing, recipients do not have to repay the $10,000 award.

However, recipients remain responsible for taxes associated with receiving or using the cash award. LISC states that a Form 1099 will be issued in connection with the grant.

Entrepreneurs should therefore treat the funding as taxable grant income where applicable and consult an appropriate tax professional regarding their individual circumstances.

Why Verizon Is Providing Small Business Grants

The Verizon Small Business Digital Ready Grant is part of a wider commitment by Verizon to support small businesses in adapting to the modern digital economy.

The initiative seeks to provide entrepreneurs not only with capital but also with knowledge and practical resources they can use to improve their businesses.

According to Verizon, the Digital Ready program contributes to the company’s goal of equipping one million small businesses with resources and tools to help them thrive in today’s economy.

The platform provides access to educational and entrepreneurial resources alongside potential grant funding, meaning applicants are required to participate in selected Digital Ready learning activities before they can unlock the grant application.

Key Benefits of the Verizon Small Business Digital Ready Grant

The 2026 opportunity provides several advantages to eligible entrepreneurs:

$10,000 in grant funding for selected businesses.

No repayment requirement, unlike a business loan.

One application for 2026, rather than applying separately each month.

Continued consideration in later monthly selections if an applicant is not selected initially.

Access to free Digital Ready courses and events before applying.

Educational resources relating to areas such as marketing, intellectual property, digital tools, business development, and entrepreneurship.

Funding administered independently by LISC, an established nonprofit organization with extensive experience supporting small businesses.

Applications available in English and Spanish.

A rolling selection structure extending through much of 2026.

Potential access to Verizon Small Business Digital Ready’s broader ecosystem of courses, events, advice, and entrepreneurial resources.

How to Qualify for the $10,000 Verizon Grant

Applying for the Verizon Small Business Digital Ready Grant involves more than simply submitting a funding form.

Applicants must first participate in the Small Business Digital Ready platform.

To become eligible to unlock the grant application, an entrepreneur must create or maintain a Verizon Small Business Digital Ready account and complete the required learning or event activities.

For the 2026 national grant, applicants must complete any combination of two qualifying courses or events on the Digital Ready platform.

Qualifying activities can include courses, virtual events, recorded virtual events, and eligible in-person events.

These activities must be completed between January 1, 2026 and December 7, 2026 to satisfy the grant-unlocking requirement.

For in-person events, only events identified as eligible on the Digital Ready In-Person Events page qualify. Attendees may also be required to scan an event QR code onsite so that their participation is properly recorded.

How to Apply for the Verizon Small Business Digital Ready Grant

The overall application process is designed to be relatively straightforward.

Entrepreneurs should first register for Verizon Small Business Digital Ready.

After creating an account, the business owner must complete any qualifying combination of two courses or events during 2026.

Once the required activities have been recorded, the grant application becomes available through the Funding section and grant details page.

The applicant can then submit the grant application.

After submission, no additional application is required for each monthly selection. The application remains eligible for future 2026 selections if the applicant is not chosen during the first review period in which the application is considered.

The official information indicates that an applicant may submit only one application for the 2026 national grant.

How Long Does the Application Take?

Verizon and LISC estimate that the grant application should take no more than approximately 30 minutes to complete.

Applicants are advised to use Google Chrome, allocate around 30 uninterrupted minutes, and carefully review all answers before submitting the application.

This last point is particularly important because LISC states that it cannot accept changes to an application after it has been submitted.

Entrepreneurs should therefore gather relevant business details in advance and proofread their applications carefully before final submission.

Only One Business Can Be Submitted

Business owners who own multiple companies cannot apply separately for every business.

The official eligibility rules state that owners of multiple businesses may apply for the grant on behalf of only one business.

Applicants should therefore select the business that best meets the eligibility requirements and for which the proposed use of grant funding can be clearly and credibly demonstrated.

What Happens After You Apply?

Grant applications are reviewed monthly.

For the 2026 program, reviews take place from June through December 2026.

Each month, Verizon and LISC intend to select 10 small businesses for grants.

An applicant who is not selected during one month’s review is not automatically rejected.

Instead, the application remains under consideration for subsequent 2026 grant selections.

This rolling structure gives applicants multiple potential opportunities for consideration without requiring them to repeatedly prepare and submit new applications.

How Are Grant Recipients Selected?

The grant selection process is administered by LISC and involves several stages.

The first stage includes an anonymous drawing designed to narrow the applicant pool and give eligible applicants an equal initial opportunity.

If necessary, an algorithm is subsequently used to help maintain a balanced representation of businesses across different industries and geographic areas, reducing the possibility that grants become excessively concentrated within one sector or location.

The program states that priority is given to businesses operating in under-resourced, low-to-moderate income communities, particularly businesses that may have difficulty obtaining flexible and affordable capital.

A subset of applications then undergoes a more detailed assessment.

Factors reviewed at that stage can include the accuracy of the application, potential community impact, and the proposed use of grant funding.

Selected businesses subsequently undergo verification to confirm that they are in appropriate financial and legal standing before an award is issued.

What Does It Mean to Become a Finalist?

Being identified as a finalist is an important step, but it does not automatically guarantee receipt of a $10,000 grant.

Finalists must successfully complete additional verification requirements before an award can be confirmed.

LISC may conduct a background search and request information necessary to verify the business and process grant payments.

Potential verification information may include the business owner’s date of birth, SSN, TIN or ITIN, EIN, W-9 information, and appropriate banking information for ACH payment.

The program specifically states that the verification process does not involve a credit check or credit-score pull.

LISC also states that it will not request copies of personal identity documents such as a driver’s license, passport, or green card as part of this verification process.

Applicants should nonetheless ensure they respond promptly to genuine finalist communications.

How Will Successful Applicants Be Contacted?

LISC primarily communicates with grant applicants by email.

Finalists may be notified within approximately six weeks following the end of each monthly selection period.

Applicants who are not selected in a particular month generally will not receive a rejection notice at that stage because their application continues to remain under consideration for future selections.

All applicants are expected to receive their final status by January 12, 2027.

Official grant-status communications are expected to come from an @lisc.org email address.

Applicants should therefore regularly monitor their inboxes and spam or junk folders after submitting their applications.

Important Requirement for Previous Applicants

Entrepreneurs who applied for a Digital Ready grant in a previous funding cycle should not assume that their older application automatically carries forward.

According to the 2026 program FAQ, anyone who applied for a Digital Ready grant before April 15, 2026 must submit a new application for the current $10,000 national grant.

For the current 2026 national grant process, applicants may submit only one application.

After the new application is submitted, it remains eligible for consideration for the rest of the applicable 2026 selection period.

Can Previous Verizon Grant Recipients Apply Again?

Previous Digital Ready grant recipients are not necessarily prohibited from submitting an application.

However, the official program states that priority is given to applicants who have not previously received a grant, and prior Digital Ready grant recipients are therefore less likely to receive a second award.

Former recipients should take this into account when evaluating their prospects.

Are Nonprofits Eligible?

No.

The national $10,000 grant is specifically intended for for-profit businesses.

Nonprofit organizations are not eligible under the stated eligibility requirements.

Applicants should ensure that their organization’s legal and business structure is consistent with the eligibility rules before completing the Digital Ready requirements.

Businesses Must Be Able to Complete Verification

Eligibility does not end when the online application is submitted.

Finalists must be able to provide appropriate financial and business verification documentation.

Examples specifically mentioned by the program include a W-9 and information necessary to receive funding through ACH.

Business owners who cannot adequately establish their business identity or provide the requested verification information could lose their finalist status.

Application Available in Spanish

The Verizon Small Business Digital Ready grant application is also available in Spanish.

Applicants who have unlocked the application can select the Spanish-language option.

For users browsing the Digital Ready platform in Spanish, the grant application is expected to default to Spanish.

This expands access for Spanish-speaking small business owners who may prefer completing the process in Spanish.

What Can Businesses Use the Grant For?

The official selection process reviews the proposed use of funds, meaning applicants should give careful consideration to how $10,000 would help their business.

The current public grant page does not provide a narrow, exhaustive list of permitted expenditures on the main funding page. Applicants should therefore avoid assuming that every possible business expenditure is automatically approved.

Instead, applicants should clearly explain how funding would create a credible business benefit and comply with the full program terms and conditions.

Potential needs should be described specifically and realistically rather than using vague statements such as simply saying that the money will be used for “business growth.”

A stronger application generally connects the requested funding to identifiable business needs, implementation plans, and expected outcomes.

Tips for Preparing a Strong Application

Because the program combines random selection with subsequent review and verification, no application strategy can guarantee an award.

Nevertheless, applicants should ensure that all submitted information is accurate, complete, internally consistent, and supported by business records.

When describing the proposed use of funds, business owners should clearly connect the $10,000 grant to their actual operations and explain how the investment could improve business sustainability, customer reach, productivity, employment, community impact, or growth.

Applicants should avoid overstating revenue, employment numbers, community outcomes, or other business information because finalists may be asked to verify important information before receiving the award.

Verizon Small Business Digital Ready Grant Deadline 2026

The current official page uses a rolling 2026 application structure rather than presenting one conventional application deadline for every applicant.

Applicants must complete the required combination of two qualifying Digital Ready courses or events between January 1, 2026 and December 7, 2026 to unlock the grant application.

The program states that applicants can submit the application during 2026 and remain eligible for available grant selections during the year. Grant applications are reviewed monthly from June through December 2026.

Therefore, prospective applicants should not wait until December. Completing the eligibility activities and applying earlier may allow the application to remain under consideration across more monthly selection periods.

All applicants are expected to receive their final decision no later than January 12, 2027.

Important Dates

The principal dates to remember are January 1 to December 7, 2026 for completing the required qualifying courses or events; June through December 2026 for monthly grant reviews and selections; and January 12, 2027 as the stated date by which all applicants should receive a final decision.

Why This Opportunity Matters for Small Businesses

Access to affordable capital remains one of the most difficult challenges facing small businesses, particularly those operating in communities that historically have had fewer conventional financing opportunities.

A $10,000 non-repayable grant can provide meaningful support to a small company without adding loan repayments or additional debt to its balance sheet.

The structure of Verizon Small Business Digital Ready also ensures that participants engage with educational resources before accessing the application.

This combination of entrepreneurship education and capital can be especially useful for small businesses that need both practical knowledge and financial resources to move to their next stage of development.

Conclusion

The Verizon Small Business Digital Ready $10,000 National Grant 2026 represents a significant opportunity for eligible for-profit small business owners based in the United States, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Through its partnership with LISC, Verizon will select businesses for $10,000 non-repayable grants throughout 2026, with 10 businesses expected to be selected each month from June through December.

The application process is comparatively accessible: business owners must register for Small Business Digital Ready, complete two qualifying courses or events, unlock the grant application, and submit one application for the 2026 funding cycle.

Because unsuccessful applicants can remain eligible for later monthly selections, applying earlier rather than waiting until the end of the eligibility period may maximize the number of selection rounds in which an application can potentially be considered.

Eligible entrepreneurs should begin by registering for Verizon Small Business Digital Ready, completing the required activities, and preparing accurate business information before submitting their grant application.

TITLE: Lisbon AI Safety Hub Foundations of AI Safety Fellowship 2026: 8-Week In-Person Programme in Portugal for Students and Working Professionals.

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Lisbon AI Safety Hub (LAISH) is inviting students and working professionals to apply for its Foundations of AI Safety Fellowship, an eight-week programme designed to introduce participants to the rapidly developing field of artificial intelligence safety and help them identify meaningful ways to contribute to the safe development and governance of advanced AI.

Based in Lisbon, Portugal, the Lisbon AI Safety Hub is building a community that brings together researchers, academics, policymakers and ambitious individuals who want to contribute to the development of safe and responsibly governed artificial intelligence.

The fellowship provides an opportunity for participants who may not have a technical background in artificial intelligence to understand the opportunities and risks associated with increasingly capable AI systems. Through the programme, participants will explore AI safety, understand major risks associated with advanced AI, examine governance approaches and consider practical career and professional pathways through which they can contribute to the field.

Applications for the current fellowship cohort opened on August 1, with applications closing on September 30. The cohort is scheduled to begin on October 6.

About the Lisbon AI Safety Hub

The Lisbon AI Safety Hub is a community-focused organisation working to help Portugal play a meaningful role in the development of advanced artificial intelligence and the emerging global AI safety field.

The organisation brings together people from different professional and academic backgrounds, including:

Researchers

Academics

Policymakers

Students

Technology professionals

Individuals interested in AI safety and governance

People looking for ways to contribute to the responsible development of advanced AI

LAISH takes a broad view of AI safety. Rather than treating the subject purely as a technical computer science problem, the organisation describes AI safety as a sociotechnical problem, meaning that technical research, governance, institutions, policy and human decision-making all have important roles to play.

Its goal is to help develop a community capable of contributing to safer AI development in Portugal and beyond.

What Is AI Safety?

Artificial intelligence systems are becoming increasingly capable and are being integrated into more areas of society, business, research and government.

As AI capabilities increase, an important question arises: how can humans ensure that increasingly powerful AI systems remain aligned with human intentions, values and interests?

AI safety broadly concerns the research, policies, institutions and practices needed to reduce the risks associated with advanced artificial intelligence.

The Lisbon AI Safety Hub highlights three major areas of AI safety:

1. AI Alignment

AI alignment focuses on ensuring that advanced AI systems pursue objectives that reflect what humans actually intend.

A system may technically follow an instruction while still producing an outcome that humans did not want. Alignment research therefore examines how AI systems can better understand and follow human goals and intentions as their capabilities become more powerful.

The fellowship introduces participants to the importance of alignment and the challenges involved in ensuring that increasingly capable systems remain under meaningful human direction.

2. AI Interpretability

Interpretability focuses on understanding what is happening inside AI systems.

Modern neural networks can be extremely complex, making it difficult for humans to understand precisely how they arrive at particular decisions or outputs.

Interpretability research seeks to make these systems more understandable so researchers can potentially:

Identify what AI systems have learned

Understand how systems represent information

Detect potential problems

Predict certain types of failure

Audit AI behaviour

Intervene before problems become more serious

Understanding how AI systems work internally is therefore an important part of developing safer and more reliable systems.

3. AI Governance

AI governance concerns the rules, policies, institutions and international arrangements that influence how powerful AI systems are developed and deployed.

Governance questions include:

Who should be allowed to develop frontier AI?

What safeguards should developers follow?

What limits should apply to advanced AI systems?

How should governments regulate powerful AI technologies?

Who should be held accountable when AI systems cause harm?

How can countries cooperate on AI safety?

What institutions are needed to manage increasingly capable AI?

The governance side of AI safety provides opportunities for people with backgrounds in areas such as public policy, law, international relations, economics, governance, communications and social sciences.

About the Foundations of AI Safety Fellowship

The Foundations of AI Safety Fellowship is a non-technical programme designed to give participants an introduction to AI risks and practical ways they can contribute to efforts to make advanced AI safer.

Importantly, participants do not need prior technical knowledge to apply.

The programme is structured to help participants progress from understanding the fundamental AI safety problem to considering how they personally might contribute.

The fellowship covers four main areas.

1. Why AI Safety Matters

Participants begin by developing an understanding of advanced artificial intelligence and why AI safety has become an increasingly important area of work.

This includes exploring:

The development of increasingly capable AI systems

The potential benefits of advanced AI

Potential risks associated with advanced AI

Why AI safety is becoming increasingly important

Why maintaining meaningful human control over powerful AI systems matters

The aim is to provide participants with a foundation for understanding why AI safety is considered an important emerging field.

2. Understanding the Risks

The fellowship then examines the different ways advanced artificial intelligence could affect individuals, institutions and society.

Participants explore major categories of AI risk and learn how people working in the field think about and evaluate those risks.

This part of the fellowship can help participants develop a more structured understanding of questions surrounding:

AI reliability

AI alignment

AI system behaviour

Societal impacts

Risks associated with increasingly capable systems

Potential failure modes

The challenges of managing advanced AI

Rather than requiring participants to already be experts, the programme provides an introductory pathway into these discussions.

3. Governance and Action

Another major component of the fellowship focuses on governance.

Participants examine how policy, institutions and international coordination can contribute to safer AI development.

This is particularly relevant for individuals interested in careers involving:

Public policy

Technology policy

Government

International affairs

Regulation

Research

Governance

Responsible technology

AI policy

Institutional decision-making

The governance component demonstrates that contributing to AI safety does not necessarily require becoming an AI engineer or machine-learning researcher.

4. Identifying Your Next Step

The final component focuses on helping participants identify practical ways to contribute to AI safety.

Participants are encouraged to consider how their existing skills, education, professional experience and interests could connect with opportunities in the field.

Possible pathways may include:

Career development

Academic research

Policy work

Governance

Technical research

Community building

Communications

Advocacy

Further study

Work related to responsible AI

This makes the fellowship relevant not only to people who are already working in artificial intelligence, but also to people considering a transition into the field.

Fellowship Duration, Location and Important Dates

The Foundations of AI Safety Fellowship has the following programme details:

Programme: Foundations of AI Safety Fellowship

Duration: 8 weeks

Location: Lisbon, Portugal

Format: In person

Applications opened: August 1

Application deadline: September 30

Cohort starts: October 6

Target participants: Students and working professionals

Technical prerequisites: No technical knowledge required

Applicants should take note of the September 30 application deadline and submit their applications before the closing date.

Who Should Apply?

The fellowship is particularly relevant to students and working professionals who want to learn more about artificial intelligence safety and explore ways to contribute to the field.

You may be a suitable candidate if you are:

A student interested in AI

Students who are curious about artificial intelligence, technology, research, policy or the societal effects of AI can use the fellowship to develop a foundational understanding of AI safety.

The programme may also help students identify potential areas for further study or career development.

A working professional considering a career transition

Professionals from fields outside traditional artificial intelligence can explore how their existing skills could be applied to AI safety.

For example, people with experience in policy, communications, research, governance, law, management, technology or other professional areas may find the programme useful.

Someone interested in AI governance

People interested in the rules and institutions surrounding artificial intelligence may particularly benefit from the governance component of the programme.

This can be relevant to individuals interested in government, public policy, regulation, international cooperation and technology governance.

Someone without a technical AI background

One of the important features of the programme is that no technical knowledge is required.

This means that applicants should not assume they need to be programmers, machine-learning engineers or AI researchers before they can participate.

The fellowship is designed to provide an introduction to the field and help participants understand where their own skills and interests could fit.

Why the Fellowship Is Important

Artificial intelligence is developing rapidly, and increasingly capable systems are expected to influence many areas of society.

This creates a growing need for people who can think about AI not only from a technical perspective but also from the perspectives of governance, policy, institutions and society.

A field such as AI safety therefore requires people with different backgrounds and skill sets.

The Lisbon AI Safety Hub’s approach recognises this by supporting both technical and governance-oriented work.

This broad perspective means that someone does not necessarily have to become a machine-learning researcher to contribute to AI safety.

Instead, individuals may contribute through:

Technical research

Policy development

Governance

Regulation

Academic research

Institutional design

Communications

Community building

International coordination

Other professional areas connected to responsible AI development

Other Ways to Get Involved With the Lisbon AI Safety Hub

The fellowship is only one of several ways to engage with the Lisbon AI Safety Hub.

Events and Lectures

LAISH organises events designed to help grow the AI safety community.

These include:

Film screenings

Directed discussion groups

Community meetings

Lectures from industry experts

Research discussions

Social events

The organisation states that events are primarily held in English, although Portuguese speakers are expected to be present.

Career Guidance

LAISH also offers career guidance for individuals interested in working in AI safety.

Participants can seek tailored advice about opportunities in the field and ways to develop a career that enables them to contribute to AI safety.

This can be useful for people who understand that they are interested in the field but are unsure which professional or academic direction to take.

Newsletter

The organisation publishes a newsletter covering topics such as:

Frontier AI news

Jobs

Fellowships

Opportunities within the AI safety field

The newsletter is available in English and Portuguese.

Community Discord

LAISH also maintains a Discord community where people can connect with other members, exchange resources and receive information about events and community activities.

This provides an additional way for people to remain connected to the AI safety community beyond individual programmes.

What Makes This Fellowship Different?

One of the strongest features of the Foundations of AI Safety Fellowship is its accessibility to people without technical AI expertise.

Many emerging technology programmes focus heavily on programming, mathematics, machine learning or computer science.

The Foundations of AI Safety Fellowship instead provides an introductory pathway that allows participants to understand the broader AI safety landscape before deciding how they might contribute.

The programme combines:

Understanding advanced AI

Exploring AI risks

Learning about AI governance

Considering practical career pathways

This makes it potentially valuable for people coming from different educational and professional backgrounds.

Potential Career Directions After Learning About AI Safety

Although participation in the fellowship does not automatically qualify someone for a particular job, developing knowledge of AI safety can help participants explore several career directions.

Depending on their existing background and future training, participants may consider areas such as:

AI policy

Technology governance

AI safety research

AI governance research

Public policy

Responsible AI

AI regulation

Academic research

Technology communications

AI-related programme management

International AI policy

Community development

Participants can also use the fellowship to determine whether they want to pursue more specialised technical or governance training.

APPLY HERE.

How to Apply

Interested applicants should apply through the Lisbon AI Safety Hub’s official fellowship application process.

Applications for the current cohort opened on August 1 and close on September 30.

The programme begins on October 6 and lasts for eight weeks.

Because the fellowship is listed as an in-person programme in Lisbon, applicants should carefully consider their ability to participate in the programme at the stated location.

Applicants who have questions can contact the Lisbon AI Safety Hub at:

contact@lisbonaisafetyhub.org

Important Details at a Glance

Opportunity: Foundations of AI Safety Fellowship

Organisation: Lisbon AI Safety Hub (LAISH)

Location: Lisbon, Portugal

Programme format: In person

Duration: 8 weeks

Application opening date: August 1

Application deadline: September 30

Cohort start date: October 6

Who can apply: Students and working professionals

Technical knowledge required: No

Main areas: AI safety, AI risks, alignment, interpretability and governance

Career focus: Identifying practical ways to contribute to AI safety

Contact: contact@lisbonaisafetyhub.org

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Foundations of AI Safety Fellowship a scholarship?

No. Based on the information provided, this is a fellowship programme, not a scholarship.

The provided information does not state that participants receive tuition funding, a stipend, travel support or other financial benefits. Applicants should therefore avoid assuming that the programme is fully funded unless LAISH confirms otherwise.

Do I need to know programming to apply?

No.

The fellowship specifically states that no technical knowledge is required, making it accessible to people who do not have a technical AI or programming background.

Who is the fellowship for?

The programme is intended for students and working professionals who want to learn about AI safety and explore ways of contributing to the field.

Do I need an AI degree?

No specific AI degree is listed as a prerequisite.

The programme is designed as an introduction to AI safety and does not require technical knowledge.

Is the fellowship online?

The fellowship is listed as in person in Lisbon, Portugal.

Therefore, applicants should be prepared to participate physically in Lisbon.

When does the application close?

The application deadline is September 30.

When does the cohort begin?

The cohort is scheduled to begin on October 6.

How long does the fellowship last?

The programme lasts eight weeks.

Can people from outside Portugal apply?

The information provided does not specify a nationality or citizenship restriction.

However, because the fellowship is listed as an in-person programme in Lisbon, international applicants should consider the practical requirements associated with participating in Portugal.

Is technical AI knowledge required?

No. The fellowship explicitly states that no technical knowledge is required.

What areas of AI safety are covered?

The programme introduces participants to why AI safety matters, the risks associated with advanced AI, governance and practical ways to contribute.

The wider LAISH approach also highlights areas including alignment, interpretability and governance.

Conclusion

The Lisbon AI Safety Hub Foundations of AI Safety Fellowship provides an accessible entry point into one of the world’s emerging technology fields.

As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly capable, questions about how these systems can remain safe, reliable and subject to meaningful human direction are becoming increasingly important. Addressing these questions requires more than technical expertise alone. It also requires people who understand policy, governance, institutions, research, communication and the broader societal implications of AI.

With its eight-week, in-person programme in Lisbon, the fellowship offers students and working professionals an opportunity to develop foundational knowledge of AI safety, explore the risks associated with advanced AI, understand governance approaches and consider practical ways to contribute to the field.

The fact that no technical knowledge is required makes the programme particularly accessible to people who are interested in AI safety but do not come from a computer science or engineering background.

For individuals interested in the future of artificial intelligence and the challenge of ensuring that increasingly powerful AI remains beneficial and responsibly governed, the programme could provide an important starting point.

TITLE: Leon Levy Scholarships in Neuroscience 2027

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 16, 2026

Applications are open for the Leon Levy Scholarships in Neuroscience 2027. The Leon Levy Scholarships in Neuroscience (LLSN) program aims to promote groundbreaking neuroscience research in the five boroughs of New York City. The Scholarships support the most innovative young researchers at a critical stage of their careers—their postdoctoral research—as they develop the new ideas and directions that will help establish them as independent neuroscientists.

The Scholarships seek to support exceptional young researchers as they pursue innovative investigations in neuroscience and advance their careers toward independent research by:

Cultivating excellence and innovation in a diverse neuroscience workforce and supporting postdoctoral Scholars, from all backgrounds, in preparing for a scientific career in the face of increasing competition.

Providing enhanced research autonomy to promote impactful scientific research.

Helping Scholars to develop wider professional skills such as writing grants and papers, project and budget management, promoting neuroethics, and enhanced community engagement.

Building and maintaining an engaged Leon Levy Scholar Alumni community to enhance collaboration and partnerships, encourage mentorship and networking, foster data sharing, and advance team science.

Benefits

The Leon Levy Scholarship is a three (3)-year award. Scholars will receive:

Annual stipend equals 125% of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) postdoctoral rate, according to the postdoctoral year

Fringe benefits at the host institution’s rate for postdoctoral Scholars

US$2,000 flexible technology and travel allowance as a one-time award

Annual supplement of up to US$10,000 to support care costs (e.g. dependent care)

Indirect support to the host institution will be allowed at the standard published rate if less than 20% and capped at 20%.

3-year Membership to The New York Academy of Sciences

Participation in a structured Mentorship Program for Leon Levy Scholars

Access to leadership and skills-building workshops through The New York Academy of Sciences

Access to the community of past and present Leon Levy Scholars and Fellows

Grant writing support

Eligibility

Applicant’s Eligibility

By the time of appointment on September 1, 2027, the applicant must:

Hold a doctoral degree (PhD, DPhil, MD, DDS, DVM, etc.)

Hold a full-time postdoctoral position at an eligible institution, or an institution that has obtained eligibility prior to the closing of the application period, in one of New York City’s five boroughs. Applicants must be employed by an eligible institution at the time the Scholarship begins, and should have the support of their proposed Research Advisor at the time of application.

Possess no more than three (3) years of cumulative postdoctoral experience. In other words, applicants’ doctoral degrees cannot be dated before September 1, 2024.

Conduct research in Neuroscience or one of its sub-disciplines while they hold the Leon Levy Scholarships

Be able to meet at least one of the following designated criteria at the time of appointment: be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, or U.S. permanent resident (holder of a Permanent Resident Card); holder of J-1 Research Scholar status or an H-1B Temporary Employee Status visa valid for the full tenure of the Scholarship; an individual granted deferred action status under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals Program; Indigenous individual exercising rights associated with the Jay Treaty of 1794; Individual granted Temporary Protected Status; Asylee; or Refugee. Conditional Visas will be considered.

There is no upper limit on the number of applicants per institution or per laboratory. Previous recipients of a Leon Levy Fellowship are not eligible to apply.

Institution Eligibility

Any accredited non-profit academic institution that is located within the five boroughs of New York City and conducts original neuroscience research is considered eligible.

Application

All materials must be submitted by October 16, 2026. Scholarships for the 2027 cohort of Scholars will run from September 1, 2027 to August 31, 2030.

TITLE: Adaptation Fund Climate Innovation Accelerator 2026: WFP Climate Innovation Opportunity for Scalable Solutions in Latin America and the Caribbean

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Adaptation Fund Climate Innovation Accelerator (AFCIA) 2026, implemented by the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) Innovation Accelerator in partnership with the Adaptation Fund, is inviting organizations with innovative climate adaptation solutions to apply for support to strengthen resilience, improve food security and help vulnerable communities respond to climate change.

The opportunity is particularly focused on Latin America and the Caribbean, with this edition seeking solutions that can be implemented in or have strong potential for implementation in the Dominican Republic, El Salvador and Peru.

Applications are open to established organizations developing solutions that address pressing climate adaptation challenges, including climate-smart agriculture, early warning systems, climate information, disaster risk management, water management, climate-risk financing and post-harvest losses.

Application deadline: 6 September 2026 at 11:59 p.m. UTC.

What Is the Main Goal of the Programme?

The AFCIA programme aims to support innovations that can contribute to a more resilient and sustainable future for communities facing climate-related challenges.

The programme seeks to:

Strengthen climate adaptation and resilience.

Improve food security.

Support vulnerable and climate-affected communities.

Promote gender equity and inclusion.

Create inclusive economic opportunities.

Engage young people in climate adaptation.

Encourage collaboration between innovators and humanitarian organizations.

Expand knowledge and learning around climate adaptation.

Support solutions with potential for large-scale implementation.

Promote sustainable and locally relevant approaches to climate resilience.

Rather than focusing only on ideas at an early conceptual stage, the programme is seeking innovations that have already progressed beyond the idea or early pre-seed phase and have a credible pathway toward implementation and scale.

What Types of Innovations Is WFP Looking For?

The programme is open to both low-tech and high-tech solutions.

This means applicants do not necessarily need to have developed sophisticated or highly technical technologies. What matters is whether the innovation provides a meaningful, scalable and sustainable response to a clearly identified climate adaptation challenge.

Potential solutions may involve:

Digital technologies

Climate information systems

Agricultural technologies

Early-warning systems

Financing mechanisms

Water-management approaches

Climate-smart agriculture

Disaster-risk management

Food-system innovations

Market intelligence

Communication technologies

Community-based approaches

Humanitarian innovations

Environmental solutions

Business-model innovations

The most important consideration is whether the proposed solution addresses a relevant climate adaptation problem and has credible potential for impact and scale.

Who Can Apply?

The opportunity is designed for established legal entities, rather than individual applicants.

Eligible organizations may include:

For-profit companies

Non-profit organizations

Social businesses

NGOs

International NGOs

Other established legal entities

An organization must also have a presence in at least one of the three countries of implementation: Dominican Republic, El Salvador or Peru.

This presence could include:

A country office

A permanent operational presence

A subsidiary

Long-term operations

An established partnership in the country

Organizations from outside the three countries may therefore be relevant if they have an appropriate and established presence or partnership structure in one of the target countries.

Key Eligibility Requirements

Applicants should carefully review the eligibility requirements before applying.

The innovation must:

1. Be submitted by an established legal entity

The applicant must be an established organization such as a company, NGO, social business or other legally recognized entity.

2. Have a presence in a target country

The organization should have an established presence in:

Dominican Republic

El Salvador

Peru

3. Address a relevant climate adaptation challenge

The innovation must respond to at least one of the priority areas identified for the country where it will be implemented.

4. Be beyond the idea stage

The innovation must be at least at the seed stage.

Solutions that are still only ideas, research concepts or at the early pre-seed stage are not eligible.

5. Have potential for scale

Applicants should demonstrate a clear pathway for expanding their solution beyond a small pilot.

6. Have adequate resources

The organization must have sufficient resources and capabilities to implement the proposed activities during the nine-month Sprint programme using the available funding.

7. Demonstrate willingness to collaborate

Applicants are expected to have strong intentions to:

Collaborate with relevant humanitarian stakeholders

Develop relationships with WFP country offices

Engage with local innovation ecosystems

Work with relevant partners

How Will Innovations Be Evaluated?

Eligible applications will be assessed against several important criteria.

1. Level of Innovation

The proposed solution should demonstrate genuine innovation and respond effectively to climate adaptation challenges within the identified thematic areas.

WFP will consider how novel and innovative the solution is and whether it offers a meaningful improvement over existing approaches.

2. Relevance to the Local Context

The solution must be relevant to at least one of the target countries and its identified climate adaptation priorities.

Applicants should demonstrate:

A clear understanding of the problem

The relevance of the solution

The needs of intended users

How the innovation fits the local ecosystem

The practical value of the solution

3. Financial Sustainability and Scalability

A strong application should demonstrate that the innovation can become financially sustainable.

Applicants should be able to explain:

How the solution generates or can generate sustainable revenue

How it can continue beyond programme support

What its business model looks like

How the solution can grow

What resources will be required for expansion

Scalability is an important part of the opportunity because the programme is looking for innovations capable of generating meaningful impact beyond a limited pilot.

4. Team Expertise and Capabilities

The strength of the team will also be considered.

Applicants should demonstrate:

Relevant technical expertise

Entrepreneurial capabilities

Commitment

Motivation

Ability to implement the proposed solution

Technical coherence

Appropriate leadership

Diverse and inclusive team composition

A strong solution must be supported by a team capable of turning the proposed innovation into measurable results.

5. Climate Adaptation

The innovation should make a meaningful contribution to climate adaptation.

This could involve:

Increasing resilience to climate impacts

Improving resource efficiency

Promoting sustainable practices

Helping communities prepare for climate-related shocks

Supporting adaptive decision-making

Reducing vulnerability to climate risks

6. Level of Impact

Applicants should provide evidence of the solution’s actual or potential impact.

WFP will consider whether the innovation can produce:

Tangible results

Sustainable improvements

Long-term benefits

Meaningful climate adaptation outcomes

Improvements that can extend beyond the grant or programme period

Historical evidence of impact can strengthen an application, particularly where the innovation has already been tested.

7. Environmental and Social Sustainability

Solutions must align with the environmental and social principles of the Adaptation Fund.

Applicants should therefore consider the broader environmental and social implications of their proposed innovation.

8. Gender and Inclusion

Gender equality and inclusion are important components of the programme.

Applicants should demonstrate how their solution:

Addresses diverse user needs

Promotes inclusive participation

Supports inclusive decision-making

Uses disaggregated data where appropriate

Incorporates feedback from different user groups

Considers the needs of populations that may be disproportionately affected by climate change

Application Process

Interested organizations should first carefully review the official call for applications and eligibility requirements.

The application process involves completing the online application form and providing information about the organization, the innovation, the problem being addressed, the target market or users, the solution’s impact and its potential for scale.

Official WFP AFCIA Call for Applications – English

Applications must be submitted through the official application platform.

AFCIA 2026 Application Form

The source information states that only English-language submissions will be accepted.

Important Application Deadline

SecUring sPORTs Education thRough innovative and inclusive Gender Equality Plans

SUPPORTER aims to support eight sports institutions of Central Eastern Europe in developing intersectional, innovative, inclusive and impactful Gender Equality Plans (GEPs) tailored to sports higher education institutions, and explicitly addressing gender-based violence.

The eight sports institutions will receive systematic support and mentoring towards the development of these GEPs from the core team partners (ESF, SEERC, UGOT). The multiplier effect of SUPPORTER -starting from the 8 partner institutions and gradually reaching the sports ecosystem and its various organisations in Eastern Europe and beyond – also has the potential to trigger institutional change from a gender perspective in a variety of further institutions, primarily in the (local) ecosystem of the partner institutions (e.g.: beyond RPOs), the overall sports ecosystem, and therefore, in the long-term go beyond institutional change, reach society more broadly and contribute to wide-range systemic societal changes.

ESF’s expertise

Project management and coordination

ESF, in its role as project coordinator, ensures the successful delivery of the project through adequate management and quality control mechanisms, and an efficient and proactive relation with the European Commission. ESF activities focus on ensuring:

Sound overall project administration (finance management, periodic reporting, etc.);

Smooth partner liaison and coordination;

Creation and maintenance of a secure and user-friendly environment for co-working, communicating, storing information, data and planning;

Highest quality of results through quality assurance, validation, and risk management;

Assure the adherence to highest methodological, ethical, gender equality and data management standards throughout the project;

Establishment of synergies with other projects, initiatives, communities of practice.

Mapping the organisational environment of the implementing organisations

ESF leads the task of mapping the state-of-the-art of each of the eight participating sport institutions at the start of the project, to define a baseline for the co-creation of the institutional roadmaps to inclusive gender equality. This initial reflexive activity focuses on mapping institutional arrangements, existing action plans in view of the ultimate objective of the project; and evaluate institutional framework conditions to be taken into consideration for the formulation of the institutional roadmaps to gender+ equality.

Implementing the training programme

ESF leads the implementation of the project’s training programme shape-cut for the eight sport institutional needs, designing and facilitating knowledge-transfer activities that serve as baseline for institutional capacity building for the efficient formulation and implementation of the institutional roadmaps towards gender equality, putting the already existing institutional GEPs into a practice and updating them to focus on shaping the GEPS to the needs of the faculties of sport, including GBV.

ESF leads the drafting of two policy briefs primarily addressed to policymakers. The policy briefs include the state-of-the-art description and recommendations related to the implementation of GEPs in sports institutions in the European Research Area, based on the observations made throughout the project.

ESF develops and implements the general communication and dissemination strategy of the project. In addition to this, ESF leads the initiative to create of a network of sports organisations implementing 4I-GEPs to ensure stakeholders’ awareness and further uptake after the project lifetime. Provides suitable communication tools;

Ensures awareness of the project and of the need to address gender+ equality and GBV in the sports ecosystem with well-planned, concrete actions, engaging stakeholders’ participation;

Empowers sports institutions and organisations to successfully implement inclusive gender+ equality plans;

Stimulates the different stakeholders and policy-makers to embrace the SUPPORTER learnings and ultimately advocate operational implementation and the use of the 4I-GEPS, trainings and guidelines developed through the project

Shares the new knowledge acquired with researchers.

TITLE: Re-Register – AAU-British Academy Writing Workshop for Sub-Saharan Africa (Early Career Researchers)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Important Notice: We respectfully request all stakeholders who registered to participate in this workshop to kindly re-register using this link: https://www.research.net/r/AAU-UoNRegis23 . Regrettably, we encountered technical challenges with the earlier registrations. New registrations are welcome.

Writing for Sustainable Development: Developing, mentoring and strengthening African grant and research writing for publication

The University of Nottingham, UK in partnership with the Association of African Universities (AAU), with funding support from the British Academy (BA) is inviting stakeholders to a writing workshop holding in Accra, Ghana on March 12–14, 2024.

Preamble

Higher education research acknowledges the underrepresentation of Africa in scholarly conversations and outputs with limited showing of works in reputable publication outlets (Thondhlana and Garwe, 2021; Puplampu, 2015; Mamdani, 2011). While research output in Africa is growing it continues to represent only about 2 percent of global knowledge production (Nkomo, 2015; Schemm, 2013). Further, the continent is argued to be lacking in home-grown theories and conceptual prescriptions and suffers from having its students and researchers constantly resorting to mostly western-originated books and other scholarly resources.

Literature reveals the barriers to scholarly productivity as including: resource constraints under which many universities in Africa operate; the nature and state of research infrastructures; attitudes, values and behaviours which act as barriers to scholarly outputs; leadership, political and organisational research culture as well as; the rapid changes and pressures under which universities currently operate (Puplampu et al., 2021; Mamdani, 2011; Ngobeni, 2010). Scholars also point to the continuing difficulty of many universities to overcome the lingering effects of colonial practices on the structure of higher education and the lack of research that centres on African problems and challenges. (Thondhlana and Garwe, 2021; Mamdani, 2011; Ngobeni, 2010). Consequently, many early career researchers within the region find it difficult to access and navigate opportunities for international publishing and for increasing the local, national and global impact of their work. Efforts towards repositioning Africa’s knowledge production in line with Africa Union’s Agenda 2063 and the UNESCO SDGs are underway. These series of writing workshops are aimed at addressing the gaps noted above as well as by the UNESCO’s Operational Strategy for Priority Africa.

Background

The current workshop builds on the BA writing workshop held in September 2019 whose objective was to support African early career researchers (ECRs) to increase their confidence and enhance the success rate of articles submitted to high quality publication platforms. This was inspired by the need to create more impact across the alumni through networking, harnessing, and sharing the good practices by those who have done well and strengthening the capacities of those facing challenges. Running additional workshops will also provide an opportunity to increase impact by taking on board new ECRs who will be mentored by alumni (whom they can easily identify with and get inspiration from) with the support of experts and Journal Editors. The need to train more ECRs was highlighted during the 2019 workshop as follows: “I really wish that another similar workshop could be organised for other groups’, said some workshop participants.

The focus of the 2019 workshop was on training the trainer so as to create impact through ripple effects. The emphasis of this round of workshops is on co-planning, peer learning, mentoring, networking and thereby creating an ‘intellectual community of practice’ able to document research into articles publishable in reputable outlets both in Sub-Saharan Africa and beyond. The current approach featuring joint publications creates a supportive environment for ECRs, Alumni and experts to improve their writing capacities.

The planned workshop will facilitate and strengthen mutual learning and sustainable partnerships among alumni, new ECRs, senior researchers and editors of international journals in the Global South and Global North. Such interaction is intended to strengthen the likelihood of knowledge and work generated by researchers from Sub-Saharan Africa to be recognised, funded, published more widely and cited in international journals where their knowledge and work can contribute to academic debates that shape sustainable futures of development in Africa and globally.

In preparation for this workshop, alumni and experts held a 2-day virtual workshop in August 2023. All the 12 alumni (two each from six Sub-Saharan African countries namely South Africa, Ghana, Nigeria, Kenya, Uganda and Zimbabwe) were given the opportunity to share their post-2019 workshop activities and achievements (number of articles published in high impact journals; mentorship of other ECRs; sustainable collaborations with peers and British institutions) and areas needing further capacity strengthening. This information informed the training needs and programme for the current workshop. In addition, Alumni undertook further training (by experts and peers) to strengthen their capacities to mentor and train new ECRs.

Under the auspices of the Association of African Universities (AAU) and the Women in Higher Education Network (WoHEN), we extend this workshop invitation to a broader spectrum of researchers within the African higher education sector. This is to promote the cultivation of a substantial cohort of researchers equipped with advanced writing skills, to facilitate impactful publications in high-impact journals. This concerted effort aims to reshape existing narratives and elevate Africa’s current research output and contribute significantly to the global pool of knowledge generation. We extend a special invitation to Women Early Career Researchers (ECRs) to actively engage in this transformative writing workshop.

Objectives of the March 2024 ECR writing workshop

The objectives of the workshop are to:

strengthen the capacity and develop a new cohort of ECRs with skills for quality research writing for publication; the democratisation/decolonisation of knowledge about the dynamics of international publication;

develop ECRs in Sub-Saharan Africa and alumni with skills for grant writing;

establish sustainable collaborations amongst new ECRs, alumni, African and British institutions;

increase understanding of both Global South and Global North editors of how best to support and enhance the visibility of African scholarship.

allocate alumni, ECRs and experts writing responsibilities for a special issue of the British Academy Journal and a peer reviewed edited book.

Target Attendees

The workshop targets the following:

the existing alumni group;

new ECRs researching on comparative education and management;

self-funding ECRs (from various universities and institutions)

senior academic mentors and facilitators; and

journal editors

Registration Link: https://www.research.net/r/AAU-UoNRegis23

Venue: Association of African Universities, Secretariat, Accra, Ghana

Date: 12–14 March 2024

Facilitators

The workshop will draw on the expertise of the following editors, senior scholars and facilitators:

Dr Yuwei Xu, University of Nottingham, Nottingham Children & Society; Pedagogy, Culture and Society; Teachers and Teaching: Theory and Practice

Professor Tony Bush, University of Nottingham, Nottingham – Educational Management, Administration and Leadership (UK journal)

Professor Juliet Thondhlana, University of Nottingham, Teachers and Teaching: Theory and Practice

Felicia Nkrumah-Kuagbedzi, Senior Communications and Publications Officer, Association of African Universities

The mix of North and South journal Editors, senior academics and experts will allow for continued dialogue on experiences of writing, publishing and grant capture regionally and internationally. Collectively, we are committed to continuously support sustainable research and create impact in Africa. Journal editors, senior academics and facilitators will play a variety of roles in the workshop inclusive of: evaluating skills, organising, mentoring, facilitating and acting as international interlocutors and consultants.

TITLE: Penn State HDFS PhD Graduate Program 2027 | Application Open for Graduate Study

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Department of Human Development and Family Studies (HDFS) at Pennsylvania State University has opened applications for its Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.) graduate programme. The programme provides an opportunity for students interested in advanced graduate study in the behavioral sciences, human development and family studies.

Applicants interested in joining the programme must apply through the Penn State Graduate School admissions portal and select the Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.) degree.

The application deadline is December 1.

Prospective applicants are encouraged to carefully review the programme requirements and prepare all required documents before submitting their applications. Applicants outside the United States should also take the application deadline and Penn State’s Eastern Standard Time zone into account when submitting their applications.

About the Penn State HDFS Graduate Programme

The Human Development and Family Studies graduate programme is designed for students pursuing advanced academic and research training in areas related to human development, family studies and the behavioral sciences.

The programme follows a doctoral pathway. HDFS does not offer a terminal master’s programme.

Students who enter the programme with a bachelor’s degree are required to complete a master’s degree en route to the doctoral degree.

Applicants should therefore select the Ph.D. degree when completing the graduate application rather than applying for a standalone master’s programme.

Application Deadline

The application deadline for the Penn State HDFS graduate programme is:

December 1

Applicants are responsible for ensuring that their applications are submitted by the deadline.

Penn State is located in the Eastern Standard Time zone. Applicants submitting their applications from outside the United States should account for the time difference when determining when to submit their applications.

It is recommended that applicants avoid waiting until the final hours of the deadline to submit their materials.

How to Apply

Applications must be submitted through the Penn State Graduate School admissions portal.

University policy allows an applicant to apply to only one graduate degree programme at a time. Applicants interested in HDFS should therefore ensure that they select the Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.) degree when completing the application.

The application process will guide applicants through the general requirements established by the Graduate School as well as the programme-specific materials required by HDFS.

Applicants should review all requirements carefully before submitting their application.

Required Application Materials

Applicants to the HDFS graduate programme are expected to provide several documents as part of their application.

The required programme-specific materials include:

1. Scientific Writing Sample

Applicants are required to submit a scientific writing sample as part of the application.

The writing sample should demonstrate the applicant’s ability to communicate academic or research-related ideas effectively and provide evidence of their writing and analytical abilities.

2. Official Transcripts

Applicants must provide official academic transcripts as required by the university.

Transcripts allow the admissions committee to assess an applicant’s previous academic preparation and educational background.

Applicants should ensure that their academic records meet Penn State Graduate School requirements.

3. Curriculum Vitae or Résumé

Applicants must submit a curriculum vitae (CV) or résumé outlining their academic, professional, research and other relevant experiences.

Applicants should ensure that the document clearly presents experiences that are relevant to their intended graduate study.

4. Statement of Professional and Career Plans

Applicants are required to submit a statement describing their professional and career plans.

This statement provides an opportunity for applicants to explain their academic and professional objectives and how doctoral study relates to their long-term goals.

Applicants should use the statement to clearly communicate their motivation for pursuing graduate education and their intended career direction.

5. Three Letters of Recommendation

Applicants must provide three letters of recommendation.

Recommendation letters are an important part of the application because they can provide the admissions committee with additional insight into an applicant’s academic preparation, capabilities and potential for success in graduate study.

Applicants should select recommenders who are familiar with their academic, research or professional abilities.

Applicants from Outside the United States

International applicants may have additional requirements as part of the Penn State Graduate School admissions process.

Applicants from outside the United States should carefully review the university’s requirements for international applicants and ensure that all required documentation is provided.

International applicants should also pay particular attention to application deadlines and time-zone differences when submitting their applications.

GRE Scores Are Not Required

The HDFS graduate programme does not require GRE scores as part of the application.

The department uses a holistic review process to evaluate each applicant’s potential to succeed in the programme. Applicants will receive full consideration regardless of whether they submit GRE scores.

Although GRE scores are not required, some applicants may choose to submit them if they believe the scores would provide additional evidence of their potential for graduate study in the behavioral sciences.

For example, submitting GRE scores may be useful for applicants whose undergraduate major is not closely related to the HDFS graduate curriculum or applicants returning to graduate school after working in another field.

In such circumstances, an applicant’s academic transcripts and recommendation letters may not fully demonstrate their preparation for graduate study in the behavioral sciences. Applicants may therefore consider whether additional materials, including GRE scores, would strengthen their application.

Holistic Application Review

The HDFS programme evaluates applications using a holistic review process.

This means applicants are considered based on the overall strength and potential demonstrated through their application rather than solely on one component such as standardized test scores.

Applicants should therefore focus on presenting a complete application that accurately communicates their academic preparation, research interests, experiences, professional objectives and potential for success in graduate study.

Who Should Apply?

The programme may be suitable for students and professionals interested in pursuing advanced academic and research training related to human development, family studies and the behavioral sciences.

Applicants should carefully assess their academic background and professional objectives against the HDFS programme before applying.

Students entering with a bachelor’s degree should be prepared to complete a master’s degree en route to the Ph.D.

Important Things Applicants Should Know

Before submitting an application, prospective students should keep the following points in mind:

The application deadline is December 1.

Applications must be submitted through the Penn State Graduate School admissions portal.

Applicants may apply to only one graduate degree programme at a time under university policy.

HDFS applicants should select the Ph.D. degree.

HDFS does not offer a terminal master’s programme.

Students entering with a bachelor’s degree are required to complete a master’s degree en route to the doctoral degree.

A scientific writing sample is required.

Official transcripts are required.

Applicants must provide a CV or résumé.

A statement of professional and career plans is required.

Three letters of recommendation are required.

GRE scores are not required.

International applicants should review the additional requirements applicable to applicants from outside the United States.

Applicants submitting from another time zone should account for Penn State’s Eastern Standard Time zone.

Contact for Application Questions

Applicants who have questions about the application process can contact the HDFS academic programme coordinator.

Applicants with questions about whether GRE scores would strengthen their application or other questions about improving their application may also contact the HDFS Admissions Committee.

Conclusion

The Penn State Human Development and Family Studies Ph.D. programme provides an opportunity for applicants seeking advanced graduate education and research training in the behavioral sciences and related areas.

The programme follows a doctoral pathway, and students entering with a bachelor’s degree are required to complete a master’s degree en route to the Ph.D. Applicants must submit their applications through the Penn State Graduate School admissions portal and provide the required academic and supporting materials.

The application requires a scientific writing sample, official transcripts, a CV or résumé, a statement of professional and career plans and three letters of recommendation. GRE scores are not required, and applications are evaluated through a holistic review process.

Interested applicants should begin preparing their application materials early and ensure that their complete application is submitted by the December 1 deadline, taking Penn State’s Eastern Standard Time zone into account.

TITLE: Delegation from the African University College of Communications and the Pan African Heritage Museum visits the AAU Secretary-General

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
A three-member delegation from the African University College of Communications (AUCC) who also serve on the Council of the Pan African Heritage Museum (PAHM) on Thursday 17th February 2022 paid a courtesy call on the Secretary-General of the Association of African Universities (AAU), Prof. Olusola Oyewole, at the AAU Secretariat in Accra, Ghana.

The delegation was led by Honourable Kojo Yankah, founder of African University College of Communications (AUCC) and Executive Chairman of the Museum foundation. Other members were Prof. Kofi Asare Opoku, Chair of the Governing Council of AUCC and Rev. Prof. Pashington Obeng, Member of the Governing Council of the AUCC, both Members of the Academic Council of the Pan African Heritage Museum.

The delegation briefed Prof. Oyewole on the progress of work on the Pan African Heritage Museum, a multimillion-dollar brainchild of Hon. Kojo Yankah that is being constructed on Pomadze Hills, near Winneba Junction, in the Central Region of Ghana. The Museum which is expected to open in August 2023, is to showcase the history, culture, and achievements of the Pan African world as presented by Africans. Hon. Yankah informed the Secretary General that while the physical construction was ongoing at the site, a team in Miami, Florida was actively producing the digital version of the museum to be launched in May this year. The delegation also offered to continue to cooperate with AAU to expand its presence in North America as well as in various parts of the African diaspora.

On his part, the AAU Secretary-General assured the delegation of the support and collaboration of the AAU towards the museum project and beyond, especially in their joint quest to mobilize Africans from all parts of the world for their common good.

Based on their common interest on reaching out to the African Diaspora, the two sides agreed to merge their Diaspora homecoming meeting and conference at a joint Summit to be held in September 2022. The Pan African Writers Association (PAWA) is to be invited as a co-partner of the Summit.
