TITLE: Donor Profile: Morton E. Goulder

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Morton E. Goulder SB ’42
Patrons of Physics Fellows

by Elizabeth Chadis // MIT Physics Annual 2005

Morton E. Goulder SB ’42

There’s a twinkle in his eye as Mort Goulder talks about his years at MIT and subsequent career. “I started out as a Course XV business major. That lasted a year and I switched to EE. By the end of my second year I had had my fill of transmission lines. I decided to take the classes I liked and found exciting. Physics offered the interest and flexibility I needed…as for getting a job afterwards, I figured I would take my chances.” Mort has never regretted his physics training which he calls “magnificent.” In fact, Mort will tell you that he has never learned anything that wasn’t useful.

Mort is now President of M.E. Goulder Enterprises, a consulting firm specializing in high technology and investment management. Prior to that he co-founded Sanders Associates, where he served as director and vice-president for 22 years. He initiated and managed two of Sanders’ largest divisions: special programs (consisting of reconnaissance and intelligence systems) and electronic design—covering product design for the entire corporation.

While at Sanders, Mort also ran all of their philanthropic activities. It was there that he became interested in leveraging charitable funds to “really accomplish some good.” Since then, Mort has devoted his energy to community and educational affairs. From involvement in the city governance of Nashua, New Hampshire, to serving on MIT’s Corporation Development Committee, Mort has sought to provide innovative solutions and high tech expertise to address the problems faced by non-profit organizations.

Training in physics is magnificent… I never learned anything that wasn’t useful.
Morton E. Goulder (’42)

When the Physics Department asked Mort to join the Patrons of Physics Fellows, Mort responded enthusiastically with a one-year expendable fellowship. Mort’s gift will make it possible for a first-year graduate student to explore his or her dreams—to really take the time to determine the right area of specialization, to find a mentor, and to have the freedom to develop new insights and ideas—without having to worry where the money will come from. And, because another generous donor has offered to match all new gifts dedicated to graduate support, Mort’s contribution will have double the impact!

“MIT is a much better place today,” explains Mort. “Today’s students have mentors. They live on campus. They have UROPs.” Mort likes the changes he sees and rarely misses an opportunity to return to campus and learn something new. He still works full time at the things he enjoys—venture capital, investment management, and board work as well as charitable support. “There are always too many things to do,” he sighs.

In addition to his gift of fellowship support, Mort has also established the Morton and Claire Goulder and Family Professorship in Environmental Systems, currently held by Director of the Laboratory for Energy and the Environment, Prof. David Marks.

Mort is very pleased to support the Physics Department and looks forward to meeting the first Morton E. Goulder Fellow.

TITLE: French Government Winter Training Scholarships 2026: Fully Supported FLE Teacher Training in Vichy and Besançon, France

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Embassy of France in South Africa, Lesotho and Malawi has opened applications for its 2026 winter training scholarships in France, offering more than 10 funded places for French-language teachers and selected future French teachers from South Africa, Lesotho and Malawi.

The scholarships provide an opportunity to participate in intensive, in-person professional training in France during November and December 2026. The programme is aimed primarily at teachers of French as a Foreign Language (FLE – Français langue étrangère) working in primary schools, secondary schools and universities. A smaller number of places may also be available to students enrolled in French departments who intend to become French teachers.

Successful applicants can choose between two professional-development programmes delivered by major French-language training institutions:

CAVILAM – Alliance Française in Vichy: 30 November to 11 December 2026

CLA – Centre de Linguistique Appliquée in Besançon: 16 November to 26 November 2026

The scholarship covers major costs connected with participation, including international and domestic travel, visa-related consular fees, accommodation, meals or a living allowance, travel insurance and the cost of the training itself.

Application Deadline: Thursday, 1 October 2026 at 12:00 noon.

About the 2026 France Winter Training Scholarship Programme

The 2026 scholarship call is organised by the Embassy of France in South Africa, Lesotho and Malawi and supports in-person professional training in France.

The programme is intended to strengthen the professional skills of French-language educators in Southern Africa by giving them direct access to specialised pedagogical training offered by established French institutions.

More than 10 scholarships are available, and applicants are asked to select one of two training options according to their professional interests and development needs.

The programme is particularly relevant for educators who want to:

Improve their French-language teaching methodology

Strengthen pedagogical leadership

Develop more contemporary classroom practices

Explore approaches to oral communication and learner engagement

Understand emerging teaching tools

Integrate artificial intelligence and modern educational practices into language teaching

Build stronger professional expertise within French-language education

Apply new knowledge in their schools, universities or educational institutions after returning home

The application process places significant emphasis on applicants explaining how the training fits into their professional project and how they intend to reuse the skills acquired in their own professional practice.

Two Training Programmes Available in France

Applicants are required to indicate which of the two training programmes they prefer.

Option 1: CAVILAM de Vichy – Pedagogical Coordination Training

The first programme will take place at CAVILAM in Vichy, France, from:

30 November to 11 December 2026

The programme is titled:

“Assurer la coordination pédagogique d’un dispositif de formation”

This can broadly be understood as training focused on managing or ensuring the pedagogical coordination of a training system or programme.

This programme is particularly relevant for professionals who have, or aspire to have, responsibilities extending beyond classroom teaching.

Potentially relevant participants may include:

French-language teachers taking on coordination responsibilities

Heads of language departments

Pedagogical coordinators

Teacher trainers

Senior French-language educators

Academic managers

University lecturers involved in programme coordination

Educators responsible for curriculum implementation

Professionals supporting other teachers or training teams

The programme provides an opportunity to develop a more strategic understanding of pedagogical management and the coordination of teaching and learning activities.

Option 2: CLA de Besançon – Winter Pedagogical University

The second training programme will be held at the Centre de Linguistique Appliquée (CLA) in Besançon, France, from:

16 November to 26 November 2026

The programme is called:

“Université pédagogique d’hiver” – Winter Pedagogical University.

The Besançon programme includes three thematic modules of 10 hours each, with participants asked to select one pathway within each module.

The choices listed in the application include subjects such as:

Integrating the body, voice and movement into learning

Discovering and using youth cultures in language classrooms

Promoting wellbeing in the language classroom

Creating conditions that support effective learning

Teaching oral communication and orality with or without teaching materials

Designing and delivering a 21st-century FLE course

Rethinking teaching and learning in the age of artificial intelligence

These themes show that the programme is strongly focused on contemporary teaching practices.

Participants can therefore gain exposure to pedagogical approaches that move beyond traditional textbook-based teaching and explore learner wellbeing, youth culture, oral communication, classroom interaction and emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence.

Minimum French-Language Requirement

Applicants must have a sufficiently strong command of French to participate effectively in professional pedagogical training.

The application explicitly states that candidates must have at least:

B2 level in French.

The application later notes that pedagogical training generally requires participants to have at least B2 level and, in some cases, C1 level.

Applicants are asked to indicate their highest DELF or DALF qualification, with options ranging from DELF A1 through DALF C2.

Candidates who have not taken DELF or DALF may instead provide details of another French-language test or certification, including the name of the qualification and the assessed level.

This means that DELF or DALF certification is useful, but the form does not state that having a DELF/DALF certificate is the only way to demonstrate French proficiency.

Who Is the Scholarship Designed For?

The programme gives priority to teachers of French as a Foreign Language working at different levels of education.

The official call specifically identifies teachers working in:

Primary schools

Secondary schools

Universities

A smaller number of opportunities may also be available to:

Students in university French departments

Students intending to become French-language teachers

The application form asks practising teachers how many years they have taught French and requests information about the institution in which they currently work.

Applicants may be teaching in institutions such as:

Nursery schools

Primary schools

Secondary schools

Technical schools

Universities

Universities of technology

Alliance Française institutions

The application also explicitly includes an option for applicants who are currently students.

Countries Covered by the Scholarship

The scholarship call is specifically open in:

South Africa

Lesotho

Malawi

The application form asks applicants to select their country of residence from these three countries.

The programme therefore has a clear Southern African geographic focus.

Importantly, the application also contains specific instructions for candidates whose nationality is different from their country of residence or employment. Such applicants may be asked to provide a valid residence permit, work permit or permanent-residence document.

This indicates that the programme is not framed solely around citizenship; legal residence or employment circumstances in one of the participating countries are also relevant.

What Does the Scholarship Cover?

One of the most attractive aspects of the programme is the broad level of financial support provided by the Embassy of France.

The scholarship covers the following expenses:

Visa Consular Fees

The Embassy will cover the consular fees associated with the visa application.

Successful candidates will still be responsible for completing the visa process promptly and supplying all required documentation.

International Return Travel

The programme covers return air transport from:

South Africa

Lesotho

Malawi

to France.

Train Travel Within France

The Embassy also covers onward train transportation in France to the location of the selected training programme.

This is particularly useful because participants travelling to Vichy or Besançon will need to continue their journey after arriving in France.

Accommodation in France

Accommodation will be provided either:

In an individual studio; or

With a host family,

depending on the participant’s preference and availability.

Applicants can state their preferred accommodation arrangement in the application.

Host Family Accommodation

Participants choosing host-family accommodation receive two meals per day as part of the arrangement.

Candidates can also indicate specific needs or preferences relating to the host family, including:

Allergies

Phobias

Dietary requirements

Preferences regarding pets

Smoking or non-smoking households

Other relevant personal considerations

Individual Studio Accommodation

Participants who choose an individual studio will have access to a small kitchen area.

Meals are not included with studio accommodation.

Instead, scholarship recipients staying in studios receive an increased lump-sum maintenance allowance intended, among other things, to help cover food expenses.

Where the training institution offers a cafeteria, university restaurant or another catering arrangement that is paid for by the French Embassy, the allowance may be adjusted accordingly.

Meals and Living Allowance

Depending on accommodation arrangements, the scholarship covers meals and/or provides a maintenance allowance.

The final amount of the allowance cannot be confirmed before the beginning of the training.

Any amount communicated in advance is therefore indicative and does not represent a binding financial commitment by the Embassy.

Applicants should also be aware that the allowance is usually paid two to three days after arrival in France, once the training institution has confirmed the participant’s arrival to Campus France.

Participants must therefore bring enough personal money to cover their initial expenses, including meals during travel and during the first days in France.

Travel Insurance

The scholarship covers travel insurance for selected participants.

Training Fees

The cost of the selected training programme is also covered by the French Embassy.

Taken together, these benefits make the programme a substantially funded professional-development opportunity.

Passport Requirements

Applicants should review the passport conditions before beginning their application.

A passport should:

Be currently valid

Have been issued less than 10 years ago

Contain at least two blank pages

Remain valid for at least three months after the applicant’s expected departure from the Schengen Area

The application specifically states that temporary passports or temporary travel documents are not accepted.

Applicants are responsible for checking passport validity sufficiently early and arranging renewal if necessary.

Passport Copy Requirements

Applicants possessing a valid passport must upload a high-quality colour scan.

Accepted file formats are:

PDF

JPG

PNG

The maximum file size for this passport upload is 1 MB.

Candidates who already hold a valid visa allowing them to enter France are also asked to provide a copy.

Applicants whose nationality differs from their country of residence or employment must combine relevant documents into a single PDF, including the passport identity page and valid residence documentation.

The Embassy places significant emphasis on document quality. Blurred, poorly framed, overexposed, dark, incomplete or otherwise unreadable files may not be processed.

Required Application Documents

Applicants should prepare the complete documentation before submitting the form.

The principal documents required are:

Valid passport copy

Completed French Government training scholarship application form

French-language CV

French-language motivation letter

Additional supporting documents may be required depending on nationality and residence status.

French-Language CV

Applicants must upload their curriculum vitae in French.

The file should be named using the following structure:

SURNAME_Firstname_CV.pdf

The application system allows only one upload, so candidates should verify the document carefully beforehand.

Motivation Letter and Professional Project

Applicants must also provide a motivation letter in French.

The letter should briefly explain:

The applicant’s background

Their professional project

Why they selected the particular training programme

How the training relates to their professional development

How they intend to reuse and transfer the skills acquired into their professional practice

This is likely to be one of the most important qualitative elements of the application.

A strong motivation letter should therefore move beyond generic statements about wanting to visit France and instead demonstrate a clear connection between the training, the applicant’s current professional role and the needs of their learners or institution.

French Government Training Scholarship Application Form

Applicants must also complete the formal training scholarship dossier.

The form must be:

Completed correctly

Signed by the applicant

Completed where required by the applicant’s institution

Signed by the relevant authority

Officially stamped by the institution

The applicant’s school, university, educational institution or administration must complete, sign and stamp the section titled:

“Attestation de l’autorité locale compétente.”

The candidate must also personally sign the declaration and commitment section.

Document Quality Standards

Applicants should pay particular attention to the administrative quality of their documents.

The Embassy states that the following may not be processed:

Ordinary photographs of documents taken by mobile phone

Low-quality scans

Unreadable scans

Incorrectly completed forms

Forms completed entirely by hand

Incomplete applications

Documents missing required signatures

Documents missing institutional stamps

Candidates who need to print the application form should first complete it digitally, then obtain the necessary signatures and institutional stamp before scanning all four pages into one PDF at a minimum resolution of 200 dpi.

Employer or Institutional Authorization Is Essential

Teachers should confirm their availability with their employer before applying.

The application asks candidates to confirm that they have:

Checked their academic calendar

Contacted their administration

Obtained authorization to be absent during the selected training period

A candidate cannot be definitively selected without written authorization from their administration.

Applicants should therefore begin this process early.

Previous French Government Scholarship Recipients May Apply

The form asks whether candidates have previously received a scholarship from the French Government.

This includes previous:

Short training scholarships

15-day training programmes

One-month training programmes

Long-term study scholarships

Other relevant French Government scholarship experiences

However, the form explicitly states that this question is for information purposes and is not eliminatory.

Therefore, having previously received a French Government scholarship does not automatically prevent a candidate from applying.

French Teacher Association Membership

The application also asks whether candidates are members of French teacher associations operating in the participating countries.

These include:

Association for French Studies in Southern Africa

French Teachers Association Lesotho

Association Malawienne des Professeurs de français

Association des Professeurs de Français du Gauteng

Association des Professeurs de Français du KwaZulu-Natal

South African French Teachers Association of Western Cape

The application does not state that membership of one of these organisations is a mandatory eligibility condition.

Visa Responsibilities for Selected Candidates

Receiving the scholarship does not remove the participant’s responsibility to complete the visa process.

Selected candidates must undertake the required visa procedures without delay and submit a complete visa application within the timetable communicated by the French Embassy.

Applicants are also expected to immediately report any difficulty that could delay or prevent issuance of the visa.

Travel Commitments

Because travel tickets are arranged and financed by the French Embassy, scholarship recipients must respect the travel arrangements communicated to them.

Participants must ensure that they arrive at the airport on time and have all required travel documents.

If a participant misses a flight because of circumstances attributable to them—for example lateness, failure to appear for boarding or missing/non-compliant travel documents—additional ticket modification or replacement costs may remain the participant’s responsibility.

Attendance Requirements

Successful candidates commit to attending the entire training programme.

They must participate consistently throughout the programme and provide feedback to the French Embassy after returning home.

The scholarship should therefore be viewed as a serious professional-development commitment rather than simply an opportunity for international travel.

Early Departure and Possible Repayment

Recipients who voluntarily interrupt their stay and return before the end of the training programme may be required to reimburse expenses already incurred in relation to:

Accommodation

Meals

Transport

Applicants should therefore ensure they can attend the complete programme before accepting an award.

Application Timeline

The key dates for applicants are:

Application Deadline: Thursday, 1 October 2026 at 12:00 noon

CLA Besançon Training: 16–26 November 2026

CAVILAM Vichy Training: 30 November–11 December 2026

After submitting the online form, applicants automatically receive an email containing a copy of their responses.

Applications can be modified until the deadline on 1 October 2026 at noon.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Candidates interested in the programme should begin by carefully reviewing the two available training programmes and determining which one aligns most closely with their current responsibilities and longer-term professional goals.

A competitive application should clearly demonstrate:

Relevant professional or academic connection to French-language teaching.

At least B2-level French proficiency.

A clear professional reason for choosing the selected programme.

The ability to apply the knowledge after returning home.

Institutional support for participation.

A valid passport meeting all Schengen requirements.

Carefully prepared and professionally presented documentation.

Availability for the full training period.

Candidates should avoid generic motivation statements and instead demonstrate how the scholarship will create measurable value for their students, institution, teacher network or wider French-language education community.

Why This Scholarship Is Important for French-Language Educators

Professional-development opportunities of this kind offer more than short-term classroom training.

For teachers of French in South Africa, Lesotho and Malawi, participation provides direct exposure to French pedagogical institutions and current approaches to FLE teaching.

Participants can potentially return with new knowledge relating to:

Curriculum design

Teacher coordination

Innovative teaching methods

Oral-language instruction

Classroom wellbeing

Youth culture

Artificial intelligence in education

Contemporary FLE methodology

Professional networking

The requirement to explain how acquired skills will be reinvested in professional practice also reinforces the programme’s multiplier effect: the benefits are intended to extend beyond the individual scholarship recipient.

Conclusion

The French Government Winter Training Scholarships in France 2026 provide an exceptional professional-development opportunity for French-language teachers and selected future French teachers based in South Africa, Lesotho and Malawi.

With more than 10 scholarships available, successful participants will attend one of two specialised in-person training programmes in France during November and December 2026.

Candidates can choose between the CAVILAM Vichy pedagogical coordination programme, running from 30 November to 11 December 2026, and the CLA Besançon Winter Pedagogical University, running from 16 to 26 November 2026.

The scholarship covers major participation costs, including visa-related consular fees, return transportation to France, onward train travel, accommodation, meals or a maintenance allowance, travel insurance and training fees.

Applicants must demonstrate at least B2-level French, prepare a French CV and motivation letter, obtain the required institutional authorization and submit complete, high-quality supporting documentation.

The final deadline is:

Thursday, 1 October 2026 at 12:00 noon.

TITLE: Association of African Universities and the African Academy of Sciences Record Key Successes Under the Science Granting Council’s Research Management Project

The SGCI Annual Forum is being hosted by the National Research Foundation of South Africa, in Cape Town, South Africa, from 4th -6th December 2022. The meeting is being attended by over 120 participants consisting of all the key stakeholders of the Science Granting Councils Initiative – including the development and funding agencies, 17 Science Granting Councils from the 17 participating African countries under the project, the project council members, project advisors, project executive committee members, implementing partners, researchers, doctoral students, and other invited guests. The Association of African Universities, which is the lead for the Research Management Project, is being represented by Professor Damtew Teferra, Director of Research and Programmes; Ms. Nodumo Dhlamini, Director of ICT, Communications and Knowledge Management; Mrs. Ruth Issambo Nyarko, Project Officer for the ​Science Granting Councils Initiative and Mrs. Felicia Nkrumah Kuagbedzi, Senior Communications and Publications Officer for the AAU. From the AAS side, the representatives are Dr Obed Ogega, Programmes Manager and Mr Roland Opisa, Programme Officer.

The Science Granting Councils Initiative (SGCI) is a multilateral initiative established in 2015 that is strengthening the institutional capacities of 17 public science funding agencies in Sub-Saharan Africa to support research and evidence-based policies that will contribute to economic and social development. Since its inception, the SGCI has provided significant financial and technical support to strengthen the Science Granting Councils in the 17 participating countries of the initiative, namely- Botswana, Burkina Faso, Cote D’Ivoire, Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, Nigeria, Rwanda, Senegal, Sierra, Leone, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia and Zimbabwe. This second phase of the SGCI is scheduled to end on the 28th February 2022.

The Association of African Universities and the African Academy of Sciences are the implementing partners of the component of the initiative focusing on Strengthening the capacity of Science Granting Councils in Research Management. Under this component, impactful successes and outcomes have been recorded, empowering the SGCs to effectively facilitate harnessing the potential of research to promote inclusive growth and development, and eradicate poverty in the region.

The huge successes recorded under the Research Management component of the Initiative, as highlighted in the presentation by the AAU and AAS include the training and provision of technical support to the Councils on research excellence, research ethics and the Good Financial Grant Practices – a certification which strategically positions institutions to be considered for funding by major public and private funders.

It was also reported that a total of three SGCs have completed the pre-certification process- Kenya, Uganda, and Zimbabwe; four SGCs are going through the pre-certification process – Namibia, Mozambique, Tanzania and Zambia and five SGCs have attended planning meetings to prepare to undertake the pre-certification exercise- Botswana, Burkina Faso, Cote d’Ivoire, Ghana and Senegal.

The AAU and AAS with the support of the Uganda National Council for Science and Technology (UNCST) have also supported the councils to establish and effectively implement a generic online grants management system, which is well equipped with multi-lingual functionalities, and which will greatly improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the Councils in managing their grant processes.

The partners have also trained a total of seventy-four (74) staff from the SGCs, including monitoring, evaluation and learning experts; grants officers; software developers; project managers; and ICT technical support staff on the use of the Generic Online Grants Management System developed under the Project.

These trainings, as reported, were held in the following SGCI participating countries – Ghana (12-13 April 2022, 20 staff trained); Burkina Faso (5th – 6th May 2022, 15 Staff trained); Zimbabwe (14th – 15th June 2022, 15 Staff Trained); Malawi (14th – 15th July 2022, 9 Staff trained); Cote d’Ivoire (21st – 22nd September 15 Staff trained).

Overall, a total of 7 Councils were reported to have implemented the Generic Online Grants Management System developed by the UNCST through funding support from the project. These are the Uganda National Council for Science and Technology; the Research Council of Zimbabwe, Fonds National de la Recherche et de l’Innovation pour le Developpement, Burkina Faso; the National Commission on Research, Science and Technology, Namibia; Fonds pour la Science, la Technologie et l’Innovation, Cote d’Ivoire; the Ministry of Environment, Science, Technology and Innovation, Ghana; and the National Commission for Science and Technology, Malawi.

Responding to the paucity of current resources, frameworks, and procedures for quality research management, the project has also produced three key manuals for usage by the participating councils and other general stakeholders. First is the Grant Management Digitalization Framework; second – the Ethics in Research and Innovation: a Guiding Framework for Science Granting Councils and finally a Manual on Research Excellence

Again, the Research Management component of the Science Granting Councils Initiative conducted National and Regional Studies focusing on Deepening Knowledge and Implementation of Research Ethics in the African Context. A digital course on the Research Quality Plus Framework to strengthen the capacity of SGCs in research excellence was also developed under the project.

The Association of African Universities, and the African Academy of Sciences, further created the requisite platform to support peer-to-peer learning and promote knowledge sharing among the councils. Among others, the project organised a peer-to-peer learning meeting in Uganda from 26th – 28th October 2022 in collaboration with the Uganda National Council for Science and Technology, which featured 35 participants from 12 SGCs. It built the capacity of Councils to facilitate implementation of online research permit issuance systems and developed Guidelines on Staff Exchange and Learning Visits which was widely disseminated among the SGCs. Additionally, participants at the SGCI Annual forum were informed that the AAU and AAS organised a collective lessons learning meeting focusing on the Online Grants Management Systems and facilitated the general visibility of the project through the engagement of the media and other key stakeholders. Contributing to the discussions at the forum, Prof. Damtew Teferra highlighted the need for the project partners and stakeholders to scale the project from its current coverage of 15 countries to the rest of the continent to ensure that the entire continent benefits from the Science Granting Councils Initiative.

The 2022 Annual Forum by the Science Granting Councils Initiative is being hosted alongside other key Science/Research Events including the World Science Forum, the Global Research Council Africa Regional Consultative Meeting, The Academic Symposium by the SGCI, and the NRF Carnegie Corporation PERKA final Conference on Early Career Researcher Development in the Post PhD Phase.

TITLE: Donor Profile: Virgil Elings

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Virgil Elings PhD ’66
$3.5 Million Gift to Name the Center for Theoretical Physics (now MIT Center for Theoretical Physics — a Leinweber Institute (CTP-LI))

by Elizabeth Chadis // MIT Physics Annual 2004

Virgil Elings (PhD ’66) donates gift to name the Center for Theoretical Physics
Virgil Elings, originally from Des Moines, Iowa, earned his SB in Mechanical Engineering from Iowa State University in 1961 and his PhD in Physics from MIT in 1966. He spent the next 20 years on the physics faculty of the University of California at Santa Barbara. While on sabbatical leave in 1987, Elings co-founded Digital Instruments, which designs and sells scanning probe microscopes (SPMs). These microscopes magnify objects 10–20 million times, enabling scientists to view materials at the atomic level. In 1998, the company was acquired and Elings retired a year later. Today, he spends time at his horse ranch, tending his lavender fields, and enjoying his vintage motorcycle museum. In addition to his philanthropic support of civic projects in Santa Barbara, where he lives, Elings made a $3.5 million gift to the Department of Physics. Director of Development Elizabeth Chadis caught up with Virgil Elings while visiting MIT recently to help celebrate the 80th birthday of his friend and former thesis advisor, Professor of Physics Emeritus Louis S. Osborne.

Elizabeth Chadis: Virgil, tell us about your experiences as a grad student working with Louis Osborne.

Virgil Elings: Lou was absolutely great. He taught me the important things in life (one of which is not high energy physics). I had the job [in the Osborne group] of trying to understand the klugy electronics in the experiment, which was documented mostly in the mind of Sergio Tatzari, who was heading back to Italy. One day, as I was puzzling over the wiring, Lou came in and ripped all the wiring out. I said to him, “Are you crazy?” and he replied, “I think you can figure it out and redo it,” and then he left. Did he understand, I wondered, that my background was in mechanical engineering and if I couldn’t understand the stuff he had just delayed the experiment for a very long time? Wow, no one ever had confidence in me like that. My dad wouldn’t even let me replace spark plugs in his car when I was young. I always remembered that lesson when working with others and it has worked really well in my business, determining when people are smart and then giving them free rein.

One of the most important things I learned at MIT was from Bill Lobar, Lou’s [Professor of Physics Emeritus Louis S. Osborne] technician. I asked him one day to show me how the oscilloscope worked, since I’d forgotten whatever I’d learned in undergraduate labs. Bill said, ‘fiddle with the knobs, you’ll figure it out.’ He was right, and it works with almost everything in life. I’ll bet Lou fostered that kind of thinking.

Virgil Elings (PhD ’66)

Lou was always on the edge of technology (which, of course, I didn’t realize at the time). We had probably the world’s first mini-computer (the LINC prototype built by Lincoln Labs, which was later sort of copied by DEC) on-line in the experiment, and it was then connected by phone lines from Harvard to MIT to an IBM computer. The LINC was given to Lou on condition that he wouldn’t ask why it didn’t work. This thing had 4k bits of magnetic core memory and was a bear to program.

I had the dubious honor of being in the Cambridge Electron Accelerator when the liquid hydrogen bubble chamber blew up. After getting myself (and my data) out of the building, I called Lou. I told him something blew up and he wanted to know what, thinking it some trivial event. I said the whole place blew up, and he thought I was exaggerating. Lou went outside his house, looking out toward Cambridge, and saw a big black cloud; he finally got the message. When he got to the site, I told him that when I went back into the building to get my data, I’d heard a voice from the dark experimental hall yelling for help. At that moment, the fire department was still busy pouring water into the hall, which could have drowned the person. Lou, after being ignored by the Captain (“This is an atomic plant, we can’t go down there.”), found a Sergeant and they went down into the hall and carried out a fellow, who had broken his back. Again, Lou knew what was important, even as his experiment burned.

EC: What initially led you to MIT?

VE: Dave Frisch asked that same question at a meeting he held for graduate students at his house. He expected answers like, “I knew the professors were great,” and stuff like that. Instead, Frisch was blown away by the random answers. I remember one student saying, “I saw MIT on someone’s sweatshirt so I thought I might apply.” As for me, I refused to check the square, “Would you come without financial aid?” so I got a Whitney Fellowship. Stanford wouldn’t give me aid, so I went to MIT. We both won. I went to the best place and MIT got its money back (a thousandfold).

EC: There’s a rumor you rode your motorcycle up and down the Infinite Corridor. Clearly, motorcycles have always been important in your life.

VE: Early in my life, motorcycles were a source of freedom (especially in Boston, where I could park anywhere). Now I collect them because I enjoy the diversity of engineering. To me, they’re sort of a bank account I can enjoy. No relation to high energy physics, and there doesn’t need to be. No relation to lavender farming, either.

EC: Virgil, is there anything else you want to share with the MIT physics community?

VE: I think one of the downsides of a PhD education is that it usually sets the tone for the rest of one’s life, especially if one goes into academics—in which case you typically do the same thing the rest of your life. I wish people would treat it more as an experience, not as a basis for life. Life is too rich for that. I enjoyed my time at MIT and, as I said, learned important things from Lou. So, I am glad to help with the gift.

TITLE: NASA Lunar Dust Mitigation Intern 2027: Apply for a Hands-On Undergraduate Research Internship at NASA Glenn Research Center

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
NASA is offering an exciting Lunar Dust Mitigation Intern opportunity for students interested in materials engineering, aerospace engineering, materials science, laboratory research, coatings, vacuum systems, and the technologies needed to support future lunar exploration. Based at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, Ohio, this full-time, in-person internship provides students with the opportunity to contribute to research addressing one of the important technical challenges associated with operating on the Moon: lunar dust.

The internship is part of NASA’s Spring 2027 intern session and will involve hands-on laboratory work alongside NASA personnel. Students will assist with the development, characterization, and testing of passive coatings designed to reduce the adhesion of lunar dust to surfaces.

The deadline to register is September 14, 2026.

About the NASA Lunar Dust Mitigation Internship

Lunar dust presents a significant challenge for future Moon missions. The Moon’s surface is covered by extremely fine particles of lunar regolith, and these particles can be abrasive, electrically charged, and difficult to control.

Lunar dust can interfere with mission operations in several ways. It can reduce visibility, change the optical properties of surfaces and equipment, and interfere with mission-critical components. Because future lunar exploration will involve increasingly complex spacecraft, instruments, habitats, vehicles, and other equipment operating on or around the lunar surface, developing effective approaches to managing lunar dust is an important area of research.

NASA is therefore investigating passive lunar dust mitigation coatings. These coatings are intended to reduce the amount of lunar dust that adheres to surfaces without requiring external electrical power or continuous human interaction.

The selected intern will assist NASA personnel in developing these coatings and evaluating how well they perform under environmental conditions relevant to lunar missions.

What the Intern Will Work On

The internship is designed to provide substantial hands-on laboratory experience. The intern will work with NASA personnel on research related to the development and testing of materials intended to mitigate lunar dust.

Depending on the specific research activities assigned, the work may include:

Depositing coatings onto surfaces using sputter deposition.

Characterizing the physical and material properties of coating materials.

Testing coating performance.

Conducting experiments under environmental conditions that simulate aspects of the lunar environment.

Using vacuum chambers to evaluate coating behavior.

Performing laboratory experiments and recording results.

Supporting materials research and experimental investigations.

Conducting some desk-based and computer-related work associated with laboratory research.

Assisting with the analysis and interpretation of experimental results.

The work is expected to combine practical laboratory activities with research, experimentation, documentation, and computer-based tasks.

Why Lunar Dust Mitigation Matters

Lunar dust is fundamentally different from ordinary dust encountered on Earth. Its fine particles can be highly abrasive and can become electrically charged, allowing them to adhere to surfaces and potentially spread to areas where they can cause operational problems.

For future lunar missions, dust mitigation could be important for protecting:

Scientific instruments

Optical systems

Sensors

Mechanical components

Spacecraft surfaces

Lunar vehicles

Habitats

Spacesuits and equipment

Mission-critical hardware

NASA’s research into passive coatings is particularly significant because a passive solution could potentially reduce dust adhesion without requiring additional power or constant intervention.

This makes materials research an important part of preparing technologies for sustained lunar exploration.

Hands-On Laboratory Research Experience

One of the major features of this NASA internship is its emphasis on hands-on laboratory experience.

Rather than being exclusively desk-based, the intern will participate in practical research activities involving coating deposition, materials characterization, experimentation, and testing.

Students may gain exposure to laboratory procedures involving:

Coating deposition

The intern may assist with depositing specialized coatings onto surfaces using techniques such as sputtering.

Materials characterization

Students may investigate the properties and performance of materials using microscopy, spectroscopy, or other characterization techniques.

Vacuum systems

The work may involve vacuum chambers and high-vacuum systems used to simulate environmental conditions relevant to space.

Experimental design

Interns may contribute to planning experiments, defining test conditions, collecting observations, and evaluating results.

Performance testing

Coatings will need to be tested to determine whether they can effectively reduce the adhesion or effects of lunar dust.

This combination makes the opportunity particularly relevant to students who want practical research experience in engineering, materials science, or space-related technology.

Preferred Skills and Experience

NASA identifies several skills and areas of experience that would be advantageous for applicants.

Preferred experience includes:

Materials engineering

Laboratory research

Materials characterization

Microscopy

Spectroscopy

Experimental design

Vacuum chambers

Coating deposition

Materials processing

Materials characterization testing

Sputtering

E-beam deposition

High-vacuum systems

Research involving space environments

However, applicants should not be discouraged if they do not possess every skill listed.

NASA specifically notes that prior experience with these specialized techniques is not a requirement because of the unique nature of the work. The most important quality is a willingness to learn.

This is an important consideration for undergraduate students who may have a strong academic foundation but limited exposure to specialized NASA laboratory equipment or lunar-environment research.

Academic Backgrounds Relevant to the Internship

The opportunity lists a broad range of preferred majors, particularly within engineering and physical sciences.

Relevant academic disciplines include:

Engineering

Aerospace, Aeronautical, and Astronautical/Space Engineering

Ceramic Sciences and Engineering

Chemical Engineering

Electrical, Electronics, and Communications Engineering

Electromechanical Engineering

Engineering Chemistry

Engineering Mechanics

Engineering Physics

Applied Physics

Manufacturing Engineering

Materials Engineering

Mechanical Engineering

Metallurgical Engineering

Polymer and Plastics Engineering

Physical Sciences

Materials Science

The broad range of eligible majors reflects the interdisciplinary nature of lunar dust mitigation research. The work combines principles from materials science, engineering, physics, chemistry, manufacturing, surface science, and space-environment research.

Who Should Consider Applying?

This opportunity could be particularly valuable for undergraduate students who are interested in:

Space exploration

NASA research

Lunar missions

Materials science

Aerospace engineering

Mechanical engineering

Chemical engineering

Materials engineering

Metallurgy

Laboratory research

Advanced materials

Space environments

Students who are considering graduate studies or careers involving aerospace research, advanced materials, spacecraft technology, or space systems may also find the experience valuable.

NASA Glenn Research Center

The internship will take place at NASA’s Glenn Research Center (GRC) in Cleveland, Ohio.

NASA Glenn is a major NASA research center with expertise spanning areas of aerospace technology, propulsion, materials, power systems, communications, and other technologies supporting space exploration and aviation.

Working in this environment can give interns exposure to professional research practices and the processes involved in developing and evaluating technologies for demanding aerospace applications.

For a student interested in materials and space technology, an internship at a NASA research center can provide an opportunity to see how academic concepts are applied to real-world engineering and research challenges.

What Students Can Learn

Although the specific activities will depend on the intern’s assignment, the opportunity can provide exposure to several valuable areas of technical and professional development.

These may include:

The internship can therefore help students connect classroom knowledge with practical research.

A Strong Opportunity for Students Interested in Space Technology

Future lunar exploration will require technologies that can function reliably in environments significantly different from those found on Earth. Dust mitigation is one of the many engineering challenges that must be addressed as NASA and its partners work toward increasingly capable lunar missions.

The development of passive coatings represents one potential approach to reducing the effects of lunar dust. By helping investigate these materials, an intern can contribute to research connected to a practical challenge in lunar exploration.

The opportunity also demonstrates how materials engineering can play a direct role in space exploration. Students do not necessarily have to study a degree explicitly titled “space engineering” to contribute to space technology. Materials science, mechanical engineering, chemical engineering, physics, metallurgy, ceramics, polymers, and related disciplines can all contribute to solving aerospace problems.

No Specialized Experience Required

One of the most encouraging aspects of this internship is NASA’s statement that specific prior experience is not required.

The work involves specialized techniques, including sputtering, coating deposition, microscopy, spectroscopy, and vacuum systems. However, NASA recognizes that students may not have previously worked with all of these technologies.

Instead, the opportunity emphasizes the importance of being willing to learn.

Applicants should therefore focus on demonstrating:

Commitment to hands-on research

Students with relevant laboratory or engineering experience can highlight it, but lack of experience with every listed technology should not automatically discourage an otherwise suitable applicant.

Application Deadline

The registration deadline is September 14, 2026.

Applicants should complete the registration and application process before the deadline and carefully review all requirements and instructions provided through NASA’s internship system.

Because this is an in-person, full-time opportunity with a specific citizenship requirement, prospective applicants should verify their eligibility before investing significant time in preparing their application.

How to Apply

Interested students should use NASA’s official internship opportunities platform and search for the opportunity using:

Tips for a Strong Application

Students applying for this opportunity can strengthen their application by clearly connecting their academic background and interests to the work described in the internship.

Consider highlighting:

Mention coursework related to materials, engineering, chemistry, physics, mechanics, manufacturing, or other relevant technical areas.

2. Laboratory experience

If you have completed laboratory courses, research projects, university experiments, or independent technical projects, explain what you did and what you learned.

3. Research experience

Describe any research involving materials, coatings, surfaces, environmental testing, characterization, or experimental methods.

4. Technical skills

Clearly identify relevant skills such as microscopy, spectroscopy, experimental design, materials characterization, CAD, laboratory equipment, data analysis, or other applicable technical abilities.

5. Willingness to learn

Because NASA specifically emphasizes willingness to learn, applicants without extensive specialized experience should demonstrate curiosity and adaptability.

Conclusion

The NASA Lunar Dust Mitigation Intern opportunity offers undergraduate students a chance to participate in hands-on research addressing a genuine engineering challenge associated with future lunar exploration. Based at NASA Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, Ohio, the Spring 2027 internship combines laboratory experimentation with materials research, coating development, characterization, and testing under simulated environmental conditions.

The opportunity is particularly relevant to students studying materials engineering, aerospace engineering, mechanical engineering, chemical engineering, metallurgy, polymer science, ceramics, physics, materials science, and other related disciplines.

While experience with sputtering, microscopy, spectroscopy, vacuum chambers, coatings, or materials characterization is advantageous, NASA makes clear that specialized prior experience is not mandatory. A strong willingness to learn is considered especially important.

With a September 14, 2026 registration deadline, eligible students interested in contributing to technologies for future lunar missions should review the opportunity and submit their applications before the closing date.

TITLE: FAPESP Young Investigator Grant for International Researchers 2026: Up to BRL 2.5 Million for Researchers to Establish Research Programs in Brazil

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The São Paulo Research Foundation (FAPESP) has launched the Young Investigator Grant for International Researchers 2026, a major research funding opportunity designed to attract outstanding researchers from around the world to establish or consolidate independent research careers at leading higher education and research institutions in the State of São Paulo, Brazil.

The international call seeks researchers with strong academic trajectories, internationally recognized expertise, demonstrated research achievements, and the potential to become scientific leaders in strategically important fields.

Under the 2026 call, FAPESP plans to support up to 20 outstanding researchers, with successful projects receiving funding of up to BRL 2.5 million per proposal. A Young Investigator Fellowship may also be requested in addition to this funding limit.

Research projects will have a duration of 60 months, providing successful researchers with substantial time and resources to establish laboratories, build research teams, develop independent research programs, and pursue internationally competitive scientific work in São Paulo.

Applications must be submitted by November 19, 2026.

About the FAPESP Young Investigator Grant for International Researchers

The Young Investigator Grant for International Researchers is an initiative of the São Paulo Research Foundation (FAPESP).

FAPESP is a public foundation of the State of São Paulo with a mission to support research across all fields of knowledge at higher education and research institutions throughout São Paulo.

The Foundation operates in close collaboration with the scientific community, and research proposals submitted for FAPESP support undergo peer review involving specialists in relevant disciplines.

Through this dedicated international call, FAPESP aims to strengthen São Paulo’s scientific and technological leadership by attracting researchers currently based outside Brazil who have the expertise and potential to develop independent, high-impact research programs.

The 2026 initiative is expected to support up to 20 researchers.

Purpose of the 2026 International Call

The central purpose of the FAPESP Young Investigator Grant for International Researchers is to attract outstanding scientific talent from abroad to research institutions in São Paulo.

FAPESP is seeking researchers who can establish or consolidate their research careers in the state while creating independent and internationally competitive research programs.

The initiative is particularly focused on candidates who demonstrate:

Outstanding expertise in their respective fields;

Originality and independence in research;

Strong scientific achievements following completion of their doctorate;

Potential for scientific leadership;

Ability to establish an independent research program;

Capacity to create new research collaborations;

Potential to conduct high-impact research; and

A research trajectory demonstrating international competitiveness.

Successful applicants are expected to establish a research laboratory and develop a dedicated research program at an institution located in the State of São Paulo.

Research Areas Supported by the FAPESP Young Investigator Grant 2026

Projects submitted under this international call must fall within the strategic research themes identified by FAPESP.

The eligible research areas are:

Biotechnology

Energy Transition

Biodiversity, Sustainable Production and Food Security

Digital Transition and Artificial Intelligence

Quantum Science and Technology

Human and Animal Health

Public Security

These fields reflect areas that FAPESP considers strategically important for strengthening scientific and technological development.

Projects approved specifically under the artificial intelligence research theme will be affiliated with the recently established São Paulo Artificial Intelligence Research Center, which is supported by FAPESP, MCTI/CGI.br and São Paulo State Universities.

Who Can Apply?

The 2026 call is specifically designed to attract researchers who are currently living and working outside Brazil.

Researchers of all nationalities may apply, provided they satisfy the program’s eligibility requirements.

Applicants must have been living and working abroad for at least two years after completing their PhD.

Eligible professional experience abroad can include:

Postdoctoral appointments;

Research fellowships;

Permanent academic positions;

Permanent research positions; or

Other qualifying appointments at research institutions.

Applicants must also be residing abroad when they submit their proposals.

The successful researcher is expected to relocate to São Paulo and establish or consolidate their research career at an eligible research institution in the state.

Research Experience and Leadership Requirements

Simply holding a PhD is not sufficient to make an application competitive.

FAPESP expects applicants to demonstrate significant achievements since completing their doctoral studies.

Their academic and research trajectory should provide evidence of:

Original scientific contributions;

Research independence;

Leadership capacity;

Scientific impact;

International research experience;

Ability to establish an independent research program;

Capacity to build research collaborations; and

Potential to undertake ambitious research at the frontier of knowledge.

Applicants must demonstrate outstanding expertise and leadership within their respective fields through the quality, originality, relevance, and impact of their scientific achievements.

Establishing a Research Program in São Paulo

An important feature of the program is that successful researchers are not simply expected to conduct a temporary research visit in Brazil.

Applicants should be prepared to establish a research laboratory and develop a dedicated research program at an institution in the State of São Paulo.

Successful candidates are expected to become fully integrated into their host institutions and demonstrate a strong commitment to both the proposed project and their research position.

This makes the program particularly relevant for international researchers seeking an opportunity to establish or consolidate an independent academic and scientific career in Brazil.

Independent Research Requirement

Competitive proposals must present a clearly defined and independent research line led by the applicant.

Researchers may collaborate with established research groups on particular topics, and such collaborations are permitted and encouraged.

However, the proposed project should demonstrate the applicant’s own scientific independence and ability to lead an internationally competitive research program.

This distinction is important because FAPESP is seeking researchers capable of developing new scientific directions rather than merely joining existing projects as supporting researchers.

Funding Available

One of the most significant features of the FAPESP Young Investigator Grant for International Researchers 2026 is the scale of funding available.

The maximum funding available per proposal is BRL 2,500,000.

This amount represents the maximum requested project budget under the call.

Importantly, the Young Investigator Fellowship may be requested in addition to the BRL 2.5 million funding limit.

Funding will follow the applicable FAPESP criteria and regulations for the Young Investigator Grant.

Young Investigator Fellowship

A Young Investigator Fellowship may be awarded for up to the full duration of the research grant.

The fellowship can continue until the Principal Investigator obtains a permanent position at a university or research institution in the State of São Paulo.

This arrangement is intended to provide researchers with support while they establish themselves within São Paulo’s research ecosystem.

During implementation of the project, Principal Investigators are encouraged to apply for permanent positions available at their host institution or other universities and research institutions within São Paulo.

This creates a potential pathway toward a longer-term academic or research career in Brazil.

Funding for Research Team Members

Successful applicants may also request scholarships and fellowships for members of their research teams in accordance with the applicable FAPESP rules.

Potential categories include:

PhD scholarships;

Master’s scholarships;

Scientific Initiation scholarships;

Postdoctoral Fellowships; and

Other eligible fellowship modalities under FAPESP rules.

For this particular call, however, only one scholarship or fellowship of each modality can be included in a proposal.

For each requested fellowship, the applicant must provide a one-page summary explaining the research objectives, work plan, and implementation schedule associated with that position.

Relocation Support for International Researchers

Successful applicants currently living abroad may also qualify for relocation support.

According to the call, this can include airfare for the successful applicant in accordance with FAPESP’s applicable relocation-support rules.

This is particularly important because the program requires selected researchers to establish their research activities within the State of São Paulo rather than conducting the project remotely from another country.

Number of Researchers to Be Supported

FAPESP states that a maximum of 20 fellowships will be awarded under this international call.

The program is therefore selective and aimed at researchers with particularly strong academic records and ambitious research proposals.

Candidates should ensure that both their scientific track record and proposed research clearly demonstrate originality, impact, independence, and international competitiveness.

Project Duration

Research projects submitted under the program must have a duration of:

60 months

This represents a five-year research period.

Upon request and subject to evaluation by FAPESP, both the project and associated fellowship may potentially be extended by up to 12 additional months.

The five-year structure provides researchers with substantial time to establish laboratories, recruit and develop research teams, generate scientific outputs, establish collaborations, and consolidate independent research programs.

Potential Long-Term Career Pathway

The program may also serve as a pathway toward longer-term academic and scientific careers within São Paulo.

During implementation, Principal Investigators are encouraged to apply for available permanent positions at their host institution or other eligible universities and research institutions in the state.

Researchers who obtain permanent positions after completing their projects may potentially continue their work through other FAPESP funding mechanisms.

This can include the Young Investigator Grant – Phase 2, provided the researcher satisfies the relevant eligibility criteria and successfully completes the applicable merit-review process.

Documents Required for Application

Applicants must prepare a comprehensive proposal package.

1. Short CV

Candidates must submit a short CV in English of no more than five pages.

It should include relevant researcher identification information, including:

Scopus ID;

Google Scholar profile; and

Web of Science ResearcherID.

Applicants must also provide a career summary of no more than 400 words.

The CV should explain the applicant’s most important scientific achievements and their relevance to the proposed research project.

Candidates must identify their five most important publications, explaining their leadership role in the research and the scientific impact of those contributions.

The CV must additionally identify the applicant’s three most significant invited talks, academic degrees, and previous professional appointments.

2. Research Trajectory Letter

Applicants must provide a letter of no more than two pages explaining how their research trajectory evolved toward the central concept underlying the proposed project.

The letter should highlight significant findings, observations, scientific developments, and experiences that contributed to the development of the proposed research direction.

3. Research Project

Applicants must submit a detailed research project demonstrating:

Clearly defined objectives;

Originality;

Scientific ambition;

Strong scientific rationale;

Potential advances at the frontier of knowledge;

International competitiveness;

Feasibility of implementation; and

The research team’s capacity to complete the work successfully.

The main body of the research project must not exceed 20 pages, including references, excluding annexes and supporting documents.

4. Fellowship Work Plans

If scholarships or fellowships are requested for team members, applicants must clearly describe the activities associated with each position.

A one-page summary must be submitted for every requested fellowship, including the research objectives, work plan, and implementation schedule.

5. Budget Information

Applicants must enter requested budget items through FAPESP’s SAGe system.

Vendor quotations must be provided for capital equipment that will be purchased in Brazil or abroad when its value exceeds the threshold specified under FAPESP regulations.

Language of Application

Research proposals must be submitted in English.

Applicants should therefore ensure that their scientific arguments, methodology, objectives, expected results, and broader research rationale are presented clearly and professionally in English.

How to Apply

Applications must be submitted through FAPESP’s SAGe system.

Applicants using the English interface should navigate through:

New Proposal > Special Programs > YIG – Young Investigator Grant > Grant for International Researchers > Call for Proposals (2026)

Candidates should prepare their documentation well before the deadline because the application involves several substantial components, including a research proposal, academic CV, research-trajectory letter, fellowship plans where applicable, and budget documentation.

Evaluation Process

The proposal submission and evaluation process consists of three major stages:

Submission of the proposal;

Evaluation by external reviewers and FAPESP’s evaluation process; and

Online presentation and interview for selected candidates.

Initial Eligibility Assessment

An Evaluation Committee will assess whether the applicant and proposed research align with the objectives and expected profile of the international Young Investigator Grant.

The assessment considers factors including:

Originality and innovation;

Potential scientific impact;

Potential societal impact;

Scientific quality;

Research relevance;

Project feasibility;

Potential contribution to advancing knowledge;

Applicant’s scientific background;

Research achievements; and

Career trajectory.

Full Proposal Evaluation

Full proposals will be sent to at least two external reviewers.

A FAPESP evaluation panel will consider these assessments when reviewing the applications.

Among the issues considered will be the project’s potential impact on its field, its relationship to existing scientific work, and whether it provides new approaches to relevant research challenges.

Reviewers and the evaluation panel will also consider the applicant’s capacity to establish new strategic collaborations with research institutions at local, regional, and international levels while maintaining scientific independence.

Interview Stage

Candidates whose full proposals receive a positive recommendation may be invited to participate in an online oral presentation and interview with members of the Evaluation Committee.

Applicants should therefore be prepared not only to submit a strong written proposal but also to explain and defend their proposed research program, its significance, methodology, feasibility, originality, and potential impact.

Application Deadline

The deadline for submitting full proposals is:

November 19, 2026

Applicants should ensure that all required materials are submitted through the appropriate FAPESP system before the deadline.

Results Announcement

FAPESP expects the final results to be announced beginning in:

June 2027

Successful projects should normally begin before December 2027, except where exceptional circumstances apply.

Key Dates at a Glance

Call Announcement: September 2026

Full Proposal Deadline: November 19, 2026

Final Results: From June 2027

Expected Project Start: Before December 2027

Project Duration: 60 months

Possible Extension: Up to 12 months, subject to request and FAPESP evaluation

Why This Opportunity Matters for International Researchers

The FAPESP Young Investigator Grant for International Researchers represents more than short-term project financing.

It provides successful researchers with the opportunity to establish an independent research program within one of Brazil’s largest scientific and academic ecosystems.

The combination of substantial research funding, a five-year project period, potential fellowship support, research-team scholarships, relocation assistance, and the possibility of pursuing permanent academic positions makes the program particularly relevant to internationally mobile researchers seeking to build independent scientific careers.

The emphasis on independence is also important. FAPESP is looking for applicants capable of leading their own research directions and developing internationally competitive programs rather than simply participating in existing research activities.

Tips for Preparing a Competitive Application

Applicants should begin preparing well before the November deadline because the application requires extensive scientific and administrative documentation.

Researchers should ensure that their proposals clearly demonstrate:

Why the proposed research question matters;

What makes the research original;

How it advances the frontier of knowledge;

Why the applicant is particularly well positioned to conduct the project;

How the project differs from existing research;

Whether the proposed methodology is scientifically rigorous and feasible;

What scientific or societal impact could result;

How the researcher will establish an independent research line;

How the project could strengthen research capacity in São Paulo; and

How the applicant’s previous achievements demonstrate leadership potential.

Applicants should also ensure that their CV, trajectory letter, and research proposal tell a coherent scientific story.

Conclusion

The FAPESP Young Investigator Grant for International Researchers 2026 offers an exceptional opportunity for accomplished early-career and emerging independent researchers currently based outside Brazil to establish ambitious research programs in the State of São Paulo.

With up to BRL 2.5 million in project funding, the possibility of an additional Young Investigator Fellowship, relocation support, research-team scholarships and fellowships, and a 60-month project duration, the program provides substantial resources for researchers seeking to build independent and internationally competitive scientific programs.

Researchers from all nationalities may be considered, provided they satisfy the eligibility conditions, including having lived and worked abroad for at least two years after completing their PhD and being based abroad when submitting the application.

Research proposals can address strategically important areas ranging from biotechnology and artificial intelligence to energy transition, quantum science, health, biodiversity, sustainable production, food security, and public security.

Eligible researchers interested in establishing or consolidating their research careers in São Paulo should begin preparing their applications well ahead of the November 19, 2026 deadline.

Scientific Structures

Image: Uploaded from Freepik. © Wirestock

The Committee on Radio Astronomy Frequencies (CRAF)

The Committee on Radio Astronomy Frequencies (CRAF) is an Expert Committee hosted and administered by the European Science Foundation. Established in 1988, it represents all the major radio astronomical observatories in Europe.

The Committee’s mission is to coordinate activities to keep the frequency bands used by radio astronomers in Europe free from interference. CRAF works towards this task by:

Promoting the policies and position of radio astronomy and space sciences in Europe in discussions with the major public and private telecommunications agencies.

Acting as the European voice together with other groups of radio astronomers in discussions within the international bodies that decide on the use of radio spectrum.

Initiating and encouraging scientific studies aimed at reducing radio astronomy interference at source and the effects of interference.

In addition, the Committee works on behalf of IRAM (Institut de Radio Astronomie Millimétrique) and IVS (International VLBI Service for Geodesy and Astrometry), which use radio astronomy bands for their scientific research.

The Committee also assists EISCAT (the European Incoherent Scatter Scientific Association), whose passive experiment using radar equipment in the polar ionosphere faces severe interference problems.

Membership, Structure, and Funders

The Committee is chaired by Dr. Benjamin Winkel (Max-Planck-Institut für Radioastronomie, Germany)

At present, CRAF has 26 members from 23 countries from Europe and South Africa. The membership list is available on the CRAF Website

CRAF is funded by the following Member Institutions:

TITLE: Visiting PhD Fellowship 2027 at United Nations University-WIDER — Fully Funded Research Opportunity for PhD Students

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The UNU-WIDER Visiting PhD Fellowship Programme 2027 offers doctoral students an opportunity to strengthen their PhD research while working with one of the world’s leading development economics institutes. This fully funded fellowship allows researchers to access UNU-WIDER’s resources, collaborate with experts, and advance research focused on developing economies.

Application form will become available on the 1st of September, 2026. The deadline for applications is 30 September 23:59 UTC+3.

For PhD candidates seeking international research exposure, publication opportunities, and academic networking, this programme provides a strong platform to enhance both dissertation quality and career development.

Visiting PhD fellows typically spend three consecutive months at UNU-WIDER before returning to their home institution. During the programme, fellows prepare one or more research papers and present a seminar on their research findings. They may also have the opportunity to publish their research in the WIDER Working Paper Series.

You can read about previous experiences from the programme, here.

About the UNU-WIDER Visiting PhD Fellowship Programme

The Visiting PhD Fellowship Programme enables registered doctoral students to:

Use UNU-WIDER’s research resources and facilities

Collaborate with researchers on shared research interests

Develop research papers related to their dissertation or thesis

Present a seminar based on their research findings

Potentially publish in the WIDER Working Paper Series

Fellows usually spend three consecutive months at UNU-WIDER before returning to their home institution.

Fellowship Duration and Research Activities

During the three-month fellowship period, participants are expected to:

Advance their doctoral research

Engage with UNU-WIDER researchers and academic discussions

Prepare research outputs suitable for publication

Present their research in a seminar setting

The programme is designed to strengthen research quality and support policy-relevant academic work.

Eligibility Criteria

Applicants must:

Be currently enrolled in a PhD programme

Demonstrate ability to conduct research on developing economies

Possess strong quantitative and/or qualitative analytical skills

Be fluent in written and spoken English

Although UNU-WIDER is an economics-focused institute, researchers from other social science disciplines may apply if their work aligns with development-related themes.

Submissions on topics related to the UNU-WIDER work programme are particularly welcome.

Priority Applicants

Applications are especially encouraged from:

Early-career researchers

Female researchers

Researchers from developing countries

PhD candidates at later stages of their studies

The programme is highly competitive. In recent years, approximately one percent of applications were successful.

Financial Support

When the fellowship is undertaken in Helsinki, UNU-WIDER provides:

A travel grant covering travel to and from the applicant’s institution or country of residence

Medical insurance during the fellowship period

A monthly stipend of EUR 2,100 to support living expenses in Helsinki

The programme does not cover expenses related to dependents.

Application Timeline and Deadlines

UNU-WIDER accepts applications twice each year.

September Application Cycle

Application form opens: 1 September (00:00 UTC+3)

Deadline: 30 September (23:59 UTC+3)

Fellowship period: March to June (following year)

March Application Cycle

Application form opens: 1 March (00:00 UTC+3)

Deadline: 31 March (23:59 UTC+3)

Fellowship period: September to November (same year)

The online application link becomes active one month before each deadline.

Application Requirements

Applicants must submit:

Completed online application form

Updated curriculum vitae (CV)

Reference letter from PhD supervisor

The reference letter must be sent directly by the supervisor to:

phdreference@wider.unu.edu

This letter also confirms the applicant’s enrolment in a PhD programme.

Applications submitted by email or post are not accepted.

Selection Process

Applications are assessed competitively based on eligibility and research alignment

Final decisions are communicated by email within four weeks after the deadline

Selected applicants must confirm acceptance within two weeks of notification

Why Apply for the UNU-WIDER Visiting PhD Fellowship?

This fellowship is ideal for doctoral researchers who want to:

Strengthen their dissertation with international research support

Work closely with leading development economists

Build academic and policy research networks

Increase opportunities for publication

Enhance future academic and professional prospects

How to Apply

Interested candidates should complete the online application form once it becomes available during the application window.

If you are interested in participating in this programme you should complete and submit the application form. For more details on the submission and for practical information on the programme, please see our frequently asked questions page.

Apply

Contact Information

If you have questions about the programme or you experience any problems with your online application, please first check our questions and answers page. If you are still experiencing problems please contact us at the following email address: phdfellow@wider.unu.edu

Please note that replies may take up to five working days.

The UNU-WIDER Visiting PhD Fellowship 2026 is a highly competitive and valuable opportunity for doctoral students conducting research on developing economies. With financial support, access to expert researchers, and opportunities to publish, the programme provides a strong environment for advancing high-quality, policy-relevant research.
