TITLE: ARC East of England Research and Impact Fellowships 2027: Research and Health Care Fellowship Opportunity in the UK

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The ARC East of England Research and Impact Fellowships 2027 are now open for applications, offering health and care professionals an opportunity to develop their research, evidence-based practice, service improvement, and implementation skills while working on practical projects within health and care settings.

The fellowship programme is designed for professionals who already have hands-on experience in the health, care, and voluntary sectors in the East of England and want to develop their ability to conduct research, evaluate services, implement evidence-based improvements, and create meaningful impact in practice.

Applications are open for the April 2027 intake, with the deadline set for 9 December 2026 at 12:00 noon.

Opportunity Overview

Opportunity: ARC East of England Research and Impact Fellowships

Year: 2027

Start date: April 2027

Deadline: 9 December 2026 at 12:00pm

Location: East of England, United Kingdom

Fields: Health, social care, research, service improvement, evidence-based practice and implementation

Fellowship types: Research Fellowship and Impact Fellowship

Target applicants: Health, care and voluntary sector professionals working in the East of England

About the ARC East of England Fellowship Programme

The Applied Research Collaboration (ARC) East of England Fellowship programme was established in 2010 to strengthen research capacity across the health and care sectors in the East of England.

Since its establishment, more than 170 ARC Fellowships have been awarded across the region.

The programme provides professionals with an opportunity to develop their research and evidence-based practice capabilities while remaining closely connected to the real-world challenges facing health and care organisations.

The programme is particularly valuable because it brings together research and practice.

Rather than focusing only on academic research, fellows are encouraged to work on practical projects that can help improve services, inform decision-making, strengthen professional practice, and generate positive outcomes for patients, service users and communities.

With annual fellowship calls planned between 2026 and 2031, more than 60 fellows are expected to receive training during this period. The programme therefore represents an important investment in developing research and improvement capacity across the East of England health and care system.

What Is the ARC East of England Fellowship?

The ARC East of England Fellowship supports professionals who already have practical experience in health and care and want to develop their ability to use research and evidence to improve services.

As a fellow, you will have the opportunity to lead a small-scale research or improvement project connected to your professional environment.

The fellowship is designed to help participants develop skills in areas including:

Research methods

Applied research

Service evaluation

Evidence-based practice

Service improvement

Change management

Implementation of research evidence

Knowledge translation

Dissemination of research findings

Evaluation and audit

Applying evidence to real-world health and care settings

The programme is particularly suitable for people interested in working at the point where research, policy and professional practice meet.

Two Fellowship Routes Are Available

Applicants can apply for one of two fellowship routes:

1. ARC Research Fellowship

The Research Fellowship focuses on conducting local applied research and evaluation projects.

This can include areas such as:

Applied research

Service evaluation

Audits

Evidence generation

Evaluation of existing practices

Research designed to address local health and care challenges

The goal is to help fellows develop the skills and confidence needed to generate and use evidence to improve health and care services.

A Research Fellow may therefore identify a practical problem within their organisation or professional environment and develop a research or evaluation project to better understand the issue.

The findings can then help inform improvements in service delivery or professional practice.

2. ARC Impact Fellowship

The Impact Fellowship is designed for professionals who are particularly interested in taking existing evidence and putting it into practice.

Instead of primarily focusing on generating new research evidence, the fellowship focuses on how evidence can be implemented, communicated, shared and used to create real-world improvements.

This route can therefore be particularly relevant to professionals interested in:

Implementing evidence-based interventions

Improving services

Knowledge mobilisation

Disseminating research findings

Supporting organisational change

Changing professional practice

Improving health and care outcomes

The Impact Fellowship aims to develop the knowledge and skills required to ensure that research does not remain confined to academic publications but is translated into meaningful improvements in health and care settings.

What Type of Projects Should Applicants Consider?

Prospective applicants are encouraged to think carefully about the health and care problem they want their fellowship project to address.

Projects should have a clear connection to real-world health, care or voluntary-sector practice.

Applicants are also encouraged to consider the 10 Year Health Plan for England and how their proposed work could contribute to the three major shifts identified in the plan.

These are:

From Hospital to Community

This shift focuses on moving appropriate care away from hospitals and closer to where people live.

Projects could therefore explore ways of strengthening community-based services, improving access to care outside hospitals, or supporting better coordination between different parts of the health and care system.

From Analogue to Digital

Digital transformation is another major priority.

Applicants could consider how technology, digital systems, data, digital communication or other innovations can improve the way health and care services are delivered.

Potential projects could explore areas such as digital access, digital health interventions, technology-enabled care or the use of data to improve decision-making.

From Sickness to Prevention

The third shift focuses on prevention rather than responding only after people become ill.

Projects could therefore examine approaches that help prevent illness, identify health risks earlier, support healthier behaviours, or improve population health.

Applicants should consider how their proposed research or impact project can contribute to one or more of these broader priorities.

Why Apply for the ARC Fellowship?

The fellowship provides an opportunity for professionals to develop research and improvement capabilities while working on an issue that is relevant to their organisation or professional environment.

Develop Research Skills

Fellows can strengthen their understanding of research methods and learn how to develop and conduct applied research projects.

Gain Experience in Evidence-Based Practice

The programme helps participants understand how evidence can be identified, evaluated and used to inform decisions and improve services.

Develop Service Improvement Skills

The fellowship can help professionals develop practical skills in identifying problems, designing improvements and evaluating whether changes are achieving their intended results.

Learn About Change Management

Health and care improvements often require organisational and behavioural change. The programme provides an opportunity to develop skills for managing and supporting change.

Create Real-World Impact

One of the strongest aspects of the fellowship is its emphasis on applying knowledge to real-world health and care challenges.

Rather than research being conducted purely for academic purposes, fellows are encouraged to generate knowledge or implement evidence that can contribute to improvements in practice.

Build Research Capacity

The fellowship contributes to developing research capacity within health and care organisations across the East of England.

By participating, fellows can become better equipped to contribute to research, evaluation and improvement activities within their organisations.

The ARC East of England Fellowship is intended for professionals who are already working across the health, care and voluntary sectors in the East of England.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Applicants interested in this fellowship should begin by identifying a clear issue within their professional setting.

A strong proposal should ideally demonstrate:

A clearly defined problem

Explain the health, care or service issue that needs to be addressed.

Why the issue matters

The organisation in which the project will take place

A well-designed project should be sufficiently focused to be achievable while still producing useful learning or impact.

Nationality and Race

The information provided for this opportunity does not specify a nationality, race or ethnic restriction.

However, the key eligibility requirement is connected to the applicant’s professional role and location: applicants should be working within the relevant health, care or voluntary-sector organisations in the East of England.

Therefore, nationality or race should not be presented as the primary eligibility criterion. Applicants should instead verify their professional and organisational eligibility through the official fellowship guidance.

Conclusion

The ARC East of England Research and Impact Fellowships 2027 provide an opportunity for health, care and voluntary-sector professionals to strengthen their research, evaluation, implementation and service improvement skills while addressing practical challenges within their working environments.

With two routes available, applicants can choose between a Research Fellowship, focused on applied research and evaluation, or an Impact Fellowship, focused on implementing and disseminating evidence-based improvements.

The programme is particularly valuable for professionals who want to bridge the gap between research and practice and use evidence to create meaningful improvements in health and care.

TITLE: United Nations Chemicals and Waste Management Study Programme 2026: Fully Funded Youth Scholarships to Attend UN Programme and Global Framework on Chemicals Conference in Geneva

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Young people interested in chemicals and waste management, environmental health, sustainable development, international environmental governance, and United Nations processes have an opportunity to participate in the United Nations Chemicals and Waste Management Study Programme 2026 in Geneva, Switzerland.

The Chemicals and Waste Youth Platform (CWYP) and the United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR) are offering up to eight fully funded scholarships to eligible youth, students, recent graduates, and early-career professionals to participate in the second edition of the Study Programme from 9–13 November 2026.

The opportunity will also provide selected participants with additional opportunities to engage in youth activities and negotiations connected to the Global Framework on Chemicals First International Conference (GFC IC-1) from 14–20 November 2026.

The scholarship is particularly valuable for young people from developing countries and other eligible groups who want practical exposure to United Nations environmental processes, professional development opportunities, expert-led learning, and youth participation in international chemicals and waste governance.

Application deadline: Friday, 11 September 2026, at 23:59 UTC.

United Nations Chemicals and Waste Management Study Programme 2026: Overview

The November 2026 Study Programme is being organized following the successful inaugural edition held in July 2026.

The programme is intended to provide young participants with an opportunity to understand how chemicals and waste management issues are addressed within the United Nations system and international environmental governance.

Selected participants will take part in structured learning, professional development, expert sessions, site visits, career activities, and collaborative work.

The programme will be held in Geneva, Switzerland, from 9–13 November 2026, followed by opportunities related to the Global Framework on Chemicals First International Conference from 14–20 November 2026.

Key details

Opportunity: United Nations Chemicals and Waste Management Study Programme 2026

Scholarship provider/organizers: Chemicals and Waste Youth Platform and UNITAR

Scholarships available: Up to 8 fully funded scholarships

Target participants: Youth, students, recent graduates and early-career professionals

Age requirement: 18–35 years at the time of application

Location: Geneva, Switzerland

Study Programme: 9–13 November 2026

Additional GFC IC-1 opportunities: 14–20 November 2026

Travel period required: 8–20 November 2026, inclusive

Funding: Fully funded travel support for selected scholarship recipients

Application deadline: 11 September 2026 at 23:59 UTC

Expected notification: Successful applicants are expected to be contacted by 19 September 2026

Certificate: UNITAR Certificate of Completion

Application: Online application form

What Is the United Nations Chemicals and Waste Management Study Programme?

The United Nations Chemicals and Waste Management Study Programme is a youth-focused learning and professional development programme connected to the international chemicals and waste management agenda.

It gives participants the opportunity to look beyond theoretical discussions and gain exposure to how chemicals and waste issues are addressed through international institutions and United Nations processes.

According to the programme information, participants will have opportunities to see the “behind the scenes” aspects of chemicals and waste processes within the UN system in Geneva. They will also participate in interactive training with experts and receive guidance concerning career pathways in the United Nations and international environmental governance.

The programme is therefore particularly relevant to young people who want to understand the intersection between:

Environmental governance

Chemicals management

Waste management

Environmental health

Sustainable development

International policy

Multilateral negotiations

United Nations processes

Youth participation

Environmental careers

Up to 8 Fully Funded Scholarships Available

One of the most significant features of the 2026 opportunity is the availability of up to eight fully funded scholarships.

The scholarships are intended to support eligible young participants who may otherwise face financial barriers to attending the programme in Geneva.

The organizers have outlined several forms of financial and logistical support for successful scholarship recipients.

The support includes international travel, accommodation, programme fees, and reimbursement of certain additional costs subject to the organizers’ conditions and approval.

Because the number of scholarships is limited, applicants should prepare carefully and ensure that their applications demonstrate genuine motivation, relevant interests, and a clear commitment to sharing what they learn.

What Does the Fully Funded Scholarship Cover?

The scholarship package includes several important components.

1. Economy-Class Round-Trip Flight

Selected scholarship recipients will receive economy-class, round-trip flight tickets, which will be booked by the Organizing Team.

This support is designed to enable eligible participants to travel to Geneva and return to their home country after the programme and associated activities.

2. Hotel Accommodation

Hotel accommodation will be arranged by the Organizing Team.

This removes a major cost associated with participating in an international programme in Geneva, where accommodation can otherwise represent a substantial portion of a participant’s travel budget.

3. Study Programme Fees

The scholarship covers the fees associated with participating in the Study Programme.

Selected participants therefore do not need to independently finance the programme participation costs covered under the scholarship.

4. Meals, Visa Fees and Transportation

The scholarship information also states that meals, visa fees and transportation costs can be reimbursed against receipts and subject to approval by the Organizing Team.

Applicants should therefore retain appropriate receipts and follow the organizers’ instructions concerning reimbursable expenses.

Important funding condition

Although the opportunity is described as fully funded, applicants should understand that certain expenses are handled through reimbursement and require receipts and approval.

The scholarship information also makes clear that visa approval is at the discretion of the relevant host and transit countries, while registration for the Study Programme and GFC IC-1 is subject to the decisions of UNITAR and the GFC Secretariat respectively. Completing the application does not guarantee admission or participation.

Who Can Apply for the Scholarship?

The opportunity is specifically aimed at young people who meet a defined set of eligibility requirements.

Applicants must satisfy the stated criteria.

Age Requirement

Applicants must be between 18 and 35 years old at the time of application.

This means the opportunity is designed for young adults, including students, recent graduates and professionals in the early stages of their careers.

Learn More

Country and Community Eligibility

Applicants must meet one of the programme’s geographic or community eligibility categories.

They must be from a:

Low- and Middle-Income Country (LMIC)

Least Developed Country (LDC)

Small Island Developing State (SIDS)

Alternatively, the applicant may be a representative of Indigenous Peoples.

This is an important part of the eligibility criteria and should be carefully reviewed before applying.

Availability for the Full Programme

Applicants must be available to travel to and remain in Geneva from 8–20 November 2026, inclusive.

They must also be committed to participating in the full duration of the programme.

This requirement is particularly important because the opportunity extends beyond the five-day Study Programme itself. Participants may also engage in activities connected to GFC IC-1 during the subsequent period.

Application Deadline Requirement

Applicants must submit a completed application by the stated deadline:

11 September 2026 at 23:59 UTC.

What Kind of Applicants Are the Organizers Looking For?

Meeting the minimum eligibility requirements does not automatically mean that an applicant will be selected.

The Selection Team will evaluate applications based on the quality and sincerity of the applicants’ written responses.

In particular, the programme seeks applicants who can demonstrate:

Clear motivation for participating

Relevant interests or experience

Alignment with chemicals and waste management or related fields

Interest in environmental health or international environmental governance

Connection between the programme and their career aspirations

A commitment to sharing knowledge after the programme

An interest in contributing to follow-up activities within their communities, organizations or networks

This means that applicants should not simply state that they want to travel to Geneva or attend a United Nations event.

A stronger application should demonstrate why the programme matters to the applicant’s current activities, interests and future plans.

Applicants Must Use Their Own Voice

The organizers have provided an important warning concerning the application.

Copy-pasted AI-generated responses are not permitted.

The programme emphasizes that sincere and personalized applications are more valuable than responses that simply appear grammatically perfect.

Applicants are encouraged to explain what genuinely excites them about the programme, describe relevant projects they are working on, and share experiences or stories that help the Selection Team understand who they are.

This is especially important for applicants preparing written responses.

Instead of producing generic statements such as “I am passionate about environmental sustainability,” applicants should explain:

What sparked their interest in the subject.

What they are currently doing.

What environmental or chemicals-related challenge they have encountered.

What project they are working on.

What they hope to learn.

How they intend to apply the knowledge after returning home.

How they could contribute to their community or professional network.

The objective should be to communicate an authentic personal story.

What Will Participants Learn?

The November Study Programme includes several components designed to provide participants with both technical knowledge and practical exposure.

According to the programme information, the programme will include:

Expert lectures

Technical workshops

Site visits

Career sessions

Collaborative innovation activities

Exposure to UN chemicals and waste processes

Professional development

Guidance on career pathways in international environmental governance

These activities can give participants a more comprehensive understanding of the international chemicals and waste management system.

Expert Lectures and Technical Workshops

Participants will attend expert lectures and technical workshops addressing thematic areas connected to chemicals and waste management.

These sessions can provide opportunities to learn directly from experts working in the field and to better understand the challenges involved in managing chemicals and waste at international and national levels.

The technical component is particularly relevant for participants pursuing careers or projects related to environmental policy, environmental health, sustainable development, chemicals management, waste management or related disciplines.

Site Visits in Geneva

The programme will also include site visits to Geneva-based institutions.

The information provided specifically mentions visits to places such as:

Palais des Nations

A hazardous waste management facility

These visits can provide participants with practical exposure to institutions and facilities relevant to international governance and chemicals and waste management.

This practical element can complement the classroom-style learning and expert sessions.

Career Sessions and United Nations Career Pathways

Another major component of the programme is career development.

Participants will receive insights into United Nations internship and entry-level recruitment processes.

The sessions are intended to provide guidance concerning career pathways within the UN system and international environmental governance.

For young professionals and recent graduates interested in international organizations, this can provide useful exposure to how careers in multilateral institutions can develop.

Pollution Solutions Lab

The programme will feature the Pollution Solutions Lab, described as a flagship CWYP-UNITAR innovation and “hackathon” session.

During this activity, participants will work collaboratively to develop practical project proposals addressing chemicals and waste management challenges.

This component moves beyond passive learning.

Participants will have an opportunity to collaborate with other young people, think about real-world environmental challenges, and develop practical responses.

The experience may be particularly useful for applicants interested in:

Environmental innovation

Project development

Social impact

Sustainability

Policy solutions

Entrepreneurship

Youth-led environmental action

UNITAR Certificate of Completion

Participants who complete the programme will receive a UNITAR Certificate of Completion.

The certificate can serve as evidence of participation in an international training programme focused on chemicals and waste management and related areas.

Applicants should, however, view the certificate as one component of the broader learning experience. The programme’s practical sessions, expert engagement, site visits, collaborative work and exposure to international environmental governance are also important aspects of the opportunity.

What Is UNITAR?

The United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR) has been involved in capacity building since 1963.

According to the programme information, UNITAR provides more than 500,000 learning initiatives annually.

Through its Division for Planet, UNITAR’s Chemicals and Waste Management Programme supports countries in implementing international agreements related to chemicals and waste.

The programme information identifies several important international agreements and frameworks associated with this work, including:

Basel Convention

Rotterdam Convention

Stockholm Convention

Minamata Convention

Global Framework on Chemicals

As of 2026, UNITAR also serves as the host of the Inter-Organization Programme for the Sound Management of Chemicals (IOMC) Secretariat.

What Is the Global Framework on Chemicals?

The Study Programme is connected to the Global Framework on Chemicals (GFC) and its First International Conference.

The Global Framework on Chemicals is described as a comprehensive policy framework for a planet free of harm from chemicals and waste.

It was adopted in September 2023 at the fifth International Conference on Chemicals Management.

The framework addresses a broad range of chemical safety issues, including:

Highly hazardous pesticides

Endocrine-disrupting chemicals

Pharmaceutical pollutants

Safer chemicals management

Chemical production

Chemical use

Chemical disposal

The framework replaced the earlier Strategic Approach to International Chemicals Management (SAICM) and establishes five strategic objectives and 28 targets, with many intended to be achieved between 2030 and 2035.

Why Youth Participation in the Global Framework on Chemicals Matters

The programme highlights youth participation as an important component of the Global Framework on Chemicals process.

According to the information provided, the GFC’s multistakeholder and multisectoral model creates opportunities for youth and other civil society groups to participate directly in discussions and negotiations.

Youth participants can potentially:

Propose text and resolutions.

Deliver interventions during negotiations.

Participate alongside country delegates.

Meet country and stakeholder delegations.

Advocate for youth priorities.

Participate in the Youth Forum on Chemicals and Waste.

Contribute to policy discussions concerning chemicals and waste.

This makes the opportunity relevant not only to students and professionals seeking training but also to young people interested in environmental policy advocacy and international negotiations.

Global Framework on Chemicals First International Conference

Following the Study Programme, additional youth engagement opportunities will be coordinated around the Global Framework on Chemicals First International Conference (GFC IC-1).

The Study Programme takes place from 9–13 November 2026, while the associated GFC IC-1 opportunities run from 14–20 November 2026.

The programme information states that youth delegates may be expected to participate in activities including:

The three-day Youth Forum on Chemicals and Waste

This gives selected young people an opportunity to move from learning about international environmental governance to actively participating in it.

However, applicants are also permitted to submit a new application if there have been significant changes to their:

The programme emphasizes the importance of the written responses.

Selection will consider whether applicants demonstrate:

Career alignment

TITLE: Can the marked Arctic Ocean freshwater content increases of the last two decades be explained within observational uncertainty?

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Le Bras, I. A.-A., & Timmermans, M.-L. (2025). Can the marked Arctic Ocean freshwater content increases of the last two decades be explained within observational uncertainty? Journal of Geophysical Research-Oceans, 130(2), e2024JC021061. https://doi.org/10.1029/2024JC021061

The freshwater content of the Arctic Ocean has increased dramatically in the last two decades, particularly in the Beaufort Gyre. However, quantifying the sources of this change is an observational challenge and has historically been limited by methodological differences across studies. Here we derive observation-based freshwater budgets from volume and mass budgets for the Arctic Ocean and the Beaufort Gyre from 2003 to 2020. Our budgets include all sources and sinks (river runoff, precipitation minus evaporation, land ice melt, sea ice export, sea ice melt, and ocean fluxes) as well as volume and mass storage terms measured by satellite. We find that Arctic freshwater changes are dominated by changes in the Beaufort Gyre, and we reconcile this with previous studies that argue for freshwater compensation between the Beaufort Gyre and the rest of the Arctic. We use inverse methods to close the volume and mass budgets within observational uncertainty and link the observed Arctic freshwater changes to the sources and sinks. Our budget analysis demonstrates that small changes to the ocean fluxes (smaller than we can measure) can account for all freshwater storage changes in the Arctic, highlighting the need for more careful accounting and detailed ocean observations in this rapidly changing environment.

TITLE: Mellon/ACLS Dissertation Innovation Fellowship 2026–27: $42,000 Stipend for Innovative PhD Research in the Humanities and Social Sciences

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Mellon/ACLS Dissertation Innovation Fellowship is now accepting applications from doctoral students developing innovative approaches to dissertation research in the humanities and interpretive social sciences.

Supported by a grant from the Mellon Foundation, the fellowship is designed for early-stage PhD students whose dissertation projects seek to move beyond conventional research methods, formats, disciplines or approaches. The program provides financial support, research and professional development funding, and external mentorship to help doctoral researchers develop ambitious and potentially field-changing projects.

Up to 45 fellowships will be awarded for the 2027–28 academic year. Each fellowship lasts approximately nine to twelve months, beginning between July 1 and September 1, 2027.

Fellowship Benefits

The Mellon/ACLS Dissertation Innovation Fellowship provides substantial financial and professional support.

The award includes:

$42,000 base stipend for the fellowship year.

Up to $3,000 for research and travel expenses.

Up to $5,000 in professional development funding for skills acquisition or additional research.

An additional $2,000 stipend for the external mentor.

A one-year fellowship period covering the 2027–28 academic year.

The possibility of undertaking the fellowship at the fellow’s home institution or another appropriate research location.

The fellowship is intended to give doctoral students dedicated time away from normal coursework, teaching and assistantship responsibilities so they can concentrate on specialized research, training and dissertation development.

What Is the Mellon/ACLS Dissertation Innovation Fellowship?

The fellowship is specifically designed to support dissertation projects that expand the traditional boundaries of doctoral research.

Rather than primarily supporting dissertations that are already well underway or approaching completion, ACLS seeks to support students at a formative stage of their doctoral research. The program allows fellows to reconsider how their research questions are investigated, how evidence is collected and analyzed, how scholarly knowledge is communicated, and even what form the final dissertation might take.

Innovation can take many forms. A project could introduce:

New research methodologies.

Interdisciplinary approaches.

Digital research methods.

Collaborative research.

Community-engaged research.

Alternative dissertation formats.

New modes of scholarly communication.

Critical or unconventional approaches to established fields.

Partnerships with organizations outside academia.

ACLS is particularly interested in applicants who can demonstrate that their proposed approach has the potential to move their field in an important new direction.

Who Is the Fellowship Designed For?

The program is intended for early-stage doctoral researchers rather than students whose dissertations are already substantially complete.

ACLS describes the fellowship as an intervention at the formative stage of dissertation development. This means applicants should be at a point where the fellowship can meaningfully influence the direction, methodology, format or development of their dissertation.

Because doctoral programs differ considerably, ACLS provides a flexible eligibility window. Some eligible applicants may be applying shortly before achieving candidacy or ABD status, while others may already have achieved candidacy but only after the specified eligibility date.

However, the program requires applicants to have completed all required coursework by the time the fellowship begins.

Examples of Innovative Research Activities

The fellowship can support a wide range of activities depending on the needs of the proposed dissertation.

Examples include:

Interdisciplinary Research and Training

A fellow may undertake directed interdisciplinary research or methodological training with scholars within their university or at another institution.

This could allow a doctoral researcher to acquire expertise that is not traditionally part of their primary discipline.

New Dissertation Formats

Applicants may explore alternative ways of presenting scholarly research rather than relying exclusively on the conventional dissertation format.

This could include innovative forms of scholarly communication and dissertation design.

Digital Methods

The fellowship can support intensive training in digital research methods where these methods are necessary for the project.

Community Collaboration

Applicants may develop equitable collaborations with community partners, particularly where community knowledge and participation are central to the research.

Non-Academic Practicum

A fellow may undertake a short-term practicum with a non-academic organization, such as a cultural, policy or social justice organization.

This can provide experience with applied research, community-engaged research or site-based collaborative approaches.

These examples are not exhaustive. ACLS emphasizes that innovation may be transdisciplinary, interdisciplinary, digital, collaborative, critical, methodological or related to publication and scholarly communication.

External Mentorship Opportunity

One distinctive feature of the Mellon/ACLS Dissertation Innovation Fellowship is the provision for external mentorship.

The purpose of the external mentor is to expand the fellow’s advisory network beyond their existing doctoral supervision structure.

An external mentor may be:

From another department at the fellow’s university.

From another academic institution.

From outside academia.

The mentor should bring expertise, perspectives or networks that can strengthen the dissertation project.

Importantly, the external mentor must be outside the fellow’s existing advising relationships within their program or department.

The fellowship provides a separate $2,000 stipend for the external mentor.

Support for Underrepresented Research and Perspectives

ACLS places considerable emphasis on broadening the range of voices, subjects, perspectives and methodologies represented within academic research.

Projects that thoughtfully engage with communities or topics that have historically been underrepresented or understudied in higher education are encouraged.

The program welcomes research addressing different historical periods, communities and regions of the world, provided the research falls within an eligible field.

ACLS also encourages institutional diversity by welcoming applications from doctoral students in eligible departments at all accredited institutions of higher education in the United States.

Eligibility Requirements

Applicants must satisfy several important requirements.

Applicants Must:

Be a PhD student in a humanities or social science department in the United States.

Be able to undertake a full year of sustained specialized research and training.

Be released from normal coursework, teaching and research assistantship responsibilities during the fellowship.

Have completed at least two years of the PhD program.

Have completed all required doctoral coursework by the start of the fellowship.

Not have advanced to PhD candidacy/ABD status before January 1, 2026.

Have applied for this fellowship no more than once previously.

Intend to complete their dissertation after May 31, 2029.

Applicants must also be prepared to devote the fellowship period to the proposed research and training.

They cannot accept teaching or research assistantships, other major fellowships, internships or similar internal or external awards during the fellowship tenure.

Fields and Degrees That Are Not Eligible

The program has a specific disciplinary focus.

It does not accept applications from students pursuing professional or applied PhDs, terminal degrees that are not PhDs, or doctoral programs outside the humanities and interpretive social sciences.

The source specifically excludes programs and fields including:

Business.

Clinical or counseling psychology.

Creative or performing arts.

Education.

Engineering.

Filmmaking.

Law.

Library and information sciences.

Life and physical sciences.

Public administration.

Public health.

Medicine.

Public policy.

Social work.

Social welfare.

Applicants who are uncertain about whether their department or interdisciplinary program qualifies are encouraged to contact ACLS before applying.

Race, Nationality and Geographic Eligibility

The competition welcomes eligible doctoral students regardless of race, ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, religion, national origin, disability, age or other aspects of identity.

The important geographic requirement is that applicants must be enrolled in an eligible PhD program at an accredited institution of higher education in the United States.

Therefore, the fellowship is not restricted to a particular racial, ethnic or national group. International students may potentially be eligible if they are doctoral students in an eligible U.S.-based PhD program and satisfy all other requirements.

Evaluation Criteria

Applications will be assessed according to several major criteria.

1. Contribution to Knowledge

Reviewers will consider whether the proposed project has the potential to advance the applicant’s field and make an original and significant contribution to knowledge.

2. Innovation

The project should demonstrate the potential to challenge scholarly conventions or expand prevailing ideas about what constitutes important scholarship.

Innovation may come through:

Research format.

Methodology.

Subject matter.

Theoretical framework.

Interdisciplinary collaboration.

Community partnerships.

3. Feasibility

Applicants must demonstrate that the proposed work can realistically be completed within the fellowship period and the broader doctoral timeline.

An innovative idea must therefore be accompanied by a credible plan for implementation.

4. Engagement With Underrepresented Communities

Reviewers will consider how thoughtfully the project engages with communities historically underrepresented in higher education and how those experiences may influence the applicant’s research and scholarly practice.

5. Applicant Preparedness

The review process will also consider whether the applicant is adequately prepared to complete the proposed research, taking into account the resources and constraints surrounding their academic journey and project.

Application Requirements

Applicants must submit their applications online through the ACLS fellowship administration system.

The application package must include several components.

Completed Application Form

Applicants must complete the official online fellowship application form.

Research Proposal

The proposal must be no more than seven pages, double-spaced, with one-inch margins and written in Arial or Helvetica 11-point font.

The proposal should explain:

The aims of the research.

What the applicant plans to accomplish during the fellowship.

The innovative approach being taken.

Why the fellowship is important at this particular stage of the doctoral project.

Training or workshops that will be required.

Research travel.

Research permissions.

Other resources necessary to advance the project.

How the applicant plans to secure necessary research permissions.

The role of an external mentor, if already identified.

The qualities and expertise sought in an external mentor if one has not yet been selected.

How success will be measured during the fellowship year.

The full scholarly output of the dissertation.

Optional Supporting Materials

Applicants may submit up to two additional pages containing images, musical scores or similar supporting non-text materials.

These materials must be unannotated.

Project Timeline

Applicants must provide a one-page timeline using the ACLS-provided template.

The timeline should outline:

Activities during the fellowship year.

The expected trajectory after the fellowship.

The period leading toward completion of the dissertation.

The timeline must use Arial or Helvetica 11-point font.

Bibliography

Applicants must provide a bibliography of key primary and secondary sources.

The bibliography must be:

No more than two pages.

Single-spaced.

Unannotated.

In Arial or Helvetica 11-point font.

Prepared with one-inch margins.

Personal Statement

A personal statement of no more than two pages is required.

The statement should describe the applicant’s journey as a scholar and explain how their personal experience, research interests and desire to transform academic research methods and formats come together in their work.

Work Sample

Applicants must submit a brief work sample of no more than 15 pages total.

The sample should include a brief explanation of its context and its relationship to the proposed project.

The formatting requirements include double spacing, one-inch margins and Arial or Helvetica 11-point font, with citations included within the page limit.

Recommendation Letter

Applicants must provide one letter of recommendation.

The letter must come from:

The applicant’s dissertation advisor; or

A faculty member who is eligible to serve as the applicant’s dissertation advisor.

Institutional Statement

The applicant’s institution must also provide a statement, preferably from the department chair, director of graduate studies or dean.

The institution must confirm several important matters, including that:

Existing institutional financial support will be paused during the fellowship and that the fellow will be allowed to retain and resume the remaining support afterward.

The institution will allow the fellow to remain enrolled during the fellowship.

Tuition and fees will be waived or covered.

The institution can accommodate the student’s exploration of non-traditional approaches to scholarly research and dissertation development.

Transcripts Are Not Required

An important application detail is that transcripts are not required for this fellowship application.

Applicants should nevertheless ensure that all other required components are complete and properly formatted before submission.

AI Use in the Application

The fellowship’s guidelines explicitly allow applicants to use AI tools such as ChatGPT or Claude when preparing their applications.

However, the responsibility remains entirely with the named applicant to ensure that the application is accurate and properly sourced.

Applicants are responsible for:

Factual accuracy.

Proper acknowledgement of sources.

Correct referencing.

Avoiding plagiarism.

Checking for errors or omissions.

Ensuring that any AI-generated material accurately represents their research.

ACLS also encourages applicants to disclose where and how AI assistance was used in the application for transparency.

Additional Opportunity Through CHCI

Fellows may have an additional opportunity through a partnership between ACLS and the Consortium of Humanities Centers and Institutes (CHCI).

Through this partnership, fellows may have the opportunity to spend all or part of their fellowship period in residence at selected CHCI member organizations.

CHCI is an international membership organization of interdisciplinary research centers with more than 170 members and affiliates across 23 countries.

This is an optional enhancement to the fellowship and does not require a separate application.

APPLY HERE

Application Support and Applicant Resources

ACLS provides resources to help prospective applicants understand the competition and prepare their applications.

Applicants can access:

Application office hours.

Webinars explaining the application process.

Live Zoom sessions with program staff.

Frequently Asked Questions.

Guidance relating to research permissions.

Information about requesting reviewer feedback.

The listed office-hour sessions include dates in August, September and October 2026, giving prospective applicants several opportunities to ask questions before the application deadline.

Application Deadline

The deadline for the Mellon/ACLS Dissertation Innovation Fellowship 2026–27 competition is:

Wednesday, October 28, 2026, at 5:00 PM Eastern Time (ET).

Completed applications must be submitted through the ACLS online fellowship administration system by the stated deadline.

Applicants should not wait until the final hours to submit, particularly because the application contains several components, including a research proposal, timeline, bibliography, personal statement, work sample, recommendation letter and institutional statement.

Fellowship Timeline

The fellowship will cover the 2027–28 academic year.

Key dates and stages include:

Application deadline: October 28, 2026, at 5 PM ET.

Notification: Late April 2027.

Fellowship start: Between July 1 and September 1, 2027.

Fellowship duration: Nine to twelve months.

Fellowship year: 2027–28 academic year.

Up to 45 fellowships will be awarded.

Who Should Consider Applying?

This fellowship may be particularly suitable for doctoral students who believe their dissertation could benefit from moving beyond traditional disciplinary or methodological approaches.

It may be a strong fit for a student who wants to:

Introduce digital methods into a humanities project.

Develop interdisciplinary research.

Work with community partners.

Experiment with alternative dissertation formats.

Develop new forms of scholarly communication.

Undertake specialized methodological training.

Build relationships with researchers outside their home institution.

Work with organizations outside academia.

Explore research topics involving historically underrepresented communities.

Develop a dissertation that combines multiple disciplines or methodologies.

The strongest applicants will need to demonstrate not simply that their project is interesting, but why innovation is necessary and how the proposed innovation will strengthen the dissertation and contribute to the field.

Important Things Applicants Should Know

Before applying, prospective candidates should carefully consider several key conditions.

First, this is not primarily a fellowship for doctoral students who are already close to completing their dissertations. The program is designed to support research at a formative stage.

Second, applicants must have completed their required coursework by the time the fellowship begins.

Third, applicants must not have advanced to PhD candidacy/ABD status before January 1, 2026.

Fourth, the fellowship requires a significant commitment of time. Fellows cannot simultaneously hold teaching or research assistantships, other major fellowships, internships or similar awards during the fellowship period.

Finally, the proposed research should demonstrate genuine innovation rather than simply presenting a conventional dissertation project with minor modifications.

Learn More About This Opportunity HERE

How to Prepare a Strong Application

A competitive application should clearly connect the research problem, innovative approach, fellowship timing and expected outcomes.

Applicants should make it easy for reviewers to understand:

What the dissertation is about.

What is innovative about the proposed research.

Why conventional approaches are insufficient for the project.

What new methods, formats or collaborations will be introduced.

Why the fellowship year is the right time to pursue these innovations.

What training and resources are required.

How the proposed work will contribute to the broader field.

How the project can realistically be completed within the proposed timeline.

How the research engages with communities, particularly those historically underrepresented in higher education, where relevant.

What the final scholarly outputs will look like.

The proposal should therefore demonstrate both intellectual ambition and practical feasibility.

Conclusion

The Mellon/ACLS Dissertation Innovation Fellowship 2026–27 is a major funding opportunity for early-stage PhD researchers in the humanities and interpretive social sciences who want to develop innovative, interdisciplinary, digital, collaborative, critical or otherwise unconventional approaches to dissertation research.

With a $42,000 base stipend, up to $8,000 in combined research, travel and professional development funding, a separate $2,000 external mentor stipend, and a nine-to-twelve-month fellowship period, the program provides doctoral researchers with both financial support and the time needed to substantially develop their projects.

The fellowship is open to eligible doctoral students regardless of race, ethnicity, gender, religion, national origin or other identity, but applicants must be pursuing an eligible PhD in the humanities or interpretive social sciences at an accredited U.S. institution.

For applicants whose dissertation research challenges traditional academic boundaries, this fellowship offers an opportunity to rethink not only what they research, but how doctoral research can be conducted, communicated and shared.

The application deadline is October 28, 2026, at 5:00 PM Eastern Time. Prospective applicants should begin preparing early, particularly because the application requires multiple documents and institutional support.

Applications are open for the UNESCO/Japan Young Researchers’ Fellowships Programme 2026. Established in 2001 under the Japanese Funds-in-Trust for the Capacity-Building of Human Resources, the UNESCO/Japan Young Researchers’ Fellowships Programme, also known as the UNESCO/Keizo Obuchi Research Fellowships Programme, is a long-standing initiative supported by the Government of Japan to strengthen research capacities and promote international knowledge exchange in areas aligned with UNESCO’s mandate.

Under the 2026 cycle, UNESCO and the Government of Japan will award 10 fellowships to highly qualified young researchers from Africa, Small Island Developing States, Ukraine and Türkiye. Benefits

Selected fellows may receive a fellowship grant of up to US$10,000. The grant will be provided as a lump-sum contribution and is intended to cover costs directly related to the approved research stay in Japan.

The grant may cover:

international and domestic travel for the approved itinerary;

accommodation;

medical insurance;

personal subsistence in Japan, including meals, local transportation and incidental expenses;

other research-related expenses, where applicable.

Eligibility

Applicants must:

be nationals of one of the invited Member States or Associate Members;

be no more than 40 years old at the time of application;

hold at least a Master’s degree or equivalent in a field relevant to the proposed research and demonstrate strong academic and research potential;

demonstrate sufficient proficiency in reading and writing in the language of instruction or supervision at the proposed host institution in Japan;

have obtained acceptance from an academic supervisor at a Japanese university or research institution, who will oversee the proposed research.

Application

Step 4: Submit your application to the National Commission for UNESCO of your home country, at least 2 weeks before the required deadline.

Step 5: As soon as you are informed by the National Commission for UNESCO of your country that you are nominated as a candidate for this programme, you should communicate your the online application form and the supporting documents to keizoobuchi.fellowships@unesco.org.

Note: Only applications nominated by the National Commission will be accepted by UNESCO.

Step 6: Letters of nomination, along with all the application documents should be submitted to UNESCO by the National Commissions no later than 30 September 2026, midnight Paris time. Candidates who submit incomplete applications, or submit the online applications beyond this deadline won’t be considered.

TITLE: Finding the Right Investment in Foreign Currencies

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Foreign currency investment can offer investors an opportunity to diversify their portfolios, gain exposure to growing economies and potentially benefit from movements in exchange rates. However, currencies can move quickly in response to economic, political and global events, making it important to approach foreign currency investment with research rather than speculation. Finding the right foreign currency investment begins with understanding what drives the value of a currency and determining whether the opportunity fits your financial goals, investment horizon and tolerance for risk.

Understand What You Are Investing In
Investing in a foreign currency is different from simply exchanging money before travelling. An investor is effectively taking a position on how one currency may perform relative to another. For example, someone holding British pounds who invests in US dollar-denominated assets has exposure to movements between the pound and the dollar. Even when the underlying investment performs well, changes in the exchange rate can increase or reduce the investor’s eventual return. This means that investors should consider two things: the quality of the investment itself and the potential movement of the currency in which it is denominated.

Look at the Strength of the Economy
A country’s economic condition can have a significant influence on its currency. Before investing, examine indicators such as economic growth, inflation, employment, government debt, trade performance and consumer confidence. A growing economy does not automatically mean that its currency will appreciate, but understanding these indicators provides useful context. Investors should also consider the country’s longer-term economic prospects. Is the economy becoming more productive and competitive? Is it attracting international investment? Is it heavily dependent on a single commodity or industry? These questions provide a broader picture than simply looking at today’s exchange rate.

Pay Attention to Interest Rates and Inflation
Central banks play an important role in currency markets. Decisions about interest rates can affect how attractive a currency is to international investors. Higher interest rates can sometimes increase demand for a currency because investors may seek better returns on deposits and fixed-income investments. However, the relationship is not always straightforward. Very high interest rates may also indicate serious inflation or economic instability. Inflation is equally important. Persistent high inflation reduces purchasing power and can place downward pressure on a currency over time. Investors should therefore examine interest rates alongside inflation rather than treating either indicator in isolation.

Consider Political and Institutional Stability
Currencies respond not only to economics but also to politics. Elections, conflicts, changes in government policy, trade disputes, sanctions and political instability can significantly affect investor confidence. Countries with credible institutions, predictable economic policies and relatively stable political environments may present different currency risks from countries experiencing frequent policy changes or political uncertainty. Before investing, consider what could realistically change within the country during your intended investment period.

Decide How You Want to Gain Currency Exposure
Buying physical foreign currency is only one way of gaining exposure. Depending on the investor’s circumstances and jurisdiction, foreign currency exposure may also come through foreign-currency bank accounts, international bonds, overseas shares, funds, exchange-traded funds and other financial instruments. For example, an investor who believes strongly in the long-term prospects of the US economy may decide that investing in carefully selected US assets is more appropriate than simply holding dollars. The important question is not merely, “Which currency should I buy?” but “What investment gives me the most appropriate exposure to this currency and economy?”

Understand Currency Pairs
Currencies are valued relative to other currencies. This is why foreign-exchange markets use currency pairs such as GBP/USD, EUR/USD or USD/JPY. Suppose GBP/USD is 1.30. Broadly, this means £1 buys approximately US$1.30. If the pound strengthens against the dollar, the exchange rate changes accordingly. For an investor, the relevant question is therefore not simply whether the dollar is “strong”. It is whether the dollar is likely to strengthen or weaken relative to the investor’s home currency during the investment period.

Do Not Chase a Currency Because It Is Rising
One of the biggest mistakes investors can make is entering an investment simply because its recent performance looks impressive. A currency that has appreciated considerably may already reflect much of the positive economic information available to the market. Likewise, a currency that has fallen sharply is not automatically a bargain. Ask why the movement occurred and whether the conditions responsible for it are likely to continue. Successful investing requires separating a genuine long-term opportunity from short-term market excitement.

Calculate the Real Cost of Investing
Exchange rates displayed online are not necessarily the rates an investor will receive. Banks, brokers and money-transfer providers may charge transaction fees or incorporate a margin into their exchange rates. Some investments also carry management, trading, custody or withdrawal fees. Imagine converting £10,000 into another currency, investing it and later converting the proceeds back into pounds. Your real return will depend on the investment performance, currency movement, transaction costs, applicable taxes and other fees. These costs should be calculated before committing capital.

Diversify Instead of Betting Everything on One Currency
Currency movements are difficult to predict consistently. Concentrating a large proportion of wealth in one foreign currency can therefore create significant risk. Diversification can reduce dependence on the performance of one country, currency or economic environment. Depending on an investor’s circumstances, this could mean spreading investments across different geographical markets, currencies and asset classes. The objective is not to find one “perfect” currency. It is to construct a portfolio capable of performing across different economic conditions.

Know Your Reason for Investing
Before purchasing any foreign currency investment, be able to answer a simple question: Why am I making this investment? Perhaps you are diversifying your savings, preparing for future expenses in another country, investing internationally, protecting against weakness in your domestic currency or pursuing long-term capital growth. Your purpose should influence your strategy. Someone saving for university fees in the United States has a fundamentally different reason for holding dollars from someone attempting to profit from short-term movements in the foreign-exchange market. The appropriate level of risk will therefore be different.

Think Long Term and Manage the Risk
Foreign currency investment should form part of a wider financial strategy rather than becoming a gamble on the next exchange-rate movement. Before investing, consider how much you can afford to lose, how long you intend to remain invested and what circumstances would cause you to reconsider the investment. Investors should be particularly cautious with leveraged foreign-exchange trading, where relatively small currency movements can produce disproportionately large losses. The strongest approach combines economic research, diversification, disciplined risk management and a clear understanding of personal financial objectives.

The Bottom Line
Finding the right foreign currency investment is less about predicting which currency will suddenly rise and more about understanding the economies, institutions and investments behind those currencies. Research economic fundamentals. Follow central-bank decisions. Understand inflation and interest rates. Consider political risk. Calculate transaction costs. Diversify your exposure and, above all, understand why the investment belongs in your portfolio. Foreign currencies can provide useful opportunities within a diversified investment strategy, but they also introduce risks that should not be underestimated. A good investment decision is therefore not simply about finding a strong currency. It is about finding an appropriate investment, at an acceptable level of risk, that supports your wider financial goals.

TITLE: Tribute to Dr. Rispa Achieng’ Odongo – From the Association of African Universities

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Secretary General of the Association of African Universities (AAU) on behalf of the Governing Board and African Universities, expresses the profound shock of the AAU at the passing of Dr. Rispa Odongo, on Saturday, April 20th, 2022.

Dr. Rispa Odongo was the Chairperson of the Technical Working Group (TWG) for the development of the African Standards and Guidelines for Quality Assurance in higher education (ASG-QA), which is one of the tools developed under the Harmonization of African Higher Education Quality Assurance and Accreditation (HAQAA) Initiative, a Pan African Quality Assurance and Accreditation System (PAQAF). The Association of African Universities, is one of the partners of the HAQAA initiative and worked closely with her under this initiative.

In March 2019, she facilitated a workshop organized by the AAU in collaboration with the African Quality Assurance Network (AfriQAN) on Good Practices in quality assurance in higher education, to enlighten Quality Assurance (QA) agencies and HEIs on current developments in QA . This was hosted at the University of Nairobi, Kenya.

Dr. Rispa Odongo worked for the Commission for University Education (CUE), Kenya from 1993 to 2016 and was the Head of Department of Curriculum (Programme Accreditation) between 2004 and 2013. Following her retirement from the CUE in 2016 after 23 years of service, she served in a number of regional and international positions offering expertise in Quality Assurance. She also worked and consulted for various institutions (on higher education related assignments), including UNESCO and the Inter-University Council for East Africa (IUCEA).

She earned a Doctorate of Education in Higher Education Leadership from Walden University, USA, a Postgraduate Certificate in Quality Assurance from the University of Melbourne, Australia, a Master of Science in Animal Production and Health from the University of Edinburgh (U.K) and a Bachelor of Veterinary Medicine from the University of Nairobi (Kenya).

Dr. Rispa Odongo was a mentor to many people, and made impacts nationally, regionally and globally. Africa has indeed lost a distinguished daughter. Our condolences go out to her family, country and the entire African Higher Education fraternity.

Applications should be received by 30th November 2019.

Annex

Extract from relevant sections of the Project Appraisal Document – Africa Higher Education Centers of Excellence for Development Impact (ACE Impact) Project (P164546)

1. The proposed project consists of three components: Component 1: Establishing new and scaling-up well-performing existing ACEs (from ACE I) for development impact; Component 2: Fostering regional partnerships and scholarships; and Component 3: Enhancing national and regional project facilitation, and monitoring and evaluation (M&E). Component 1 will aim to strengthen capacity in the ACEs and their host institutions (supply-side), while Component 2 will aim to strengthen non-ACE institutions in the region and allow students to benefit from the capacity in the ACEs (demand-side). Component 3 will aim to support national and regional facilitation of the project and M&E related activities. Financing for Component 1 and 2 will be result-based, while financing for Component 3 will be cost-based.

Component 1: Establishing new and scaling up well-performing existing Africa Centers of Excellence (from ACE I) for development impact (Total: US$198 million; of which IDA and government contributions are 50 percent each)

Component 1 aims to build and strengthen the capacity of 16 competitively selected centers located in higher education institutions across West and Central Africa. Component 1 has two sub-components: Sub-component 1.1 will establish new ACE Impact centers for skills development and knowledge generation (through applied research) to address development challenges, that are not addressed under the ACE I project. Sub-component 1.2 will provide additional support to well-performing ACEs participating in the ongoing ACE I project (these ACE Impact centers will be referred to as renewals) to scale-up impact on development challenges, to strengthen regional collaboration, and ensure that these ACEs are fully fiscally sustainable). Additional funding will support the best engineering and technology institutions hosting ACEs from Sub-components 1.1 and 1.2, to strengthen institutional impact.

Each ACE Impact center (new and renewals) supported through Component 1 will focus activities on a specific regional development challenge. Each of these centers is targeted in scope and will deliver postgraduate education and applied research programs developed in coordination with relevant stakeholders. While the center workplans are focused, a multidisciplinary approach will be essential to achieve the goals of each center.Component 2: Fostering Regional Partnerships and Scholarships (Total: US$40 million of which the IDA contribution is US$23 million and government contribution is US$17 million)

Component 2 seeks to expand the regional impact of the ACEs funded under Component 1 by providing demand-side funding for partnering institutions and regional students to purchase training and consulting services from the ACEs that are most relevant. Component 2 has two sub-components: Sub-component 2.1 will finance regional institutional partnerships through support to Emerging centers, while Sub-component 2.2 is optional and will finance governments’ contribution towards the PASET RSIF.Component 3: Enhancing National and Regional level Project Facilitation, and Monitoring and Evaluation (Total: US$13.5 million; of which US$10 million is in IDA grant and $3.5 is in IDA credit)

Component 3 will support regional and national project facilitation and monitoring and evaluation (M&E).Sub-component 3.1: Regional-level project facilitation and monitoring and evaluation (M&E) (Total:US$10 million in IDA grant).

Through a regional IDA grant of US$10 million, Sub-component 3.1 will fund the Association of African Universities (AAU), which will continue as the Regional Facilitation Unit (RFU), to facilitate the ACE Impact I project’s regional activities and support the centers under the project. Activities will include: M&E activities such as development of an online M&E database platform, verification of results, benchmarking of ACE host universities, and graduate tracer studies; site supervision visits of ACEs by independent experts; communications, safeguards support, capacity-building; and knowledge-sharing and networking among ACEs and governments. The RFU will also liaise with ongoing regional and national initiatives in order to strengthen the ACE regional networks, including through digital networking platforms.Sub-component 3.2: National-level project facilitation (Total:US$3.5 million in IDA credit).

Under Sub-component 3.2 activities in Burkina Faso and Ghana will be coordinated by the national agencies responsible for tertiary education. The total allocation, including contingencies, will be US$3.5 million. This sub-component will finance project implementation support at the national level in the countries where the ACE Impact I investments exceed US$25 million. These are the National Council for Tertiary Education (NCTE) for Ghana and the Ministry of Higher Education, Research and Innovation (MESRSI) for Burkina Faso. The MESRSI of Burkina Faso currently hosts the Project Implementation Unit (PIU) of its IDA -Funded national higher education project (mentioned earlier in the document). This same MESRSI-PIU will play the national facilitator role for ACEs in Burkina Faso. The objective is to provide national level support to the centers, within their respective countries. Performance of these national level facilitation agencies will be measured by the degree to which the ACE Impact centers in the respective countries achieve the project objectives including compliance with fiduciary, safeguard and anti-corruption guidelines. The activities will include supervision and training related to educational, research, implementation, fiduciary and safeguards aspects; as well as national M&E and minor TA.Procurement

For all Implementing Agencies, procurement under the proposed project will be carried out in accordance with the following World Bank procedures: (a) the World Bank Procurement Regulations (PR) for IPF Borrowers, dated July 2016 and revised in November 2017, and August 2018; and (b) “Guidelines on Preventing and Combating Fraud and Corruption in Projects Financed by IBRD Loans and IDA Credits and Grants”, dated October 15, 2006 and revised in January, 2011 and as of July 1, 2016 and other provisions stipulated in the FAs. STEP will be the platform for preparing, reviewing and clearing Procurement Plans as well as reviewing of prior review procurement activities.

Each component of the project will have its own procurement arrangements. Procurement activities under Component 1 and Sub-component 2.1 will be implemented by the selected education institutions in the Borrower countries, and the Bank funds will be disbursed against a set of DLIs to finance the non-procurable expenditures as defined under the EEPs. Other expenditures, the non-EEPs, including procurement of goods and civil works under the project will be procured together with the institutions’ other operating requirements and needs, following the institutions’ own procurement procedures. These non-EEPs will be financed by the institutions’/governments’ own funds and therefore, the procurement plans for those activities will not be prepared in STEP nor will they be reviewed and cleared by the Bank. If any such procurable expenditures are at any point to be included for Bank-financing, the center and its host institution shall be required to follow the PR as stated in Bank Guidance on IPF with DLI (dated April 25, 2018) Section III 23,24,25 and Annex 2 for the entire budget line of each of such procurable expenditures. The procurement plans for such procurement activities will be prepared, reviewed and cleared in STEP, as well as any prior review procurement. Contributions towards Sub-component 2.2 will be disbursed directly upon project effectiveness to icipe, the RFU for the Bank-financed Africa Regional Scholarship and Innovation Fund for Applied Sciences, Engineering and Technology project. Component 3 will finance inputs-based expenditures for facilitation, coordination and study activities by AAU, NCTE and MESRSI-PIU, and these institutions will follow the Bank’s Procurement Regulations when implementing the activities under the project.

Consistent with the above procurement arrangements, different procurement assessments were carried out for various institutions by the Bank during project preparation. For each of the coordinating entities (AAU, NCTE and the MESRSI-PIU), a procurement capacity assessment was carried out as required for any implementing agency for an IPF. In addition, the Bank carried out a limited procurement assessment of a select number of the ACE Impact I centers (in Ghana and Burkina Faso). The limited assessment focused on select centers hosted in universities that did not participate in the ACE I project and so are not familiar with the program. The full summary of the completed procurement assessments and suggested measures to address identified inadequacies and risks are provided in Annex 2. A brief highlight of the summary is given below.

AAU, each center, MESRSI-PIU and NCTE will have in place adequate capacity to ensure the timely implementation of procurement activities. AAU will also have the responsibility of procurement activities under the regional level activities (under Component 3) they will support and in accordance with the PR and using STEP for procurement planning and prior reviews. AAU will also engage a well-qualified and experienced procurement consultant proficient in Bank procurement requirements and procedures, to undertake procurement at AAU. The procurement consultant will more importantly act as an advisor to the ACE Impact centers, supporting them in procurement related activities. The limited assessment indicated a lack of staff that are solely dedicated to the centers’ project procurement activities. The universities must delegate a dedicated procurement staff from the Department or hire one to handle procurement activities for the centers.

Since the centers will utilize their own institutions’/national procurement guidelines, there will be limited oversight by the Bank’s procurement team. Given the peculiarities associated with procurement of science equipment and research supplies, centres may propose separate guidelines that are specific for procurement of science goods and allow the centres to be efficient in implementing their projects on schedule. Such additional guidelines must be consistent with the general principles of procurement, should be included in the Procurement Manuals of the centers and should be approved by the World Bank procurement specialist in the country. To ensure compliance by the centers and to monitor their procurement activities, the National Steering Committee will review the procurement audits of the centers within their respective countries at least once a year. Overall, the procurement risk rating for the project is High.

TITLE: The PRO-RES Framework for Ethical Evidence

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
PUBLICATIONS

The PRO-RES Project has produced a guidance FRAMEWORK that encourages policymakers and their advisors to seek evidence for their decisions from research that has been conducted ethically, responsibly and with integrity.

Together these three ‘pillars’ comprise a normative framework.

A normative framework is a collection of principles, values and standards for right action that is seen as morally binding upon the members of a group and serves to guide, control, and/or regulate proper and acceptable behaviour. That is, such a framework contains advice and guidance on how one ‘ought’ to behave in producing ethical evidence. The framework constructed by the PRO-RES Project is based upon principles of normative ethics which refers to the grounds of meaning or acceptance of decisions about why certain behaviour is right or wrong.
