TITLE: INVITATION – Education Collaborative Virtual Conference 2020

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Stakeholders of African Higher Education are invited to join the Education Collaborative virtual conference as we share context-specific successful university strategies, administration, teaching and learning approaches in this COVID -19 period; obtain insight on ways to capitalize on our innovations to create a “new normal” for institutions in the near future for the transformation of the African continent.

This will be a one-day virtual conference on zoom – with a live broadcast on Facebook, AAU TV, and YouTube.

Theme: Changing the Narrative of African Education

Tuesday 16th June 2020

Participation is free

Scheduled sessions are as follows:

Executive Conference

Join university executives in African higher-ed to share, learn, and reimagine the future of higher education, to give context to current issues and strategize for continuity after a disruptive world.

Stakeholders forum: The COVID-19 Test of Ghana’s Educational System: Policy Implications and New Pathways

Time: 10:00-11:00 AM GMT

Though the novel virus has ravaged different sectors of the economy across the world, one area undeniably affected is the educational system. In Ghana specifically, schools from the basic to the tertiary levels, have remained closed for the last two months, with its related challenges. As the government of Ghana and other African countries prepare to ease these restrictions on gatherings and school closures, there is the need to assess the higher educational system, the lessons we’ve learned, the gaps that have arisen, and the challenges we’ve overcome, and chart new pathways to maximize the almost-disguised-opportunities that this pandemic has opened up for education delivery in Ghana.

Panel session: Transitioning to online: The contextual realities of the go, no-go decision

Time: 11:30-12:30 AM GMT

The COVID-19 pandemic has no doubt brought education leaders to the point of making some of the toughest decisions in their careers. Transition online or not to transition online, and to what extent. In our African-context, that decision is not a simple go-no-go-decision. Besides the continent-specific challenges, there also exist institution-specific challenges. In weighing the factors to transition online or not, the right decision in a crisis such as this for some is a no-go decision.

In an emergency, “speed trumps perfection”, and one size does not fit all. Join education leaders on the African continent as they discuss the actual factors that went into making the decisions they made in the face of COVID-19 campus shutdowns.

Faculty and Administrator workshop

Join faculty, course trainers, administrators, departmental teams, classroom facilitators, to explore faculty-administrator collaborations, develop hands-on techniques to facilitate classroom instruction and continuity during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, and build a network of support in Africa.

Parallel Sessions: 2:00-3:00 PM GMT

Workshop A: What next? Implications of our new normal on the future of teaching and learning in Africa.

“COVID19 is widely seen as the unwanted, uninvited enemy of 2020. And for good reason. […] But for just a moment, I invite you to consider how this unwanted enemy may in fact be the best gift Higher Ed could have ever asked for. Many schools will adapt in the short-term and then return to the status quo. But the perceptive and innovative institutions will seize on this once-in-a-lifetime opportunity and be transformed by it.” (Andrew Allen, 2020)

In this COVID-19 pandemic, higher-ed institutions with prior face-to-face instructional pedagogies have redesigned courses to match with the online teaching and learning. How and what can we carry forward to transform how we teach and learn for the better? This session unpacks the approaches adopted in this period and what it holds for the future of instruction in African higher institutions

Workshop B: Integrating immersive learning methods: The future of higher education

Local and regional universities are best suited to solve the pressing needs of learners today, but if they don’t adapt quickly, their value proposition won’t be enough to serve students and competitors will take their place. This is the best opportunity we’ve had in decades to re-design higher ed. And embedding learning by doing into the academic design is the key to our future as institutions.

Facilitator: Andrew Allen, Director of the Magelli Office of Experiential Learning, Illinois Gies College of Business

Parallel Sessions: 3:30-4:30 PM GMT

Workshop A: Re-thinking remote access online for students with disability

As schools adopt remote learning channels during this COVID-19 pandemic, are the needs of students with disabilities being fully considered? What are some of the opportunities that these transitions have presented for inclusion of students with disabilities, and what are some of the challenges faced in developing institutions’ capabilities to support in this period. What lessons and practicalities does this hold for the future of instruction and administration of higher-ed in Africa?

Workshop B: Preparing Students for work after the New Normal

The World Bank’s report in 2017 indicates that the expeditious change in technology, information, and related developments are creating corresponding changes in the world of work on the continent. The present pandemic has fast-tracked this change with the emergence of new forms of work; with remote working revealing new possibilities for expenditure and resource management. The nature of work post-COVID19 will likely take on a new look that will require new strategies for talent and career development. As educators, join this session to look into this trend, identify new administrative and teaching approaches to adequately prepare students for a changing future of work.

TITLE: Team4Tech Experience AI Cohort 2026 | Free AI Education Training for NGOs in Africa

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Team4Tech is inviting education-focused nonprofits and NGOs operating in Africa to apply for its Experience AI Cohort, a free, structured learning programme designed to help nonprofit staff and teachers build practical knowledge and confidence in artificial intelligence and machine learning.

Developed by the Raspberry Pi Foundation and Google DeepMind, Experience AI provides research-based educational resources for teachers and students aged 11–14. Through the three-month cohort, selected organizations will participate in live virtual sessions, self-paced learning, coaching, and peer-learning activities to develop the skills needed to introduce AI literacy to their learning communities.

About the Experience AI Cohort

The programme will run from September through early December 2026 and will support participating NGOs in understanding the foundations of AI and implementing Experience AI lessons with teachers and learners.

Participants will explore how AI is used in everyday life, how computers learn from data, and how issues such as limited datasets can contribute to bias. They will also gain practical experience training and testing machine learning models and learn strategies for identifying misinformation in an increasingly AI-driven world.

The programme will also introduce participants to AI-related career pathways, helping educators prepare young people for a future where AI and digital skills are increasingly important.

What Participants Will Learn

Through the Experience AI programme, participants will:

Explore how artificial intelligence is used in the world today.

Understand how computers learn from data using machine learning.

Discover how limited datasets can contribute to bias.

Train and test a machine learning model to address a real-world problem.

Develop strategies for distinguishing facts from false information in the age of AI.

Learn about careers and opportunities related to artificial intelligence.

Build confidence in delivering practical AI learning experiences.

What Participating NGOs Will Receive

Selected organizations will have access to:

Research-based Experience AI resources and coursework.

Live virtual learning and peer-learning sessions.

Self-paced learning modules.

Coaching and facilitation from Team4Tech.

Opportunities to strengthen staff knowledge and practical AI skills.

An implementation stipend upon successful completion of the required course activities.

The stipend can be used to support the organization’s implementation of the learning and strategies developed through the cohort.

Who Can Apply?

The opportunity is intended for education nonprofits and NGOs operating in Africa that are interested in using Experience AI lessons to strengthen AI literacy among teachers and learners.

Participating organizations are expected to nominate 2–4 staff members who can commit approximately 15–20 total hours over three months.

Organizations should also be prepared to:

Complete asynchronous learning activities and assignments.

Attend six live virtual sessions focused on peer learning, sharing, and feedback.

Complete pre- and post-cohort surveys.

Complete a follow-up survey approximately 4–6 months after participation.

Develop plans for implementing Experience AI within their organization and learner community.

Participants should also be comfortable completing coursework and participating in coaching sessions in English.

Who Will Benefit?

The programme is particularly relevant to organizations working with teachers and young learners aged 11–14.

By participating, NGOs can build their internal capacity to introduce young people to foundational AI concepts, responsible use of technology, machine learning, bias, misinformation, and AI-related careers.

Organizations will also have the opportunity to share their learning with additional staff and teachers. Applicants are asked to indicate how many additional educators they expect to train on Experience AI lessons within the following 6–12 months.

Expected Impact

Experience AI can help participating organizations strengthen their education programmes by giving educators practical tools and knowledge to introduce AI concepts in an accessible way.

Through the cohort, participating NGOs can develop strategies for integrating AI literacy into their existing programmes, help teachers become more confident in discussing AI with students, and give learners opportunities to understand how AI systems work rather than simply using AI tools.

The programme can therefore contribute to stronger digital skills, AI awareness, critical thinking, and career readiness among young people.

Important Dates

Application Deadline: September 4, 2026

Selection Decisions: September 16–18, 2026

Programme Period: September 2026 – early December 2026

Up to 10 NGOs operating in Africa are expected to participate in the cohort.

How to Apply

Interested NGOs should complete the Experience AI Cohort application form before the September 4, 2026 deadline.

Application: Apply for the Experience AI Cohort

For questions specifically about the Experience AI cohort, applicants can contact Michelle Mwangi at michelle@team4tech.org. For other questions, contact community@team4tech.org.

Conclusion

The Team4Tech Experience AI Cohort 2026 provides African education nonprofits with an opportunity to strengthen their staff capacity in artificial intelligence and bring practical AI learning experiences to teachers and young people.

With free coursework, live sessions, coaching, research-based resources, and an implementation stipend, the programme can help participating organizations take meaningful steps toward building AI-ready learning communities.

TITLE: McDonald’s Chicago Community Impact Grants 2027: Up to $200,000 for Chicago Nonprofits Supporting Youth Workforce Readiness and Food Access

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The McDonald’s Chicago Community Impact Grants Program 2027 is now open for applications from eligible Chicago-based organizations working to improve opportunities and outcomes for young people.

Through the 2027 grant cycle, McDonald’s is committing an additional $4 million to support local nonprofit organizations addressing two important challenges affecting young people in underserved Chicago communities: workforce readiness and development and food access and insecurity.

Selected organizations can receive project-based grants ranging from $50,000 to $200,000, with up to 25 grants expected to be awarded. The initiative is designed to support programs that create measurable improvements in the lives of young people between the ages of 16 and 24.

Applications opened on September 1, 2026, and the application deadline is September 30, 2026, at 11:59 PM Central Time (CT).

Overview of the McDonald’s Chicago Community Impact Grants 2027

McDonald’s has a longstanding connection to Chicago, where the company is headquartered. Through its community investment efforts, the company supports programs intended to strengthen communities, expand access to opportunity and address pressing local challenges.

The Chicago Community Impact Grants Program was launched in 2022 in partnership with The Chicago Community Trust. Since its launch, McDonald’s reports that it has invested more than $12 million in support of local organizations and reached more than 100,000 people across Chicago.

For the 2027 cycle, McDonald’s is providing an additional $4 million to continue supporting organizations that are creating meaningful change in Chicago.

The 2027 initiative places particular emphasis on empowering young people and helping them overcome barriers that can prevent them from accessing education, employment, economic opportunity and adequate food.

The program is organized around two major priorities:

Fostering Communities: Pathways to Empowerment

Feeding Futures: Food Access and Insecurity

Organizations applying for funding should ensure that their proposed project clearly aligns with at least one of these priority areas.

1. Fostering Communities: Pathways to Empowerment

The first priority area focuses on workforce readiness and development for youth ages 16–24.

McDonald’s recognizes that young people do not all follow the same pathway to employment and economic success. Some face significant barriers involving transportation, financial knowledge, access to professional networks, mentorship, training and exposure to potential careers.

Through the Fostering Communities priority, the grant program seeks to support organizations implementing programs that take a holistic approach to removing these barriers.

The goal is not simply to provide young people with short-term activities. Rather, supported programs should help participants develop the knowledge, skills, experience and support systems they need to move toward meaningful employment and long-term economic opportunity.

What types of workforce programs can be funded?

Eligible organizations may request funding for direct workforce-readiness services and initiatives such as:

Apprenticeships that provide young people with practical, hands-on work experience.

Pre-employment training designed to prepare participants for entering the workforce.

Post-employment training that helps young workers strengthen their skills and succeed after securing employment.

Career exposure opportunities that introduce young people to different industries, occupations, professional environments and career pathways.

Other workforce development activities that directly contribute to improving employment readiness and access to opportunity.

The emphasis is on programs that provide practical benefits and can demonstrate meaningful outcomes for young participants.

Holistic support services

The program also recognizes that workforce participation can be affected by challenges outside the classroom or workplace.

Consequently, applicants may include funding requests for holistic support services that directly strengthen their core workforce programming.

Examples include:

Transportation and mobility assistance

Transportation can be a significant barrier for young people attempting to participate in training, apprenticeships, interviews, internships or employment.

Organizations may therefore incorporate transportation or mobility support where it directly contributes to successful participation in their workforce programs.

Financial literacy education

Financial literacy can help young people better understand budgeting, saving, responsible financial decision-making and other issues associated with economic independence.

Programs may incorporate financial literacy when it directly supports their broader workforce-readiness objectives.

Mentorship and coaching

Mentorship and coaching can provide participants with guidance, encouragement, professional insight and accountability as they navigate education, training and employment pathways.

Applicants can therefore include appropriate mentoring and coaching components as part of a broader workforce development program.

The key consideration is that these support services should directly enhance the organization’s core workforce programming, rather than operate as unrelated activities.

2. Feeding Futures: Food Access and Insecurity

The second priority area focuses on food access and food insecurity among youth ages 16–24 in underserved communities.

As a global food company, McDonald’s states that it seeks to play a positive role in the communities it serves, including through initiatives that improve access to food.

The Feeding Futures priority is intended to support organizations developing practical responses to food insecurity and barriers to accessing food.

Programs can focus on providing direct food assistance, expanding local food production, improving access to food in underserved neighborhoods or developing community-led approaches to addressing systemic barriers.

Examples of eligible food-access initiatives

Funding may support programs such as:

Food banks and food pantries that provide consistent access to nutritious food and meals.

Community gardens that promote local food production and community participation.

Urban farms that expand local food production and improve food availability.

Mobile markets that bring food to neighborhoods experiencing limited access to grocery stores and other food sources.

Community-led solutions designed to remove systemic barriers to food access.

Other direct services and initiatives that align with the program’s food access and food insecurity objectives for young people ages 16–24.

Organizations should demonstrate how their proposed project addresses an identifiable food-access challenge and how young people in underserved Chicago communities will benefit.

Who Should Apply for the McDonald’s Chicago Community Impact Grants?

The program is designed for Chicago-based organizations serving young people ages 16–24 through programs aligned with one of the two priority areas.

Applicants should not simply demonstrate that they work with young people. Their proposed project must have a clear connection to either:

Workforce readiness and development; or

Food access and food insecurity.

Organizations should also be able to demonstrate that they have the experience, systems and financial capacity necessary to responsibly manage grant funding and implement the proposed project.

Grant Eligibility and Selection Criteria

McDonald’s has established several criteria that applicants must satisfy.

1. Serve youth ages 16–24

Applicants must operate programs serving young people between the ages of 16 and 24.

The proposed program should clearly demonstrate how it will benefit this population and how it aligns with one of the two focus areas.

2. Demonstrate measurable impact

Applicants should have a track record of delivering programs that produce meaningful outcomes.

Organizations should be able to demonstrate evidence of:

Successful program delivery.

Positive outcomes for participants.

Measurable community impact.

Effective engagement with the communities they serve.

A strong application should therefore go beyond describing activities and explain what changes the organization has achieved or expects to achieve.

3. Demonstrate organizational and financial capacity

Organizations must have the organizational and financial systems necessary to successfully implement and manage the proposed project.

This means applicants should be able to demonstrate responsible stewardship of resources and the ability to administer grant funding effectively.

4. Maintain strong community relationships

Applicants should have established relationships within the communities they serve.

McDonald’s is looking for organizations with credibility and a reputation for:

Responsible stewardship.

Integrity.

Community service.

Meaningful community engagement.

Positive relationships with the populations they serve.

How McDonald’s Will Evaluate Applications

This is a competitive grantmaking process. Submitting an application does not guarantee funding.

Eligible applications will be reviewed, evaluated and scored using the program’s published criteria.

Several major factors will influence the assessment.

Financial Health

McDonald’s will consider the organization’s:

Financial stability.

Stewardship of resources.

Funding diversity.

Ability to sustain its operations.

Capacity to effectively implement the proposed program.

Applicants should therefore present a credible picture of their financial health and demonstrate that they can responsibly manage the proposed grant.

Program Alignment

The proposed project must demonstrate strong alignment with one of the two 2027 priorities:

Feeding Futures: Food Access and Insecurity, or

Fostering Communities: Pathways to Empowerment.

A proposal that does not clearly connect its activities and intended outcomes to these priorities is likely to be less competitive.

Impact

McDonald’s will assess the organization’s ability to demonstrate meaningful and measurable outcomes.

Applicants should clearly explain:

Who will benefit.

What problem the project addresses.

What activities will be implemented.

How many people are expected to benefit.

What outcomes are expected.

How progress and success will be measured.

Organizational Brand and Reputational Risk

McDonald’s will also consider an organization’s credibility, community reputation and alignment with its values and community-impact priorities.

This means applicants should demonstrate that they are trusted organizations with a responsible approach to serving their communities.

How Much Funding Is Available?

The 2027 Chicago Community Impact Grants Program will provide $4 million in additional funding.

Individual grant awards will range from:

Minimum grant: $50,000

Maximum grant: $200,000

The final amount awarded to each organization will depend on the strength of its application and its alignment with the goals of the Chicago Community Impact Grants Program.

McDonald’s expects to award up to 25 grants.

Importantly, this is a competitive process. Being eligible does not mean an organization will automatically receive funding.

Funding decisions will take into consideration factors including:

Alignment with the program’s focus areas.

Expected community impact.

Financial health.

Organizational capacity.

Geographic focus.

Community credibility.

Overall application strength.

The strength and feasibility of the proposed project.

What Makes an Application Competitive?

Because funding is competitive, organizations should avoid treating the application as simply a request for financial assistance.

A strong application should demonstrate a clear connection between the organization’s existing work, the proposed project and the objectives of the grant program.

Applicants should consider emphasizing the following areas.

Clearly define the problem

Explain the specific challenge affecting youth ages 16–24 in the Chicago community being served.

TITLE: WFP Fellowship Programme 2026: Research Opportunities for Master’s, Doctoral and Postdoctoral Researchers

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) is offering an important pathway for researchers and academics who want to connect advanced research with real-world humanitarian action through its Fellowship Programme and academic partnerships.

Through collaboration with universities, research institutions and think tanks, WFP creates opportunities for researchers to contribute knowledge, evidence and innovative ideas to some of the world’s most urgent challenges, including hunger, food insecurity, resilience, humanitarian assistance and sustainable development.

The WFP Fellowship Programme is particularly relevant for Master’s students, doctoral researchers and postdoctoral researchers who want to gain practical exposure to the work of a major United Nations humanitarian organization while contributing to research and evidence-based solutions.

About the World Food Programme

The World Food Programme (WFP) is a United Nations organization focused on combating hunger and providing food assistance and humanitarian support to people affected by conflict, disasters and other crises.

Its work extends beyond emergency food assistance. WFP also works in areas such as food security, nutrition, supply chains, resilience, social protection, humanitarian logistics, research, policy development and capacity strengthening.

Because many of the challenges WFP addresses are complex and interconnected, research and evidence play an important role in helping the organization design effective interventions.

The organization’s collaboration with universities and research institutions is therefore intended to bring academic knowledge closer to humanitarian operations and ensure that research can contribute to practical solutions.

What Is the WFP Fellowship Programme?

The WFP Fellowship Programme provides opportunities for qualified researchers and academics to contribute directly to WFP’s work while receiving mentorship and professional exposure.

According to WFP, fellows can include Master’s and PhD students or graduates, researchers and professors with relevant technical knowledge. Fellowship opportunities can take place across WFP’s headquarters, regional bureaux and country offices, depending on the specific opportunity.

The programme is designed to create a bridge between academic research and humanitarian practice.

Rather than research remaining exclusively within an academic environment, fellows have the opportunity to connect their knowledge and research interests with real-world challenges faced by communities and humanitarian organizations.

This can make the experience especially valuable for individuals interested in careers in:

Food security

Humanitarian affairs

International development

Nutrition

Public policy

Agricultural development

Social protection

Climate resilience

Humanitarian logistics

Supply-chain management

Monitoring and evaluation

Research and analysis

Programme design

Evidence-based policymaking

Connecting Academic Research With Humanitarian Action

One of the central objectives of WFP’s academic partnerships is to close the gap between academic research and humanitarian implementation.

Universities and research institutions produce substantial amounts of research, but translating academic findings into practical solutions can sometimes be challenging.

WFP’s collaboration model seeks to address this gap by creating opportunities for researchers to engage with humanitarian professionals and operational realities.

Through these collaborations, academic research can help generate evidence-based proposals and locally relevant solutions.

At the same time, humanitarian organizations can benefit from new research, analytical methods, technical expertise and innovative approaches developed within universities.

This creates a two-way exchange of knowledge.

Opportunities Available Through WFP’s Academic Partnerships

WFP’s engagement with academia extends beyond fellowships. Its academic partnership activities can include several forms of collaboration.

1. Fellowship Opportunities

The Fellowship Programme allows qualified Master’s, doctoral and postdoctoral researchers and other eligible academic professionals to contribute to WFP’s work.

Fellows work under the mentorship and guidance of experienced professionals, giving them the opportunity to understand how humanitarian organizations operate and how research can inform programmes and policies.

WFP states that fellowship opportunities are generally offered for periods ranging from 3 to 12 months, depending on the assignment. The fellowship is sponsored by an academic institution, research organization or governmental body with a valid Fellowship Partnership Agreement with WFP, rather than being directly financed by WFP itself.

2. Secondments

WFP also facilitates secondments between WFP and academic or research institutions.

Secondments allow expertise to move in both directions.

For example, an academic or researcher may gain practical exposure within WFP, while WFP professionals can engage with academic institutions and research environments.

This exchange can strengthen institutional relationships and encourage the development of research that is more closely connected to humanitarian needs.

3. Speaking Opportunities

Universities can also engage with WFP through lectures, seminars, conferences and other academic events.

WFP experts may participate in academic discussions and share knowledge about humanitarian operations, food security, hunger, development and related issues.

This gives students and researchers the opportunity to learn directly from professionals working in the field.

4. Study Visits

Universities can organize visits to WFP headquarters in Rome, Italy.

These visits can give students and faculty members an opportunity to learn more about:

WFP’s global mandate

Humanitarian operations

Food security

WFP priorities

International development

The organization’s operational structure

The role of research and evidence in humanitarian decision-making

Such visits can provide valuable exposure to the work of a major international organization.

Why the WFP Fellowship Is Valuable for Researchers

Participating in a WFP fellowship or academic collaboration can provide several professional and academic advantages.

Practical Humanitarian Experience

Researchers can gain exposure to the practical realities of humanitarian work.

This is particularly valuable for students whose academic programmes are heavily research-based but who want to understand how evidence is used in real-world settings.

Mentorship From Experienced Professionals

The programme provides opportunities to work under the mentorship of experienced WFP professionals.

This can help researchers better understand professional standards, operational decision-making and the relationship between research and programme implementation.

Exposure to International Development

WFP operates internationally and addresses hunger and food insecurity in a wide range of contexts.

Working with the organization can therefore provide insight into international development and humanitarian systems.

Strengthening Research Skills

Researchers can develop their ability to conduct research that is relevant to policy and programme implementation.

This can be particularly useful for individuals pursuing academic careers, research careers or positions within international organizations.

Networking and Collaboration

Academic partnerships can create opportunities to interact with researchers, academics, humanitarian professionals and other specialists.

These relationships may be valuable for future research collaborations and professional development.

Contributing to Real-World Solutions

Perhaps one of the most important advantages is the opportunity to contribute to research and ideas that can potentially inform humanitarian interventions.

The goal is not simply to produce academic knowledge but to help advance practical and locally led solutions to hunger and food insecurity.

Who Can Benefit From the Fellowship Programme?

The programme is primarily relevant to individuals with an academic or research background.

WFP identifies fellows as including:

Master’s students

PhD students

Master’s graduates

PhD graduates

Researchers

Professors and other academic professionals

Applicants are expected to have an appropriate technical foundation relevant to WFP’s areas of work. WFP’s current fellowship guidance states that candidates typically have completed at least an undergraduate programme and possess advanced technical knowledge relevant to the organization’s work.

Specific fellowship vacancies may impose additional requirements, so applicants should always check the requirements attached to the particular opportunity.

General Eligibility Requirements

The precise requirements can vary depending on the fellowship, sponsoring institution and assignment.

However, WFP’s current fellowship information identifies several general requirements.

Academic Background

Applicants should generally be:

Master’s or PhD students or graduates;

Researchers; or

Professors/academic professionals.

They should have a strong technical foundation relevant to the area in which they intend to work.

Sponsorship

An important point prospective applicants should understand is that WFP’s fellowship programme is not structured as a standard scholarship where WFP directly pays the fellow.

WFP states that fellows must be financially sponsored by an academic institution, research organization or governmental body that has a valid Fellowship Partnership Agreement with WFP.

The sponsoring organization is responsible for supporting the fellow financially and may cover expenses such as:

Stipend

Round-trip appointment and repatriation travel

Accommodation

Visa fees

Medical insurance

Other assignment-related costs

The exact support available can depend on the sponsoring organization and the specific fellowship arrangement.

Language

English proficiency is required for the general fellowship programme.

Knowledge of additional WFP working or official languages can be an advantage and may be required for particular duty stations or assignments.

WFP identifies Arabic, Chinese, French, Russian and Spanish, alongside English and Portuguese as a working language, among its relevant language competencies.

Computer Skills

Candidates are expected to be proficient in Windows Microsoft Office.

Applicants should therefore be comfortable working with common digital productivity tools and preparing professional documents and analytical materials.

Interpersonal and Teamwork Skills

Applicants should demonstrate the ability to work collaboratively in multicultural environments.

This is particularly important because WFP operates across different countries and humanitarian contexts, requiring staff, fellows and partners to work with people from diverse cultural and professional backgrounds.

Which Countries Can Apply?

The WFP Fellowship Programme is connected to WFP’s international academic partnerships and is not presented as an opportunity restricted to one particular race, ethnicity or continent.

There is no racial restriction stated in the general fellowship eligibility information.

Applicants should, however, understand that eligibility can depend on the specific fellowship vacancy, the sponsoring institution and the terms of the relevant Fellowship Partnership Agreement.

WFP operates internationally, including in countries across Africa, Asia, the Middle East, Latin America and the Caribbean, among other regions. Its country network includes Ghana and numerous other countries.

Therefore, candidates from African countries, including Ghana, may be relevant to the programme where they meet the academic, technical, sponsorship and assignment-specific requirements.

The safest approach is to review the eligibility requirements of the specific fellowship opportunity rather than assuming that nationality alone guarantees eligibility.

What Areas of Research Could Be Relevant?

Because WFP’s mandate covers a broad range of humanitarian and development activities, researchers from several disciplines may find the programme relevant.

Potential areas include:

Food security and hunger

Nutrition

Agriculture and food systems

Humanitarian assistance

International development

Public policy

Climate change and resilience

Social protection

Supply-chain management

Humanitarian logistics

Economics

Data analysis

Monitoring and evaluation

Research methodology

Conflict and food insecurity

Sustainable livelihoods

Disaster response

Programme design and implementation

The suitability of a particular academic background will depend on the specific fellowship or research assignment.

How Academic Partnerships Strengthen WFP’s Work

WFP’s collaboration with universities is not only about providing opportunities to students and researchers.

The partnerships also support WFP’s broader organizational mission.

Academic collaboration can help WFP:

Generate new evidence;

Explore innovative approaches to hunger and food insecurity;

Strengthen research capacity;

Improve programme design;

Encourage locally led solutions;

Connect humanitarian operations with academic expertise;

Support knowledge exchange;

Develop the next generation of humanitarian professionals; and

Keep humanitarian programming informed by emerging research.

This approach recognizes that solving hunger requires more than emergency food assistance. It also requires strong research, policy, innovation, evidence and collaboration.

Research That Can Lead to Practical Impact

An important feature of the WFP academic partnership model is its focus on research that can be connected to real-world outcomes.

For example, research conducted by students and academics can contribute to understanding how communities experience food insecurity, how climate shocks affect livelihoods, how humanitarian interventions can become more effective, or how food systems can become more resilient.

WFP has previously highlighted academic partnerships in which Master’s and PhD students conduct research connected to resilience and food security programming.

One example is the partnership with the Sahel University Network, involving universities in Burkina Faso, Niger, Senegal, Chad and Mali, where Master’s and PhD students conducted research connected to WFP resilience sites.

This illustrates how academic research can move beyond theoretical analysis and contribute to practical humanitarian programming.

Important Information About the Deadline

No application deadline is stated in the information provided for the WFP Academia and Think Tanks/Fellowship Programme page.

This means applicants should not assume that there is a single annual closing date for the overall programme.

WFP fellowship opportunities may become available according to institutional partnerships, funding arrangements and specific assignments. Prospective applicants should therefore monitor WFP’s official fellowship opportunities and the requirements of individual vacancies.

How to Approach a WFP Fellowship Opportunity

Researchers interested in pursuing this pathway should take a strategic approach.

Step 1: Identify Your Research Area

Determine how your academic work connects to WFP’s mandate.

Your research should ideally address a relevant humanitarian, food-security, development, nutrition, resilience, policy or operational issue.

Step 2: Check Your Academic Status

Confirm whether you qualify as a Master’s student, doctoral student, graduate, researcher or academic professional under the requirements of the specific fellowship.

Step 3: Review Sponsorship Requirements

Because WFP fellowship participants generally require sponsorship from an eligible academic, research or governmental institution, applicants should investigate whether their university or research organization has the appropriate partnership arrangement with WFP.

Step 4: Prepare Your Academic Documents

Depending on the opportunity, applicants may need materials such as:

Curriculum vitae;

Academic transcripts;

Research proposal;

Research statement;

Motivation letter;

Proof of academic status;

References; and

Evidence of technical or research experience.

The exact documents should be determined from the specific opportunity.

Step 5: Connect Your Research to WFP’s Mission

A strong application should make a clear connection between the candidate’s research and WFP’s objectives.

Instead of simply describing an academic research topic, applicants should explain why the research matters and how it could contribute to improved humanitarian or development outcomes.

Step 6: Monitor WFP Opportunities

Because fellowship opportunities may not operate according to one universal annual deadline, prospective applicants should regularly check WFP’s official opportunities and academic partnership information.

Why This Opportunity Stands Out

The WFP Fellowship Programme is particularly attractive because it combines academic research, professional mentorship and humanitarian impact.

For a researcher, the experience can provide an opportunity to understand how evidence is transformed into policies, programmes and operational decisions.

For universities, partnerships with WFP can strengthen institutional research networks and provide students and faculty with exposure to international humanitarian work.

For WFP, academic collaboration provides access to research expertise and emerging ideas that can contribute to its efforts to address hunger and food insecurity.

This creates a mutually beneficial relationship between academia and humanitarian practice.

Important Considerations Before Applying

Prospective applicants should keep several points in mind.

First, the fellowship programme should not automatically be treated as a conventional scholarship. WFP’s current information indicates that fellows are financially sponsored by eligible academic, research or governmental institutions rather than receiving direct financial support from WFP.

Second, meeting the general fellowship requirements does not necessarily guarantee selection.

Specific assignments may have additional technical, academic, language or professional requirements.

Third, applicants should carefully distinguish between WFP’s general academic partnership programme and individual fellowship vacancies. The general Academia and Think Tanks page describes the overall collaboration framework, while specific fellowship opportunities may contain additional requirements.

Finally, candidates should rely on the official WFP requirements attached to the particular opportunity before making application decisions.

APPLY HERE

Visit the OFY Website HERE for more Graduate fellowship programmes

Conclusion

The WFP Fellowship Programme provides an important opportunity for researchers and academics to connect scholarship with humanitarian action.

Through fellowships, secondments, university visits, speaking engagements and research collaborations, the World Food Programme is strengthening the relationship between academic institutions and humanitarian organizations.

For Master’s students, doctoral researchers, postdoctoral researchers, academics and other qualified research professionals, the programme can provide valuable exposure to international humanitarian work while creating opportunities to contribute to evidence-based approaches to hunger, food security, resilience and development.

The opportunity is particularly relevant to researchers who want their work to have practical impact beyond academia. By connecting research with WFP’s operational experience and global mandate, participants can contribute to locally led solutions while developing their own academic and professional capabilities.

Although no single deadline is stated for the overall programme, interested researchers should regularly monitor WFP’s official fellowship opportunities and consult their universities or research institutions regarding sponsorship and partnership arrangements.

Ultimately, WFP’s academic partnerships demonstrate that tackling hunger requires collaboration across sectors. Universities generate knowledge, researchers produce evidence, humanitarian professionals bring operational expertise, and organizations such as WFP provide platforms through which these resources can be connected to real-world challenges.

For researchers seeking to build a career at the intersection of academia, food security, humanitarian action and international development, the WFP Fellowship Programme is therefore a pathway worth exploring.

TITLE: Commonwealth Master’s Scholarships 2027/28: Fully Funded UK Scholarships for Students from Developing Commonwealth Countries

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Commonwealth Master’s Scholarships 2027/28 provide an opportunity for talented and motivated graduates from eligible low- and middle-income Commonwealth countries to pursue full-time taught Master’s degrees at universities in the United Kingdom.

Funded by the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office, the scholarship programme is designed to support individuals who demonstrate academic potential, leadership capacity and a commitment to sustainable development but who may not otherwise be able to afford postgraduate study in the UK.

The programme is administered by the Commonwealth Scholarship Commission in the UK, commonly known as the CSC, under the framework of the Commonwealth Scholarship and Fellowship Plan. It aims to develop skilled professionals, researchers, leaders and innovators who can contribute to the development of their home countries after completing their studies.

For the 2027/28 academic year, applications are scheduled to open on 8 September 2026, with the closing deadline set for 20 October 2026 at 16:00 British Summer Time (BST). Applicants must also apply through an approved nominating agency, and those agencies may establish earlier internal deadlines.

About the Commonwealth Master’s Scholarships

The Commonwealth Master’s Scholarship is one of the Master’s-level programmes offered by the Commonwealth Scholarship Commission in the UK.

The CSC operates within the wider Commonwealth Scholarship and Fellowship Plan, which promotes educational exchange, professional development, international collaboration and sustainable development across Commonwealth countries.

The scholarship is supported by the UK government through the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office. Its central purpose is to enable talented people from eligible developing Commonwealth countries to acquire advanced knowledge and practical skills that can contribute to social, economic and institutional development.

The programme is particularly intended for candidates who:

Have strong academic and professional potential.

Come from eligible low- and middle-income Commonwealth countries.

Have a clear interest in sustainable development.

Would not otherwise be able to finance postgraduate study in the UK.

Intend to use their knowledge and skills to contribute to their home countries and communities.

The CSC seeks to attract people from diverse backgrounds and support them in becoming future leaders, innovators and change-makers.

Scholarship Purpose and Development Focus

Commonwealth Master’s Scholarships are not simply designed to support individual academic advancement. They are also connected to the UK’s international development priorities.

The programme seeks to build human capacity in Commonwealth countries by supporting postgraduate education in fields that can contribute to sustainable development. Scholars are expected to gain knowledge, professional networks and practical experience that can be applied after their return to their home countries.

The scholarship programme combines several objectives:

Developing advanced skills: Scholars gain specialist knowledge through postgraduate study at a UK university.

Supporting sustainable development: Academic programmes are expected to connect with development needs and challenges.

Strengthening institutions: Graduates can contribute to universities, public institutions, businesses, civil society organisations and other sectors.

Encouraging international collaboration: Scholars become part of a wider Commonwealth network that supports cooperation between countries and institutions.

Developing future leaders: The CSC supports individuals with the potential to create positive change in their professional fields and communities.

The scholarships are offered under the CSC’s six development themes. Applicants should therefore demonstrate how their proposed Master’s programme relates to development priorities and how the knowledge gained may contribute to meaningful outcomes in their home country.

More information about the development themes is available through the official CSC development themes page.

What the Scholarship Supports

The Commonwealth Master’s Scholarships are designed to enable successful candidates to undertake full-time taught Master’s study at a UK university.

The scholarship is intended for applicants who could not otherwise afford to study in the United Kingdom. The precise financial terms, allowances and conditions should be checked in the official scholarship guidance for the relevant application year.

Applicants should carefully review the official financial assistance information before applying, as the scholarship’s funding arrangements may include specific conditions relating to:

Tuition fees.

Living and maintenance support.

Travel arrangements.

Allowances and other approved expenses.

Scholarship duration.

University placement.

Immigration and visa requirements.

Return to the scholar’s home country after completion.

Candidates should not assume that every cost associated with studying in the UK will automatically be covered. All financial provisions should be confirmed through the official CSC guidance and scholarship terms.

Study Level and Programme Type

The Commonwealth Master’s Scholarships support:

Full-time taught Master’s programmes.

Study at eligible universities in the United Kingdom.

Postgraduate programmes that align with the CSC’s development themes.

Academic programmes that can contribute to sustainable development in eligible Commonwealth countries.

The scholarship is not intended to fund every type of postgraduate programme. Applicants should carefully review the official restrictions on eligible courses and confirm that their chosen programme meets the CSC’s requirements.

The CSC’s frequently asked questions indicate that the programme does not fund MBAs or research-based Master’s programmes. Applicants should therefore distinguish between a taught Master’s programme and a research Master’s programme before preparing an application.

Commonwealth Master’s Scholarships 2027/28 Important Dates

The official application timetable for the 2027/28 academic year is as follows:

Activity
Date

Applications open
8 September 2026

CSC application deadline
20 October 2026 at 16:00 BST

Expected period of study
September/October 2027

Nominating agencies submit candidates
December 2026

July 2027

Applicants must remember that nominating agencies may set their own deadlines, which may be earlier than the CSC’s final deadline.

Therefore, candidates should not wait until 20 October 2026 before contacting their national nominating agency. An applicant who misses the agency’s internal deadline may not be considered, even if the CSC application portal remains open.

Who Can Apply?

The Commonwealth Master’s Scholarships are intended for candidates from eligible low- and middle-income Commonwealth countries.

To be considered, applicants must generally satisfy the following eligibility requirements.

1. Citizenship or Refugee Status

Applicants must:

Be a citizen of an eligible Commonwealth country;

Have been granted refugee status by an eligible Commonwealth country; or

Be a British Protected Person.

Applicants who do not fall within one of these categories may not be eligible for this particular scholarship programme.

2. Permanent Residence

Applicants must be permanently resident in an eligible Commonwealth country.

This requirement is important because the programme is designed to support candidates who are connected to eligible Commonwealth countries and who are expected to use their knowledge and skills to contribute to development in those countries.

Temporary residence, study residence or a short-term stay in an eligible country may not be sufficient. Applicants should review the official eligibility rules carefully if their citizenship and residence countries differ.

3. Academic Qualification

By the relevant start date, applicants must normally hold:

A first degree of at least upper second-class honours standard, commonly referred to as a 2:1; or

A lower second-class degree together with a relevant postgraduate qualification, usually a Master’s degree.

The exact interpretation of degree classifications may vary by country and education system. Applicants should provide accurate academic records and ensure that their qualifications meet the CSC’s minimum standard.

Candidates should also confirm whether their proposed UK university requires a particular degree subject, grade, prerequisite course or professional qualification for admission.

4. Financial Need

The scholarship is aimed at candidates who would not otherwise be able to afford to study in the United Kingdom.

Applicants should be prepared to explain their financial circumstances and why scholarship support is necessary for them to undertake the proposed Master’s programme.

Financial need is an important part of the programme’s purpose. Applicants should provide truthful, clear and consistent information about their circumstances rather than treating the scholarship as a general funding opportunity available regardless of financial need.

5. Availability to Begin Study

Successful candidates must be available to begin academic studies in the UK at the start of the UK academic year in September or October 2027.

Applicants should consider:

Their graduation timeline.

University admission requirements.

Visa processing.

Passport validity.

Academic commitments in their home country.

The timing of any employment or professional obligations.

Candidates who cannot begin the programme within the required period may not be able to take up the scholarship.

Eligible Commonwealth Countries

Only applicants from countries listed by the Commonwealth Scholarship Commission as eligible for the Commonwealth Master’s Scholarships can apply.

The eligible countries span several regions, including Africa, Asia, the Caribbean and the Pacific.

The official list may also include other eligible territories and Commonwealth countries. Applicants should consult the CSC’s current eligible-country list rather than relying only on examples.

The CSC has also indicated that it particularly welcomes applications from Small Island Developing States, in line with commitments associated with the 2024 Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting.

How the Application Process Works

The Commonwealth Master’s Scholarship is an agency-nominated scholarship. This means applicants do not simply submit a direct application to the CSC and wait for consideration.

Candidates must generally complete two connected application steps:

Apply through the CSC’s online application system.

Apply to an approved nominating agency or organisation.

The CSC identifies two broad types of nominators:

National nominating agencies.

Selected non-governmental organisations and charitable bodies.

National nominating agencies are the main application route for many candidates.

Step 1: Identify the Appropriate Nominating Agency

Applicants should first identify the nominating agency responsible for their country or the approved organisation through which they intend to apply.

For example, the CSC lists the following nominating agency for Ghana:

Registrar of Scholarships

Scholarships Secretariat

Accra, Ghana

Applicants from Ghana should verify the latest application instructions, eligibility requirements, submission method and internal deadline directly with the Ghana Scholarships Secretariat.

Each nominating agency may establish:

Its own application form.

Its own deadline.

Additional eligibility requirements.

Additional supporting documents.

A national selection process.

Specific subject or development priorities.

Interview or screening procedures.

Meeting the CSC’s general eligibility requirements does not automatically mean that an applicant meets the requirements of the nominating agency.

Step 2: Apply Through CSC Central

Applications to the Commonwealth Scholarship Commission are submitted through the official online application system, known as CSC Central.

Applicants should create an account, complete the application form and upload the required supporting documentation before the deadline.

The official CSC page advises candidates to use the save function regularly to avoid losing information. Applicants should also be aware that:

Refreshing the browser window may cause them to exit the form.

Unsaved information may be lost.

Applications cannot be edited after submission.

Applicants should use the system’s navigation buttons rather than relying on the browser’s back buttons.

Clicking the CSC logo may return the user to the login screen.

Two-factor authentication may be required when accessing the system.

Applicants should avoid waiting until the final day to submit their forms because the online system may experience heavy traffic near the deadline.

There is a template application form and guidance document available to assist applicants when applying.

Step 3: Apply for University Admission

Applicants should also research and apply for admission to suitable UK universities and Master’s programmes.

The scholarship application and university admission process are connected but separate. Applying for the scholarship does not necessarily constitute an application for admission to a university.

Candidates should:

Identify relevant UK universities.

Review eligible taught Master’s programmes.

Check academic and English-language requirements.

Review tuition fees and course duration.

Prepare a personal statement or study proposal where required.

Apply for admission according to the university’s instructions.

Seek an offer of admission as early as possible.

The CSC advises applicants to seek admission to their proposed UK university at the time of, or as soon as possible after, submitting their scholarship application.

Applicants should also understand that receiving a university offer does not automatically guarantee a Commonwealth Scholarship.

Nominating Agencies and Their Role

Nominating agencies play a central role in the Commonwealth Master’s Scholarship process.

They are responsible for identifying and recommending candidates to the CSC. Each agency is allocated an agreed number of nominations and conducts its own selection process.

A nominating agency may assess applicants based on:

Academic performance.

Leadership potential.

Development impact.

Professional experience.

Proposed course of study.

Commitment to returning or contributing to the home country.

Financial need.

National development priorities.

Quality and clarity of the application.

Because agencies may use different procedures, applicants should contact their relevant nominating body for precise instructions.

There are two types of nominator invited to participate in the Master’s Scholarship programme:

National nominating agencies – this is the main route of application.

Selected non-governmental organisations and charitable bodies.

A nomination is an important stage in the process, but it is not a guarantee that the CSC will award the scholarship. Final selection is made by the Commonwealth Scholarship Commission from the pool of nominated candidates.

Applicants can find general information about applying for a Commonwealth Scholarship on the advice for applicants page.

Selection Process and Criteria

After nominating agencies submit their candidates, the CSC reviews the applications and conducts its selection process.

Applications are assessed against the Commission’s eligibility and selection requirements. Incomplete applications or applications that do not include required supporting documents may not be considered.

The selection process generally considers factors such as:

Academic Merit

Applicants should demonstrate strong academic achievement and the ability to succeed in postgraduate study.

Academic records, degree classifications and relevant qualifications may be considered when assessing academic merit.

Development Impact

The proposed course should be relevant to development needs. Applicants should explain how the knowledge and skills gained in the UK could contribute to their home country or wider communities.

A strong application should connect:

The applicant’s academic background.

The proposed Master’s programme.

A specific development challenge.

The applicant’s future plans.

The expected benefits to the home country.

Leadership Potential

The CSC seeks individuals who demonstrate potential to become leaders and innovators.

Leadership does not necessarily mean holding a senior political or managerial position. It may be demonstrated through:

Community initiatives.

Research projects.

Professional responsibilities.

Volunteer activities.

Youth development.

Entrepreneurship.

Public service.

Advocacy.

Educational work.

Contributions to civil society.

Applicants should provide concrete examples rather than relying only on general statements about being passionate or hardworking.

Commitment to Home-Country Development

Candidates should show how they intend to use their training after completing their studies.

Applicants may discuss how they plan to contribute through:

Public policy.

Education.

Healthcare.

Research.

Agriculture.

Technology.

Environmental sustainability.

Governance.

Economic development.

Social innovation.

Civil society.

Private-sector development.

The proposed impact should be realistic, specific and connected to the applicant’s experience and career goals.

Financial Circumstances

Because the scholarship is intended for candidates who cannot otherwise afford UK study, applicants may need to demonstrate their financial need.

Information provided about financial circumstances should be accurate and consistent throughout the application.

The Six CSC Development Themes

Commonwealth Master’s Scholarships are offered under the CSC’s six development themes.

Applicants should review the official themes and identify the theme that most closely relates to their proposed course and development objectives.

When preparing an application, candidates should explain:

Which development challenge they want to address.

How their proposed Master’s programme relates to that challenge.

Why UK study is relevant to their goals.

How they will apply the knowledge gained.

Who is likely to benefit from their future work.

How their plans connect to sustainable development.

Applicants should avoid selecting a development theme merely because it sounds attractive. The theme should be clearly connected to the proposed programme and the applicant’s future plans.

How to Choose a Suitable UK University and Course

Choosing the right university and course is an important part of the application process.

Applicants should consider the following factors.

Course Relevance

The proposed Master’s programme should be closely related to the applicant’s academic background, professional experience or future development goals.

Candidates should be able to explain why the course is necessary for their career progression and development objectives.

University Strengths

Applicants should research:

Course content.

Faculty expertise.

Research centres.

Practical learning opportunities.

Industry and institutional partnerships.

University rankings where relevant.

Graduate outcomes.

Student support.

International student services.

Rankings should not be the only deciding factor. Course relevance, academic supervision, learning structure and practical opportunities may be more important for the applicant’s objectives.

Course Structure

Candidates should review:

Course duration.

Required modules.

Optional modules.

Dissertation or project requirements.

Assessment methods.

Placement opportunities.

Attendance requirements.

Campus location.

Start date.

Applicants should ensure that the programme is a full-time taught Master’s course that meets CSC requirements.

University Admission Requirements

Each university may have different requirements concerning:

Academic qualifications.

English-language proficiency.

Work experience.

References.

Personal statements.

Transcripts.

Passport documentation.

Professional registration.

Portfolio or writing samples.

Applicants should begin checking these requirements early.

Documents and Information Applicants Should Prepare

The exact supporting-document requirements may vary according to the application instructions and nominating agency. However, candidates should prepare the following materials in advance where applicable:

Academic certificates.

University transcripts.

Evidence of degree classification.

Curriculum vitae or résumé.

Personal statement.

Study or development-impact statement.

References.

Proof of citizenship.

Proof of permanent residence.

Passport or identity document.

Evidence of English-language proficiency, if required.

University course information.

Admission application details.

Employment or professional experience information.

Details of publications, awards or leadership activities.

Applicants should ensure that names, dates, qualifications and employment details are consistent across all documents.

Documents should be clear, authentic and uploaded in the format required by the CSC or nominating agency.

Practical Advice for Preparing a Strong Application

Start Early

The application process involves several stages, including identifying a nominating agency, researching universities, preparing documents and completing the online form.

Starting early allows applicants to address missing transcripts, request references and investigate university admission requirements.

Understand Both Deadlines

Applicants should distinguish between:

The deadline set by their nominating agency.

The final CSC application deadline.

The agency deadline may be earlier. Missing the agency deadline may prevent an applicant from being nominated.

Research the Course Carefully

Applicants should not select a course only because the university is well known. The course should clearly support their academic interests, professional plans and development objectives.

Connect the Course to a Development Challenge

A strong application should explain the relationship between the proposed study and a real development issue.

For example, an applicant might connect a Master’s programme to:

Improving education systems.

Strengthening public health.

Advancing climate resilience.

Promoting inclusive economic growth.

Supporting digital transformation.

Improving governance.

Expanding access to technology.

Developing agricultural productivity.

Addressing gender inequality.

Strengthening research and innovation.

Demonstrate Evidence of Impact

Applicants should provide examples of what they have already done. These examples may come from employment, research, community service, volunteering, entrepreneurship or academic projects.

Instead of writing only that they are committed to development, candidates should explain:

What they did.

Who benefited.

What challenge they addressed.

What results were achieved.

What they learned.

How the proposed Master’s programme will build on that experience.

Prepare a Realistic Future Plan

Applicants should explain how they will use their training after completing the scholarship.

A realistic plan may include:

Returning to a current profession.

Working in a relevant public institution.

Developing a community initiative.

Conducting research.

Supporting policy development.

Training other professionals.

Establishing partnerships.

Contributing to education or healthcare.

Working with NGOs or development organisations.

Check All Requirements Before Submission

Before submitting the application, candidates should confirm that:

They meet the citizenship requirement.

They are permanently resident in an eligible country.

Their academic qualifications meet the minimum standard.

Their proposed course is eligible.

They have applied to the relevant nominating agency.

All required documents are included.

Their personal statements are complete.

Their references are properly arranged.

Their application has been submitted before the deadline.

Important Application Warnings

Applicants should take note of several important points.

A Nomination Is Not a Scholarship Award

Being nominated by a national agency or approved organisation does not guarantee final selection. The CSC makes the final decision after assessing the nominated applications.

Agency Requirements May Differ

Nominating agencies may establish additional eligibility requirements or use different selection procedures. Applicants must follow both the CSC requirements and the nominating agency’s instructions.

Late Applications May Not Be Accepted

The CSC has stated that late applications cannot be accepted if applicants run out of time to submit their forms. Candidates should submit well before the deadline.

Submitted Applications Cannot Be Edited

Applicants should carefully review their forms before clicking the final submission button because applications cannot be edited after submission.

Be Careful with Fraudulent Requests

The CSC advises applicants to be cautious of third-party websites or individuals requesting personal information, money or supporting documentation. Applicants should use the official CSC website and official application system.

Supporting documents should only be submitted through the authorised application process. The CSC has also warned that it will not ask applicants to attend in-person screening events as part of its scholarship selection process.

Official Application Deadline

The official deadline for Commonwealth Master’s Scholarship applications for the 2027/28 academic year is:

20 October 2026 at 16:00 BST

Applications are scheduled to open on:

8 September 2026

However, applicants must confirm the deadline of their national nominating agency because agencies may require applications earlier than the CSC deadline.

How to Apply

Interested candidates should follow these steps:

Review the official Commonwealth Master’s Scholarships information.

Confirm that their country is on the eligible-country list.

Identify the appropriate national nominating agency or approved organisation.

Check the nominating agency’s additional requirements and internal deadline.

Research eligible full-time taught Master’s programmes at UK universities.

Prepare academic, personal and professional documents.

Create an account on the CSC Central application system.

Complete the CSC application form.

Submit the required documents before the CSC deadline.

Complete the separate application process required by the nominating agency.

Apply for university admission as early as possible.

Monitor email communications for updates.

The official application information is available on the Commonwealth Master’s Scholarships page.

Applicants can also review the CSC’s national nominating agencies and the official Scholarships and Fellowships section.

Conclusion

The Commonwealth Master’s Scholarships 2027/28 offer an important postgraduate study opportunity for talented graduates from eligible low- and middle-income Commonwealth countries who want to pursue full-time taught Master’s degrees in the United Kingdom.

Beyond academic funding, the programme is designed to strengthen professional capacity, support sustainable development and build a network of future leaders and innovators across the Commonwealth.

Applicants should begin preparing early, research suitable UK courses, understand the CSC’s development themes, identify their nominating agency and carefully follow both the agency’s requirements and the CSC’s application procedures.

The main CSC application deadline is 20 October 2026 at 16:00 BST, but candidates should check whether their nominating agency has an earlier deadline. A well-prepared application should clearly demonstrate academic ability, financial need, leadership potential and a realistic plan for contributing to development after completing the Master’s programme.

TITLE: Allyn Vine

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
By Hannah Piecuch

An early sketch of a deep-sea submersible by Allyn Vine. From the beginning, safety features were a top priority, including a way to release the sphere containing people (which never was necessary).
Photo courtesy of Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution Archives
© Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution
In the late 1950s, when the idea of a human-occupied submersible was just an engineering sketch, WHOI’s newly-formed Deep Submergence Group started calling it “Alvin” after WHOI scientist Allyn Vine, a vocal advocate for developing a scientific submersible to study the deep sea.

Vine’s argument for human exploration of the ocean proved persuasive. At a 1956 symposium convened by the National Academy of Sciences and National Research Council, members passed a resolution to create a national program that would develop vehicles capable of transporting humans to the deep sea. Six years later, in 1964, Alvin was ready to dive.

“A good instrument can measure almost anything better than a person can if you know what you want to measure. But people are so versatile, they can sense things to be done and can investigate problems. I find it difficult to imagine what kind of instrument should have been put on the Beagle instead of Charles Darwin.”

-Al Vine

Vine worked closely with the U.S. Navy during the war years. His research included testing antifouling paints, studying the transmission of sound in the sea, developing underwater explosives, designing the first deep-sea cameras, making current and drift predictions to locate downed aviators on life rafts, and troubleshooting issues with submarines.

In peacetime, Vine threw himself into adapting war technologies for science, with a particular interest in exploring the deep sea. Vine wasn’t at his namesake’s commissioning ceremony, because he was deep beneath the surface of the Atlantic Ocean in the French submersible Archimede.

TITLE: IBRO Parenthood Grant 2026 for Early-career Researchers

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: August 15, 2026

Applications are open for the IBRO Parenthood Grant 2026. These grants ensure continuity for scientific projects run by early-career researchers who are approaching parental leave.

Pregnancy, parental leave, and adoption leave often coincide with a busy time in researchers’ lives. The challenges researchers may face in maintaining continuity in their research can sometimes result in a perceived reduction in competitiveness in terms of producing results, publishing papers and obtaining grants. By supporting early career researchers, the grant seeks to empower them to navigate the balance between personal situations and their successful scientific endeavors.

The IBRO Parenthood Grant aims to counter any disadvantage by providing funds that can be used to cover research-related expenses such as reagents, facility costs, outsourcing experiments or data acquisition, transportation of non-commercial samples or reagents. In addition, funds can be used for travel and child-care expenses to attend a conference, or for grant writing or consultation services.

Grants

The maximum grant amount an applicant can request varies based on the region where they reside and is determined by the corresponding IBRO Regional Committee. Note the specific amounts below:

Africa: $3,000 USD

Asia-Pacific: $2,000 USD

Latin America region: $2,500 USD

Pan-Europe region: $4,000 USD

US/Canada: $3,000 USD

Eligibility

Applicants should be early career principal investigators (maximum 7 years in this role).

Any extended breaks from research (e.g. previous maternity or adoption leave) are accepted and should be justified in the application.

Applicants must have at least one published, peer-reviewed paper in at least the capacity of the corresponding author.

Applicants or their partner must either:

be pregnant (at least 4 months),

have given birth in the last four months before the grant application deadline, or

be close to adoption, assuming the role of the primary caregiver.

Application

The application form asks for the following information:

Applicant Details: A brief description of the applicant’s academic background and current research focus

Grants Received: A list of grants that you have received, including IBRO grants

Research Proposal: A detailed description of the research project for which you request IBRO support

Motivation and Impact Statement: A comprehensive explanation of your motivation in applying for this program and the impact of the requested funds to your research project and laboratory

Budget Request: A detailed budget breakdown, specifying the proposed items to be funded by IBRO

Curriculum Vitae (CV): A copy of the applicant’s CV

Confirmation of independent Principal Investigator status: Signed and dated letter your institution of affiliation confirming your PI role

Confirmation of pregnancy, birth, or adoption: Official letter confirming your pregnancy, birth, or adoption

Terms and conditions: Agreeing with terms and conditions as stipulated in the IBRO Privacy Policy and payment guidelines
