TITLE: ESRC Studentship Funding 2027: Fully Funded PhD Opportunities in the UK for Social Science Researchers

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The White Rose Doctoral Training Partnership (WRDTP) has announced its call for nominations for ESRC studentship funding for doctoral research students commencing their studies in October 2027.

The funding provides an opportunity for prospective PhD researchers to undertake doctoral study in a wide range of social science disciplines at participating universities in the United Kingdom. Depending on the applicant’s previous academic and research training, successful candidates may receive funding through different award structures, including doctoral programmes that incorporate a research-training master’s year.

The WRDTP brings together seven partner universities and supports high-quality doctoral research addressing important social, economic and interdisciplinary issues.

Prospective applicants should note that the number of studentships advertised for the 2027 intake is currently provisional because ESRC Doctoral Training Partnerships are undergoing a mid-term review during 2026. The final number of available awards may therefore be adjusted following the review.

What Is the WRDTP ESRC Studentship?

The White Rose Doctoral Training Partnership is a doctoral training partnership that provides funding and research training for postgraduate researchers working in the social sciences.

The Economic and Social Research Council (ESRC) is one of the UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) research councils and supports research and postgraduate training in the social sciences.

The WRDTP offers studentships at seven partner universities:

University of Bradford

University of Hull

University of Leeds

Manchester Metropolitan University

University of Sheffield

Sheffield Hallam University

University of York

Applicants do not apply directly to the WRDTP for funding. Instead, candidates apply for an eligible PhD programme at one of the partner universities and are subsequently nominated by their university for WRDTP studentship consideration.

What Does the ESRC Studentship Fund?

The WRDTP provides several categories of doctoral studentships for students beginning their research degrees in October 2027.

These include:

1. WRDTP Pathway Awards

Pathway Awards support applicants who develop their own doctoral research proposals.

These awards are intended for impactful social science research that engages with key themes and challenges identified through the WRDTP’s interdisciplinary pathways.

Successful candidates undertake their research under the supervision of academic experts whose research interests align with the proposed doctoral project.

The Pathway Awards include interdisciplinary research opportunities and other specialist awards.

2. Advanced Quantitative Methods Awards

The Advanced Quantitative Methods (AQM) Awards support doctoral research involving advanced quantitative research methods.

These awards are particularly relevant to candidates whose proposed research requires sophisticated quantitative approaches to investigate social science questions.

Applicants interested in research involving statistical analysis, quantitative modelling, large datasets or other advanced quantitative methodologies may find this pathway particularly relevant.

3. Advanced Data Analytics Awards

The Advanced Data Analytics (ADA) Awards support doctoral projects involving advanced data analytics within the social sciences.

These awards are particularly relevant to research involving data-intensive approaches and analytical techniques.

Candidates considering research at the intersection of social science and data analytics should examine the specific eligibility and application requirements of the relevant department.

4. WRDTP Collaborative Awards

Collaborative Awards are different from the student-led Pathway, AQM and ADA awards.

Collaborative projects are designed by academic colleagues at WRDTP partner universities in collaboration with partners from sectors such as:

Private-sector organisations

Public-sector organisations

Third-sector organisations

Other external partners

Students can subsequently apply for studentships connected to the available collaborative projects.

This structure provides doctoral researchers with an opportunity to conduct research involving external organisations and real-world research challenges.

5. WRDTP/Stuart Hall Foundation Awards

The WRDTP also includes specialist awards delivered in collaboration with the Stuart Hall Foundation.

According to the current WRDTP eligibility information, these awards are specifically open to Black British students, including applicants identifying as Black or Black British African, Black or Black British Caribbean, Black or Black British other, or Mixed Black or Black British.

However, international students are not eligible for the WRDTP/Stuart Hall Foundation Awards.

How Long Does the WRDTP PhD Funding Last?

The WRDTP structures its awards according to the applicant’s previous academic qualifications and research training.

There are three principal programme structures.

+3.5 Programme

This provides funding for a 3.5-year PhD.

It is generally intended for applicants who already have a social science master’s degree and have completed approximately 60 or more credits, or an equivalent amount, of master’s-level social science research training.

This option is therefore particularly relevant to applicants who already have substantial postgraduate research training.

+3.75 Programme

This provides funding for an integrated PGCert/PhD programme lasting approximately 3.75 years.

It is generally intended for applicants who have a social science master’s degree but have not completed the required core research training.

The integrated structure enables the student to obtain additional research training before or alongside their doctoral research.

1+3.5 Programme

This provides funding for:

One year of master’s-level study; followed by

A 3.5-year PhD.

It is generally intended for applicants who do not already have a social sciences master’s degree.

This route may therefore be particularly important for graduates whose undergraduate degree is in a different field or who do not yet possess the postgraduate social science research training normally expected for direct doctoral entry.

Applicants are advised to select the appropriate structure according to their academic and research background and to discuss the choice with their proposed supervisor.

Who Can Apply?

The WRDTP ESRC studentships are intended for prospective doctoral researchers who want to undertake eligible social sciences PhD research at one of the WRDTP’s seven partner universities.

Applicants must satisfy both:

The admission requirements of their chosen university, school or department; and

The minimum eligibility requirements established for ESRC-funded studentships.

Applicants must hold an offer for a PhD place in an eligible school or department and intend to undertake a social science research project that falls within the ESRC’s remit.

The applicant’s proposed research must therefore be academically suitable for an eligible social science department and must fall within the relevant ESRC research scope.

Academic Qualification Requirements

The WRDTP states that applicants must meet the entry requirements of the school or department through which they are applying.

In addition, the ESRC requires studentship applicants to have qualifications equivalent to a good honours degree at first-class or upper-second-class level, or demonstrate equivalent ability through a combination of qualifications and/or experience.

Recognised equivalent international qualifications can be considered.

Applicants must satisfy the requirements of their chosen university as well as the ESRC’s minimum academic threshold.

Because individual universities and departments can impose additional requirements, prospective applicants should check the PhD entry requirements of their intended department before preparing their application.

Can International Students Apply?

Yes. International applicants can apply for WRDTP ESRC studentships, subject to the relevant eligibility requirements.

However, the WRDTP states that the ESRC limits the proportion of studentships available to international applicants to 30% of awards.

This means that international applicants can be considered, but the WRDTP cannot award more than 30% of its studentships to international candidates in a given year. Each partner university also has limits on the number of international candidates it can put forward.

Therefore, international applicants should contact their chosen department early to find out how that university manages the selection and nomination of international candidates.

For international students who are successfully awarded a standard WRDTP studentship, the WRDTP universities have agreed to cover the difference between the UK and international tuition fee rates. This means successful overseas students are not expected to personally pay the international fee gap.

However, the studentship does not cover costs such as visa fees, the Immigration Health Surcharge, flights or other expenses associated with moving to the United Kingdom.

Can Applicants from Africa Apply?

Yes. Applicants from African countries can be eligible to apply for the standard WRDTP ESRC studentships as international candidates, provided they meet the academic, university, departmental and ESRC requirements.

This means prospective applicants from countries such as Ghana, Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda and other eligible countries worldwide can potentially be considered.

Nationality alone does not guarantee eligibility. International candidates must obtain admission to an eligible PhD programme and must also go through the university’s nomination and selection process.

The 30% limit on international studentships is particularly important for applicants outside the UK.

Who Is Not Eligible?

Several restrictions apply.

Applicants Already Undertaking a PhD

Applicants who have already commenced a PhD are not eligible to apply for a WRDTP studentship, whether they are studying in the UK or internationally.

Applicants who have a PhD offer with a start date before 1 October 2027 should contact their university about possible deferral options. Deferring the start date may allow them to be considered for the 2027 WRDTP competition, subject to all other requirements.

Distance-Learning PhDs

Remote, online or distance-learning PhD programmes are not eligible for ESRC funding.

The funded study must be undertaken in accordance with WRDTP and ESRC requirements, including the requirement to reside within a reasonable travel distance of the university.

International Applicants for the Stuart Hall Foundation Award

Although international applicants can apply for standard WRDTP ESRC studentships, they are not eligible for the WRDTP/Stuart Hall Foundation Awards, which have specific eligibility criteria for Black British students.

Where Can Successful Applicants Study?

WRDTP studentships are available through eligible schools and departments at the partnership’s seven universities.

The partner universities are:

University of Bradford

University of Hull

University of Leeds

Manchester Metropolitan University

University of Sheffield

Sheffield Hallam University

University of York

Not every department at each university is necessarily eligible, so applicants should confirm that their proposed PhD department participates in the WRDTP.

For example, eligible departments include areas such as management, politics and international studies, law, sociology, social policy, education, geography, healthcare, psychology and other relevant disciplines, depending on the university.

Is Political Science Eligible?

Political and social science research can fall within the WRDTP’s remit where the proposed research is appropriate for an eligible department and falls within the ESRC’s scope.

For example, the University of Leeds lists its School of Politics and International Studies among its eligible departments.

Applicants with backgrounds in political science, public policy, international relations, development studies, sociology, economics, management and related fields should therefore investigate the specific PhD departments and research areas available at each partner university.

Eligibility ultimately depends on the proposed research, department, admission requirements and WRDTP/ESRC criteria.

What Does the Funding Cover?

WRDTP ESRC studentships provide substantial financial support for successful doctoral researchers.

The funding covers UK tuition fees and maintenance at the standard UKRI rate.

For international students, the WRDTP universities have agreed to cover the difference between UK and international tuition fees for studentship holders.

Students may also have access to additional funding opportunities during their studentship, including support connected with:

Research training

Overseas fieldwork

Difficult language training

Overseas institutional visits

Other approved research-related activities

The exact level of stipend is linked to the applicable UKRI rate for the relevant academic year and is revised periodically.

Applicants should therefore check the current UKRI rates when planning their finances.

Important Costs Not Covered

Although the studentship provides significant financial support, applicants should not assume that every cost associated with studying in the UK will be paid.

For international students in particular, the WRDTP states that UKRI studentship awards do not cover:

UK visa costs

Immigration Health Surcharge

Flights to or from the UK

Other relocation expenses

International applicants should therefore budget separately for these costs.

Application Deadline

The current WRDTP application guidance states that applicants must submit the following by:

Deadline: 17:00, 20 January 2027

Applicants must submit:

An application for a PhD study place; and

A WRDTP Studentship Application Form.

The studentship application is separate from the university’s ordinary PhD admission application.

Important: University Deadlines May Be Earlier

The 20 January 2027 deadline should not necessarily be treated as the first deadline an applicant needs to worry about.

Individual departments and schools may establish earlier internal deadlines so that they have sufficient time to review applications and determine which candidates they will nominate.

Applicants should therefore contact their preferred department as early as possible and confirm:

The PhD application deadline

The department’s internal WRDTP deadline

Supervisor requirements

Research proposal requirements

Any additional documents required

The university’s process for international applicants

The WRDTP does not accept direct applications from individual candidates. Universities nominate candidates to the WRDTP.

How the Application Process Works

The process generally involves several stages.

Step 1: Identify an Eligible University and Department

Choose one of the seven WRDTP partner universities and identify an eligible school or department that matches your proposed research.

Step 2: Develop Your Research Idea

Applicants seeking a Pathway, AQM or ADA studentship should develop a strong doctoral research proposal that aligns with the relevant research pathway and the expertise of potential supervisors.

Step 3: Find a Potential Supervisor

Applicants should contact potential supervisors and discuss their research proposal.

This is particularly important because the university, rather than the applicant, ultimately nominates candidates for WRDTP consideration.

Step 4: Apply for the PhD

Submit your PhD admission application to the chosen university according to its own requirements and deadline.

Step 5: Complete the WRDTP Studentship Application

Applicants must also complete the separate WRDTP Studentship Application Form.

Step 6: University Selection and Nomination

The university or department assesses applicants using its own fair and equitable process.

TITLE: Fully Funded PhD in Global Talent Mobility and Europe’s Strategic Autonomy at Utrecht University: €4,051 Monthly Salary

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Utrecht University in the Netherlands is inviting applications for a fully funded four-year PhD position in Global Talent Mobility and Europe’s Strategic Autonomy. The opportunity is hosted by the Faculty of Geosciences, within the Department of Human Geography and Spatial Planning, and is designed for highly motivated researchers interested in innovation, international mobility, human capital, economic geography, and the future of Europe’s knowledge and innovation systems.

This is a particularly attractive opportunity for prospective doctoral researchers who want to pursue an interdisciplinary research career while working with large-scale datasets and internationally recognised researchers.

The successful candidate will investigate how Europe’s ambitions for technological innovation, competitiveness, resilience, and strategic autonomy are connected to the movement of highly skilled international talent, particularly people who have completed PhDs in STEM-related fields.

Unlike a conventional scholarship that simply provides a study allowance, this opportunity is a paid PhD employment position. The selected candidate will be employed by Utrecht University and receive a gross monthly salary, alongside holiday pay, a year-end bonus, pension arrangements, leave benefits, and professional development opportunities.

Host Institution

Utrecht University

Faculty

Faculty of Geosciences

Department

Department of Human Geography and Spatial Planning

Research Sections

The successful candidate will be based in the Economic Geography Section of the Department of Human Geography and Spatial Planning, while working closely with the Innovation Studies Section at the Copernicus Institute of Sustainable Development.

The two research groups provide an interdisciplinary environment combining economic geography, innovation studies, migration research, and related social science disciplines.

PhD Research Topic

Global Talent Mobility and Europe’s Strategic Autonomy

The PhD project focuses on an increasingly important question: How does Europe’s ability to innovate and maintain strategic autonomy depend on the international mobility of highly skilled talent?

Talent has become a critical resource for modern innovation systems. Highly educated researchers and professionals contribute to scientific discovery, technological development, entrepreneurship, and knowledge transfer.

At the same time, Europe and other regions are facing major changes in the international movement of skilled workers and researchers. Geopolitical tensions, migration restrictions, national security concerns, and changing international relationships may influence where highly skilled people choose to study, work, conduct research, and build their careers.

These developments could have significant consequences for global knowledge networks and innovation.

The PhD project therefore seeks to understand the relationship between:

Global talent mobility

International migration

Doctoral education

Human capital

Innovation

Scientific research

Technological development

Economic geography

Institutional environments

Europe’s strategic autonomy

International knowledge networks

A particular focus will be placed on STEM PhD recipients, who are important contributors to science- and technology-based innovation.

What Will the PhD Research Investigate?

The project will examine how doctoral training, international mobility, and institutional environments influence where knowledge is produced and where that knowledge is eventually transformed into technological and economic value.

The research will connect perspectives from economic geography and innovation studies to investigate questions surrounding the movement of global talent and the consequences of that movement for innovation systems.

The successful candidate will have the opportunity to develop unique datasets and use quantitative and mixed-method research approaches.

The research may involve combining several types of information, including:

PhD recipient data

Career information

Publication records

Patent data

Survey data

Administrative data

Online data

Individual mobility information

Other relevant sources concerning career trajectories and preferences

Online data

International conferences

National conferences

Other scholarly events

TITLE: Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters Scholarships 2026–2027: Study Across Europe with Fully Funded Scholarship Opportunities

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters (EMJM) programme offers an exceptional opportunity for students from around the world to pursue an international master’s degree through a consortium of universities located in different countries.

Unlike a conventional master’s programme where students may remain at one university for the entire duration of their studies, Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters are designed around international mobility. Students typically study at several universities and may also participate in research projects, traineeships, fieldwork, thesis preparation and other academic activities in different countries.

The programme is supported by the European Union’s Erasmus+ programme, and selected master’s programmes can provide highly competitive scholarships to the best-ranked applicants worldwide. Depending on the individual programme, scholarships can contribute toward participation costs as well as travel, visa and living expenses.

For students seeking an internationally recognised master’s degree, exposure to different academic systems, multicultural learning environments and international professional networks, Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters can be one of the most valuable study opportunities available.

Opportunity Category

Scholarship / International Master’s Degree Programme

The Erasmus Mundus opportunity combines postgraduate study with competitive scholarship funding. Students apply to individual Erasmus Mundus Joint Master programmes rather than submitting one general application to Erasmus Mundus.

What Are Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters?

Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters are prestigious international master’s programmes that are jointly designed and delivered by a consortium of higher education institutions.

A participating programme normally brings together at least three higher education institutions from at least three different countries. The consortium may also include associated partners from academic, research, professional, governmental, business or other non-academic sectors.

This structure gives students the opportunity to experience higher education across different countries and institutions while completing one coordinated master’s programme.

Depending on the programme, students may move between participating universities during their studies. The exact mobility pathway varies from one master’s programme to another, so prospective applicants should carefully examine the official programme website before applying.

Why Study an Erasmus Mundus Joint Master?

There are several reasons why Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters are attractive to international students.

1. Study in multiple countries

One of the defining characteristics of an Erasmus Mundus Joint Master is international mobility.

Rather than completing the entire programme at one university, students may spend different parts of their master’s degree at different institutions within the consortium.

This can expose students to:

Different European higher education systems

International academic perspectives

Multiple research environments

Different cultures and languages

International professional networks

Diverse student communities

Cross-border approaches to research and problem-solving

The specific countries and universities involved depend on the master’s programme selected.

2. International academic experience

Erasmus Mundus programmes bring together students and academics from different parts of the world.

Studying in such an environment can help students develop a broader understanding of their academic discipline while learning to work with people from different cultural and professional backgrounds.

This can be particularly valuable for graduates interested in international development, public policy, communication, science, technology, environmental studies, business, social sciences and other disciplines where international collaboration is important.

3. Prestigious master’s programmes

Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters are developed and delivered by international university consortia.

The participating institutions work together to create an integrated programme rather than simply offering separate courses under a common name.

Students therefore receive an academic experience built around collaboration between the participating institutions.

4. Opportunities for research and practical experience

An Erasmus Mundus Joint Master is not necessarily limited to traditional classroom-based learning.

Depending on the programme, students can undertake:

Academic coursework

Research activities

Traineeships

Practical projects

Fieldwork

Thesis preparation

Master’s thesis research

Thesis defence

The exact combination varies according to the selected programme.

This makes it important for applicants to examine individual programme curricula before deciding which Erasmus Mundus master’s programme best matches their academic and professional objectives.

Erasmus Mundus Scholarships

One of the most attractive features of the programme is the availability of competitive scholarships.

Some Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters offer full scholarships to the best-ranked students worldwide.

Scholarship arrangements vary according to the specific programme and the applicable funding rules. However, the official Erasmus Mundus information indicates that scholarships can cover or contribute toward major costs associated with participating in the master’s programme.

Potential areas of financial support include:

Participation or programme costs

Travel expenses

Visa-related expenses

Living allowance

Because funding conditions can differ between programmes and application cycles, applicants should not assume that every Erasmus Mundus master’s programme provides exactly the same scholarship package.

The individual master’s programme website should always be checked for the current scholarship amount, eligibility conditions, payment arrangements and covered expenses.

How Long Are Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters?

Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters generally last between one and two academic years.

Programmes can comprise:

60 ECTS credits

90 ECTS credits

120 ECTS credits

The duration depends on the specific master’s programme.

Applicants should therefore examine the programme description carefully to determine:

Programme duration

Number of semesters

Required mobility periods

Participating universities

Study locations

Internship or traineeship requirements

Research requirements

Thesis requirements

Graduation arrangements

What Degree Will You Receive?

Students who successfully complete an Erasmus Mundus Joint Master may receive either a joint degree or multiple degrees, depending on the structure of the programme.

Joint degree

A joint degree is a single degree certificate issued on behalf of at least two higher education institutions within the consortium.

Multiple degrees

A multiple-degree arrangement means that the student receives at least two degree certificates from two higher education institutions belonging to the consortium.

The precise degree arrangement is established by the individual Erasmus Mundus Joint Master.

Students should therefore review the degree structure before applying and understand which institutions will award the qualification.

Who Can Apply for Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters?

Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters are designed for students from around the world.

The programme information states that students from all over the world are welcome to apply. Therefore, the opportunity is not restricted to applicants from European countries.

Applicants from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, the Caribbean, Oceania and other regions may be eligible, provided they satisfy the requirements of the particular master’s programme they select.

However, international eligibility does not mean that every applicant automatically qualifies for every programme. Each Erasmus Mundus master’s programme establishes its own academic and admission requirements.

Academic Requirements

The general requirement is that applicants must:

Hold a bachelor’s degree or first degree; or

Be in the final year of their bachelor’s degree and graduate before the master’s programme begins.

Applicants may also qualify if they can demonstrate an equivalent level of learning.

Where an equivalent qualification is used, it must be officially recognised in accordance with the relevant national legislation and practices of the country where the degree is awarded.

This means prospective applicants should carefully verify whether their existing qualification is considered equivalent to a bachelor’s degree for their selected Erasmus Mundus programme.

Final-Year Bachelor’s Students

Students who have not yet completed their bachelor’s degree may still be able to apply.

However, applicants in their final year must graduate before the Erasmus Mundus Joint Master begins.

This is particularly important because applicants should not assume that being accepted while completing a bachelor’s degree means they can postpone graduation indefinitely.

Students should check the individual master’s programme for its specific documentation and graduation verification requirements.

Eligibility for Applicants from Africa

Students from African countries can apply to Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters.

There is no general restriction limiting the opportunity to European applicants. Applicants from African countries can compete for available places and scholarships alongside eligible applicants from other parts of the world.

For example, prospective applicants from countries such as:

Kenya

Uganda

Tanzania

Rwanda

Ethiopia

Ghana

Nigeria

South Africa

Zambia

Zimbabwe

Botswana

may explore the available catalogue and determine whether they meet the admission requirements of individual programmes.

Nationality alone, however, does not guarantee admission or a scholarship. Academic qualifications and programme-specific eligibility requirements remain important.

Application Process

One of the most important things prospective applicants should understand is that there is not one universal application form for all Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters.

Students apply directly to the institution or consortium running their chosen programme.

The application process can therefore differ significantly from one master’s programme to another.

Step 1: Search the Erasmus Mundus catalogue

The first step is to explore the official Erasmus Mundus catalogue and identify master’s programmes relevant to your academic background and career objectives.

When searching the catalogue, applicants should pay attention to:

Programme title

Academic discipline

Participating universities

Participating countries

Programme duration

Mobility requirements

Admission requirements

Application deadline

Scholarship availability

Required documents

Language requirements

Step 2: Visit the master’s programme website

After identifying an interesting programme, applicants should visit its official programme website.

The programme website is the authoritative source for the specific admission requirements and application instructions.

Applicants should not rely solely on general Erasmus Mundus information because individual master’s programmes can have different requirements.

Step 3: Check the academic requirements

Applicants should determine whether their bachelor’s degree or equivalent qualification is accepted.

They should also review any programme-specific requirements relating to:

Academic discipline

Previous coursework

Grade requirements

Professional experience

Language proficiency

Research experience

Technical skills

Other qualifications

Step 4: Check scholarship requirements

If funding is important to you, determine whether the programme offers Erasmus Mundus scholarships and whether you need to complete any additional scholarship-related section of the application.

Some programmes may assess applicants for scholarships as part of the main application process, while others may provide specific instructions.

Step 5: Prepare the required documents

The exact documents vary by programme, but applicants should expect to provide some combination of:

Bachelor’s degree certificate

Academic transcripts

Proof of graduation or expected graduation

Curriculum vitae

Motivation letter

Proof of language proficiency, where required

Identification documents

Recommendation letters, where required

Other programme-specific supporting documents

Applicants should follow the official programme instructions carefully because submitting an incomplete application can affect eligibility.

Step 6: Submit before the programme deadline

Once the application is complete, submit it through the application system specified by the master’s programme.

Do not assume that there is one universal Erasmus Mundus deadline.

The deadline is determined by the individual programme.

When Is the Erasmus Mundus Application Deadline?

There is no single universal deadline for all Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters.

The official Erasmus Mundus information states that, in most cases, applications should be submitted between October and January for programmes beginning during the following academic year.

However, the exact deadline depends on the master’s programme.

Applicants should therefore check the official website of their selected programme for the precise application deadline.

Important deadline advice

Because many programmes have competitive scholarship selection processes, prospective students should begin preparing well before October.

Waiting until the final days of an application period can create problems if you need:

Academic transcripts

Recommendation letters

Language test results

Certified documents

Passport or identification documents

A strong motivation statement

Additional programme-specific documentation

Deadline: Generally October to January for programmes starting in the following academic year, but the exact deadline varies by master’s programme.

What Makes the Scholarship Competitive?

Erasmus Mundus scholarships are highly competitive because they are intended for the best-ranked applicants.

Applicants therefore need to do more than simply meet the minimum admission requirements.

A strong application should demonstrate a clear connection between the applicant’s:

Academic background

Professional or extracurricular experience

Motivation for the chosen programme

Career objectives

Relevant skills

Interest in the programme’s academic focus

International or cross-cultural interests

Potential contribution to the programme community

How to Strengthen Your Application

Research the programme carefully

Do not apply simply because a programme offers a scholarship.

Read the curriculum, mobility structure, research areas, participating universities and career outcomes.

Your motivation statement should demonstrate that you understand what the programme offers.

Match your background to the programme

Applicants should clearly explain how their previous academic and professional experiences prepare them for the master’s programme.

For example, if your bachelor’s degree is in communication, you should identify relevant communication, research, media, digital, development, public relations or related experience when applying to an appropriate programme.

Build a strong motivation statement

A strong motivation statement should explain:

Why you want to study the programme

Why the subject is important to you

Why you selected that particular Erasmus Mundus programme

What experience you bring

What you hope to learn

How the programme fits your career plans

What you intend to contribute after graduation

Avoid writing a generic statement that could be submitted to any university.

Demonstrate international motivation

Because Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters are inherently international, applicants should demonstrate their ability and willingness to learn and collaborate in multicultural environments.

International exposure can come from education, work, volunteering, research, community projects or other relevant experiences.

Start early

Applicants should begin preparing months before the deadline.

A useful preparation timeline could include:

Several months before applications open

Research programmes

Compare academic requirements

Identify suitable programmes

Review scholarship conditions

Before the application deadline

Prepare your CV

Draft your motivation letter

Request recommendation letters

Obtain academic documents

Check language requirements

Prepare any required tests

Before submission

Review every requirement

Check document formats

Proofread the application

Confirm the correct application portal

Submit before the deadline

Advice and Support for Applicants

Prospective applicants can also find resources through the Erasmus Mundus Association, which provides information and resources intended to help applicants understand the programmes and application process.

These resources can include programme contacts, events involving national volunteer representatives and stories from successful applicants.

Learning from previous applicants can help prospective students better understand the application process and prepare a stronger submission.

No Application date yet. In most cases, you should submit your application between October and January for courses starting the following academic year.

Erasmus Mundus in Numbers

The Erasmus Mundus programme has a substantial international track record.

According to the official Erasmus+ information referenced by the programme, almost 50,000 students have participated since 2004.

This long history demonstrates the scale and international reach of Erasmus Mundus and highlights the programme’s role in facilitating international postgraduate education.

Erasmus Mundus Opportunities Beyond Students

Although this opportunity is focused on students seeking master’s degrees, Erasmus+ also provides other forms of support.

Grants for higher education institutions

Erasmus+ provides grants to higher education institutions to develop and run Erasmus Mundus Joint Master programmes.

Institutions interested in participating should consult the official Erasmus+ information for organisations.

Opportunities for researchers

Researchers may also find related opportunities under the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions, including postdoctoral fellowships and staff exchanges.

Other Erasmus+ opportunities

Erasmus+ also provides various opportunities and forms of support for students, staff and other eligible participants.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Erasmus Mundus available to students from Africa?

Yes. Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters welcome applications from students around the world. African students can apply provided they meet the requirements of the particular master’s programme.

Do I need to already have a master’s degree?

No. The general requirement is a bachelor’s degree or equivalent first degree. Students in the final year of their bachelor’s degree may also apply, provided they graduate before the master’s programme begins.

Can final-year undergraduate students apply?

Yes. Final-year bachelor’s students can apply, but they must complete and graduate from their bachelor’s programme before the Erasmus Mundus master’s programme begins.

Are Erasmus Mundus scholarships fully funded?

Some Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters offer full scholarships to the best-ranked students worldwide. Scholarship coverage can include participation costs and contributions toward travel, visa and living expenses. The exact funding package varies by programme.

Can I choose any university in Europe?

No. Applicants apply to specific Erasmus Mundus Joint Master programmes, each of which has its own consortium of participating universities. Students follow the mobility structure established by their chosen programme.

How many universities participate in an Erasmus Mundus Joint Master?

An Erasmus Mundus Joint Master normally involves at least three higher education institutions from at least three different countries, together with associated partners.

How long does an Erasmus Mundus master’s degree take?

The programmes generally last between one and two academic years and may comprise 60, 90 or 120 ECTS credits.

Will I receive one degree or several degrees?

Depending on the programme, you may receive either a joint degree issued on behalf of multiple institutions or multiple degrees issued by two or more institutions in the consortium.

Is there one Erasmus Mundus application deadline?

No. Each master’s programme establishes its own deadline. In most cases, applications are submitted between October and January for programmes beginning in the following academic year.

Where do I apply?

You apply directly to the institution or consortium running the Erasmus Mundus Joint Master programme you have selected.

Where can I find available programmes?

You can search the official Erasmus Mundus catalogue for the latest programmes available.

Conclusion

The Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters programme represents a major opportunity for international students seeking an advanced degree in a highly international academic environment.

With master’s programmes delivered by consortia of universities across different countries, students can gain international academic exposure, participate in research and practical activities, build cross-cultural networks and potentially earn a joint or multiple-degree qualification.

The availability of competitive scholarships makes the opportunity particularly attractive to students who may otherwise find international postgraduate study financially difficult. Selected scholarship recipients can receive support toward participation costs as well as travel, visa and living expenses, depending on the individual programme.

However, prospective applicants should remember that Erasmus Mundus is not a single master’s course with one universal application deadline. The programme consists of numerous individual Joint Masters, each with its own participating universities, academic focus, admission criteria, scholarship arrangements and application deadline.

The best strategy is therefore to begin early, search the official Erasmus Mundus catalogue, identify programmes that match your academic and career goals, study the individual programme requirements carefully and submit a well-prepared application directly through the appropriate programme.

For students with a bachelor’s degree or those approaching graduation who want to experience international postgraduate education, Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters can provide a pathway to study across multiple institutions and countries while becoming part of a global academic community.

TITLE: Njala University and eLearnAfricaLMS Partner to Develop Online Program Management (OPM)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
PRESS RELEASE – Accra, Ghana (January 10, 2023)

Njala University, Sierra Leone; the Association of African University (AAU); and eLearnAfricaLMS, have signed a collaboration agreement, entitled ‘The Design and Development of Online Modules for the Programmes offered at Njala University’. The partnership will provide Njala University with inexpensive tools to incorporate eLearning solutions quickly and efficiently for blended and fully online academic programmes.

The Vice Chancellor and Principal, Professor Bashiru Mohamed Koroma expressed hope that the timely intervention by AAU and eLearnAfricaLMS would transform the pedagogical landscape and facilitate modern teaching and learning methods to provide staff and students increasing access to lecture notes, course content and other digital learning materials in Njala University. The Leadership at Njala University hope for a great and rewarding partnership.

“eLearnAfrica is a social enterprise committed to increasing and expanding access to educational and professional development opportunities throughout Africa. The instructor toolkit makes course design and presentation simple for professors. The Virtual classroom promotes thoughtful participation, learning review for mastery, and collaborative assignments and grading”. (Brook Negussie, CEO, eLearnAfricaLMS).

“eLearnAfricaLMS is a platform that makes learning easier for students. All learning materials are made available and accessible, providing a solution to the massification of classes and other related contextual factors. The task and interactions are made easy for teachers in their interactions with students”, said Dr Thomas Philip Songu, ICT Director, Njala University .

About Njala University

Njala University (or simply Njala, as it is fondly called) has had a rich history since its establishment in 1964 as a university college based on the model of the American Land Grant University. Since then, it has developed into one of the leading universities in the country, preparing undergraduate and postgraduate students for careers in a wide variety of specializations including Education, Agricultural Sciences, Environmental and Community Health Sciences, Social Sciences and Law, Natural Resources Management, and Information Technology, among others. Njala University is a multi-disciplinary University with three campuses – the Njala campus in the Moyamba District, the Bo campus in the Bo District and the newly established Bonthe campus in the Bonthe District. It also operates a location in Freetown.

About eLearnAfrica

In 2016, eLearnAfrica entered a partnership agreement with the Association of African Universities (AAU); one that would expand online learning opportunities for students enrolled in the AAU’s over 400 member institutions and other universities not yet under the umbrella of the prestigious AAU. The target was to make educational opportunities available to about 10 million African students. In pursuing this agenda, the AAU-eLearnAfricaLMS was launched by the two partners at the 15th Quadrennial General Conference of African University Leaders, on 7th July 2021.

For further details, contact Thomas Philip Songu, Director of Information and Communication Technology, at tsongu@njala.edu.sl or AAU -eLearnAfricaLMS: admin@elearnafrica.com / aaulms@aau.org

TITLE: Teacher Development Fund 2026: Up to £165,000 for Arts-Based Learning in UK Schools

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Paul Hamlyn Foundation (PHF) Teacher Development Fund supports partnerships between schools and arts or cultural organisations that use arts-based approaches to improve teaching, learning and equity for children.

The fund is designed around the belief that high-quality arts-based learning can help create more equitable classrooms where children can learn, participate and thrive.

Funding Amount and Duration

Successful applicants can receive up to £165,000 per application.

Projects are expected to run for two academic years, giving schools and arts organisations sufficient time to develop professional learning, test arts-based approaches in classrooms, evaluate their impact and build sustainable changes in teaching and learning.

What Does the Teacher Development Fund Support?

The fund focuses on developing teachers’ skills and confidence in using arts-based approaches in education. Supported projects should contribute to more equitable learning environments, particularly for pupils experiencing systemic inequity.

The programme aims to:

Improve access to learning for pupils experiencing systemic inequity.

Strengthen collaboration between schools and arts or cultural organisations.

Provide high-quality professional learning for teachers.

Enable teachers and artist practitioners to learn from and work alongside one another in classrooms.

Build evidence and practical knowledge about how arts-based learning can improve equity.

Encourage sustainable improvements in teaching and learning that continue beyond the project period.

Who Can Lead an Application?

Either of the following can act as the lead applicant:

A primary school, or

An arts or cultural organisation.

However, applications must be based on a strong partnership between schools and arts or cultural organisations.

Each project must involve:

A minimum of six schools.

A maximum of ten schools.

At least one arts or cultural organisation.

At least two teachers and one senior leader from each participating school, although some flexibility may be available for small or rural schools.

Eligible Schools and Organisations

Participating schools must operate in the state sector and can include:

Mainstream primary schools.

Specialist SEND settings.

Alternative Provision settings.

Schools working with primary-age children.

Teachers working with Nursery and Reception classes in primary schools may also be included.

Eligible arts organisations can include:

Charities.

Community organisations.

Social enterprises.

Not-for-profit companies active in the arts and culture sector.

What Will Funded Projects Work On?

The Teacher Development Fund expects projects to develop a structured professional learning programme over two academic years.

Key areas include:

Equity: Improving learning opportunities and outcomes for pupils.

Professional learning: Developing teachers’ knowledge, skills and confidence.

Arts-based approaches: Integrating creative and arts-based methods into classroom teaching.

Curriculum: Exploring how arts-based approaches can enhance curriculum delivery.

Formative evaluation: Learning from the implementation of the project and using evidence to improve practice.

Spreading practice: Sharing learning and effective approaches beyond participating schools.

Cohort learning: Creating opportunities for participating schools and practitioners to learn together.

Community of practice: Building longer-term networks for collaboration and shared learning.

What Makes a Strong Partnership?

The foundation highlights several characteristics associated with effective partnerships and practice.

These include:

Anti-racism.

Intersectionality.

Effective professional learning.

Meaningful involvement of school leaders.

Strong roles for artist practitioners.

Enquiry-driven and reflective practice.

Applicants should therefore demonstrate that the proposed partnership is more than a simple relationship between a funder, school and arts organisation. The partners should be able to show how they will work together, learn together and create meaningful improvements in teaching and learning.

Deadline

The deadline to apply for the Teacher Development Fund is 11 November 2026 at 12 noon.

Applicants should allow sufficient time to establish the required partnerships, develop the project approach, clarify participating schools and prepare the application before the deadline.

How to Apply

Applications are submitted through the Paul Hamlyn Foundation’s application system.

Applicants should also review the foundation’s detailed eligibility guidance and FAQs before applying.

Click HERE to read more and apply.

Conclusion

The Teacher Development Fund provides substantial support for schools and arts or cultural organisations seeking to use arts-based learning to create more equitable educational environments. With funding of up to £165,000, a two-academic-year project period and a strong emphasis on teacher development, partnership working, evaluation and sustainable change, the opportunity is particularly relevant to organisations with established experience in arts education and schools committed to improving outcomes for children experiencing systemic inequity.

TITLE: GRIOS launches open call for evidence synthesis on Open Science

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Network News | News | Programme Management | Research Assessment News | Science Policy Support

The Global Research Initiative on Open Science (GRIOS), hosted by the European Science Foundation (ESF), is pleased to announce the launch of its first open call for proposals to conduct in-depth evidence synthesis on key Open Science topics.

Open Science holds great promise for making research more inclusive, transparent, and impactful. Yet while many funders, research organisations, and national and international authorities have adopted Open Science policies, implementing effective strategies remains challenging. Policymakers need a solid evidence base to guide their decisions – and that evidence is often lacking.

GRIOS was established to address this gap. Its objectives are to synthesise existing knowledge on Open Science worldwide, formulate evidence-based policy recommendations, and propose a research agenda to fill current knowledge gaps.

This call will fund evidence synthesis on two priority topics identified by GRIOS funders and its Academic Advisory Board:

Incentives and research assessment – Which incentive schemes and assessment reforms increase the uptake of Open Science practices?

Research data sharing – What factors influence the effectiveness of research data sharing policies?

The call is open to individual researchers, research teams, organisations, consultancies, and consortia from all countries. GRIOS seeks proposals grounded in rigorous, transparent methods and Open Science practices. One review will be funded per topic, with a maximum budget of €80,000 per project. Projects are expected to run for 12 months.

Submissions are open from 23 April until 20 July 2026 (16:00h CEST).

TITLE: Towards the Development of Quality and Relevant African Higher Education – Infusion of Entrepreneurship and Job Creation Skills Curricula

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities whose headquarters is based in Accra, Ghana continues to build the capacity of higher education stakeholders in different subject areas. This is in line with the fulfilment of the AAU’s pledge and mandate to contribute towards quality African Higher Education (HE), superintended by a highly skilled human resource.

A total of twelve (12) top university leaders including Vice Chancellors, Deans and Directors from Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) in Ghana, Nigeria, Malawi, Eswatini and Kenya attended the AAU’s workshop. Hosted under the topic; Inculcating Entrepreneurial & Job Creation Skill, the sessions were highly interactive with diverse activities and opportunities for lesson sharing and exchanges among the delegates.

The workshop, held from the 9th – 12th of May 2022, was against a background of the rising graduate unemployment, the loss of jobs due to the COVID-19 pandemic and the inability of national governments to generate enough jobs for everyone. In addition, the workshop also sought to assist institutions in identifying gaps and opportunities for commercialization and industrialization of staff and students’ ideas, innovations and creativity. During the discussions, emphasis was placed on implementing strategies to foster attitude and mindset change of both staff and students and creating an enabling environment to support the reversal of the trend of being job seekers instead of job creators. Delegates were also encouraged to go back and make sure that their institutions do things differently for the better. The workshop proposed and discussed various high quality instructional methods/pedagogy and entrepreneurship curricula for consideration and adoption by African Universities.

In his opening remarks, on behalf of the AAU Secretary General, the Director of Research and Projects, Prof. Damtew Teffera, said that, as one of the poorest continents, Africa needs to revive its higher education systems to produce home-grown solutions to overcome its myriad of developmental challenges. He made reference to the African Development Bank (ADB)’s White Paper, published in June 2021 titled, Entrepreneurship and Free Trade: Africa’s catalysts for a new era of Economic prosperity. In this paper, the ADB advocated for entrepreneurship, as being central to all efforts towards Africa’s socio-economic transformation. Prof. Teferra added, that he was convinced the workshop would add value to the delegates’ institutions as they attempted to build more robust ecosystems and networks in the African HEIs.

The broad areas covered by the different facilitators and guest speakers included the following; The Art of Managing Emotions, Examples of Entrepreneurial Activities Outside the Curricula, The Enterprise Culture in the African HE Context, Developing an Enterprise Strategy & an Incubation Centre, Mapping out the Desired Culture in Institutions of Higher Learning, Developing the Entrepreneurial Mindset, Developing Intrapreneurs, Examining the way forward for the African HE staff & students, Skills Development for Tomorrow’s Technology, Resolving the Entrepreneurial Mindset Challenges and The Principles of Curriculum Design for Enterprise Education.

The topics were effectively presented by facilitators from diverse backgrounds, including Dr. Violet Makuku, the AAU Project Officer and Workshops Coordinator; Dr Irene Riverson-Brew, a Senior Lecturer in the University of Westminster, London, UK; Ms. Jewel Thompson, Lecturer & Business Incubator Manager, Ashesi University, Ghana; Mr. Abednego Corletey, the ICT, Senior IT Officer and Mrs. Ayesha Owusu-Barnaby, Senior Lecturer, University of Hertfordshire, UK. Their efforts were augmented by a number of guest speakers of different related backgrounds.

Some Key Highlights from the Workshop Deliberations

Entrepreneurship leadership and emotional intelligence were highlighted by Dr. Irene Brew-Riverson as being critical catalysts to successful entrepreneurial activities by an institution. Desired characteristics identified, to be possessed by leaders to achieve the target agenda of having a fully-fledged entrepreneurial university/institution included integrity, innovativeness, creativity and being a fast thinker, among others. Regarding emotional intelligence, leaders are encouraged to transfer attributes such as hope, love and happiness within their institutions to create a conducive environment for entrepreneurship to flourish. One of the delegates encouraged all stakeholders to prioritise the Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) and practice efficient monitoring and evaluation in order to realize the set goals and objectives.

Ms. Jewel Thompson, one of the facilitators, concentrated on incubators, identification and grooming of students as well as commercialization and industrialization of students’ innovations and intellectual property (Copyrights and Patents). She lamented the collapsing of some students’ innovations and promising businesses once they leave the institutions without financial support to stabilize and scale up their highly promising business ventures. Again, various units in all higher education institutions were encouraged to work collaboratively in driving their institutions’ entrepreneurship agenda instead of working in silos as was the case from a number of institutions represented by the delegates.

Institutional Work Around the Inculcation of Entrepreneurship and Job Creation Skills

The delegates’ institutions were at different levels of establishing and implementing the entrepreneurship and job creation skills programmes, including the establishment of the incubation centres. While some of the institutions offer entrepreneurship and job creation skills modules/courses to their Business School students only, others offer them as university wide courses/modules. Institutions which had incubators before the COVID-19 pandemic also reported being heavily affected by the lockdowns, sicknesses and in some cases deaths of some of the incubators’ staff.

The challenges related to the Inculcation of Entrepreneurial and Job Creation Skills in Higher and Tertiary Education

Funding was identified as one of the major challenges limiting the scaling up of viable staff and students’ innovations and business plans. Another challenge is the lack of effective collaboration among students, staff and the institution in developing and registering intellectual property (patents and copyrights), as well as commercialize and industrialize goods and services. The non-inclusion of dedicated time slots on the official calendar for mentorship and grooming of students with innovative ideas to nurture and expand them into businesses was also highlighted.

The failure of institutions to approach industry players for partnerships that could benefit the students and the institutions is one challenge that was underscored. Delegates were encouraged to also connect students, especially those with distinctions, merits and great ideas to industry so that they can be supported in cash and kind to transform their research results and recommendations to intellectual property (patents and copyrights) which can then be commercialized leading to industrialization. The industry could in turn support the institutions in cash and kind, for example, with placement for internships and funding to further develop their ideas.

Mitigation Measures, Missing Links and the Way forward

The mobilisation of alumni networks to support the ingrain of entrepreneurship and job creation skills activities were identified as being important. Dr. Violet Makuku strongly advised the institutions to treat students well if they are expected to become active alumni with an attachment to their institution after completing their studies. According to her, this helps them to develop a strong positive relationship with the institutions such that long after graduating, they will remain loyal to them and are always willing to contribute to developmental activities and initiatives.

Another proposed solution was to have mentoring and counselling services for students on the subject of entrepreneurship so that they get to understand what they are doing and how they should do it better. Closely related to this is the need to teach soft skills such as creativity, teamwork, problem solving, hard work, communication and writing skills, among others to the students. The learner-centred approaches could also help the students to further develop analytical, evaluative and examination skills, which are all critical aspects of entrepreneurship and job creation skills.

Solutions to curricula related issues were also proposed by Mrs. Ayesha Owusu-Barnaby. These include the teaching and learning of entrepreneurship and job creation skills during the first year and the last year of academic studies. Other delegates proposed that the courses could be taught from the first year to the final year so that students gradually change their attitude, ways of doing things and their mindset from being job seekers to job creators. In addition, the curricula content would need to be reviewed while new related curricula should be designed to make sure that students get the appropriate knowledge and skills that can help them to eventually commercialize and industrialize the products and services they come up with. In relation to curricula issues, Dr. Makuku emphasized that every related course should have an ICT component because of the 4th Industrial Revolution and the digitalization of the workspaces and pieces of equipment which require work-ready students.

The delegates were also encouraged to be actively involved in writing grant winning proposals and to search for grant calls that are aligned to this area. Such grants could then be used to scale-up innovations and sustain the existing incubation centres and innovation hubs. One of the key aspects to take note of would be to include the Sustainable Development goals in proposal writing.

Students and institutions were advised to start with simple solutions and the low hanging fruits where their ideas and innovations would not require a lot of capital, as they could eventually expand and obtain funding to implement larger projects.

Bringing the discussions to a close, higher education institutions in Africa were encouraged to host various events targeted at inculcating entrepreneurship and job creation skills in students. The workshop ended on a high note with the certification ceremony and an encouragement to the AAU from the delegates that such workshops should be executed throughout the whole continent at regular intervals.

Speakers Series Schedule

[CANCELLED] February 9, 2022

Duff Neill, Senior Staff Scientist, Los Alamos National Laboratory
2012-2015 Pappalardo Fellow, Quantum Field Theory
Introductory remarks: Joshua Foster, 2021-2024 Pappalardo Fellow

“The enduring dream of Drell-Levy-Yan”

Two foundational processes inform our understanding of strongly-interacting scattering at high energies: deep in-elastic scattering (DIS), which probes the structure of bound states, and fragmentation, which quantifies how the total energy of the scattering process converts into the asymptotic bound states.

Roughly speaking, the DIS process captures a snapshot in time of the spatial structure of the bound state in terms of the underlying degrees of freedom, while the fragmentation process captures the formation in time of bound states, and both are governed by scaling-laws arising from the asymptotic freedom of quantum chromo-dynamics (QCD).

But even before QCD was realized as the theory of strong interactions, Drell-Levy-Yan proposed that these two processes should be analytically connected. Knowledge of one ought to allow one to completely predict the other.

Their original formulation has not really ever been proven, and it was quickly realized may not even be true, but I will sketch how this dream is being unexpectedly reconstructed on several fronts using insights from conformal field theory being applied to real-world QCD, giving rise to a set of relations I will loosely call the “reciprocity between space and time.”

February 23, 2022

Haruki Watanabe, Associate Professor, Faculty of Engineering, The University of Tokyo
2015-2016 Pappalardo Fellow, Condensed Matter Theory/Theoretical Nuclear and Particle Physics
Introductory remarks: Senthil Todadri, Professor of Physics

“Vanishing and non-vanishing persistent currents of various conserved quantities”

Symmetries are the key in understanding the physical properties of many-body systems. The famous Noether theorem guarantees the presence of a conserved quantity for every continuous symmetry of the system. There could also be other “accidental” conserved quantities that are conserved, but are not related to continuous symmetries. Regardless of their origin, we can define a current operator for each conserved quantity that satisfies the continuity equation.

In this talk, we revisit the old problem of the scaling of “persistent currents” as a function of the system size. We find that, when the conserved quantities are given as the Noether charges associated with internal symmetries or the Hamiltonian itself, the corresponding persistent currents decay at least algebraically as the system size increases.

In contrast, the persistent currents of accidentally conserved quantities can be nonzero, even in the thermodynamic limit and even in the presence of the time-reversal symmetry.

March 9, 2022

Joshua Spitz, Associate Professor, Department of Physics, University of Michigan-Ann Arbor
2011-2014 Pappalardo Fellow, Experimental Nuclear and Particle Physics
Introductory remarks: Joshua Foster, 2021-2024 Pappalardo Fellow

“How Often Do Muon Neutrinos Turn Into Electron Neutrinos?”

The properties of the neutrino are imprinted on the evolutionary history of our Universe.

In particular, the mass of the neutrino and its behavior have affected matter dominance, galactic structure, heavy element creation, and many other fundamental characteristics of the cosmos.

Towards a complete understanding of the neutrino, the remaining mysteries mainly revolve around answering a singular question: How often do muon neutrinos turn into electron neutrinos?

The multi-faceted answer is one of the keys to bringing us into the age of astroparticle physics, in which we relate the smallest (particle) and largest (cosmic) scales.

In this talk, I will present our work in studying muon-to-electron neutrino mixing at both short and long distances, utilizing powerful accelerators and ultra-large detectors in the US, Japan and Korea.

[CANCELLED] March 23, 2022

Michael Wagman, Staff Scientist, Theoretical Physics Department, Fermilab
2017-2020 Pappalardo Fellow, Nuclear and Particle Theory
Introductory remarks: Manki Kim, 2021-2024 Pappalardo Fellow

Title and abstract forthcoming

[CANCELLED] April 6, 2022
