TITLE: NASA SSERVI CAN-5 2026 Funding Opportunity: Up to $1.8 Million Per Year for Lunar, Mars-Forward, Workforce Development and Citizen Science Research

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
NASA has released the final Solar System Exploration Research Virtual Institute Cooperative Agreement Notice-5 (SSERVI CAN-5), inviting multi-institutional research teams to compete for major cooperative agreement awards supporting lunar science, planetary exploration, NASA’s Artemis programme and research that uses the Moon to prepare for future exploration of Mars.

The final opportunity is:

SSERVI CAN-5 – NNH26ZDA016C

NASA’s Science Mission Directorate and Human Spaceflight Mission Directorate are jointly supporting the initiative. The call seeks integrated, multi-institutional teams capable of advancing fundamental and applied research on the Moon and its near-space environment, while strengthening connections between planetary science and human exploration. “Mars forward” projects that use lunar research to develop approaches relevant to eventual Mars exploration are explicitly welcomed.

The funding opportunity is particularly notable because teams can combine major scientific research with activities designed to strengthen the future STEM workforce and broaden public participation in NASA science.

The detailed CAN funding structure anticipates:

Approximately five awards

Up to approximately $1.8 million per year per team

An anticipated five-year award period

Approximately $9 million total per selected team over five years

Up to an average of $180,000 per year within the overall team budget for Workforce Development and/or Citizen Science, Science Activation or Space Apps activities

The $180,000 is important to understand correctly: it is not an additional $180,000 on top of the $1.8 million annual award. It is part of the overall annual team budget and can support the additional workforce and engagement components.

The proposal process has two stages:

Step-1 Proposal Deadline: September 29, 2026 at 11:59:59 PM Eastern Daylight Time

Step-2 Full Proposal Deadline: December 4, 2026

Only teams that submit the required Step-1 proposal may proceed to Step 2. NASA will use dual-anonymous peer review, and applicants must submit their proposals through NASA’s NSPIRES system rather than through Grants.gov.

Important update about the earlier draft

The document initially circulated for community comment was DRAFT SSERVI CAN-5, NNH26ZDA013J. That draft was issued on July 10, 2026 and closed for comments on July 28. NASA has since issued the final call as NNH26ZDA016C, so applicants should use the final announcement number and final deadlines rather than the dates or placeholders contained in the draft.

This article therefore uses NASA’s final announcement for the current solicitation number and deadlines, while drawing on the detailed CAN documentation supplied with the opportunity for the programme’s research structure, funding architecture and proposal requirements.

About NASA’s Solar System Exploration Research Virtual Institute

The Solar System Exploration Research Virtual Institute, or SSERVI, is a distributed research institute that brings together expertise from the scientific and human exploration communities.

Its premise is that:

Science enables exploration, and exploration enables science.

SSERVI is designed to create collaborative research teams rather than fund a collection of isolated individual projects.

The Institute connects researchers working across areas such as:

Lunar science

Planetary science

Space physics

Human exploration

Geology and geophysics

Engineering

Biological and physical sciences

Robotics

Sample science

Space environments

Technology

Public engagement

Workforce development

Selected teams become participating members of the broader SSERVI network and are expected to collaborate both internally and across other Institute teams.

The Institute is coordinated through SSERVI Central at NASA Ames Research Center. Its virtual structure enables geographically distributed universities, research organisations, NASA institutions, industry partners and other eligible organisations to work together on large interdisciplinary problems.

What NASA Is Looking for Through SSERVI CAN-5

NASA is not seeking disconnected small projects under this call.

It wants:

Multi-institutional, team-based, integrated research programmes.

The final announcement specifies that proposals should present innovative basic and/or applied research that advances understanding of:

The Moon

The Moon’s near-space environment

Scientific questions relevant to human lunar exploration

Research required to enable Artemis

Lunar research that can inform future Mars exploration

NASA says proposals complementing current CAN-4 SSERVI teams, or filling important research gaps not already covered by the Institute, will receive strong consideration.

Supporting NASA’s Artemis Programme

A central objective of CAN-5 is supporting NASA’s return to the Moon through:

Human missions

Robotic missions

Lunar surface research

Sample science

Exploration science

Development of scientific approaches supporting longer-duration lunar activity

The Moon is therefore not treated solely as a scientific destination.

It is also regarded as a location where researchers can develop knowledge, methods and operational experience necessary for future human exploration.

The “Mars Forward” Approach

NASA explicitly welcomes:

Mars-forward research

This means proposals may use studies of the Moon to develop:

Methods

Scientific knowledge

Operational approaches

Exploration concepts

Technologies

that could later inform Mars missions.

The Moon can serve as an intermediate environment for studying issues such as:

Long-duration surface operations

Radiation

Dust

Resource utilisation

Habitat sustainability

Robotics

Autonomous operations

Human-machine interaction

Sample handling

NASA’s final announcement specifically confirms that proposals using lunar-focused research to develop approaches to Mars exploration are welcome.

Anticipated Funding: Up to $1.8 Million Per Year

The detailed CAN funding table anticipates:

$9 million in first-year funding for all new awards

with approximately:

Five awards

at an anticipated level of:

$1.8 million per year for five years

or approximately:

$9 million per selected team over five years.

If five awards were funded at the anticipated maximum annual level across the full five-year period, the overall multi-year programme value could be substantial.

However, applicants should not interpret future-year funding as automatically guaranteed.

The detailed CAN notes that awards are generally not fully funded upfront and future-year funding depends on:

Congressional appropriations

Availability of NASA funding

Continued programme funding

Acceptable performance and award conditions

Applicants should therefore construct realistic five-year budgets while recognising the federal appropriations condition attached to out-year funding.

Up to $180,000 Per Year for Workforce Development, Citizen Science and Public Engagement

One of the most interesting features of SSERVI CAN-5 is its explicit integration of scientific research with wider workforce and community engagement.

The detailed CAN allows teams to request up to an average of:

$180,000 per year

across the proposed five-year period for the combined activities associated with:

Workforce Development Plan

Citizen Science Plan

Science Activation Plan

Space Apps Plan

Again, this amount is part of the overall SSERVI team budget rather than an additional award outside the main funding ceiling.

This provision creates an unusual opportunity for institutions that want to combine advanced lunar and planetary research with:

Student development

Postdoctoral training

STEM workforce development

Public participation in science

Science communication

Community engagement

Citizen science

NASA Space Apps activities

Workforce Development Plan

NASA places significant emphasis on preparing the next generation of researchers, scientists and engineers.

The Workforce Development Plan should describe how the team will:

Build knowledge

Develop technical or professional skills

Promote collaboration

Support professional growth

Prepare students and early-career researchers

Address changing workforce needs

The detailed CAN identifies possible activities such as:

Specialized undergraduate courses

Graduate courses

Workshops

Postdoctoral training opportunities

Field training

Internships

New degree programmes

Collaborative training initiatives

NASA also encourages partnerships that expand access to relevant knowledge and skills.

What the Workforce Development Plan Must Explain

The plan should clearly identify:

Objectives

Proposed activities

Approach

Expected outcomes

Potential impact

How the programme contributes to training future planetary scientists and engineers

How progress will be evaluated

An evaluation approach is required so the team can assess progress against its stated workforce objectives and identify areas for improvement.

Citizen Science Opportunities

SSERVI teams must also connect their activities with NASA’s broader public-engagement ecosystem.

The detailed solicitation allows proposals to include a:

Citizen Science Plan

A team may either:

Establish a new citizen-science project

Collaborate with an existing NASA-supported citizen-science project

Combine both approaches

Citizen science involves members of the public actively contributing to scientific research.

NASA expects these projects to maintain rigorous scientific standards and involve meaningful interaction between professional scientists and volunteers.

What a New Citizen Science Project Should Address

Teams proposing a new citizen-science initiative should explain issues including:

The relevant scientific field

Scientific questions being investigated

Citizen-science methodology

How the public contribution helps answer the research question

Why citizen science is an appropriate method

Relevant existing communities or platforms

Beta testing where necessary

Team expertise

How participants will be informed about project outcomes

The programme therefore treats citizen science as a genuine research method rather than simply a promotional activity.

Science Activation Plan

Teams can alternatively or additionally develop a:

Science Activation Plan

NASA’s Science Activation, or SciAct, approach aims to connect people of different ages and backgrounds with NASA science.

Activities might include:

Learning experiences

Workshops

Webinars

Educational resources

Training

Engagement with NASA subject-matter experts

Public events

Science experiences

The objective is to connect SSERVI-generated knowledge with established NASA Science Activation audiences and dissemination networks.

Space Apps Plan

Teams may also develop a:

Space Apps Plan

NASA’s International Space Apps Challenge is a global hackathon encouraging participants to use NASA data and resources to address challenges related to Earth and space.

A SSERVI team proposing a Space Apps component should consider developing relevant challenges and engaging subject-matter experts capable of supporting participants.

The detailed CAN indicates that Space Apps plans should explain:

The challenge idea

The problem participants will address

Desired outcomes

Relevant experts and support

A Citizen Science, Science Activation or Space Apps Plan Is Expected

The detailed CAN states that SSERVI proposals should contain an engagement plan involving:

Citizen Science,

Science Activation,

Space Apps,

or some combination of these approaches.

Teams should identify a relevant liaison, subject-matter experts, personnel and corresponding budget.

This means public engagement is not simply an optional paragraph added at the end of the science proposal.

It is integrated into how NASA expects SSERVI teams to contribute to the wider scientific ecosystem.

Major Scientific Research Areas

The CAN supports a broad range of lunar and exploration research.

The detailed research list is explicitly non-exhaustive, meaning teams do not have to cover every area.

Potential research areas include the following.

Fundamental Lunar Geology

Research may examine:

Origin of the Moon

Internal structure

Mass anomalies

Core structure and formation

Surface evolution

Volcanic history

Tectonic history

Thermal evolution

Planetary differentiation

Lunar magma ocean

Crater distributions

Impact history

Earth-Moon system evolution

Lunar Environment

Research may examine the environmental conditions surrounding and affecting the Moon.

Possible subjects include:

Solar wind

Space weathering

Lunar exosphere

Plasma processes

Magnetic fields

Radiation environment

Effects of deep-space radiation

Effects of lunar albedo radiation on biological systems

Lunar Volatiles

The distribution and behaviour of volatiles are important both scientifically and for future exploration.

Potential research includes:

Origin of lunar volatiles

Chemical composition

Distribution

Transport

Sequestration

Regolith interactions

Volatiles in lunar samples

Permanently shadowed regions

Temperatures and lighting conditions

Depth and distribution of resources

Lunar Regolith

Regolith research is particularly relevant to future human and robotic surface activity.

Possible subjects include:

Formation and evolution

Particle size distribution

Geotechnical properties

Geochemistry

High-fidelity simulants

Robot-regolith interactions

Plume-surface interactions

Material extraction

Gas extraction

Partial-gravity effects

Regolith interactions with crop plants

Lunar Dust

Dust can affect:

Human health

Robotic equipment

Mechanical systems

Surface operations

Scientific instruments

Relevant research could examine:

Dust composition

Dust mobility

Particle size

Charge

Adhesion

Cohesion

Plasma-driven transport

Mechanical effects on systems

Returned Samples and Meteorites

SSERVI research can also include investigations involving:

Petrology

Geochemistry

Mineralogy

Geophysical properties

Magnetic properties

Geotechnical properties

of returned lunar samples and meteorites.

Sample Management

Relevant research may address:

Sample preservation

Storage

Collection

Return protocols

New analytical methods

Sample science is particularly significant as NASA prepares for future Artemis surface activities and potential sample return.

Cosmic Rays and Solar Storms

Proposals may study galactic cosmic rays and solar events in relation to:

Crew risk

Hardware risk

Mitigation approaches

Understanding the radiation environment is essential for longer-duration human activity beyond Earth.

Robotics, Automation and Autonomous Systems

Relevant areas may include:

Robotics

Sample handling

Automated analysis

Automated operations

Telerobotics

Artificial intelligence

Machine learning

Autonomous systems

Augmented reality

Virtual reality

The detailed CAN indicates that new technological approaches are welcome where they form part of a broader integrated scientific programme.

Planetary Protection

Possible areas include:

Survival of terrestrial organisms in extraterrestrial environments

Radiation exposure

Vacuum

Extreme temperatures

Microbial management

Antimicrobial approaches

Waste management

Prevention of microbial growth and spread

The Moon as a Scientific Platform

The unique lunar environment may also support research into broader astrophysical and fundamental-physics questions.

Examples listed in the CAN include:

Low-frequency radio astronomy

Dark Ages cosmology

Gravitational-wave concepts

Tests of general relativity

Cosmic-ray astrophysics

Observations uniquely enabled by the lunar environment

The programme therefore extends beyond conventional lunar geology.

Multi-Institutional Collaboration Is Required

A defining feature of the SSERVI model is collaboration.

Teams must involve expertise from:

More than one institution.

The programme also expects varied technical expertise rather than a team composed exclusively of researchers working in a single narrow subfield.

Research tasks should be intellectually connected.

A proposal that divides funding among unrelated projects without a convincing unifying research structure is unlikely to reflect the Institute model.

Who Can Apply?

This is primarily an institutional research funding opportunity, not an individual scholarship or personal fellowship.

Eligible entities identified in the detailed CAN include several categories.

Educational Organisations

Potentially eligible institutions include:

Public institutions of higher education

State-controlled universities

Private institutions of higher education

Independent school districts

Nonprofit Organisations

The detailed CAN lists:

501(c)(3) nonprofit organisations

Eligible nonprofits without 501(c)(3) status

Government Organisations

Categories include:

State governments

County governments

City or township governments

Special district governments

Tribal governments

For-Profit Organisations

Eligible categories include:

For-profit organisations

Small businesses meeting relevant SBA size requirements

The detailed programme description also identifies research organisations such as universities, industry partners, FFRDCs, NASA Centers and other U.S. government agencies as part of the target research community.

Lead Institution Requirement

For multi-organisational proposals, one organisation serves as the:

Lead Institution

The detailed CAN states that this should be the:

Principal Investigator’s home institution.

NASA funding is provided to U.S. institutions under the solicitation framework.

The final public opportunity listing likewise states that proposers must be affiliated with institutions registered in NSPIRES and that NASA generally provides funding only to U.S. institutions.

Can International Researchers Participate?

Yes, but with an important distinction.

The opportunity is not structured as an internationally funded grant where institutions worldwide can independently lead and receive NASA funding.

Instead:

NASA generally provides funding to U.S. institutions.

International researchers and institutions may participate through collaborations conducted under NASA’s applicable no-exchange-of-funds rules.

The detailed CAN encourages U.S. proposers to collaborate with international researchers, including relevant existing SSERVI international partners and other appropriate organisations, while making clear that international lead institutions are not solicited.

Restriction Concerning China and Chinese-Owned Companies

The detailed CAN contains a specific institutional and national-participation restriction.

It states that proposals involving bilateral participation, collaboration or coordination with China or Chinese-owned companies, whether funded or under a no-exchange-of-funds arrangement, are ineligible for award under the solicitation.

Applicants involved in international partnerships should therefore read the final CAN and NASA Grants and Cooperative Agreements Manual carefully before building the proposal team.

Is Cost Sharing Required?

No.

The detailed CAN states:

Cost sharing is not required.

NASA may accept voluntary cost sharing, but it is not a prerequisite for competing for the award.

Two-Step Application Process

SSERVI CAN-5 uses a mandatory two-stage proposal process.

This is one of the most important requirements to understand.

Step 1: Preliminary Proposal

Step-1 proposals are due:

September 29, 2026 at 11:59:59 PM EDT.

Submitting Step 1 is mandatory.

NASA’s final announcement confirms:

Only proposers that submit Step 1 are eligible to submit Step 2.

What Goes Into Step 1?

The detailed CAN describes Step 1 as a short preliminary summary.

The core submission uses the NSPIRES:

4,000-character Proposal Summary field.

No full budget is required at this stage.

NASA requests information including:

Principal Investigator

Institution

Contact details

Co-Investigators and known team members

Proposed project title

Brief investigation description

The Step-1 proposal must be submitted by the organisation’s Authorized Organizational Representative, or AOR.

Teams therefore need to involve their institution’s research administration office early.

Register Early in NSPIRES and SAM

Organisations and participating investigators need to be registered in:

NASA NSPIRES

NASA also notes that organisations must have valid System for Award Management (SAM) registration before registering in NSPIRES.

The detailed CAN warns that SAM registration can take significant time.

This makes early institutional coordination especially important.

Do not wait until September 29 to begin organizational registration.

Team Members Must Confirm Participation

The detailed application instructions also require relevant team members to confirm participation through NSPIRES.

A proposal cannot be submitted if required team members have not completed their participation confirmation and organizational relationship requirements.

This is another reason Principal Investigators should build their team early.

Step 2: Full Proposal

Full proposals are due:

December 4, 2026.

The final call uses:

Dual-Anonymous Peer Review

or:

DAPR

for proposal evaluation.

Step 2 is split into:

Volume A – Anonymous material

Volume B – Non-anonymous material

Anonymous Volume A

The detailed CAN identifies major components of Volume A including:

Proposal Cover Page

Table of Contents

Executive Summary

Research Plan

Anonymized Personnel and Work Effort Table

Redacted Budget and Narrative

Open Science and Data Management Plan

References

Workforce Development Plan

Fieldwork Plan, where applicable

Citizen Science, Science Activation or Space Apps Plan

The draft specifies a substantial 35-page Research Plan, along with three-page limits for several specialized plans.

Applicants should consult the final CAN before submission for the definitive page and format limits.

Non-Anonymous Volume B

The detailed CAN describes the non-anonymous section as containing institutional and personnel information, including areas such as:

Team Collaboration and Science Management

Team agreements on acceptable behaviour

Fieldwork agreements where relevant

Contributions to SSERVI and NASA’s mission

Biographical sketches

Personnel and work-effort information

Current and pending support

Letters of commitment or support

Facilities and equipment information

High-End Computing information where required

NASA separates these materials from anonymous scientific content to protect the integrity of the dual-anonymous review.

Open Science and Data Management

SSERVI CAN-5 also places emphasis on:

Open science

Data management

Accessible research

Peer review

Responsible dissemination

Teams should therefore treat their data-management plan as a substantive component rather than an administrative afterthought.

Contribution to the Wider SSERVI Community

Selected teams are expected to contribute to the Institute beyond their own research programme.

Possible contributions may include:

Professional community development

Workshops

Seminar series

Cross-team collaboration

Research tools

Data visualisation

AI and machine-learning applications

Shared scientific facilities

Commercial space partnerships

International partnerships

The detailed CAN explicitly emphasizes that SSERVI is more than a collection of independent projects.

What NASA Will Evaluate

The final NASA announcement confirms that proposals will undergo peer review under the rules set out in the CAN.

Broad assessment considerations include:

Scientific and technical merit

Quality of the proposed research

Relevance to SSERVI

Relevance to NASA’s lunar and exploration priorities

Integration across disciplines

Open Science and Data Management

Workforce Development

Citizen Science, Science Activation or Space Apps

Team collaboration and management

Cost reasonableness

The final call also gives strong consideration to proposals that either complement existing CAN-4 teams or address important gaps in the existing SSERVI research portfolio.

Application Timeline

The major confirmed dates for the final CAN-5 opportunity are:

Stage
Date

Final CAN-5 available
2026

Step-1 proposal
September 29, 2026, 11:59:59 PM EDT

Step-2 full proposal
December 4, 2026

Anticipated award notification
Approximately nine months after Step 2, according to the detailed CAN structure

NASA’s official final announcement confirms the September 29 and December 4 proposal deadlines.

How to Apply

Applications must be submitted through:

NASA NSPIRES

They cannot be submitted as applications directly through the Grants.gov synopsis.

Open the final SSERVI CAN-5 opportunity in NSPIRES

NASA’s current announcement number is:

NNH26ZDA016C

Applicants should use this number when searching NSPIRES.

For the NASA announcement explaining the final release:

Read NASA’s SSERVI CAN-5 final text announcement

Programme questions can be directed to:

HQ-SSERVI@mail.nasa.gov

NASA requests clarification questions sufficiently before the Step-2 deadline; the final announcement specifies that questions should be submitted no later than 14 calendar days before Step 2.

Tips for Preparing a Competitive SSERVI CAN-5 Proposal

1. Do Not Treat This as an Individual Research Grant

SSERVI wants a:

Multi-institutional team

with a coherent intellectual programme.

A collection of unrelated researchers and projects is unlikely to demonstrate the integration NASA is seeking.

2. Make the Artemis Connection Explicit

Explain exactly how the proposed science contributes to:

Understanding the Moon

Lunar exploration

Artemis

Future human exploration

Do not assume reviewers will make the connection themselves.

3. Explain the “Mars Forward” Value Where Relevant

If your research can help future Mars exploration, explain:

What lunar problem is being studied

What can be learned on the Moon

How that knowledge translates to Mars

A credible Moon-to-Mars logic can strengthen the proposal.

4. Build the Workforce Plan as a Real Programme

The workforce component can represent up to an average of $180,000 per year together with public-engagement activities.

Treat it as a serious programme with:

Objectives

Beneficiaries

Activities

Expected outcomes

Evaluation

rather than a generic promise to “train students.”

5. Think Beyond Traditional Outreach

CAN-5 creates opportunities to integrate serious research with:

Citizen science

Science Activation

Space Apps

Workforce development

Teams with strong science and thoughtful engagement structures can potentially create much broader impact than through conventional outreach alone.

6. Identify the Right Institutional Lead

Because funding is primarily directed through U.S. institutions, international research groups should identify an appropriate eligible U.S. lead partner early.

The lead structure needs to be determined before Step 1.

7. Register in SAM and NSPIRES Immediately

Administrative registration can derail an otherwise strong proposal.

Confirm that:

Lead organisation has SAM registration

Institution is registered in NSPIRES

PI is registered

Co-Investigators are registered

Team members establish required organizational relationships

Required participants confirm participation

well before September 29.

8. Protect Proposal Anonymity

NASA is using dual-anonymous peer review.

Applicants should therefore carefully remove identifying information from anonymous materials.

This includes more than simply deleting the PI’s name.

The detailed CAN cautions against revealing identity through:

Institution names

Logos

Self-identifying references

Named collaborations

Possessive descriptions of previous work

Pronouns revealing team-member identity

9. Review Existing SSERVI Teams

NASA says proposals complementing CAN-4 teams or filling gaps in existing research coverage will receive strong consideration.

Before designing the proposal, review what SSERVI already funds.

Ask:

What important scientific problem is missing?

How does the proposed work complement existing teams?

What new capability would this team add?

Why does the Institute need this team now?

Key Details at a Glance

Programme: Solar System Exploration Research Virtual Institute Cooperative Agreement Notice-5

Abbreviation: SSERVI CAN-5

Final announcement number: NNH26ZDA016C

Agency: NASA

NASA directorates: Science Mission Directorate and Human Spaceflight Mission Directorate

Primary focus: Moon, lunar environment, Artemis and Mars-forward exploration research

Proposal model: Multi-institutional teams

Anticipated awards: Approximately 5

Indicative award level: Approximately $1.8 million annually per team

Indicative duration: 5 years

Indicative total per team: Approximately $9 million

Workforce/public engagement component: Up to an average of $180,000 per year within the total award budget

Cost sharing: Not required

Step-1 deadline: September 29, 2026 at 11:59:59 PM EDT

Step-2 deadline: December 4, 2026

Review: Dual-anonymous peer review

Submission system: NASA NSPIRES

Programme contact: HQ-SSERVI@mail.nasa.gov

Conclusion

The NASA SSERVI CAN-5 2026 funding opportunity represents a major opportunity for universities, research institutions, nonprofits, industry partners, government research organisations and other eligible U.S.-based institutions to build ambitious multi-institutional teams focused on the future of lunar and planetary exploration.

Under final solicitation NNH26ZDA016C, NASA is seeking research programmes that can advance fundamental and applied understanding of the Moon and its near-space environment while contributing directly to Artemis and future human exploration. Mars-forward research using lunar science to develop approaches relevant to Mars is also explicitly encouraged.

The detailed CAN funding structure anticipates approximately five awards at around $1.8 million per year for five years, equivalent to approximately $9 million per team over the proposed award period, subject to federal appropriations and continued funding.

A particularly distinctive element is the opportunity to dedicate up to an average of $180,000 per year within the overall budget to Workforce Development and Citizen Science, Science Activation and/or Space Apps activities.

This creates room for institutions to combine frontier research with serious investment in:

Students

Early-career researchers

Postdoctoral scholars

STEM workforce pathways

Public participation

Citizen science

Science communication

Community engagement

Applications use a mandatory two-stage process. Step-1 proposals are due September 29, 2026, and only Step-1 proposers can proceed to the December 4, 2026 Step-2 deadline.

For teams working in lunar science, planetary science, human exploration, workforce development or meaningful public participation in NASA science, SSERVI CAN-5 is one of the most significant NASA team-research opportunities currently open.

TITLE: MSCA Doctoral Networks 2026: European Commission Funding for International PhD Training, Research and Doctoral Careers

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA) Doctoral Networks 2026 call offers an important opportunity for universities, research institutions, businesses, public organisations, NGOs and other eligible organisations to establish international doctoral training programmes and recruit doctoral candidates from around the world.

Funded under Horizon Europe, MSCA Doctoral Networks are designed to develop the next generation of researchers through international, interdisciplinary and inter-sectoral research and training. The programme places strong emphasis on research excellence, transferable skills, innovation, entrepreneurship, career development, international mobility and collaboration between academic and non-academic sectors.

The 2026 call opens on 28 May 2026 and closes on 24 November 2026 at 17:00 CET.

Importantly, this is not a conventional individual PhD scholarship application in which a student applies directly to the European Commission. The Doctoral Networks call is primarily submitted by international consortia of eligible organisations that propose a doctoral training programme. Successful networks subsequently recruit doctoral candidates through open and merit-based vacancies.

MSCA Doctoral Networks 2026 at a Glance

Programme: Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions Doctoral Networks

Call: MSCA Doctoral Networks 2026

Category: Doctoral research and fellowship funding

Funding framework: Horizon Europe

Application opening date: 28 May 2026

Application deadline: 24 November 2026 at 17:00 CET

Applicants: International consortia of eligible organisations

Doctoral candidates: Researchers from all nationalities, subject to the programme’s eligibility requirements

Fields: Various scientific and research disciplines

Training models: Standard Doctoral Networks, Industrial Doctoral Networks and Joint Doctoral Networks

Geographical scope: International, with participation rules depending on the status of participating countries under Horizon Europe

Application platform: European Commission Funding & Tenders Opportunities Portal

What Are MSCA Doctoral Networks?

The Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions Doctoral Networks are part of the European Union’s MSCA programme, which focuses on developing research talent and strengthening research and innovation capacity.

Doctoral Networks bring together organisations from different sectors and countries to create structured doctoral programmes.

Rather than simply funding individual research projects, the programme supports networks that can provide doctoral researchers with:

High-quality research training.

International research experience.

Interdisciplinary training.

Exposure to different sectors.

Transferable skills development.

Entrepreneurial skills.

Professional networking opportunities.

Supervision and mentoring.

Career development support.

Opportunities to work with organisations outside academia.

International mobility and secondments.

Preparation for long-term careers inside and outside academia.

The programme therefore seeks to produce researchers who are not only technically strong in their particular research fields but are also equipped with the broader skills required to succeed in today’s research, innovation and professional environments.

The Three Types of MSCA Doctoral Networks

The 2026 call provides different models of Doctoral Networks. Applicants should determine which model best matches the objectives, structure and partnerships of their proposed doctoral programme.

1. Standard Doctoral Networks

Standard Doctoral Networks promote international, interdisciplinary and inter-sectoral cooperation for the training of PhD candidates across different scientific areas.

The model is designed to help researchers develop:

Research expertise.

Transferable skills.

Entrepreneurial mindsets.

Research-related competencies.

International experience.

Interdisciplinary perspectives.

Long-term career prospects.

Standard Doctoral Networks can be particularly valuable where several institutions and sectors need to work together to provide doctoral researchers with a broad training environment.

2. Industrial Doctoral Networks

Industrial Doctoral Networks are designed to strengthen the connection between academia and industry.

Doctoral candidates receive training that includes exposure to skills and environments outside academia. The programme also supports collaboration between academic and non-academic organisations.

A major feature of Industrial Doctorates is joint supervision between industry and academia.

This approach allows doctoral researchers to:

Conduct advanced research.

Gain experience outside traditional academic environments.

Develop industry-relevant skills.

Understand how research can be translated into practical applications.

Build professional networks.

Improve their employability beyond academia.

Develop an innovation-oriented mindset.

Industrial Doctoral Networks can therefore be particularly relevant to research areas where collaboration between universities, companies, businesses and other non-academic organisations can generate practical impact.

3. Joint Doctoral Networks

Joint Doctoral Networks support integrated doctoral programmes that lead to joint or multiple doctoral degrees.

These networks require deeper institutional collaboration and a joint governance structure.

The participating institutions must establish joint procedures covering areas such as:

Recruitment.

Admission.

Supervision.

Evaluation.

Doctoral training.

Governance.

Degree arrangements.

For Joint Doctorates, at least three independent legal entities within the consortium must be entitled to award doctoral degrees.

At least one institution conferring the joint, double or multiple doctoral degree must be established in an EU Member State and/or a Horizon Europe Associated Country.

Learn More HERE

Who Can Apply for MSCA Doctoral Networks 2026?

The main applicants are organisations rather than individual doctoral students.

Doctoral Networks are open to international consortia involving organisations from different socioeconomic sectors.

Eligible types of organisations can include:

Higher education institutions.

Universities.

Research institutions.

Research infrastructures.

Private-sector organisations.

Industry.

Businesses.

Small and medium-sized enterprises.

Public-sector organisations.

National governments.

Regional governments.

Local governments.

Government agencies.

Museums.

Non-governmental organisations.

Think tanks.

Charities.

Other socioeconomic actors.

This broad eligibility structure allows doctoral programmes to bring together different perspectives and expertise.

Consortium Requirements

A consortium applying for a Doctoral Network must meet specific requirements.

The minimum consortium must include at least three independent legal entities.

These entities must:

Be established in different EU Member States or Horizon Europe Associated Countries.

Include at least one organisation established in an EU Member State.

Beyond this minimum requirement, organisations from other countries around the world may also participate as beneficiaries or associated partners, depending on the applicable country-status rules.

This international structure is fundamental to the programme because MSCA Doctoral Networks are designed to promote cross-border research collaboration.

Special Requirements for Joint Doctorates

Joint Doctoral Networks have additional requirements.

At least three independent legal entities in the consortium must be entitled to award doctoral degrees.

Furthermore, at least one institution responsible for conferring a joint, double or multiple doctoral degree must be established in:

An EU Member State; and/or

A Horizon Europe Associated Country.

These requirements are intended to ensure that Joint Doctoral Networks have the appropriate institutional capacity and degree-awarding arrangements.

What Responsibilities Do Beneficiaries Have?

All beneficiaries participating in the network must recruit at least one doctoral candidate.

They must also provide appropriate arrangements for:

Hosting recruited researchers at their premises.

Supervising doctoral candidates.

Providing research training.

Supporting career development.

Participating in network activities.

Where appropriate, beneficiaries may use associated partners linked to them to host and supervise researchers.

This means organisations should not join a consortium simply as passive partners. They need to have a meaningful role in implementing the doctoral programme.

Can Organisations from Developing Countries Apply?

Yes.

Organisations based in low- and middle-income countries can also participate and may receive EU funding, subject to the specific conditions established under the MSCA Work Programme.

Organisations should therefore carefully check the applicable country participation rules before assuming that their location automatically makes them eligible or ineligible.

The Horizon Europe participating-country documentation should be consulted to determine the precise status of a country.

Organisations participating in an EU-funded programme for the first time will also need to register and obtain a Participant Identification Code (PIC).

Who Can Be Recruited as a Doctoral Candidate?

Doctoral candidates funded through MSCA Doctoral Networks must meet specific eligibility conditions.

They:

Must not already hold a doctoral degree at the date of recruitment.

Can be of any nationality.

Should be enrolled in a doctoral programme leading to a doctoral degree in at least one EU Member State or Horizon Europe Associated Country.

May, under the programme’s rules, be recruited through a beneficiary based in a non-EU, non-Associated third country in certain degree-awarding arrangements.

Are normally employed for a period of at least 3 months and up to 36 months.

May be employed for up to 48 months in the case of Joint Doctorates.

Must comply with the applicable MSCA mobility rule.

The programme therefore provides an international pathway for researchers who are beginning their doctoral careers and have not yet obtained a PhD or equivalent doctoral degree.

The MSCA Mobility Rule

One of the most important eligibility requirements for doctoral candidates is the mobility rule.

In general, a researcher must not have:

Resided in the country of the recruiting organisation; or

Carried out their main activity there, such as work or studies,

for more than 12 months during the 36 months immediately before their recruitment date.

This requirement is important because international mobility is a central component of MSCA programmes.

Prospective doctoral candidates should therefore carefully examine their residence, study and employment history before applying for a specific doctoral vacancy.

Additional Requirement for Industrial Doctorates

Researchers recruited under Industrial Doctorates must spend at least 50% of their time outside academia.

This requirement reflects the purpose of Industrial Doctoral Networks, which is to expose researchers to both academic and non-academic environments.

The arrangement enables researchers to gain practical experience and develop skills relevant to careers in industry, business and other non-academic settings.

How Long Can Researchers Be Employed?

The standard employment period for researchers in Doctoral Networks is:

Minimum: 3 months.

Maximum: 36 months.

Joint Doctorates: Up to 48 months.

Researchers may also undertake secondments as part of their research training.

In general, secondments can take place for up to half of the duration of their MSCA fellowship. However, this limitation does not apply in the same way to Industrial Doctorates and Joint Doctorates.

What Are the Benefits of MSCA Doctoral Networks?

MSCA Doctoral Networks offer extensive academic, professional and international development opportunities.

International Research Experience

Researchers become part of international networks involving organisations from multiple countries.

This can provide valuable exposure to different research cultures, methodologies and professional environments.

Interdisciplinary Training

Doctoral candidates can work across disciplinary boundaries and learn how different research fields contribute to solving complex problems.

Research Skills Development

The programme supports researchers in developing advanced research competencies relevant to their doctoral projects.

Transferable Skills

Training extends beyond technical research skills.

Researchers can develop competencies that may include:

Communication.

Project management.

Entrepreneurship.

Innovation.

Collaboration.

Networking.

Research dissemination.

Career planning.

Exposure to Non-Academic Careers

The programme places considerable emphasis on employability and career development.

Researchers can gain exposure to:

Industry.

Businesses.

SMEs.

Public-sector organisations.

NGOs.

Other non-academic environments.

This can help researchers understand career opportunities beyond traditional academic positions.

International Mobility

The programme encourages researchers to work and train across different countries and institutions.

This international experience can strengthen both academic and professional development.

Supervision and Mentoring

Doctoral Networks place particular attention on the quality of supervision and mentoring.

Industrial and Joint Doctorates also require joint supervision arrangements.

Career Development

Every recruited doctoral candidate should have a career development plan prepared jointly with their supervisor.

The plan considers the researcher’s:

Research objectives.

Training needs.

Career needs.

Teaching opportunities.

Publication planning.

Conference participation.

Other relevant professional development activities.

Research and Training Activities

Successful Doctoral Networks are expected to provide comprehensive training environments.

Researchers should have opportunities to:

Acquire new research skills.

Develop transferable competencies.

Develop entrepreneurial abilities.

Participate in interdisciplinary research.

Work with academic and non-academic organisations where appropriate.

Build professional networks.

Exchange knowledge.

Develop good scientific practices.

Strengthen research integrity.

Explore innovation and entrepreneurship.

The network should make use of the complementary strengths of its participating organisations.

Supervisory Board

Each MSCA Doctoral Network should have a clearly identified Supervisory Board.

The board plays an important role in coordinating network-wide:

Training.

Research activities.

Supervision.

Communication.

Exchange of good practices.

A strong supervisory structure can help ensure consistency and quality across the participating organisations.

Recruitment of Doctoral Researchers

MSCA Doctoral Networks are expected to recruit researchers through an open, transparent and merit-based process.

Selected projects must advertise doctoral vacancies as widely as possible.

This includes publication through the EURAXESS Jobs Portal, alongside other relevant networks and communication channels.

Doctoral candidates can therefore be recruited from around the world, subject to the programme’s eligibility requirements.

Career Development and Employability

Career development is a central element of the programme.

Doctoral training is not limited to completing a research thesis.

Networks are expected to help researchers prepare for their longer-term careers by providing opportunities for:

Training.

Teaching.

Research dissemination.

Conferences.

Networking.

Publication planning.

Professional development.

Exposure to potential employers.

Engagement with society and citizens.

The overall objective is to improve researchers’ employability and career prospects both within and beyond academia.

Green Research and Sustainability

MSCA Doctoral Networks also incorporate sustainability considerations.

Projects are strongly encouraged to adopt environmentally sustainable practices in line with the MSCA Green Charter.

Networks should report on their sustainability efforts.

Sustainability may also be considered when distinguishing between otherwise equally ranked proposals.

Applicants should therefore consider how sustainable research and project-management practices can be incorporated into their proposed network.

Learn More HERE

How to Prepare a Strong MSCA Doctoral Networks Application

The European Commission outlines six key steps for organisations preparing a Doctoral Networks proposal.

Step 1: Understand How the Funding Works

Before developing a proposal, applicants should become familiar with:

The Doctoral Networks scheme.

The MSCA Work Programme.

The relevant annexes.

Funding rules.

Eligibility requirements.

Evaluation criteria.

Different Doctoral Network modalities.

The Funding and Tenders Opportunities Portal is a central resource for prospective applicants.

The official Guide for Applicants, FAQs, proposal templates, application forms and evaluation documents should be reviewed carefully.

Applicants can also participate in information sessions and workshops.

Step 2: Confirm Consortium Eligibility

Before investing significant time in proposal development, organisations should confirm that their consortium satisfies the minimum eligibility requirements.

This includes checking:

Number of participating legal entities.

Independence of organisations.

Countries where organisations are established.

EU Member State participation.

Degree-awarding requirements for Joint Doctorates.

Recruitment responsibilities.

Funding eligibility of participating organisations.

Organisations uncertain about their eligibility can seek guidance from their MSCA National Contact Point.

Step 3: Find the Right Partners

A successful proposal requires a strong international and diverse consortium.

Potential coordinators and partners can begin by examining existing institutional relationships.

They can also use the opportunity to establish new partnerships with organisations in Europe and elsewhere.

Useful partner-search resources include:

MSCA Matchmaking.

Funding and Tenders Opportunities Portal.

European Enterprise Network.

MSCA National Contact Points.

For Industrial Doctoral Networks, organisations seeking stronger research-business collaboration can particularly benefit from contacting the European Enterprise Network.

Step 4: Start Drafting the Proposal

Once the consortium and project concept are established, applicants should begin drafting the proposal around the official award criteria and requirements.

Applicants should carefully review:

Award criteria.

Budget structure.

MSCA Financial Guide.

Horizon Europe Programme Guide.

Gender dimension and inclusiveness.

Dissemination and exploitation.

Open science.

Research integrity.

Intellectual property management.

Communication and dissemination.

The proposal should demonstrate not only strong research ideas but also the quality of the training environment, supervision, career development and collaboration arrangements.

Step 5: Ask Others to Review the Proposal

Applicants should not wait until the final days before asking for feedback.

Draft proposals can be reviewed by:

Colleagues.

Institutional research-support teams.

MSCA National Contact Points.

Experienced researchers.

Previous applicants.

Peer review can help identify weaknesses, unclear sections, missing information and inconsistencies before submission

Step 6: Submit the Application

The MSCA Doctoral Networks 2026 call opens on 28 May 2026.

The application deadline is:

24 November 2026 at 17:00 CET.

Applications must be submitted through the European Commission’s Funding and Tenders Opportunities Portal.

Applicants should become familiar with the Electronic Submission Service before the deadline.

The European Commission strongly recommends submitting proposals well before the closing time to avoid last-minute technical or administrative problems.

Proposals can be updated, downloaded or withdrawn up until the deadline.

Learn more and apply HERE

Important Resources for Applicants

Prospective applicants should use official resources when preparing their proposals.

These include:

MSCA Doctoral Networks programme information.

MSCA Work Programme 2026–2027.

General annexes.

Guide for Applicants.

Funding and Tenders Opportunities Portal.

MSCA Financial Guide.

Horizon Europe Programme Guide.

Evaluation forms.

MSCA National Contact Points.

EURAXESS Worldwide.

EURAXESS Jobs Portal.

MSCA Matchmaking platform.

European Enterprise Network.

CORDIS database of previously funded projects.

The European Commission also provides information sessions and other support opportunities for applicants.

Where Can Applicants Find Examples of Previous Doctoral Networks?

The CORDIS database, the European Commission’s official database of EU-funded research projects, can be used to explore previously funded Doctoral Networks.

Studying previously funded projects can help prospective applicants understand:

The types of research areas supported.

How international consortia are structured.

How academic and non-academic organisations collaborate.

How training programmes are designed.

How networks integrate career development.

How research and innovation objectives are presented.

Applicants should use previous projects for understanding and inspiration while ensuring that their own proposal responds directly to the current call requirements.

Application Deadline

The MSCA Doctoral Networks 2026 application deadline is 24 November 2026 at 17:00 CET.

The call opens on 28 May 2026.

Applicants are strongly encouraged to begin preparations early because building an international consortium, developing the research programme, preparing training plans and completing the proposal can require significant coordination.

How to Apply for MSCA Doctoral Networks 2026

The MSCA Doctoral Networks 2026 call is submitted through the European Commission’s Funding and Tenders Opportunities Portal.

Apply through the Funding & Tenders Opportunities Portal

Prospective applicants should also consult the official MSCA Doctoral Networks guidance before beginning the submission process.

MSCA Doctoral Networks official page

The official MSCA page should be used to confirm the latest requirements, eligibility rules, programme conditions and supporting documents.

Pro Tip for Applicants

Start early and build the consortium before drafting the full proposal. A strong MSCA Doctoral Networks application requires more than an excellent research idea. Applicants should carefully match partners to the scientific objectives, training programme, supervision structure, international mobility, non-academic engagement and career-development goals. Reviewing the official Work Programme and Guide for Applicants early can help prevent eligibility and proposal-design problems later.

Conclusion

The MSCA Doctoral Networks 2026 call provides a major opportunity to develop international doctoral training programmes and strengthen research collaboration across Europe and the wider global research community.

Its distinctive strength lies in combining doctoral research with international mobility, interdisciplinary training, transferable skills, industry and non-academic exposure, supervision, career development and networking.

The programme supports three major models: Standard Doctoral Networks, Industrial Doctoral Networks and Joint Doctoral Networks, allowing consortia to select an approach that best fits their research and training objectives.

For organisations, success begins with establishing an eligible and complementary international consortium, identifying a strong research and training concept, understanding the funding and evaluation requirements, and developing a proposal that demonstrates high-quality research, supervision, training and career development.

For prospective doctoral researchers, the opportunity is particularly relevant because successful networks recruit doctoral candidates from around the world through open and merit-based processes. However, individual researchers do not submit the main Doctoral Networks proposal themselves; they normally apply for doctoral vacancies advertised by successful networks.

With the 24 November 2026 at 17:00 CET deadline approaching, organisations interested in establishing a Doctoral Network should begin consortium building, partner identification, proposal development and internal review as early as possible.

TITLE: SUPPORTER achieves key milestone in driving gender equality in sports

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
SUPPORTER Reaches Key Milestone with Endorsement of 4I-GEPs

25 August 2025

As coordinator and communication leader of the SUPPORTER project, ESF is pleased to announce a key milestone: eight sports higher education institutions from Central and Eastern Europe, with the support of expert partners University of Gothenburg, South East European Research Centre, and ESF, have successfully developed, endorsed, and published their Inclusive, Innovative, Intersectional, and Impactful Gender Equality Plans (4I-GEPs).

About the SUPPORTER Project

SUPPORTER is an EU-funded project that aims to foster gender related, sustainable, and transformative institutional changes in sports higher education institutions, paying specific attention to the challenge of gender-based violence and leading to the development of (4I-GEPs).

The Development of the 4I-GEPs

The 4I-GEPs developed within SUPPORTER are the result of three years of collaborative and evidence-based work. Each institution carried out a gender equality audit, co-designed tailored roadmaps, and worked through mentoring, training, and mutual learning activities. This participatory process ensured that the final plans are both adapted to the specific needs of the sports sector and aligned with European guidelines for institutional change.

TITLE: Royal Commonwealth Society Recruitment 2026: Apply for the Digital Communications and Public Affairs Officer Role in London

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Royal Commonwealth Society (RCS) is currently accepting applications for an exciting professional opportunity in London, United Kingdom. The organisation is recruiting a Digital Communications and Public Affairs Officer to support its growing communications, digital engagement, public affairs and stakeholder outreach activities.

This full-time position presents an excellent opportunity for communications professionals who are interested in international affairs, digital storytelling, youth engagement, public affairs and the Commonwealth. The successful candidate will contribute to some of the Royal Commonwealth Society’s most visible programmes and events while helping the organisation expand its digital presence and connect with audiences across the Commonwealth and beyond.

The position is based in London, United Kingdom, with a salary of £27,000 to £29,000 per year. The Society states that flexible working arrangements may be considered for the right candidate. Applications must be received by the opening of business on Tuesday, 29 September 2026.

About the Royal Commonwealth Society

The Royal Commonwealth Society is a long-established organisation dedicated to improving the lives and prospects of people across the Commonwealth.

Founded in 1868, the Society operates as a non-partisan organisation independent of governments. Its work brings together political and diplomatic representatives, civil society organisations, businesses, young people and other stakeholders from across the Commonwealth.

The RCS works across the Commonwealth’s 56 member countries, focusing particularly on three interconnected areas: education, equality and inclusion, and the environment. Its wider mission is to connect, convene and equip people to advance Commonwealth values and contribute to a fairer world for Commonwealth citizens.

The Society also delivers and supports internationally recognised initiatives, programmes and events involving young people, governments, diplomatic representatives and civil society.

Its Strategic Plan for 2025–2030 places particular emphasis on strengthening collaboration across the Commonwealth, developing young leaders and advancing progress towards the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals through initiatives connected with education, equality and environmental sustainability.

Why the Royal Commonwealth Society Is Expanding Its Digital Communications

The recruitment comes at an important period for the Royal Commonwealth Society.

The organisation will celebrate its 160th anniversary in 2028, and it is developing an ambitious programme of communications and digital engagement aimed at introducing the Society and the wider Commonwealth to new audiences around the world.

One of the major initiatives associated with this expansion is Digital Commonwealth Day, which is intended to complement the Society’s annual Commonwealth Day Celebration at Westminster Abbey.

Digital content, video, social media and online storytelling are expected to play an increasingly important role in allowing audiences outside London to engage with Commonwealth Day activities and other programmes.

The new Digital Communications and Public Affairs Officer will therefore have a significant operational role in implementing this expanding digital strategy.

About the Digital Communications and Public Affairs Officer Position

The Digital Communications and Public Affairs Officer will be responsible for supporting and delivering the Royal Commonwealth Society’s day-to-day communications and digital activities while also contributing to public affairs and stakeholder engagement.

This is not solely an administrative communications position. It is designed as a practical and creative role involving written content, social media management, website administration, photography, video, digital campaigns, events and stakeholder communications.

Candidates should therefore be comfortable moving between different communication formats and audiences.

The position will involve contributing to several major Royal Commonwealth Society programmes, including Commonwealth Day, Digital Commonwealth Day, the Queen’s Commonwealth Writing Competition, the Commonwealth Youth Photography Competition and preparations for the Society’s 160th anniversary.

The Queen’s Commonwealth Writing Competition itself is one of the Society’s most established education initiatives and is recognised by the RCS as the world’s oldest international writing competition for schools, having been delivered by the organisation since 1883.

Key Responsibilities

The successful candidate will undertake a broad range of communications, digital engagement, public affairs and events responsibilities. These include:

Developing engaging communications and digital content for the RCS website, social media platforms, email communications and other digital channels; managing website content including news, blogs, campaign materials and events; creating and scheduling professional content for LinkedIn, Facebook, Instagram and X; producing short-form videos, photography, graphics and other visual material; using Canva and similar digital communication tools; producing the Society’s monthly newsletter; capturing interviews, photographs and videos during events; creating stories highlighting young people, partners and RCS initiatives; monitoring digital performance and using analytics to improve engagement; identifying emerging platforms and communication opportunities; supporting communications surrounding Commonwealth Day and Digital Commonwealth Day; producing pre-event, live-event and post-event digital content; working with youth networks, Commonwealth partners and stakeholders; supporting communications for the RCS’s 160th anniversary; assisting with major programmes and events; contributing to briefings, speeches and correspondence; developing relationships with external organisations and Commonwealth stakeholders; and representing the RCS at appropriate events and networking opportunities.

Commonwealth Day and Digital Commonwealth Day

A particularly significant element of the role will involve communications surrounding the annual Commonwealth Day Celebration at Westminster Abbey.

Commonwealth Day forms an important part of the RCS calendar and brings together participants and representatives connected with the Commonwealth.

The successful applicant will assist in creating communications before, during and after the event while helping the Society expand participation through Digital Commonwealth Day.

The Royal Commonwealth Society’s wider convening role regularly brings together governments, diplomatic representatives, civil society, businesses and young people, meaning that communications surrounding these programmes can potentially reach diverse audiences across numerous regions and professional sectors.

Essential Skills and Experience

The Royal Commonwealth Society is looking for an individual with strong written and verbal communication abilities and excellent attention to detail.

Applicants are expected to have relevant experience in areas such as communications, marketing, digital communications or public affairs.

Strong practical experience with digital and social media content is particularly important. This includes experience creating short-form video and producing material suitable for public-facing digital channels.

Candidates should also be comfortable managing websites and producing content for general audiences.

Professional familiarity with major social media platforms is expected, alongside experience using design and content creation software such as Canva or equivalent tools.

The successful applicant should be capable of managing multiple assignments and deadlines simultaneously while working creatively and proactively.

Strong interpersonal and collaborative skills are also important because the position involves regular interaction with internal colleagues, partners, youth networks, diplomatic stakeholders and external organisations.

An interest in areas such as international affairs, the Commonwealth, advocacy or youth engagement is specifically relevant to the position.

UK Right-to-Work Requirement

One particularly important eligibility condition should be carefully considered before applying.

Applicants must have the right to live and work in the United Kingdom.

The vacancy announcement does not state that visa sponsorship will be provided. International candidates should therefore not assume that being a citizen of a Commonwealth country automatically makes them eligible for employment.

Candidates outside the United Kingdom should first establish whether they already possess an appropriate UK immigration or employment status permitting them to take up the position.

Desirable Experience

While not mandatory, candidates will be particularly competitive if they have experience working with website content management systems, especially Wix.

Knowledge of video-editing software and digital analytics would also strengthen an application.

Other useful backgrounds include experience designing digital campaigns, developing online communities, promoting youth-led programmes and supporting high-profile events involving external organisations or partners.

Candidates who already understand the Commonwealth system or the mission and programmes of the Royal Commonwealth Society may also be able to demonstrate stronger alignment with the organisation.

Applicants should also be aware that the position may occasionally require work outside normal working hours because of the nature of events, communications activities and programmes.

Salary and Working Arrangement

The advertised annual salary is:

£27,000–£29,000

The position is advertised as full-time and is based in London, United Kingdom.

The Royal Commonwealth Society indicates that flexible working arrangements may be considered for an appropriate candidate. However, applicants should not interpret this as confirmation that the position is fully remote.

Candidates should assess their ability to work from London and participate physically in major events and activities associated with the position.

How to Apply for the Royal Commonwealth Society Vacancy

Applicants are required to submit two principal documents:

A CV of one to two pages, together with a statement of suitability explaining how the applicant meets the person specification and why they want to work for the Royal Commonwealth Society.

Applications should be sent to the email address specified on the official vacancy page.

The prescribed email subject format is:

Communications, Digital & Public Affairs Officer – [Your Last Name]

Applicants should follow this format carefully, as clear compliance with application instructions demonstrates attention to detail—an ability that is particularly relevant for a professional communications position.

What to Include in the Statement of Suitability

The statement of suitability should not simply repeat the applicant’s CV.

A competitive application should demonstrate evidence of relevant achievements and connect those achievements directly with the requirements of the position.

Candidates may strengthen their statement by explaining their experience managing organisational social media channels, developing communication campaigns, creating digital or video content, maintaining websites, preparing newsletters, supporting events and working with external stakeholders.

Where possible, applicants should quantify their achievements.

For example, rather than merely stating that they managed social media accounts, an applicant could explain how their campaign increased engagement, audience reach, followers or participation.

Candidates should also explain why the Royal Commonwealth Society’s work in education, equality, environmental sustainability, youth empowerment or international engagement is personally and professionally relevant to them.

Application Deadline

The official application deadline is:

Opening of business on Tuesday, 29 September 2026.

Applicants should avoid waiting until the final day to submit their documents.

Applications received after the deadline may not be considered.

Interview Dates

The Royal Commonwealth Society has already announced provisional interview dates.

The first interview is scheduled for 7 October 2026, while the second interview is scheduled for 14 October 2026.

Both interview stages are expected to take place in person at Guildhall in the City of London.

This is particularly important for applicants who are currently based outside London, as shortlisted candidates may need to make appropriate arrangements to attend the interviews physically.

The Society also notes that because of capacity limitations, it cannot provide individual feedback to candidates who are not invited to interview.

Why This Opportunity Could Be Valuable for Communications Professionals

The Royal Commonwealth Society vacancy offers exposure to a distinctive combination of international communications, youth engagement, public affairs, major events and digital storytelling.

The successful applicant could work on communications connected with internationally recognised Commonwealth initiatives while interacting with organisations and individuals from government, diplomacy, civil society, youth networks and other sectors.

The timing is also noteworthy. The Society is implementing its Strategic Plan 2025–2030 while preparing for its 160th anniversary and developing new digital initiatives designed to connect audiences internationally.

The RCS has reported significant reach through its existing programmes. Its recent strategic update stated that more than 7.5 million people watched its Commonwealth Day Celebration, while more than 121,000 young people participated in the Queen’s Commonwealth Writing Competition over the preceding five-year period.

For an early-career or developing communications professional, the position therefore provides the possibility of working across campaigns with substantial international visibility.

Important Advice Before Applying

Applicants should review the official vacancy announcement carefully before preparing their documents.

A generic CV and cover letter are unlikely to demonstrate the level of alignment expected for a communications-focused role.

The strongest applications should clearly demonstrate practical communications experience, creativity, digital capability, writing ability, stakeholder engagement and genuine interest in the Society’s mission.

Applicants should also ensure that any claims made about digital communications experience can be supported with specific examples, outcomes, campaigns, portfolios or measurable results where appropriate.

Most importantly, candidates should confirm that they satisfy the UK right-to-work requirement before submitting an application.

Conclusion

The Royal Commonwealth Society Digital Communications and Public Affairs Officer Recruitment 2026 represents a strong professional opportunity for candidates seeking experience at the intersection of communications, digital media, international affairs, youth engagement and public affairs.

With an annual salary of £27,000–£29,000, involvement in major Commonwealth programmes, and opportunities to contribute to initiatives such as Commonwealth Day, Digital Commonwealth Day and the RCS’s 160th anniversary programme, the position could provide valuable professional exposure within an internationally focused organisation.

Interested candidates should prepare a focused one-to-two-page CV and statement of suitability demonstrating how their experience meets the person specification.

The final application deadline is the opening of business on Tuesday, 29 September 2026.

Candidates should consult the official Royal Commonwealth Society vacancy announcement for the complete application instructions before submitting their application.

TITLE: Call for Applications: African Food Baskets Country Researchers Program 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 6, 2026

Applications are open for the African Food Baskets Country Researchers Program 2026. The Alliance for Food Sovereignty in Africa (AFSA) invites applications from qualified African researchers to support the first phase of the African Food Baskets initiative. Ten Country Researchers will be selected—one from each participating country—to document the foods, dishes, beverages, recipes, food sources, menus, stories, proverbs and cultural knowledge that shape their country’s food heritage.

The initiative forms part of the TAFS Project, funded by Sida, and contributes to AFSA’s My Food Is African campaign. It aims to preserve and promote African food knowledge while building a continental resource for advocacy, research, education, communication and policy engagement.

Scope of Work

The selected Country Researcher will:

Attend the AFSA online training on the African Food Baskets Toolkit and complete the practice exercises.

Prepare a short country workplan identifying the communities or food territories to be documented, the knowledge holders to be engaged and the fieldwork schedule.

Conduct community entry, explain the purpose of the initiative and obtain consent from communities and individual participants before any documentation begins.

Collect data using the KoboToolbox modules, meeting at least the minimum country data package set out.

Collect and caption photographs and other media in line with the consent recorded in Form 7.

Complete the Field Data Quality and Validation Checklist and validate the findings with the communities concerned before final submission.

Submit the complete country data package to AFSA together with a short narrative report of no more than eight pages covering the process followed, the people engaged, the main findings, foods identified as being at risk, and recommendations.

Benefits

Each selected researcher will receive USD $1,000 as facilitation for the assignment. This amount is paid after the complete country data package has been submitted and accepted by AFSA, and it covers the researcher’s time, local travel, communication and community engagement costs.

Eligibility

Applicants must:

Be a national of, or be resident and actively working in, the country they are applying to document.

Hold a background in research, preferably in food systems, agriculture, agroecology, nutrition, anthropology, sociology, development studies, environmental studies, cultural heritage or a related field. A postgraduate qualification is an advantage, but strong demonstrated field research experience will also be considered.

Have practical experience of qualitative fieldwork, community interviews or participatory documentation.

Be able to work in at least one of English, French or Portuguese, and be able to communicate in the main local language of the communities to be documented, or arrange reliable interpretation.

Have access to a smartphone, tablet or computer and be willing to learn KoboToolbox. Prior experience with KoboToolbox or similar mobile data collection tools is an advantage.

Be able to take clear, well composed photographs of foods, dishes and food environments, or work with someone who can.

Be available for the full period.

Application

Submit the following in a single email:

A curriculum vitae of no more than two pages with at least two referees.

A country concept note of no more than three pages setting out the communities or food territories you would work with, why you have chosen them, the knowledge holders you would engage, how you would obtain consent, and how you would manage fieldwork within two months.

One example of previous relevant work, such as a report, article, thesis chapter or documentation product.

Where applicable, the name of the AFSA member organisation you are affiliated with.

Applications must be submitted to afsa@afsafrica.org by 6 September 2026 and may be submitted in English, French or Portuguese.
