TITLE: University of Maryland Do Good Accelerator Fellows 2026: $2,000 Stipend, Coaching and Social Impact Support

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The University of Maryland Do Good Accelerator Fellows Program is an opportunity for current University of Maryland, College Park students who are developing projects, social ventures, or initiatives designed to create meaningful change in society, the environment, or the future.

Organized by the Do Good Institute at the University of Maryland, the Accelerator Fellows Program is designed to give students the practical support, mentorship, resources, workspace, and time they need to move promising ideas forward and increase their social impact.

For students who are already implementing a project and want to strengthen, test, develop, or scale their work, the program provides an opportunity to spend a semester working within a supportive environment alongside coaches and other students pursuing social impact.

The Fall 2026 Accelerator Fellows Program will run for eight weeks, from September 28 through November 20, 2026. Selected fellows are required to dedicate 8 hours per week to the Do Good Accelerator and will receive a $2,000 stipend upon successful completion of the fellowship.

Applications open on August 3, 2026, and close on September 14, 2026.

About the University of Maryland Do Good Accelerator Fellows Program

The Do Good Accelerator Fellows Program is a student-focused initiative created to help University of Maryland students turn ideas and social impact projects into stronger, more sustainable initiatives.

The program recognizes that having a good idea is only the beginning. Students working on social ventures often need access to experienced guidance, resources, a dedicated workspace, development opportunities, and a community of people who understand the challenges involved in creating impact.

The Accelerator provides these forms of support through an intensive eight-week program.

Participants can use the fellowship to:

Explore and develop an existing project.

Test an idea or approach.

Improve a project that is already operating.

Strengthen the impact of a social venture.

Develop strategies for scaling an initiative.

Receive individualized coaching.

Learn practical skills through workshops and webinars.

Connect with other students working on meaningful projects.

Access resources and workspace.

Dedicate structured time to advancing their initiative.

The program is particularly suited to students who have moved beyond the initial idea stage and are already implementing their projects.

Fall 2026 Accelerator Fellows Program

The Fall 2026 cohort is an eight-week fellowship program designed for current University of Maryland, College Park students.

Unlike opportunities that focus primarily on developing an idea from scratch, the Accelerator specifically identifies the ideal fellow as someone who is already in the implementation phase and is currently making an impact within the community.

This means applicants should ideally have more than just an idea. They should be able to demonstrate that they are actively working on a project, initiative, organization, social venture, or other form of impact-driven work.

The program can then provide the support needed to help the student take that work to the next level.

Fall 2026 Program Dates and Timeline

Applicants should keep the following dates in mind:

Application Opens: August 3, 2026

Application Closes: September 14, 2026

Fall Fellows Notified: September 24, 2026

Program Begins: September 28, 2026

Program Ends: November 20, 2026

Program Duration: 8 weeks

Application Deadline

The application deadline for the University of Maryland Do Good Accelerator Fellows Program Fall 2026 cohort is September 14, 2026.

Students interested in the opportunity should complete their applications and submit all required information before the deadline.

Applicants are encouraged not to wait until the final day to apply, particularly if additional information or preparation is required for the application.

What Does the Do Good Accelerator Fellows Program Offer?

The University of Maryland Do Good Accelerator provides several forms of support intended to help fellows strengthen their projects and increase their impact.

1. One-on-One Coaching and Advising

One of the central features of the fellowship is individualized coaching.

Each week, fellows participate in one-on-one coaching sessions designed to address the specific needs of their projects.

This is particularly valuable because social impact initiatives can face very different challenges depending on their stage of development.

Through coaching, students can receive guidance as they work through issues related to developing, testing, improving, or scaling their projects.

The individualized nature of the coaching also allows fellows to focus on the areas where their particular initiative needs the most attention.

2. Workshops and Webinars

Fellows will participate in developmental activities designed to expose them to useful tools, knowledge, and resources.

The program includes:

Workshops

Webinars

Panel discussions

Community events

Other developmental programming

These activities are intended to help students develop diverse skills that can contribute to the success of their projects.

Rather than simply receiving theoretical information, fellows can use what they learn to address practical challenges within their initiatives.

3. Dedicated Workspace and Resources

The program provides fellows with access to workspace and resources through the Do Good Accelerator.

Having a dedicated environment can be particularly useful for students balancing academic responsibilities with project development.

The fellowship creates structured time for students to focus on their initiatives and work alongside other students who are also pursuing social impact.

4. Community of Like-Minded Students

Another important component of the program is the opportunity to become part of a community of students working on projects intended to create positive change.

Fellows participate in group activities and community programming where they can interact with peers who are also developing their own initiatives.

This environment can encourage:

Collaboration

Knowledge sharing

Peer learning

Networking

Exposure to different approaches to social impact

New ideas and perspectives

Being surrounded by other students who are actively working on meaningful projects can also help participants remain motivated throughout the fellowship.

$2,000 Stipend for Successful Fellows

Selected Fall 2026 fellows will receive a $2,000 stipend upon successful completion of the fellowship.

This is an important financial benefit for students because the program requires fellows to dedicate 8 hours each week to the Do Good Accelerator.

The stipend is therefore tied to successful completion of the fellowship rather than simply being an upfront award.

Applicants should understand the program’s participation requirements before applying and be prepared to commit the required time throughout the eight-week program.

Weekly Time Commitment

Fall 2026 fellows are required to work 8 hours per week at the Do Good Accelerator.

During those weekly hours, students will participate in activities including:

One-on-one coaching sessions.

Independent work on their projects.

Workshops and webinars.

Panel discussions.

Community activities.

Other developmental programming.

This structure is intended to balance focused independent project work with mentorship and collaborative learning.

Students considering applying should evaluate their academic schedules and other commitments to make sure they can consistently dedicate eight hours each week to the program.

Who Should Apply?

The Accelerator Fellows Program is particularly relevant for students who are already actively working on an initiative.

The University of Maryland identifies the ideal student as someone who is in the implementation phase and is currently impacting the community.

A strong prospective applicant could therefore be someone who:

Has an established social impact project.

Is actively implementing an initiative.

Has already begun creating community impact.

Is developing a social venture.

Wants to test or improve an existing approach.

Wants to scale an existing project.

Needs professional coaching and guidance.

Would benefit from structured development time.

Wants access to workshops and useful resources.

Is interested in learning alongside other student changemakers.

Simply having an idea may not make someone the strongest candidate because the program specifically emphasizes students who are already implementing their work.

What Types of Projects Can Benefit From the Program?

The information provided does not restrict the Accelerator to one particular social impact sector.

The program broadly refers to ideas and projects that could change:

Someone’s life

The environment

The future

This creates room for students working on different types of social impact initiatives.

Potential examples could include projects addressing:

Community development

Education

Environmental sustainability

Social entrepreneurship

Public service

Nonprofit initiatives

Community empowerment

Other social or environmental challenges

However, applicants should focus on accurately describing their actual project rather than attempting to reshape their initiative simply to fit a perceived category.

The strongest applications are likely to clearly explain the problem being addressed, what the project is doing, the impact already achieved, and what additional support is needed to move the initiative forward.

Eligibility Requirements

The Fall 2026 Accelerator Fellows Program is open to all current University of Maryland, College Park students.

This is the primary eligibility requirement explicitly stated in the program information.

Applicants should be:

Current students at the University of Maryland, College Park.

Working on a project, initiative, or social venture that can benefit from the Accelerator’s support.

Ideally, in the implementation phase of their project and already creating community impact.

Able to commit 8 hours per week during the fellowship.

Able to participate in the program from September 28 to November 20, 2026.

Academic Major Requirements

The announcement does not state that applicants must study a particular subject.

Therefore, no specific major or field of study should be assumed to be required based on the available program information.

GPA Requirement

No minimum GPA requirement is stated in the provided announcement.

Students should nevertheless carefully review the official application portal for any additional requirements or questions that may apply during the application process.

Age Requirement

No specific age requirement is stated in the program information provided.

Nationality and Geographic Eligibility

The announcement does not identify a nationality requirement or restriction.

However, the program is specifically open to current University of Maryland, College Park students.

Consequently, this should not be treated as a general fellowship open to anyone around the world.

International students who are currently enrolled at the University of Maryland, College Park may potentially qualify because eligibility is based on current student status rather than a stated nationality or continental restriction.

Someone who is not currently enrolled at UMD College Park would not qualify based on the eligibility criteria provided.

Race and Ethnicity Requirements

The provided program information does not specify any race, ethnicity, or racial eligibility requirement.

The opportunity is described as being open to all current University of Maryland, College Park students.

Program Benefits at a Glance

Successful fellows can benefit from:

$2,000 stipend upon successful completion.

Eight-week structured fellowship experience.

One-on-one coaching and advising.

Workshops and webinars.

Panel discussions and community events.

Access to workspace.

Dedicated time to work on a project.

Developmental activities and resources.

Networking with like-minded student innovators.

Opportunities to strengthen an existing social impact initiative.

Support for exploring, testing, or scaling a project or social venture.

How to Apply for the University of Maryland Accelerator Fellows Program

Students interested in the Fall 2026 Accelerator Fellows Program can submit their applications through the official University of Maryland Do Good Accelerator application portal.

Application Portal:

https://webportalapp.com/sp/login/acceleratorfellows

Official Do Good Institute Website: https://dogood.umd.edu/research-impact/projects/accelerator-fellows

More fellowship opportunities visit the OFY Website HERE

Applicants should review the application requirements carefully and provide information that clearly demonstrates their project’s current stage and impact.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Although the announcement does not provide a detailed scoring rubric, applicants can strengthen their applications by clearly communicating the substance and progress of their work.

1. Explain the Problem

Start by clearly explaining the problem your initiative is addressing.

A strong description should make it easy for someone unfamiliar with your project to understand:

What problem exists?

Who is affected?

Why does the problem matter?

Why does it need attention?

2. Demonstrate That You Are Already Taking Action

Because the ideal Accelerator Fellow is in the implementation phase, applicants should clearly distinguish between an idea and an active project.

If applicable, describe:

What you have already done.

Who has benefited.

Where the project is being implemented.

How long the initiative has been operating.

What results you have achieved.

Evidence of community engagement.

Concrete examples can make the project’s progress easier to understand.

3. Explain Your Impact

Don’t simply state that your project is creating impact.

Explain what that impact looks like.

For example, applicants might discuss measurable outcomes such as:

Number of people reached.

Number of beneficiaries served.

Communities involved.

Partnerships established.

Services delivered.

Environmental outcomes.

Educational outcomes.

Revenue or sustainability progress for a social venture.

The specific measurements will depend on the nature of the project.

4. Identify Your Biggest Challenges

The Accelerator exists to provide support, so applicants should be honest about the areas where their projects need development.

Consider explaining challenges involving:

Strategy.

Scaling.

Sustainability.

Operations.

Community engagement.

Partnerships.

Measuring impact.

Project development.

Resource mobilization.

Communication.

This can help demonstrate why participating in the Accelerator would be valuable to the project.

5. Explain How the Accelerator Can Help

Applicants should connect their project’s needs with the resources available through the program.

For example, you could explain how you would benefit from:

One-on-one coaching.

Workshops.

Expert guidance.

Peer learning.

Workspace.

Dedicated project-development time.

Community connections.

Developmental programming.

The goal is to show that you understand what the Accelerator provides and have a clear reason for wanting to participate.

Why the University of Maryland Accelerator Fellowship Stands Out

The Accelerator Fellows Program is different from a conventional scholarship because its primary purpose is not simply to provide financial assistance for education.

It is designed around project development and social impact.

The $2,000 stipend is one component of the program, but fellows also receive structured coaching, developmental programming, resources, workspace, and a community of peers.

For a student who already has a project making an impact, this combination can provide both the time and support needed to strengthen the initiative.

The program can also give students an opportunity to develop practical skills beyond what they may learn through their academic coursework.

What Happens During the Eight-Week Fellowship?

The program combines several activities rather than requiring students to spend all eight hours each week in workshops.

Fellows will spend time working independently on their projects, receiving coaching, participating in developmental activities, and engaging with other students.

Independent Project Work

Students will dedicate structured time to advancing their individual projects.

This could involve developing strategies, testing ideas, improving operations, working with beneficiaries, measuring impact, building partnerships, or addressing other project-specific needs.

Coaching Sessions

Participants will engage in one-on-one sessions designed to provide personalized guidance based on the needs of their individual projects.

Developmental Programming

Workshops, webinars, panel discussions, and community events will expose fellows to tools and resources that can support their development.

Peer and Community Engagement

Group activities provide opportunities to interact with other students pursuing social impact and learn from their experiences.

This combination creates a structured environment in which students can both work on their projects and learn how to improve them.

Questions About the Program

Students who have questions about the Accelerator Fellows Program can contact Kisha McNeill, Do Good Accelerator Manager.

Email: kisham@umd.edu

Kisha McNeill serves as Manager of the Do Good Accelerator at the University of Maryland Do Good Institute.

Applicants with questions about eligibility, the application process, or the fellowship structure can contact the program manager for clarification.

Important Things Applicants Should Know

Before applying, prospective fellows should keep several points in mind.

The Opportunity Is University-Specific

This is not a fellowship that is open to the general public. Applicants must be current University of Maryland, College Park students.

The Program Prioritizes Implementation

The university specifically identifies students who are already in the implementation phase and impacting their communities as ideal candidates.

The Stipend Is Conditional

The $2,000 stipend is provided upon successful completion of the fellowship.

There Is a Weekly Time Commitment

Selected fellows must work 8 hours per week at the Do Good Accelerator.

The Program Is Eight Weeks

The Fall 2026 cohort begins on September 28, 2026, and concludes on November 20, 2026.

The Application Deadline Is September 14, 2026

Students interested in applying should submit their applications by September 14, 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the University of Maryland Accelerator Fellows Program a scholarship?

No. It is a fellowship program focused on student projects, social impact, and venture development. Although fellows receive a $2,000 stipend upon successful completion, the program also provides coaching, workshops, resources, workspace, and developmental opportunities.

How much is the stipend?

Selected fellows receive a $2,000 stipend upon successful completion of the fellowship.

How long is the program?

The Fall 2026 program lasts eight weeks.

How many hours per week are required?

Fellows are required to work 8 hours per week at the Do Good Accelerator.

Who can apply?

The program is open to all current University of Maryland, College Park students.

Do I need to be in a particular major?

No particular academic major is specified in the provided announcement.

Is there a minimum GPA?

The announcement does not state a minimum GPA requirement.

Can international students apply?

The announcement does not impose a nationality restriction, but applicants must be current University of Maryland, College Park students. Therefore, international students who meet that student-status requirement may potentially apply.

Can someone who is not a UMD student apply?

Based on the stated eligibility criteria, no. The program is specifically open to current University of Maryland, College Park students.

Does my project have to be fully developed?

Not necessarily. The program supports students who are exploring, testing, or scaling projects. However, the university states that the ideal student is in the implementation phase and currently impacting the community.

When does the Fall 2026 program begin?

The program begins on September 28, 2026.

When does it end?

The Fall 2026 program ends on November 20, 2026.

When is the application deadline?

The application closes on September 14, 2026.

Conclusion

The University of Maryland Do Good Accelerator Fellows Program offers current University of Maryland, College Park students an opportunity to turn ongoing social impact work into stronger, more developed, and potentially more scalable initiatives.

With a $2,000 stipend, one-on-one coaching, workshops, webinars, panel discussions, community activities, workspace, and dedicated project-development time, the program provides more than financial assistance. It creates a structured environment in which students can work directly on their initiatives while learning from coaches, resources, and fellow student changemakers.

The opportunity is particularly relevant for students who have moved beyond the idea stage and are already implementing a project or social venture that is creating community impact.

For eligible students, the September 14, 2026 deadline is the key date to remember. Those selected will begin the eight-week Fall 2026 program on September 28, 2026, and complete it on November 20, 2026.

Students who are currently enrolled at UMD College Park and have a project they are actively developing should consider using this opportunity to gain structured support, strengthen their initiative, expand their skills, and increase their social impact.

TITLE: 1,500 witness inauguration of the AAU North Africa Regional Office in Cairo, Egypt

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities North Africa Regional Office (AAU NARO) was launched at a high-level, colourful and well attended ceremony hosted by Al-Azhar University in Cairo, Egypt on the 12th March 2019. Al-Azhar University, which was founded in October 975 AD, is a founding member of the Association of Africa Universities.

An impressive number of one thousand five hundred (1500) delegates graced the occasion including Prof Ahmed El-Tayeb the Grand Imam of Al-Azhar University, Prof Khaled Abdel Ghaffar the Egypt Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research, Prof Mohamed Hussein Al Mahrasawy the President of Al-Azhar University, Ambassador Abdulhamid Bu Zaher the Representative of the African Union Commission, Prof Orlando Antonio Quilambo the AAU President, Prof Etienne Ehouan Ehile the AAU Secretary General, Mr Peter Kwasi Kodjie the Secretary General of the All Africa Students Union (AASU), Diplomats, Dr Faiza Mohamed Osman Mahmoud the Coordinator of the AAU East Africa Regional Office, Staff of the AAU Secretariat, Academics from other universities in Egypt, Academics and administrative staff from several African countries, Staff and Students from Al Azhar University and the general public.

The AAU North Africa Regional Office, hosted by Al-Azhar University, is the second AAU Regional Office to be launched – after the East Africa Regional Office (EARO) was launched at the University of Khartoum in Sudan on the 14th of March 2018.

The main goal of the AAU North Africa Regional Office is to increase the impact of AAU’s activities in North Africa and maximise the benefits of AAU to the membership universities in North Africa. This decentralization of the Association’s activities is expected to help improve both the visibility of the AAU and the quality of Higher Education in Africa.

The Grand Imam, Sheikh Professor Ahmed El-Tayeb pledged his support for the AAU North Africa Regional Office and spoke about the need for peace in the world and the eradication of extremism. The Grand Imam is the Head of Sunni Islam’s most prestigious seat of learning at Al-Azhar University. The influential Cleric previously met Pope Francis in February 2019 and they brokered an agreement pledging that Al-Azhar and the Vatican will work together to fight extremism, hateful attitudes and hostility.

In his address the President of Al-Azhar University Professor Mohamed El-Mahrasawy said that Egypt was proud of belonging to Africa and emphasized that Al-Azhar University was not a local or regional institution, but an international institution, where more than 33,000 students from all over the world are studying. He indicated that there were currently 5,000 African students studying at Al-Azhar University.

In his remarks the Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research of Egypt, Professor Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, brought greetings from the President of the Arab Republic of Egypt, Abdel Fattah el-Sisi. He reiterated the Government of Egypt’s unflinching support for the AAU North Africa Regional Office – saying that this regional office tied in neatly with the Agenda 2063 vision of an integrated continent.

The President of the Association of African Universities Professor Orlando Antonio Quilambo stated that the idea of establishing regional hubs of the AAU was not only for increasing the visibility of the Association’s programmes “but more importantly to facilitate effective networking among ourselves first at the country levels, sub-regional levels and then at the continental level”. He said that the current AAU Governing Board had committed itself to pursue this agenda during its four-year mandate.

Professor Etienne Ehile thanked the Government of Egypt, the Grand Imam and the leadership of Al-Azhar University for working hard to make the launch of the AAU North Africa Regional Office a reality. He emphasized that there was a need for African countries to work together to tap into the capacities that are resident in other African countries – citing the example that Al-Azhar University had the capacity to train medical students while most sub-Saharan universities had limited capacities.

A Good Will message was presented by Dr Faiza Mohamed Osman Mahmoud the Coordinator of the AAU East Africa Regional Office. She congratulated Al-Azhar University and the AAU on the successful launch of the North Africa Regional Office – pledging to work closely with them.

The Secretary-General of the All Africa Students Union (AASU), Mr Peter Kwasi Kodjie expressed AASU’s desire to collaborate closer with students in the sub-region.

Various Diplomats and members of the AAU Governing Board that were present also presented their good will messages. The distinguished members of the AAU Governing Board that were present are:

Prof. Hassan Mohamed H. KAAFI – Vice Chancellor, Plasma University, Somalia.

Prof. Theresia K. NKUO-AKENJI – Vice-Chancellor, University of Bamenda, Cameroon

Prof. Bakri Osma SAEED – Vice Chancellor, Sudan International University, Sudan

Prof. Edward AKO – Rector, Université de Maroua, Cameroon

Prof. Nicholas N.N. NSOWAH-NUAMAH – President, Dominion University College, Ghana

The week’s events in Cairo include the Maiden African Universities Olympics that will officially commence on the 14th of March 2019 – organized by the Association of African Universities in collaboration with Al Azhar University and the Ministry of Youth and Sport of Egypt.

TITLE: World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) Fellowship 2026-2027

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: August 6, 2026

Applications are open for the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) Fellowship 2026-2027. The World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) is a United Nations specialized agency. Its WIPO Knowledge Center (WKC) is the custodian of the knowledge repository, which is an authoritative source for global IP academic research. The WKC oversees WIPO’s physical and digital library collection, in addition to the dissemination of WIPO publications.

The WKC team requires a qualified Fellow to support the library and knowledge services by collecting, analyzing, and reporting data that informs evidence-based decision-making. Working closely with colleagues, the fellow will contribute to the assessment of library services, digital resources, and user engagement, helping to identify opportunities to improve discoverability, accessibility, and service delivery.

Fellowships aim to provide fellows with experience to strengthen their knowledge and professional competence, which they can apply in their professional field once they have completed their fellowship with WIPO.

Duties

The Fellow will provide support in the following areas:

Collect, validate, and manage quantitative and qualitative data relating to library services, digital collections, and information resources.

Gather, monitor, and analyze usage statistics from library platforms, repositories, websites, and other digital services.

Produce regular statistical reports to support strategic planning and operational decision-making.

Analyze trends in resource usage, identifying patterns and opportunities for improvement.

Assist in developing and maintaining key performance indicators (KPIs) for library services and digital initiatives.

Contribute to the evaluation of digital resources, collections, and services using evidence-based assessment techniques.

Assist in collecting and analyzing citation, bibliometric, altmetric, and other research impact data, where applicable.

Prepare reports, presentations, and briefing materials summarizing analytical findings for internal stakeholders.

Collaborate with colleagues to improve workflows for data collection, reporting, and assessment.

Perform other related duties as required.

Benefits

A fellowship may be granted for a period of up to 12 months with the possibility to renew.

Stipend: CHF 6,000 monthly.

WIPO shall contribute towards the cost of the fellow’s travel on engagement and separation from service. If necessary, WIPO may provide assistance in obtaining an entry visa to Switzerland.

WIPO contributes towards the medical insurance and provides accident insurance coverage during the course of the fellowship.

Eligibility

Have at least a first-level degree in library, information science, knowledge management or a related field. Recognized professional qualification.

At least two years of professional experience working in a library, knowledge management, research support, or related environment.

Experience collecting, managing, and analyzing library or information-related data.

Experience working with usage statistics, service metrics, or other performance data to support assessment activities.

Experience preparing analytical reports and presenting findings to support decision-making.

Experience using spreadsheet software and data analysis tools.

Desirable Qualities

Experience working with integrated library systems, institutional repositories, discovery platforms, or digital library services.

Experience using business intelligence, dashboard, or data visualization tools.

Experience working with bibliometric, altmetric, or research impact indicators.

Experience with SQL, Python, R, or other analytical tools would be an advantage.

Application

The Fellowship will take place in Geneva, Switzerland and it cannot be carried out remotely. Anticipated Start Date is October 1, 2026.

TITLE: Why Nursing Careers Matter More Than Ever Today

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Nursing matters more than ever because healthcare is no longer built around brief doctor visits or simple treatment plans. People are living longer, managing more stress, and facing health concerns that affect daily life in complex ways.

That shift has placed nurses at the center of care, education, and problem-solving. For anyone considering the profession, nursing stands out as one of the most direct ways to help others while building a stable and flexible career.

Why Nursing Is Changing

Healthcare is evolving quickly, and nursing is evolving with it. Hospitals, clinics, schools, long-term care centers, and community programs all need nurses who can do more than follow routines. Patients often have medical, emotional, and social needs that overlap, so care now depends more on prevention, education, and teamwork.

The profession is shifting from a role focused mainly on treatment toward one built around leadership, prevention, and stronger preparation. Nurses are increasingly expected to guide patients, mentor peers, and shape how care is delivered across entire systems. These broad changes are exactly what people mean when they discuss the future of nursing, which is less about responding to illness after it appears and more about helping people understand their health before small concerns become serious problems.

Technology has also changed healthcare, but it has not replaced the human side of nursing. Digital tools can track symptoms, organize records, and monitor vital signs, yet they cannot reassure a frightened family member or notice subtle confusion in a patient. Nurses are often the people who catch those small but important changes early.

More Than Bedside Care

Many people still picture nurses mainly at the bedside, checking vital signs and giving medication. Those duties remain essential, but they represent only part of a much broader field. Nursing now offers many paths instead of one narrow role.

Nurses may teach families how to manage chronic illnesses like diabetes, support students in schools, coordinate services for older adults, or explain complicated treatment plans to patients who feel overwhelmed. Some work in public health and focus on prevention. Others advocate for people who feel anxious, confused, or unheard.

This expanded role matters because healthcare can become complicated very quickly. One patient may need medication, transportation, follow-up care, mental health support, and clear instructions all at once. Nurses often help connect those pieces. In practice, they frequently act as caregivers, educators, coaches, and care coordinators at the same time.

What Communities Need Now

Communities today face serious and often overlapping health challenges. An aging population means more people are living with long-term conditions such as heart disease, arthritis, and memory-related disorders. Mental health concerns are also being discussed more openly, which is important because ignoring them has never made them disappear.

Access to care remains another major issue. Some people live far from healthcare services. Others cannot afford regular visits, do not have reliable transportation, or simply do not know where to begin. Even health information can be hard to trust, especially when conflicting advice online leaves patients more uncertain than informed.

Nurses help close these gaps in practical ways. They explain care in plain language, recognize warning signs early, and help patients stay on track with treatment. In many communities, nurses are the steady and trusted presence people rely on. That trust matters because people are more likely to ask questions, follow care plans, and seek help before a crisis when they feel heard and respected.

The Rise of Nurse Leaders

Nurses are taking on leadership roles more often, and leadership in nursing goes far beyond executive titles or formal management positions. Strong nurse leaders guide teams, solve everyday problems, and improve the experiences of patients and families. Because nurses see what care looks like in real settings, their perspective is especially valuable.

Leadership can begin early in a nursing career. A nurse might mentor a new colleague, suggest a better workflow, or speak up when a process is not serving patients well. Those actions matter because leadership often starts with awareness and the belief that a better approach is possible.

This shift also creates meaningful career growth. Nurses who build communication skills, decision-making ability, and professional confidence can move into roles that influence staffing, policy, education, and systems of care. That benefits healthcare organizations, but more importantly, it improves outcomes for the people receiving care.

Education Opens New Doors

Continuing education can change a nursing career in practical and personal ways. It does more than add credentials to a resume. It can open paths to leadership, teaching, care coordination, and specialized practice areas that better match a nurse’s interests and strengths.

Some nurses discover that they want to mentor others. Teaching future nurses can be deeply rewarding because the experience of one professional can shape many careers and, in turn, many patients’ lives. Others want to improve healthcare systems, lead teams, or strengthen care delivery. Additional education can help make those transitions possible.

Education also builds confidence. Greater knowledge often leads to stronger judgment, broader opportunities, and better patient outcomes. In nursing, learning is never only theoretical. It directly affects how well professionals respond to real situations involving real people. That is why growth in this field matters so much.

A Career With Purpose

Nursing offers something many careers cannot: a clear sense of purpose. On the best days, nurses help people heal, feel safer, or better understand what comes next. On the hardest days, they still provide support during moments that matter deeply. That work leaves a lasting impact on both patients and the professionals who care for them.

There are practical benefits as well. Nursing generally offers strong job stability, and the profession can adapt to different stages of life. Some nurses thrive in fast-paced hospitals, while others prefer schools, clinics, home health, public health, or community-based settings. That flexibility makes nursing appealing to people who want a career that can evolve over time.

It is also a profession that depends on both analytical thinking and interpersonal skills. Nurses assess symptoms, solve problems, make decisions, and build trust all at once. That balance is part of what makes the role so valuable. The work is serious and demanding, but it also offers a direct way to improve lives.

Looking Ahead

Nursing will remain essential because healthcare will always need people who can make it clearer, more compassionate, and more human. As healthcare systems continue to change, nurses will keep connecting treatment with trust, information with action, and complex systems with the people they are meant to serve.

TITLE: Ireland Civil Society Fund 2027: Up to €800,000 Per Year for Overseas Development Projects

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Government of Ireland’s Civil Society Fund 2027 is now open, offering substantial grant funding to eligible civil society organisations implementing overseas development projects. Through the fund, the Department of Foreign Affairs can provide up to 100% of eligible annual project costs, with grants of up to €800,000 per year for projects lasting as long as five years.

The Civil Society Fund is designed to support development interventions delivered by civil society organisations and aligned with Ireland’s international development priorities. The programme also recognises the importance of sustained responses to long-term humanitarian crises, although sudden-onset acute emergency responses are not eligible.

The 2027 call involves a two-stage application process. Organisations must first establish their eligibility and, if eligible, will subsequently receive the full application form. Irish-based organisations that believe they meet the requirements are required to submit an Eligibility Form by 5pm on Friday, 11 September 2026. Eligible organisations will then be invited to submit the full application by 5pm on Monday, 2 November 2026.

Ireland Civil Society Fund 2027 at a Glance

Opportunity
Details

Programme
Civil Society Fund 2027

Funder
Government of Ireland / Department of Foreign Affairs

Implementing department
Development Cooperation and Africa Division

Opportunity type
Overseas development grant

Maximum funding
Up to €800,000 per annum

Maximum project duration
Up to five years

Funding level
Up to 100% of annual project costs for successful applications

Eligible applicants
Irish civil society organisations and specifically invited international civil society organisations

Application structure
Eligibility Form followed by full application for eligible organisations

Initial eligibility deadline
5pm, Friday, 11 September 2026

Full application deadline
5pm, Monday, 2 November 2026

Eligibility notification
Late September 2026

Appraisal period
December 2026/January 2027

Funding decisions
March/April 2027

Project focus
Overseas development projects

Long-term humanitarian crises
Eligible

Sudden-onset acute emergency responses
Not eligible

What Is the Civil Society Fund?

The Civil Society Fund (CSF) is a funding mechanism through which the Government of Ireland supports civil society organisations implementing overseas development projects.

The fund provides financial support for organisations undertaking development work outside Ireland and is intended for interventions that contribute to international development objectives.

Rather than being an individual funding opportunity, this is an organisational grant programme. Applications are submitted by qualifying civil society organisations rather than individuals.

For successful applicants, the Department can fund up to 100% of annual project costs, subject to the applicable grant ceiling and other requirements.

The maximum grant available is €800,000 per annum, while projects can have a duration of up to five years.

This means that organisations selected for multi-year support could potentially receive significant funding over the life of a project, although the exact amount awarded will depend on the approved project, annual costs, funding conditions and assessment process.

What Does the Civil Society Fund Support?

The fund is intended to support overseas development projects implemented by eligible civil society organisations.

The programme is therefore particularly relevant to organisations that already have the capacity, experience and institutional structures necessary to design and implement development interventions outside Ireland.

Potential applicant organisations should carefully examine the official 2027 Call for Applications to determine whether their proposed intervention fits within the fund’s specific policy priorities, geographic requirements and thematic criteria.

The fund is not simply a general-purpose organisational funding programme. Applicants must propose eligible development interventions and satisfy the requirements established in the official call.

Up to €800,000 Per Year in Grant Funding

One of the most significant features of the Civil Society Fund is its maximum funding level.

Successful applicants can receive:

Up to €800,000 per year

The fund can also support projects lasting:

Up to five years

The Department states that, for successful applications, it will fund up to 100% of annual project costs, up to the maximum grant limit.

This can provide eligible civil society organisations with substantial resources to implement development programmes over an extended period.

However, organisations should not interpret the €800,000 figure as an automatic award. It is the maximum available grant per annum, and funding decisions will depend on the quality, relevance, eligibility and assessment of each application.

Important Organisational Income Requirement

Applicants should pay particular attention to the Civil Society Fund’s organisational income requirement.

Income received from the Department, whether directly or indirectly, must not exceed 49% of the applicant organisation’s overall income.

The calculation is based on an average of the organisation’s published audited accounts over the previous three years.

Importantly, in-kind income is excluded from this calculation.

This requirement means organisations should review their financial records before proceeding with an application.

An organisation that relies too heavily on income from the Department of Foreign Affairs may not satisfy this particular eligibility requirement.

Applicants should therefore examine their audited accounts for the relevant three-year period and calculate the proportion of overall organisational income originating directly or indirectly from the Department.

Long-Term Humanitarian Crises Are Eligible

The Civil Society Fund makes an important distinction between long-term humanitarian crises and sudden-onset emergencies.

Interventions addressing long-term humanitarian crises can be eligible for support.

This creates an opportunity for organisations working on sustained humanitarian challenges where development and humanitarian needs persist over an extended period.

However, the fund does not support responses to sudden-onset acute emergencies.

Therefore, organisations proposing projects should distinguish clearly between:

Long-term humanitarian crises requiring sustained interventions; and

Sudden-onset emergencies requiring immediate emergency response.

A proposal focused primarily on responding to a newly occurring acute emergency would not meet this aspect of the fund’s eligibility.

Who Can Apply?

The Civil Society Fund is primarily open to Irish civil society organisations that meet the eligibility criteria set out in the 2027 Call for Applications.

The opportunity also allows for participation by a limited number of international civil society organisations, but there is an important restriction.

International organisations cannot simply apply independently because they discover the call.

The Government states that a limited number of international civil society organisations may be invited to the Civil Society Fund each year, based on policy priorities.

Therefore:

Irish-based civil society organisations that meet the requirements can proceed through the published eligibility process.

International civil society organisations are eligible only if specifically invited.

An international organisation that has not been invited should not assume that it can submit an application.

This distinction is particularly important for NGOs and development organisations based in Africa, Asia, Latin America and other regions.

Can African NGOs Apply?

African civil society organisations should not assume that the Civil Society Fund is an open global grant competition.

The official information specifically states that a limited number of international civil society organisations may be invited each year.

Therefore, an African NGO, for example, would need to determine whether it has been specifically invited to participate in the 2027 Civil Society Fund.

Being an NGO, having a strong development project or operating in a country relevant to international development does not, by itself, establish eligibility under the international-organisation provision.

Potential international applicants should consult the official 2027 Call for Applications and use the contact details provided by the Department if they need clarification.

Eligibility Is the First Stage

The Civil Society Fund uses a staged application process.

Organisations do not immediately submit the full grant application.

Instead, eligible Irish-based organisations begin by completing an Eligibility Form.

This first stage allows the Department to determine whether the organisation meets the basic requirements before inviting it to submit the full application.

This means organisations should treat the Eligibility Form as an important part of the application process rather than as a simple registration exercise.

First Deadline: Eligibility Form

Irish organisations that intend to apply must submit their completed Eligibility Form to the Civil Society Fund mailbox by:

5pm on Friday, 11 September 2026

This is the first major deadline.

Organisations should not wait until the final day because they need to gather supporting documents and ensure that the submission is complete.

The Department specifically requests that applicants also provide supporting documentation, including:

A Tax Clearance Certificate or equivalent

Accounts for the last three years

Relevant safeguarding policies

The Eligibility Form and supporting documents should therefore be prepared together.

What Happens After the Eligibility Form?

Organisations that submit a completed Eligibility Form will be notified about their eligibility in late September 2026.

Organisations determined to be eligible will then receive the full application form by email.

This creates a two-stage process:

Stage 1: Eligibility

Submit:

Completed Eligibility Form

Tax Clearance Certificate or equivalent

Three years of accounts

Safeguarding policies

Deadline: 5pm, 11 September 2026

Stage 2: Full Grant Application

If the organisation is confirmed as eligible, the Department will email the full application form.

The completed application must then be submitted by:

5pm on Monday, 2 November 2026

Applicants should understand that submitting the Eligibility Form does not automatically mean that the organisation will be invited to submit a full proposal. The organisation must first be assessed as eligible.

Second Deadline: Full Application

The full application deadline is:

5pm on Monday, 2 November 2026

The Department states that applications received after the relevant deadlines will not be considered.

Organisations should therefore plan backwards from the deadline and leave sufficient time for:

Internal review

Financial verification

Safeguarding review

Senior management approval

Legal review where necessary

Final editing

Submission

Printing and signing of the required hard copy

Hard Copy Submission Requirement

The application process also includes a subsequent hard-copy submission.

After submitting the application form, applicants must submit a hard copy of the application form, signed by the legal representative of the organisation.

The hard copy should be sent to:

Civil Society Fund
Civil Society Unit
Development Cooperation and Africa Division
Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
Riverstone House
23–27 Henry Street
Limerick
V94 R7YE
Ireland

Organisations should therefore allow sufficient time for the physical document to reach the Department after completing the electronic application requirements.

Safeguarding Requirements

Safeguarding is an important component of the eligibility documentation.

Applicants are required to provide their safeguarding policies alongside the Eligibility Form.

This is particularly relevant because organisations receiving development funding may work directly with:

Children

Women and girls

People experiencing poverty

Displaced populations

Refugees

People with disabilities

Communities affected by conflict

Other vulnerable or marginalised groups

Organisations should ensure that their safeguarding policies are current, formally approved and appropriate to the nature of their proposed development work.

Financial Documentation

Applicants must also provide accounts covering the last three years.

These documents are important for demonstrating the organisation’s financial position and for assessing compliance with the Civil Society Fund’s income requirements.

Organisations should ensure that their accounts are:

Complete

Published or formally audited where required

Consistent across the relevant three-year period

Readily available for submission

Compatible with the information provided in the Eligibility Form

Financial information should be carefully checked before submission because discrepancies between the eligibility form and financial statements could create problems during assessment.

Tax Clearance

Applicants must include a Tax Clearance Certificate or equivalent with their eligibility submission.

This is another indication that the fund is designed for established organisations with appropriate financial and legal structures.

Organisations should verify that their tax documentation is valid and meets the Department’s requirements before submitting the Eligibility Form.

Application Assessment Timeline

Following the application process, the Department intends to assess applications during:

December 2026 and January 2027

Funding decisions are expected to be communicated in:

March/April 2027

The timeline therefore provides applicants with several months between the full application deadline and the expected funding decision.

However, organisations should not assume that funding will be available before the official notification of a decision.

Important Application Rules

Applicants should pay close attention to the Department’s procedural requirements.

Late applications are not accepted

The Department states that forms received after the relevant deadlines will not be considered.

This applies to the relevant stages of the process, so applicants should submit their documents before the stated closing times.

Individual meetings are not available

Once the Call for Applications is issued, representatives of applicant organisations cannot request individual meetings concerning the application form until funding decisions have been communicated.

This means organisations should rely on the official documentation and the designated Civil Society Fund contact channel for questions.

Attempts to influence the decision can lead to disqualification

The Department explicitly states that any attempt to influence the outcome of the decision-making process in relation to grant applications will result in disqualification.

Applicants should therefore maintain a professional and transparent application process and avoid inappropriate attempts to influence officials or the assessment process.

Organisations based in Ireland that consider they meet the criteria set out in the 2027 Call for Applications and who wish to apply for funding can download an Eligibility Form.

How Organisations Should Prepare

Although applicants should rely on the official call for the complete requirements, organisations can begin preparing immediately.

1. Review the eligibility requirements

Start by reading the full 2027 Call for Applications carefully.

Do not begin with the project narrative before confirming that the organisation itself is eligible.

2. Review three years of financial records

Check the organisation’s published audited accounts for the relevant three-year period.

Calculate the proportion of organisational income received directly or indirectly from the Department to determine whether the organisation satisfies the 49% income requirement.

3. Prepare safeguarding documentation

Make sure safeguarding policies are current and can be provided with the Eligibility Form.

4. Confirm tax clearance

Obtain the relevant Tax Clearance Certificate or equivalent documentation.

5. Examine the proposed development project

The project should clearly correspond to the objectives and eligibility requirements of the Civil Society Fund.

Organisations should be able to explain:

What development problem they are addressing

Where the project will operate

Who will benefit

Why the intervention is necessary

What outcomes are expected

How activities will produce those outcomes

How progress will be measured

How the intervention will be sustained

How risks will be managed

Why the organisation is appropriately positioned to implement it

6. Build a realistic budget

Because funding can cover up to 100% of annual project costs for successful applications, organisations should prepare a realistic and well-supported project budget.

The budget should correspond directly with the activities and expected results of the project.

7. Plan for a multi-year intervention where appropriate

Projects can last for up to five years.

Organisations with interventions requiring sustained implementation should consider how activities, outcomes, partnerships and financing would develop over the full project period.

8. Begin internal approvals early

The application may require approval from senior management, a board, legal representatives or other authorised personnel.

Organisations should therefore avoid leaving internal approval until the final days before submission.

Why the Civil Society Fund Is Significant

The scale and duration of the Civil Society Fund make it potentially valuable for established development organisations.

A maximum annual grant of €800,000 provides considerably more funding capacity than many small community or seed grants.

The possibility of funding projects for up to five years also makes the programme relevant to interventions that require long-term implementation rather than short-term activities.

Longer-term development programmes may involve:

Institutional strengthening

Community development

Capacity building

Education

Health

Gender equality

Poverty reduction

Governance

Human rights

Livelihood development

Resilience building

Long-term humanitarian support

However, the specific thematic and geographic priorities of the 2027 call should always be checked before preparing a proposal.

Important Distinction: Grant Funding vs Individual Funding

This opportunity is a grant for civil society organisations, not an individual scholarship or fellowship.

Individuals cannot apply for the €800,000 grant as individuals.

Similarly, students, job seekers and individual researchers should not treat the Civil Society Fund as a personal funding programme.

The applicant is the eligible organisation, which must demonstrate the institutional, financial, legal and safeguarding capacity required by the programme.

What International Organisations Should Know

International civil society organisations should pay particular attention to the invitation requirement.

The Government of Ireland states that only a limited number of international civil society organisations may be invited each year.

Eligibility is determined according to policy priorities, and only organisations specifically invited are eligible to apply.

Therefore, international NGOs should not assume that the publication of the call means that every international organisation worldwide can submit an application.

This is especially important for organisations headquartered outside Ireland.

Geographic Eligibility

The Civil Society Fund supports overseas development projects, meaning the programme is relevant to development activities implemented outside Ireland.

The official page also provides an OECD DAC Country Codes / ODA recipients resource as one of the key documents for the call.

Organisations should consult the official 2027 Call for Applications and the OECD DAC list to determine whether their proposed project location meets the relevant development-assistance requirements.

For African organisations, geographic relevance should therefore be assessed alongside the separate requirement concerning whether an international organisation has been specifically invited.

Key Documents

Applicants should review the official programme documents before preparing their submission.

The key documents include:

2027 Call for Applications

OECD DAC Country Codes / ODA Recipient List

2027 Civil Society Fund Eligibility Form

The official Civil Society Fund webpage also provides access to these documents and additional programme information.

Application Deadlines

There are two critical deadlines for the 2027 Civil Society Fund.

Eligibility Form

5pm, Friday, 11 September 2026

This is the deadline for eligible Irish-based organisations to submit the completed Eligibility Form and required supporting documents.

Full Application

5pm, Monday, 2 November 2026

Only organisations that are confirmed as eligible will receive the full application form and proceed to this stage.

Organisations should not confuse the two deadlines. The 11 September 2026 deadline is the first-stage eligibility deadline, while 2 November 2026 is the deadline for the full application.

Key Takeaways for Prospective Applicants

Before applying, organisations should remember the following:

The Civil Society Fund supports overseas development projects.

It is an organisational grant, not an individual funding opportunity.

Successful projects can receive up to €800,000 per year.

Projects can run for up to five years.

The Department can fund up to 100% of annual project costs, subject to the grant limit and applicable conditions.

Departmental income must not exceed 49% of the applicant organisation’s overall income, calculated using the average of published audited accounts over three years.

Long-term humanitarian crisis interventions are eligible.

Sudden-onset acute emergency responses are not eligible.

Irish civil society organisations can apply if they meet the requirements.

International civil society organisations must be specifically invited to apply.

The first stage requires an Eligibility Form.

Applicants must provide financial accounts, tax clearance documentation and safeguarding policies.

The Eligibility Form deadline is 5pm, 11 September 2026.

Eligible organisations will be notified in late September 2026.

The full application deadline is 5pm, 2 November 2026.

Applications received after the relevant deadlines will not be considered.

Appraisal is expected in December 2026/January 2027.

Funding decisions are expected in March/April 2027.

A signed hard copy of the application must subsequently be submitted to the Civil Society Fund in Limerick.

Attempts to influence the funding decision can result in disqualification.

Conclusion

The Ireland Civil Society Fund 2027 represents a significant funding opportunity for eligible civil society organisations implementing overseas development projects. With grants of up to €800,000 per annum, the possibility of projects lasting up to five years, and funding of up to 100% of annual project costs, the programme can provide substantial support for well-designed and strategically relevant development interventions.

However, organisations should pay close attention to the eligibility conditions. The opportunity is primarily available to Irish civil society organisations, while only a limited number of international civil society organisations specifically invited by the Government of Ireland may apply. It is therefore not an open global grant competition for every NGO.

The application process has two important stages. Irish organisations intending to apply must first submit the Eligibility Form and required documentation by 5pm on Friday, 11 September 2026. Organisations that are confirmed as eligible will receive the full application form and must submit it by 5pm on Monday, 2 November 2026.

Prospective applicants should begin preparations early by reviewing the official call, checking their financial eligibility, preparing their three years of accounts, confirming tax clearance, reviewing safeguarding policies and developing a strong project concept aligned with the fund’s requirements.

The Civil Society Fund can be particularly valuable for established organisations seeking substantial, multi-year support for overseas development work, but applicants should carefully verify all eligibility, thematic, geographic and financial requirements in the official 2027 Call for Applications before submitting.

Official information and application documents:
Government of Ireland – Civil Society Fund 2027
