TITLE: LSE FLIA Creatives in Residence 2026: One-Year Opportunity for African Creatives to Collaborate with the London School of Economics

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the Firoz Lalji Institute for Africa (FLIA) Creatives in Residence Programme at the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE). The programme offers African creatives and members of the African diaspora an opportunity to become affiliated with one of LSE’s leading Africa-focused institutes, work alongside academics and researchers, develop creative responses to major social-science questions, and contribute to public conversations about Africa and the wider world.

The current open call was announced by LSE on 9 September 2026. Each selected Creative in Residence will initially be affiliated with FLIA for one year, with the possibility of renewal. Applications are explicitly open to people of African nationality or African descent.

The programme sits at the intersection of creative practice, academic research and public engagement. FLIA intends the residency to help artists and other creative practitioners translate complex social-science research into compelling forms that can reach audiences beyond academia.

The application deadline is 7 October 2026.

About the FLIA Creatives in Residence Programme

The Creatives in Residence Programme is run by the Firoz Lalji Institute for Africa, part of the London School of Economics and Political Science in London.

The programme is designed to connect Africa’s creative industries with LSE’s academic community. Its central premise is that creative practice can help researchers communicate difficult or complex ideas in forms that are accessible, memorable and capable of engaging wider audiences.

FLIA describes the programme as a way of bringing creatives with a record of creativity, innovation and leadership into dialogue with academic research. Creatives may work alongside scholars, contribute to research communication and use their artistic or professional practice to broaden the impact of academic work.

The programme is therefore not simply an opportunity to spend time at LSE independently. Successful applicants are expected to become active participants in the Institute’s intellectual community and create outputs that connect their own creative practice with wider issues being researched and debated at FLIA.

Host Institution: Firoz Lalji Institute for Africa at LSE

The Firoz Lalji Institute for Africa is LSE’s principal institute focused on Africa.

Its mission is to place Africa at the centre of research, teaching, policy engagement and public debate. The Institute supports interdisciplinary scholarship, evidence-based policymaking and collaboration between researchers and institutions in Africa and elsewhere.

FLIA works across a wide range of disciplines and combines research with public engagement, policy work, leadership development and creative communication.

Its activities include initiatives such as:

The Programme for African Leadership

The Hub for African Thought

Africa at LSE

The LSE Africa Summit

Public events and policy engagement

Academic research programmes

Creative communication initiatives

The Creatives in Residence Programme

This broader institutional environment means selected residents can potentially interact not only with academics, but also with students, policy specialists, public-engagement teams and members of LSE’s wider African intellectual network.

What Is the Purpose of the Residency?

The programme seeks to create stronger connections between creative industries and academic research.

Academic research often addresses complex topics such as inequality, political change, social movements, technology, conflict, climate change, economic transformation and identity. Such work can sometimes remain inaccessible to audiences outside universities.

FLIA wants its Creatives in Residence to explore different ways of communicating these issues.

Creative approaches could potentially involve fields such as:

Film

Documentary

Photography

Visual arts

Graphic design

Illustration

Digital media

Writing

Journalism

Storytelling

Performance

Multimedia

Cultural production

Other forms of creative communication

The official announcement does not limit applications to one artistic medium. Its emphasis is instead on using creative practice to communicate research and engage wider audiences.

Residency Duration

Each successful Creative in Residence will initially be affiliated with FLIA for:

One year

The appointment may subsequently be renewed. FLIA holds an annual open call through which creatives can apply to join the programme.

The one-year structure gives residents time to develop meaningful relationships with researchers and create outputs that go beyond a short workshop or temporary visit.

Applicants Must Be Able to Spend Time in London

Although the residency lasts for an initial one-year period, the official call includes an important practical requirement.

Successful applicants must be able to spend time in London so that they can integrate into FLIA’s intellectual community.

Applicants based outside the United Kingdom should take this requirement seriously when considering whether they can participate.

The announcement does not state that residents must permanently relocate to London for the entire year. It says they must be able to spend time there. Applicants should therefore discuss practical expectations with FLIA if selected.

Who Can Apply?

The current call states clearly that applications are open to:

Anyone of African nationality or African descent.

This means eligibility is not limited to people currently living on the African continent.

African nationals may apply, and members of the African diaspora may also be eligible where they are of African descent.

FLIA’s wider fellowship guidance further describes Creatives in Residence as academics and non-academics who work in or on the creative industry in Africa.

This is therefore a deliberately broad opportunity that can accommodate both formally trained academics and creative practitioners whose expertise comes primarily through professional practice.

Is an Academic Degree Required?

The current application announcement does not specify a mandatory bachelor’s degree, master’s degree, PhD or other academic qualification.

That is an important distinction from traditional academic fellowships.

FLIA’s visiting fellowship guidance states that Creatives in Residence may include academics and non-academics working in or on Africa’s creative industries.

Applicants should therefore focus primarily on demonstrating the quality of their creative practice, relevant experience, leadership, past work and the strength of the project they propose to undertake.

What Kind of Applicant Is FLIA Looking For?

The wider programme description indicates that FLIA seeks creatives with a track record of creativity and leadership who can connect with academic research and help generate change through creative outputs.

A competitive applicant would therefore ideally be able to demonstrate:

Previous creative work of strong quality

An established creative practice

Leadership or initiative within the creative sector

Interest in Africa and African issues

Capacity to collaborate with academics and researchers

Ability to communicate complex ideas creatively

A clear and achievable project proposal

Capacity to produce a substantial creative output

Willingness to engage with the FLIA community

Availability to spend time in London

The exact weight FLIA gives to each factor is not specified in the announcement, so applicants should not treat this as a formal scoring rubric.

What Must Selected Creatives Produce?

FLIA has set several expectations for appointed Creatives in Residence.

During the residency, successful applicants are expected to:

Produce one creative output

Contribute to either the Institute’s blog or the Hub for African Thought

Participate in at least one event during their term

These requirements demonstrate that the programme combines creative production, written or intellectual contribution and direct community engagement.

The residency is therefore structured around tangible outputs rather than being only an honorary affiliation.

What Could the Creative Output Look Like?

The current announcement does not prescribe a particular medium.

FLIA’s broader creative engagement work demonstrates its interest in many forms of communication, ranging from blogs and podcasts to paintings, comics and other creative media.

Depending on the applicant’s profession, a proposed output might therefore potentially involve:

A short film

Documentary project

Photography series

Visual exhibition

Multimedia project

Podcast

Graphic narrative

Illustration project

Written creative work

Performance

Digital storytelling project

Research-based artistic installation

Public-facing communication campaign

Applicants should make sure that the proposed format is appropriate for their own expertise and relevant to the subject they intend to explore.

Proposal Themes

The official announcement gives applicants considerable flexibility when choosing a project.

Proposals may align with, but are not restricted to:

FLIA’s research themes

LSE’s five strategic themes

Gaps in existing thematic work

Existing FLIA research projects

The LSE Africa Summit theme of reparations

This flexibility means applicants do not need to force their proposal into a narrowly predetermined subject.

However, showing a meaningful connection between a proposed creative project and FLIA’s research priorities could help demonstrate why LSE is an appropriate place to undertake the work.

FLIA Research Themes for 2026–2029

FLIA’s current research strategy identifies five major thematic areas for 2026–2029:

1. Trade and Industry

This theme considers African economic transformation, industrial development, trade and the ways African countries and institutions exercise agency within changing global geopolitical and economic systems.

2. Women, Peace and Security

This area examines issues including justice, human rights, women’s participation in peace and security, conflict and gender-based violence.

3. Sustainable Multispecies Futures

This research stream examines relationships between humans, animals and environments, particularly in the context of climate change and ecological sustainability.

4. Activism, Influence and Change

This theme examines how citizens, organisations and movements bring about change by understanding power, building coalitions, developing narratives and engaging institutions.

5. Digital Cooperation and Sovereignty

This area explores digital public infrastructure, governance, technology, data, digital sovereignty and the effects of emerging technological systems on societies and states.

Applicants could use these themes as inspiration, but they are not required to restrict themselves exclusively to them.

LSE’s Wider Strategic Themes

FLIA states that its research agenda also connects with LSE’s focus on five major global challenges:

Political economy

Inequality

Sustainability

Future technologies

Democracy

A creative proposal could therefore potentially address one or several of these areas from an African perspective.

Reparations as a Possible Theme

The current call specifically mentions reparations in connection with FLIA’s Summit theme.

This opens space for proposals examining reparations through creative approaches connected to areas such as:

Colonialism

Slavery and historical injustice

Cultural restitution

Memory

Heritage

Economic justice

Identity

Diaspora experiences

Museums and cultural property

Political movements

Historical narratives

Applicants should develop their proposals according to their own expertise rather than assuming that reparations is mandatory. The official call explicitly says proposals are not restricted to the suggested themes.

Connection with the Programme for African Leadership

The broader Creatives in Residence Programme also has a strong connection with FLIA’s Programme for African Leadership (PfAL).

FLIA states that one responsibility of Creatives in Residence is to inspire, engage and facilitate access to development opportunities in creative industries for students and alumni associated with the Programme for African Leadership.

Residents may therefore have opportunities to interact with emerging African leaders studying or engaging with LSE.

Supporting Africa’s Creative Economy

A further purpose of the programme is to advance FLIA’s work around Africa’s creative economy.

The programme is designed not only around artistic production but also around broader questions about how the creative industries can contribute to African social, cultural and economic development.

This makes the residency potentially relevant to professionals working in sectors including:

Film and television

Media

Photography

Publishing

Design

Digital content

Music

Cultural production

Creative entrepreneurship

Visual communication

Art

Storytelling

Technology-enabled creative industries

Current FLIA Creatives in Residence

FLIA currently lists several Creatives in Residence whose professional backgrounds illustrate the diversity of practitioners involved in the programme.

Current residents include:

Chude Jideonwo, a media entrepreneur whose career spans advertising, public relations, television, radio, print and digital media

Dr Tunde Alabi-Hundeyin II, a documentary filmmaker and media creative working on culture, identity, power and social justice

Ian Mangenga, a social designer and AI ethics and governance researcher focusing particularly on technology, identity, access and African women

Ama Ofeibea Tetteh, founder and lead consultant at Chapter54 with a background across graphics, communications, research and programme management

Their profiles demonstrate that the programme is not confined to one artistic discipline or career trajectory.

How Creative Practice Can Strengthen Research Communication

FLIA has a history of using creative methods to make academic research more accessible.

The Institute has worked with different formats including visual arts, comics, photography and other public-facing approaches to communicate complex research findings.

Such work reflects a broader recognition that conventional academic publications do not always reach communities, policymakers or general audiences effectively.

Creative practitioners can help transform data, historical research, interviews and theoretical concepts into experiences and narratives that are easier for wider audiences to understand and engage with.

Required Application Materials

According to the official announcement, applicants should submit three principal components:

Previous examples of their work

A proposal describing the project they plan to undertake during the residency

A summary of the outputs they hope to produce by the end of the fellowship

Applicants should make sure that each component clearly demonstrates both their creative credentials and the feasibility of their proposed project.

Preparing Examples of Previous Work

Past work is likely to be important because the programme seeks people with an established track record of creative practice.

Applicants should therefore select examples that best demonstrate:

Artistic or creative quality

Originality

Ability to communicate ideas

Experience addressing social or public issues

Leadership in creative practice

Relevance to African contexts where applicable

Capacity to complete ambitious projects

Depending on the medium, examples could potentially include portfolios, publications, films, photographs, recordings, project links or other appropriate evidence.

Applicants should use accessible links or formats where necessary and ensure that reviewers can easily understand their contribution to each project.

Preparing the Project Proposal

The official announcement does not prescribe a specific word count for the project proposal.

A strong proposal should nevertheless explain:

What the applicant wants to create

The issue or research question the project addresses

Why the topic matters

Why FLIA and LSE provide a suitable environment

How the project connects with African experiences, debates or creative industries

Which FLIA or LSE themes are relevant

What creative method will be used

Which audiences the applicant wants to reach

What can realistically be completed during the residency

What final output or outputs are anticipated

These are practical suggestions rather than additional formal requirements published by LSE.

Preparing the Output Summary

Applicants must also provide a summary of the outputs they hope to produce by the end of the fellowship.

This section should be concrete.

For example, rather than stating only that the applicant intends to “raise awareness,” it may be stronger to identify specific deliverables such as a film, photographic series, digital publication, exhibition, podcast series or other defined creative product.

The official call expects at least one creative output from appointed residents.

Application Method

Applications should be sent directly to Mark Briggs at the Firoz Lalji Institute for Africa.

Application email:
m.a.briggs@lse.ac.uk

Applicants should include the required materials covering previous work, their project proposal and anticipated outputs.

The announcement does not specify a separate online application portal.

Application Deadline

The application deadline is:

7 October 2026

The official call was published on 9 September 2026 and states that applications close on 7 October.

Prospective applicants should allow enough time to prepare a clear portfolio and project proposal rather than waiting until the deadline.

Is the Residency Funded?

The current official call does not state a stipend, salary, grant amount, travel allowance, accommodation support or visa funding.

Applicants should therefore not assume that these costs are covered.

Because successful applicants must be able to spend time in London, international candidates who require clarity regarding travel, accommodation, visa arrangements or financial support should contact FLIA directly before making major commitments.

Why the FLIA Creatives in Residence Programme Is Distinctive

Several aspects differentiate this opportunity from a conventional arts residency.

First, participants become affiliated with a major social-science institution rather than working exclusively within an arts organisation.

Second, the programme actively encourages collaboration between creative practitioners and academic researchers.

Third, selected residents are expected to produce public-facing outputs, participate in events and contribute to the Institute’s intellectual life.

Fourth, the programme focuses strongly on Africa and African perspectives, while situating those perspectives within global debates.

Finally, the one-year initial affiliation allows for a longer and potentially deeper relationship than many short-duration creative residencies.

Important Information at a Glance

Detail
Information

Programme
FLIA Creatives in Residence

Host institution
Firoz Lalji Institute for Africa, London School of Economics

Location
London, United Kingdom

Initial affiliation
One year

Renewal
Possible

Eligibility
African nationals or people of African descent

Degree requirement
No specific degree requirement stated

Required presence
Must be able to spend time in London

Required output
At least one creative output

Additional participation
Contribute to FLIA blog or Hub for African Thought and participate in at least one event

Application materials
Previous work, project proposal, summary of intended outputs

Application email
m.a.briggs@lse.ac.uk

Deadline
7 October 2026

Funding amount
Not specified in the current call

Conclusion

The LSE Firoz Lalji Institute for Africa Creatives in Residence Programme 2026 provides African creatives and members of the African diaspora with an unusual opportunity to combine creative practice with academic research at one of the world’s best-known social-science institutions.

Selected creatives will join FLIA for an initial one-year affiliation, collaborate within its intellectual community and develop projects that can turn complex social-science ideas into compelling forms of public communication.

The call is particularly broad in terms of professional background. Applicants do not need to follow a single artistic discipline, and the official announcement does not impose a specific academic degree requirement. What matters most is a meaningful creative track record, a strong project proposal, clearly identified outputs and the ability to spend time in London.

Applicants may connect their projects with FLIA’s research priorities, LSE’s broader strategic themes, existing research projects, gaps in current work or the theme of reparations. Successful residents will be expected to deliver at least one creative output, contribute to FLIA’s blog or Hub for African Thought and participate in at least one event during the residency.

The deadline to apply is 7 October 2026.

TITLE: Mohamed Ali Foundation Fellowship Programme 2027

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 20, 2026

Applications are open for the Mohamed Ali Foundation Fellowship Programme 2027. The fellowship is established to devote scholarly attention to the Abbas Hilmi II Papers held at Durham University and to make the collection’s strengths more widely known to scholars. Fellows will work on the collection to shed light on an important period of Egyptian history, and a transformative era in East-West relations.

In this, the final year of the fellowship programme, the panel is particularly interested in applicants working on the following topics:

Infrastructure in its social and political context;

The use of new technologies in promoting and publicising the Khedive to a wide audience;

Gender dynamics within the Khedival family and Egyptian society at large during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries;

The Khedive’s estate and holdings, with a focus on the management of these assets through such mechanisms as waqf;

The nationalist movement and its relation to the Khedive;

Political activism, especially by secret organizations using e.g. assassination as a means of protest.

Benefits

Fellows will be awarded an honorarium upon completion of their fellowship, and accommodation and all meals will be provided for the duration of the fellowship; a research travel grant is also available to each fellow.

Eligibility

Fellows will be early career (post-doctoral) or established scholars.

The nature of the collection will often require good reading knowledge of Arabic, Ottoman Turkish, French, and English.

Application

Applicants are required to undertake the following:

Complete the Application Form

Send a copy of your Project Proposal (2-3 pages) alongside a copy of your CV (Curriculum Vitae) in support of your application to maf.fellow@durham.ac.uk

Note you will be required to complete both stages of this process in order for your application to be considered.

For more information, visit Mohamed Ali Foundation Fellowship.

TITLE: AAU PRESS RELEASE ON THE CORONAVIRUS PANDEMIC (COVID-19)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Disruption of Educational Activities and Proposed Responses

The Association of African Universities (AAU) has observed with growing concern developments related to the outbreak of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. The life-threatening nature and rapid transmission of this disease has been felt globally – its significant impact on the global education systems is also being felt, especially in African countries. Numerous African higher education institutions (HEIs) and other educational institutions have been ordered to close in order to contain the spread of COVID-19. UNESCO (2020) monitoring estimates that 776.7 million children and youth worldwide will be obstructed by the closure of schools resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic.

HOW AFRICAN UNIVERSITIES ARE RESPONDING TO THE COVID-19 PANDEMIC

The AAU is also pleased to note various initiatives by African Universities to actively participate in high-end research towards finding a cure for COVID-19. Examples of universities involved in COVID-19 research include the African Centre of Excellence for the Genomics of Infectious Disease (ACEGID) at Redeemer’s University, Ede, Nigeria that is leading the way in fighting COVID-19 in Africa (Read More Here). The University of Ghana Health Services and Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research formed a Joint Emergency Response Team (UG ERT) to bring education and awareness on preventive measures and diagnosis of COVID-19 at the University of Ghana campuses (Read More Here). Makerere University in Uganda has developed a dedicated website to provide Africa with facts and research based information on COVID-19.

Numerous African universities have also established COVID-19 emergency response teams. The University of Cape Coast in Ghana is highly applauded for being one of the first African universities to take decisive actions in a bid to contain the spread of the virus. The University of KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa has launched a “WAR ROOM” for confronting the coronavirus outbreak. Additional responses by universities in South Africa can be found here.

THE OPPORTUNITIES PRESENTED BY COVID-19

The COVID-19 safety measures that have been announced by African governments in relation to the closing educational institutions and banning gatherings have a negative impact on the continuation of teaching, learning and research activities of HEIs. Even though this appears to be a negative outcome we see it as an opportunity that African universities can explore to introduce technology-based platforms for teaching, learning and research. Based on our ongoing assessments of technology adoption by African universities we are aware that a significant number of the African universities have implemented some kinds of eLearning management systems. However, we are also aware that most African universities had not yet enforced technology-supported teaching and learning – this includes those that do have eLearning management systems installed on their campuses. This is the appropriate moment for our HEIs to move decisively to institutionalize technology-based teaching and learning.

PRECAUTIONS RECOMMENDED BY THE AAU

Though most universities in Africa, have taken measures to mitigate the negative impact of the pandemic, the AAU is adding its voice and encouraging African HEIs to take the necessary steps to reduce the impact of COVID-19. The AAU therefore urges all African HEIs to consider the following:

Abide by the public notices and advice issued by their Governments and other relevant authorities, in relation to the COVID-19 pandemic.

Activate their Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery Plans proportionate to the current circumstances and to review these plans as the situation changes.

Urgently move to implement alternative methods of delivering teaching and learning using technology and other distance learning techniques.

Plan for bigger disruptions – so that HEIs are prepared if the COVID-19 pandemic takes longer to contain.

Teach and learn about the COVID 19 virus. This includes engaging with communities (via non-physical means) to educate them on preventive measures and correct the growing misinformation about the pandemic; educate various stakeholders against COVID-19 related discrimination and provide support for students and faculty in isolation.

Ensure all electronic channels of communication are always activated and fully functional to facilitate ongoing engagements with the universities’ communities.

WHAT THE AAU IS DOING AS A RESPONSE TO THE COVID-19 PANDEMIC

The AAU wishes to assure all its Member Universities, other African HEIs and stakeholders that it remains committed to its mandate and will provide the necessary support and advocacy to mitigate the impact of the COVID pandemic on education in the continent and help ensure that the COVID-19 impact on education is minimal.

The AAU is doing the following as a response to the COVID-19 pandemic:

We are conducting a brief assessment on the preparedness of African universities to adjust to the COVID-19 safety measures introduced by African governments. We request that Vice Chancellors, Deputy Vice Chancellors or their appointees complete this brief survey from here: https://www.research.net/r/COVID19AAU

The AAU is organizing an Online Teaching & Learning Webinar on the 30th March 2020 as one of AAU’s direct support to the African Higher Education community. The webinar will discuss the Effective Integration of Online Education and our guest speaker will be Professor Safary Wa-Mbaleka who is currently the Director of the Adventist University of Africa Online, based in Nairobi, Kenya. Please register for this webinar here: https://www.aau.org/webinars/aauregis.php?webinar_id=23

AAU has postponed its face to face capacity building initiatives that were scheduled for the month of March and April 2020 in various African countries. We are putting measures in place to continue these programs using online delivery methods.

RECOMMENDED RESOURCES

Various resources are provided by the World Health Organisation (WHO) (https://www.who.int/emergencies/diseases/novel-coronavirus-2019/technical-guidance)

National Centers for Diseases Control in African countries (e.g. Nigeria Centre for Disease Control is on Twitter via @NCDCgov)

The Commonwealth of Learning various Resources and Tools on the COVID-19 crisis: https://www.col.org/news/press-releases/keeping-doors-learning-open-covid-19

Free access to the scientific literature on COVID-19: https://pages.semanticscholar.org/coronavirus-research

EDUCAUSE Resource Web Page on COVID-19: https://library.educause.edu/topics/information-technology-management-and-leadership/covid19

The Chinese Experience in Maintaining Undisrupted Learning in COVID-19 Outbreak: https://iite.unesco.org/news/handbook-on-facilitating-flexible-learning-during-educational-disruption/

ABOUT THE ASSOCIATION OF AFRICAN UNIVERSITIES (AAU)

The Association of African Universities (AAU) is an international non-profit, non-governmental organization created by African universities to promote cooperation among themselves on the one hand, and between them and the international academic community on the other. AAU is the Implementing arm of the African Union Commission on Higher Education matters and the Coordinator of The Continental Education Strategy for Africa (CESA-16-25). Created in 1967, the AAU is the Voice of Higher Education in Africa. It aims to improve the quality of African Higher Education, and to strengthen its contribution to Africa’s development by supporting the core functions of higher education institutions and facilitating critical reflection and consensus building on issues affecting Higher Education in Africa.

TITLE: Canon Collins RMTF Scholarships for Postgraduate Study in South Africa 2027

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: August 14, 2026

Applications are open for the Canon Collins RMTF Scholarships for Postgraduate Study 2027. They will provide funding for up to a maximum of two years for Masters and PhD with the ability to reapply for a third year. Continued funding depends upon satisfactory progress and academic reports.

In 2027, they will be making awards only to those studying in three areas:

Justice, which includes Climate Justice, Law, Economics and Politics

Education policy and practice

Humanities, which includes Literature, History, Anthropology and the Arts

Scholarship

They will provide funding for up to a maximum of two years for Masters and three years for PhD. The value of the scholarship package will range from R20,000 to R100,000 depending on student circumstances. They support both full and part-time study and will consider applications from those who wish to study by distance learning.

They also organise an annual conference for current scholars and hold several smaller events throughout the year. Scholarship holders are expected to participate in these activities and to become part of and contribute to their network.

Eligibility

In addition, to be considered for a scholarship under this programme you must:

be a national of, or hold recognised refugee status in, one of the following countries: Angola, Botswana, Eswatini (Swaziland), Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Zambia and Zimbabwe

be ordinarily resident in one of the above countries;

be applying for, or currently enrolled in, a Master’s or PhD programme at a South African university;

hold, or expect to obtain in the year of application:

a good Honours degree (minimum Second Class Upper Division or equivalent) if applying for Master’s study;

or good Master’s degree if applying for PhD study;

demonstrate a sustained commitment to social justice through at least two years of active engagement in activities that contributed to addressing social, educational, economic, environmental, cultural, or human rights challenges in their community, country, or region. Such engagement may include, but is not limited to, community-based initiatives, advocacy, teaching or mentoring, public service, civil society or NGO involvement, social impact research, professional practice, or leadership in activities that promote equity and inclusion;

be pursuing studies or research that contribute to understanding, responding to, or addressing a significant social justice challenge affecting Southern Africa;

if applying for PhD study, have identified a supervisor (or prospective supervisor) who has agreed in principle to supervise the proposed research, and submit a draft research proposal as part of the application.

Application

Applicants must complete and submit a short online application by 14 August 2026 at 16:00 SAST.
